May there be well-being! Homage to the Lord of the Ganas! May there be no obstacle! Hariḥ Om!
[I bow] to the supreme ruler of those who are higher, the beginningless beginning of the three worlds.
Having prostrated with my head before Hiraṇyagarbha, I shall compose this exposition on memory. ||1||
And likewise Svāyambhuva Manu, who was instructed by the Self-born One;
through whose grace this world has come to possess the eye of Dharma. (2)
And this which was explained from the beginning by Bhṛgu, who was authorized by Manu, the seer of all things directly perceived. (3)

And his disciples' disciples, as well as others who have exerted themselves in all the scriptures—those compassionate ones, knowers of the Vedas and the Śāstras, by whom this [work] has been explained. (4)
Out of ignorance, or failing to understand the Dharmaśāstra of great significance, one may either think, "This is crooked," or again, "This is difficult to comprehend. (5)
Or rather, this distinction has been explained by those who are unwise, who have not properly heard the meaning of the scriptures, and who are deluded by mere exegesis (arthavāda). (6)
Out of a constant love for the Dharma, I shall speak this according to reality for the sake of refuting all those who have gone astray. (7)
Who would not constantly speak that which is delightful to contemplate, of manifold meaning, and unsurpassed, being endowed with the authority of words, sentences, and valid cognition? (8)
What is its connection? This is stated:

The continuous succession of births and deaths, characterized by the conjunction with and separation from bodies, senses, and objects for the purpose of experiencing the desirable and the undesirable, has as its cause the various forms of ignorance and is rooted in the authority of diverse types of knowledge. As some have said: "Furthermore, merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), being the causes of what is desired and undesired for the person (*puruṣa*), must always be either acquired or avoided. Just as in the world there are garlands and the like, or poison and the like... And the definitive knowledge derived from the authority of the Vedas and the *Smṛti* scriptures takes precedence over the objects of perception, inference, or other traditional authorities (*āgama*). This being so, just as the Veda teaches that the highest good (*śreyaḥ*) for a person consists in the *agnihotra* and other rites through their performance, those seeking the highest good exert effort based on the Vedic scriptures. Likewise, from the *Smṛti*, there is the excellence resulting from the performance of practices such as the *Aṣṭakā* rites; therefore, the scripture (*āgama*) which is the basis for that must also be respected. Thus, this *Dharmaśāstra* is commenced as the means for understanding and practicing the performance of the *Aṣṭakā* and other ritual observances.
Approaching Manu as he sat with a one-pointed mind, the great seers honored him according to custom and spoke these words. 1.1.

In this context, *Manu* refers to a specific person named Svāyambhuva, who is capable of performing the duties pertaining to his distinguished status; he is not anyone else. This is further specified in other Smṛtis such as: “Having composed this treatise... and “Manu, the son of the Self-born, spoke. Furthermore, he demonstrates that the name *Manu* is etymologically significant because he possesses the power to perceive all things and is able to specifically know and speak of all matters at will; therefore, from the act of *manana* (thinking/contemplating), he is called *Manu*. If he is such a speaker, then it is appropriate for him to be questioned regarding the most subtle *dharmas*. One who is not of such a nature would not be qualified. His qualification is described as *ekāgram* (one-pointed). *Akarmātmatā* (the state of being beyond action) is what is expressed here. Because he goes to the forefront (*agra*) when grasping the meaning, his mind (*manas*) is directed toward the Supreme Reality (*paramārtha*) in a single effort within the region of the heart known as the "forefront"; thus he is *ekāgra*. The meaning is that he is one whose mind is undistracted and whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is oriented toward awakening to the Supreme Goal. Alternatively, it means one whose mind is fixed on the perception of the inquiry into *dharma*. Or, *ekāgra* is another qualification for him. *Āsīnam* means seated, not lying down or standing. Although one might be able to speak of *dharmas* while lying down or standing, nevertheless, out of a desire to protect proper conduct (*ācāra*)—in accordance with the principle seen in BhG 3.21, “Whatever a superior person practices”—he acted thus so that others would not lose their adherence to such established conduct. Or, he did so knowing the minds of others, having understood that the great sages were about to inquire about *dharma*. Or, it may be due to the requirement of alerting the listeners; since Manu’s activity consists of both answering and questioning, the accusative case is used there. Thus, the three words—the qualifier and the qualified—are in the same case: “Manu, one-pointed, seated. The great sages, having approached him, performed a journey for the purpose of pleasing Manu, preceded by humility and inquiry. And those sages [approached him] through the practice of yoga and meditation, and by the vision of the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman hymns. What did they do immediately after approaching? He asks this to inquire about another action as required by the logic of the words. This is now stated: *idaṃ vacanam ābruvan* (they spoke these words). Just as the second verse follows the rule and the scripture, first the sages [approached], and afterwards they spoke these words known as the inquiry into *dharma*, which is expressed through various modes of conduct. If [the inquiry] is yet to be spoken, how then does he designate it? It is because of proximity to the present (*vartamāna-sāmīpyāt*), or because that which is called "intellect" (*buddhi*) is said to be directly perceived when situated in the self. That which is to be spoken, though belonging to the future, is treated as perceptible because of its immediacy. Thus, whether it be the future verbal expression or the perceptibility of the destruction of all *dharmas*, and so forth, it is repeated.
"You ought to tell me the duties of all the social classes (varṇas) in their proper order and sequence, as well as those of those born of intermediate castes."

The word *bhavat* denotes complete sovereignty. Thus, they address Manu—who possesses such qualities—using a term of respect (*āmantrita-śabda*) in order to draw his attention for the purpose of hearing their question: "O Blessed One (*bhagavan*), you ought to tell us the duties. This is the connection with the principal term; its qualification is "of all castes" (*sarvavarṇānām*), specifically those of the primary births. For this is intended to exclude the Śūdras. Furthermore, "according to rule" (*yathāvat*) means in the sequence of the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa. What then? Tell us about them and about those born of intermediate origins (*antaraprabhavānām*). It is not only of these [primary castes], but also of those born of intermediate origins. "Intermediate" (*antara*) refers to the middle among the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa; those who originate therein are "born of intermediate origins" (*antaraprabhavāḥ*), produced from different castes through *anuloma* (natural order) and *pratiloma* (inverse order), like a mule. Just as a mule is a distinct species due to the mixing of the seeds of a horse and a donkey, so too those born of intermediate origins, resulting from contact with women of *anuloma* and *pratiloma* unions, are distinguished as separate species. You ought to tell us, for our sake, both the general and the specific duties of these [castes] in their established forms. Now, are only those born of intermediate origins entitled [to these duties], or not everyone? On the contrary, it is the *pratilomas* [who are excluded]; the *anulomas*, however, are indeed entitled. Since it was said "and of those born of intermediate origins" with reference to them, so too the *pratilomas* are entitled by virtue of the duties of men; and thus he will say: "For the sake of a cow or for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa" (11.79), etc. And their restriction of conduct will be taught: "Fishing is for the Niṣādas" (10.48), etc. Just as they are not entitled because they lack authority over the entire range of duties, so it is the same in other cases as well. Therefore, no single person is entitled to all duties simultaneously or in succession. This has been taught in the Gautama Dharma Sūtra: "But the *pratilomas* are devoid of duty" (GDh 4.25), because of that lack of entitlement to all duties. For this reason, the Great Sages have stated the cause here: "You ought to tell us the duties," while remaining in that very state. Thus ends the first section. II.1–2. O Lord, although you are alone, you are the knower of the true meaning and purpose of the effects of this entire self-existent ordinance, which is inconceivable and immeasurable.

The word *eka* (one) has the sense of praise (*stuti*), just as in common usage it does not mean numerical oneness. The particle *hi* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). By means of a gesture (*abhinaya*), the term "of this entire" (*asya sarvasya*) indicates the *vidhāna* (ordinance); that is, the scripture (*śāstra*). But how is it an ordinance? Because it "ordains" (*vidhatta*) the scripture; thus, by the rule *kṛtyaluṭo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.113), the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the active sense, and when independence is intended, it functions as an agent. The meaning is that it ordains—that is, it demonstrates the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful. This state (*bhāva*) is the ordinance (*vidhi*), the act of ordaining (*vidhāna*), the instruction (*upadeśa*). Alternatively, it is so called because things are ordained (*vidhīyante*) by it or in it; the meaning is that it is taught therein. Such is the ordinance, which is the scripture; this is its qualification. "Of the Self-born" (*svayaṃbhuvaḥ*) means "of the eternal. And thus, this [scripture] was not composed by Manu. What is the proof for this? That the prosperity (*abhyudaya*) of Manu is an effect, and that his duty (*dharma*) is obtained from that scripture; and likewise, even though there is a scripture for the birth of Manu, his duty is the teaching of that [scripture]. If that were the case, his duty would not be the cause of prosperity through the scripture. If it were so for others as well, then the scripture would be purposeless and there would be no reason [for its existence]; likewise, if his duty were derived from another scripture, then for others too the scripture would be purposeless. Or rather, [if he were such] without [the knowledge of] Dharma, his sovereignty would not exist. What then? It is innate. If it were so for others too, the scripture would be purposeless and there would be no reason; if for others it were by means of a scripture, then for him it would be by nature without a scripture—thus there is an absence of the specific reason [for his superiority]. By this, Hiraṇyagarbha is also explained. Thus, the ordinance is eternal. If so, then how about what we shall say? That is for the sake of praise (*stuty-artha*) for that scripture. And this is another qualification: "of the inconceivable" (*acintyasya*). "Inconceivable" means beyond the reach of logical reasoning (*hetutaḥ*), not to be refuted, by which the establishment of Dharma and Adharma is not sought through inference. An example: whatever is declared to be unfit for food (*abhojya*), such as human excrement and the like, all that is fit for food because it is material (*bhautikatvāt*), just like curds and other such things. And whatever women are considered forbidden (*agamyā*), such as sisters and others, all women are approachable because they possess female organs, just like a prostitute. In the same way, one should provide examples regarding undesirable touch as well. And because the authority of the scripture is stronger, an inference contrary to it is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) here. While being material, there is a distinction between pure and impure, and while possessing organs, there is a distinction between those who may be approached and those who may not. Thus, the scripture alone is the authority. Since this is inconceivable in terms of its cause and immeasurable in terms of its result—such as the attainment of the world of Brahmā through truthful speech and other virtues—these three qualifications are for the sake of praise. Of such an ordinance, there is "one who knows the true nature of the task and its purpose, O Lord" (*kāryatattvārthavit prabho*). Regarding the ordinance, the "task" (*kārya*) is the action enjoined by the scripture. The "true nature" (*tattva*) of that task—which is performed by a person after perceiving it through the scripture—is the relationship with a qualified agent, consisting in the fitness for attaining the fruit. Like medical treatment, this action is connected to a specific agent for the sake of the fruit, and not to any other. The "true nature of the task" (*kāryatattva*) is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound where the first member is predominant (*pūrvapadārthapradhāna*), like "rice-cooking" (*odanapāka*). Just as the fruit of rice comes from the cooking of the rice and not from mere cooking, so too the fruit arises from a specific action and not from action in general; such is the meaning and purpose of the "true nature of the task. The "purpose" (*artha*) of the task, characterized by the qualification of the person entitled to it (*adhikāra*), is the universal variety of fruits, which is the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). And that is diverse: for some action, the subject's result is merely the non-occurrence of transgression (*pratyavāya*); for some, both; for some, expiation (*niṣkṛti*); and for some, the expiation of accumulated merit (*dharma*). He who knows this is "one who knows the true nature of the task and its purpose. Alternatively, the "task" of the ordinance is Dharma. Its "true nature" is not merely the performance of the act. What then? It is the fact that, being distinct from the act itself, it persists in another time, is a quality of the self (*ātmaguṇatva*), and bestows the fruit of the action. Such is the "true nature of the task" regarding Dharma; its "purpose" is the fruit, which is the universal variety of prosperity (*abhyudaya*). He who knows this—from which action a particular desired or undesired ripening of fruit arises—is the one described. He will later explain that the action is the cause of the fruit. In this way, the excellence of the author of the scripture is stated: for only one who knows the true nature of the task and its purpose is able to speak thus of his own duties, and no other. And since he possesses such lordship (*prabhutva*), the address "O Lord" (*prabho*) is appropriate. Those great seers (*maharṣis*) who have attained Dharma and have directly realized Dharma do not need to ask about Dharma; or if they did ask, they would not be "great seers. Here, a resolution is provided by means of a narrative convention (*ākhyāyikā-dharma*): assuming that the great seers asked about Dharma, this statement is for the sake of praising the scripture. Just as in the Vedas, through explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and narratives, it is said: "How indeed is this Dharma so subtle and most difficult to understand that it requires even great seers as questioners, let alone others? This praise of the scripture serves to encourage study and other such activities. Alternatively, Manu, having been questioned by the great seers—who were established on the path of accepting all the means for attaining the status of great seers—spoke these well-composed words in the form of a question on Dharma. The author of the *Smṛti*, having composed the text, refers back to them in the verse beginning "Thus knowing... (*paścād evaṃ vijānatā*); those very ones mentioned in this scripture are the great seers. Thus, in the fourth verse, which is the promise to explain Dharma, he will state this meaning: "Having honored all those great seers, he replied: 'Listen! Nor is any salutation or worship toward Manu mentioned for them, except for their status as disciples and their suitability for inclusion within his own tradition, which is a cause for affection, as indicated by the title "great seer. The term "great seer" should be applied to them as before, either through a connection with a specific power related to study and knowledge, or by referring to them as future great seers using the term "great seer" in a figurative sense (*guṇavṛtti*). Thus, the inquiry into Dharma by these existing great seers will serve the welfare of others, just as it does in the world. In this way, the meaning of the question on Dharma is stated in these three verses. The subsequent verse is now introduced for the purpose of the reply.
Thus duly questioned by those great-souled ones, he of immeasurable power, having honored all those great seers, replied: "Listen! (1.4)

That Manu was questioned by those great sages (*maharṣis*) regarding what duties (*dharmas*) should be taught "correctly and in due order for all castes (*varṇas*), and for those born of intermediate castes" (1.2). The word *samyak* ("correctly") is an adverbial modifier of the question; he was questioned correctly, not with a confused manner of inquiry. What are his characteristics? From this, the author shows the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the speaker: *amitaujāḥ*. *Ojas* is dharma pertaining to all matters, or rather, the unimpeded knowledge (*vijñāna*) which is the seed of that [dharma]; since he possesses such [knowledge] regarding all matters, he is *amitaujāḥ*. Their greatness (*mahātmatva*) has been explained by the Great-souled Ones (*mahātmabhiḥ*). He replied. Having done what? It is said, "having honored those great sages"; here, one should see the elision of the vowel *a* (i.e., *ārcya tān* becomes *ārcyākāt*). This is understood through the *saṃhitā* reading with the pause (*avagraha*) between words. The form *ārcya* is derived from the root with the suffix *lyap* (gerund) following a compound. A clearer reading is: "having honored them" (*athārccayitvā tān*). Why did he reply to the great sages? It is said thus: "Listen to that which I have been asked by you. Now, an objection might be raised: if the scripture is spoken by Manu, then the reference in the opening verse, "to Manu, who was sitting with a concentrated mind" (1.1), would contradict the fact that the speaker is seen to be someone else in this scripture composed by Manu himself. This fault would apply if he were the author, but not if he were not the author. What then is the meaning? There was a certain cultured person (*śiṣṭa*), a direct witness of all the laws of the Smṛtis, whose indications were found in the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas of all Vedic branches. Desiring to teach those Smṛti-laws—which are for the purpose of recollection—by means of a compendium (*grantha*), he designated a specific person named Bhṛgu (or Bheṣaja) as the speaker of the scripture, saying, "Whatever Manu spoke is indeed a remedy," and [designated] the great sages as the listeners. For the sake of praising the scripture, he composed the work merely as a compilation based on recollection out of compassion. Thus, it is not appropriate to say that the instruction belongs to another as its author. How then is it called "Mānava" (of Manu)? If the designation belongs to one who is not the author, it takes the name of that person because it is bound to his recollection for that purpose, just as rain intended for rice is called "rice. Even in the view that it is a narration of past events, there is no contradiction regarding the work produced by the cultured ones for that purpose. However, this is the distinction: in one case it is a figurative statement (*prakalpya-vāda*), in the other it is a narration of what actually happened (*bhūtānukathana*). And so the Paurāṇikas say: *(Note: The provided text ends abruptly here.)*
The Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, the Sāman-chants, and those mantras belonging to the Atharvans were proclaimed by the Seven Seers; but that which is based on tradition (smārta) was spoken by Manu.
And so, remaining right there, he honored all those great seers and replied, "Listen!
This universe was once enveloped in darkness, unperceived, and without distinguishing marks."
It is beyond reasoning, unknowable, as if entirely asleep. || 1.5 ||

This is improper: having been asked about *dharma*, [the author] has demonstrated the unmanifest nature of the world, yet its origin, maintenance, and dissolution are being described without having been asked. Furthermore, if this were the case, the mere removal of sorrow would not be the subject matter, nor would the origin and so forth of the world be explained. What then? The entire chapter must be understood as such; thus, the scripture from the second verse onwards should be stated as a connected sequence of meaning for the purpose of answering what was asked. Otherwise, there would be the fault of the Teacher’s negligence regarding his promise, in that he does not answer the specific *dharma* asked about with the aforementioned qualifications, but instead explains—immediately after the question—the unrelated subject matter of the Purāṇas, namely the categories of the world’s origin and so forth. To avoid this fault, this subsequent answer, which is connected in meaning, must be stated: "Served by the wise, by the good," and so on. To this we reply: Because the scripture is authoritative, this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is intended to explain the reality of the world’s origin and dissolution. How so? The transmigratory cycle (*saṃsāra*), characterized by the union with and separation from bodies, senses, objects, and desired or undesired results, has been set forth for the sake of explaining the true nature of the eternal Self—which is distinct from the body, senses, mind, and intellect—as the agent and enjoyer. This is understood through the context of the world’s origin and so forth.
These destinies, beginning with that of Brahmā, have been declared to end here; yet in this terrible, ever-continuing cycle of existence for beings,
they are said to be caused by all dharmas, both virtuous and non-virtuous, as has been stated and will likewise be stated.
Thus, by my command, all this— the mobile and immobile— was created by those great-souled ones through the application of austerity according to their respective karma. And so,
he will state in the twelfth chapter that the creation of the body and so forth for the person arises from karma alone.
Having observed with his own mind this course of the living being according to both merit and demerit, he should always fix his mind upon dharma. [12.23]

And this [creation] is intended for those two; for merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which are the means of enjoyment for the hungry ghosts (*preta*), are not established by the authority of the scriptures regarding their acquisition or avoidance. Therefore, the creation of the world and so forth, which are indicated in the Purāṇic scriptures for the sake of explaining those [merits and demerits], are here merely restated in brief for our own purpose. Thus, since the capacity for the commencement of the scripture is established, the incapacity for mere recitation, hearing, or restatement is set aside; for it is honored [by the injunction]: "This should be studied and heard by those seeking the highest good. Furthermore, just like the sections on waking, dreaming, and so forth, even those subsequent sections such as the praise of the Brāhmaṇa—which arise incidentally—should be understood as being supplementary to that very [subject]. We shall demonstrate this as follows: the collection of verses beginning with "This was then enveloped in darkness" (1.5) is to be seen as extending until the end of the chapter for the purpose of demonstrating the capacity for the commencement of the scripture, so that it does not appear to be a meaningless utterance like the words of a madman, as is the case with grammar and other sciences. Now the verse is explained. First of all, since it is improper to describe the creation and so forth of the world without first stating its unmanifest state (*avyaktāvasthā*) which exists at all times, that unmanifest state is therefore stated prior to these [descriptions of creation]. "This world existed, enveloped in darkness. In what manner was it enveloped in darkness? It was like darkness, but not darkness itself; its true existence was not perceived. How then? By the word "darkness," one understands that which has become darkened—that world which is known through its common characteristics of being known and so forth—is said to have become darkened in that state, and thus it is "unperceived. Why? Because of the absence of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). He shows that absence in this way: by the term "without characteristics" (*alakṣaṇam*), perception (*pratyakṣa*) is excluded; by "inconceivable" (*apratarkyam*), inference (*anumāna*); and by "unknowable" (*avijñeyam*), scripture (*āgama*). Since its non-existence would follow from the absence of these means of knowledge, he prevents that by saying, "as if sleeping on all sides"; we shall explain this further.

Alternatively, this world existed. In what manner? He shows that: it was "consisting of darkness," meaning its specific qualities were unmanifest; and for that reason, it was "unknowable" through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Or rather, in what manner did it exist? Direct perception does not have the past as its object, nor does it have subtle objects as its domain. [One might ask: "In that case, will it be known through inference (*anumāna*)? To this he says: "without characteristics" (*alakṣaṇam*). That by which something is characterized is a "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*); this has no characteristic, thus it is "without characteristics. This is a negation of inference based on perceived marks (*dṛṣṭaliṅga*). [One might ask: "In that case, will it be known through inference from general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*)? To this he says: "inconceivable" (*apratarkyam*). Even by inference from general observation, it is impossible to conceive how this was, such as "this was so. This is improper because one can infer that an entity endowed with other properties must have existed previously with those very same properties—just as one might infer that the world was likewise. True, this is so; however, this rejection of its being inconceivable is intended to demonstrate the extreme subtlety [of the state], and it is intended as a praise of scripture (*āgama*). Scripture is that which is free from the need for praise. Now, this statement "this was consisting of darkness" establishes the past state of the world, and since this very view holds that it was "unintelligible," and likewise that the world [is known] through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) than scripture—how then can it be known? It has been said: "from scripture. This is a praise of the authority of scripture. And thus, those scriptures which describe even an existing entity while describing it in a way that contradicts itself, do not become authoritative. How so? They say "this was consisting of darkness" and yet they perform a negation of scripture; this is not logical. Now he establishes the matter taught by scripture by means of an illustration: "as if asleep on all sides. By this, the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) of a person, having abandoned the states of waking and dreaming, is stated as an illustration. Just as this person, existing in that state, is devoid of consciousness and, with afflictions extinguished, is specifically peaceful—so too is this world in this state, unmanifest and, with distinctions extinguished, specifically peaceful. This is the meaning of the comparison. Regarding "as if asleep," the phrase "on all sides" implies that there is no partial dissolution (*antarā-pralaya*) here. Rather, it refers to the state after the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), when the entire world is called "undifferentiated" (*avyākṛta*). Furthermore, those who claim that the word *śoka* (darkness/gloom) has the same meaning as *avyakta* (unmanifest) do so either due to an unrefined intellect or out of hostility toward the treatise. Even if the meanings were identical, this is said: this is a restatement (*anuvāda*), not a tautology (*punarukta*). What, then, is the difference between these two? A restatement is a repetition of the sense, even when the words are repeated; a tautology, however, is useless, even when there is a commonality of repeated words, like the instruction to "go. If this is so, what is the purpose of the repetition here? It is to demonstrate the extreme subtlety of the Unmanifest. Of what kind are its specific qualities? The "non-specific" ones are called the "subtle elements" (*tanmātra*); subtler than those is the Ego (*ahaṅkāra*); subtler than the Ego is the Great Principle (*mahat*); and subtler than the Great Principle is the Unmanifest. Having shown the unsurpassed subtlety of the Unmanifest, one should state that the worldly illustration—"this was consisting of darkness"—and so forth, is merely conventional speech.
Then the Blessed One, the Self-Existent, unmanifest yet making this world manifest, whose power operates through the great elements and other principles, appeared as the dispeller of darkness.

The word *tataḥ* means immediately following the state of indeterminacy (*avyākṛtāvasthā*). He is called *Svayambhū* because he exists by himself; he is so designated as he assumes causes and effects according to his will. He is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the Person who is the cause of the world and the ruler of the conscious and unconscious universe. He is not merely some transmigrating soul (*saṃsāryātman*), for such a soul lacks independence. Thus says a verse from the *Gītā*:

"Though I am unborn and my nature is imperishable, though I am the Lord of all beings, yet by establishing myself in my own material nature (*prakṛti*), I manifest through my own power of illusion (*māyā*). (BhG 4.6)

But why is there this conceptualization of a self? Because, in all the Upaniṣadic scriptures, there is a prohibition against the application of the authority that establishes the distinction between dharma and adharma; and those things which are here "inexpressible" (avacanīya) are authoritative because they possess the specific quality of being as they truly are, just like the sense faculties. And so it will be said:
"One should know that Supreme Person, the ruler of all, subtler than the subtlest, radiant like gold, and accessible through the intellect in deep sleep. [12.122]
And again, there is a verse from the Gītā:
"But the Supreme Person is another, declared as the Supreme Self (Paramātman),
the imperishable Lord who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them" (BhG 15.17).

And here, our inference is based on observing the production of effects capable of performing purposeful human action, which occurs through the influence of the operation of a person possessing specific knowledge. This world as well, by virtue of being influenced by the operation of wisdom and effort, must be the effect of some non-transmigrating Person (*puruṣa*) in his own right. Thus, even by means of inference, there exists a Lord (*īśvara*), distinct from both *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*, who serves as the object of meditation for one who meditates upon the Supreme Self—not merely from scripture. And thus, in all matters, that Blessed One should be regarded as having inexhaustible causal power and unceasing capacity, even though he remains unmanifest (*avyakta*). "As if manifesting"—that is, making evident—by way of the principles beginning with *mahat*, he possesses vigor (*ojas*) operative within the great elements; that is, the power or energy produced in the principles starting with *mahat*. Or, according to another reading regarding this meaning, *mahābhūtatadvṛttenaujas* (or *mahābhūtānuvṛttaujāḥ*): he is one whose vigor follows after the great elements; he is one whose vigor persists as far as the great elements. He "became manifest" (*prādur āsīt*). The word *prāduḥ* signifies manifestation; he became manifest in the form of the initiator of *pradhāna*. And thus he is called "the dispeller of darkness" (*tamonuda*); dispelling that very state of unmanifest darkness, he is called the dispeller of darkness. By the manifestation of the principles beginning with *mahat*, as we have explained, this verse stands.
He who is perceivable by those beyond the senses, subtle, unmanifest, eternal,
consisting of all beings, and inconceivable— he himself appeared of his own accord.

The mind (*manas*) is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). How is it that, having transcended the senses, it is nevertheless perceived through [the mediation of] place, time, and effect? For this reason, it is called "perceivable by that which is beyond the senses. And so Vyāsa says:
"It is not indeed perceivable by the eye, nor by the other remaining senses which are beyond the senses;
it is grasped by those who see the subtle, with a highly refined mind."

And this being so, he is called "subtle" (*sūkṣma*). Its synonym is "unmanifest" (*avyakta*). He has the body of *prakṛti* or the body of the Great One (*mahat*). And thus say the authors of the Purāṇas: "The Lord, whose body is majesty, stood right where he had previously been; the wise one remained stationed there at the entrance of the gate-hall."

"Sanātana" means eternal indeed. Thus, he is as he has been taught. Otherwise, since everything would be subtle by comparison with the true nature (*satattva*) of the Self, this [description] would lack distinction for him. "Consisting of all beings" (*sarvabhūtamaya*): because he is permeated by the knowledge that serves as the means for the withdrawal of all beings, he should be understood as "consisting of all beings" precisely through his own power; the suffix *-maya* here denotes a state of being permeated (*bhāvanā*), as in the expression "made of clay" (*mṛnmaya*). He is "inconceivable" (*acintya*) because his power is inconceivable, as it has been said, due to the convergence of distinguished potencies. And for this reason, he himself shone forth. Others, however, describe Hiraṇyagarbha—who is already an individual transmigrating soul—as the enjoyer and the agent, acting as the instigator of *pradhāna*, just as insentient milk flows for the nourishment of the calf, and not out of a desire for me. They claim there is no such thing as a Supreme Self, asserting that the twenty-sixth principle is the proof for this. They cite the authority: "The states of existence end with this" (1.50). This must be explained in a way that does not contradict the context. The origin of Brahmā has been stated briefly in two verses. Being asked how he manifested, he speaks the following for the sake of explaining the specific process.
Desiring to emit various kinds of creatures from his own body, he first created the waters alone; into them he cast his seed. (1.8)

Having reflected, he considered: What do they call the Self? How did the body originate? Why was it produced through the sequence of the egg's formation? From that body, desiring to emit various offspring, what was his body within the egg—the body from which he, wishing to create, [issued], even as the progenitor of the circle of worldly existence (*saṃsāramaṇḍala*)? Or was the body created from *pradhāna* by him who is characterized by the impulse to emit? And what were those various offspring? The world consisting of fourteen realms. Thus there is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). And the Paurāṇikas [say]: "At the beginning, from the very body of Prajāpati, the creation of offspring occurred. Desiring thus to bring forth his own body from the egg for the sake of creating offspring, what did he do? "In the beginning, he created the waters alone, which served as the support for the egg. Because the waters being created are the object of the action, they are indicated in the accusative case. He created the waters in the beginning. Into those [waters], for the purpose of the egg's birth or the birth of the world, he cast his seed. The "seed" is the power for the production of the egg belonging to the waters. And thus, that seed, through the transformation of the waters and by the will of Prajāpati, [proceeded] according to that sequence.
That became a golden egg, radiant as the thousand-rayed sun,
within which Brahmā himself was born, the grandfather of all the worlds.

That energy, through the transformation of the waters by the will of Prajāpati, became in due order an egg made of gold (*haima*). The term *haima* is used here in a figurative sense (*upamāna*) to denote its quality; even without a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), the meaning is conveyed. For example, one says "the feet of the cock are golden" or "the ears of the donkey are saffron-colored"—in these cases, the word is used for the sake of comparison. Indeed, because of its cohesion with the waters and its lack of contraction, it is said to be "like gold," or perhaps because of its purity of essence (*tattva-śuddhi*). By which [egg] it [Brahmā] possessed a radiance equal to the thousand-rayed sun. Or rather, it is called "golden" in the sense of its accumulation (*upacaya*). In that [egg], Brahmā himself was born according to his own intention, not by the will of another like other souls, nor indeed before the production of his body. That [objection] is incorrect, because it is said that he is the Grandfather of all worlds; by whom this progenitor of all worlds is declared through both scripture and reasoning, and not anyone else. Thus, by his own will, he possesses the capacity to assume a body, unlike transmigrating souls. And now, he confirms this very process as it has been taught by means of a name.
The waters are called *nārāḥ*, for the waters are indeed the offspring of Nara;
since they were his first place of resort (*ayana*), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa. (1.10)

The waters are called *nārāḥ*. Because they were created by that Being known as Brahman for the purpose of producing the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*), and because they were his *ayana*—his path, his movement, and his support—while his body was still within the egg prior to the creation of the worlds, for that reason this Brahmā is remembered as *Nārāyaṇa*. The waters are *nārāḥ*; he whose *ayana* is these is *Nārāyaṇa*. And thus say the authors of the Purāṇas: "The thousand-headed Puruṣa, golden-hued and beyond the senses, known as Brahmā Nārāyaṇa, was then born upon the primordial waters."
That cause which is unmanifest, eternal, and of the nature of both being and non-being—from that was he, the Puruṣa, emitted; in this world, he is celebrated as Brahman. 1.11.

The two words "that" (*yat*) and "this" (*tat*), which function as pronouns for both general reference and specific designation, denote in a general sense the Cause—which is distinct from *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*. Of what? Of the world (*jagat*). By means of the one who sets *pradhāna* in motion. Of what nature? Unmanifest (*avyakta*). Here, too, the word "also" (*api*) is elided by implication; the meaning is: "both unmanifest and manifest," that is, "both embodied and bodiless. "Eternal" (*nitya*) is its qualification. The eternal cause is never a non-cause, nor is it in part existent and in part non-existent. It is designated as "existent" because its effects are observed to be of the nature of existence; and it is metaphorically called "non-existent" like a hare's horn because it is absolutely beyond perception. Released from that [Cause], that Person (*puruṣa*), known as the body composed of the elements, is celebrated in the world as "Brahmā" because he originates from Brahman. This verse concerning *pradhāna* must be explained in this way. Others, however, declare this to concern the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Thus, although bodiless, the Lord, the witness of all, fashioned the cosmic egg containing a distinguished body.
Having dwelt within that egg for a full year, the Blessed One himself,
through his own meditative concentration, divided that egg into two parts.

Having dwelt in that egg for an unspecified period of time—a *parivatsara* (the word *parivatsara* being used here to indicate the duration of the gestation and the time of birth)—he was not dependent on another like other men; rather, the meaning is that he did so by his own will. Immediately thereafter, when the period of dwelling in the womb had concluded, he divided that egg into two parts. How? Through his own meditative power (*dhyāna*). Having understood through the signs of the situation that the time of his own abiding there had come to an end, he made that egg split into two halves, one above and one below.
From those two fragments, he fashioned heaven and earth;
in between, the intermediate space, the eight directions, and the eternal abode of the waters.

The ocean that is the support of the world, or the earth, is established in sevenfold ways; yet, while the creation of the principles beginning with *mahat* exists, there is no mention of the creation of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) of the great elements. Since that [creation] was not previously stated, this [work] is commenced with the intention of explaining it. Furthermore, prior even to the creation of the body of the cosmic egg from the great elements, [the Lord] extracted from Himself the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent, and from the mind, the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), the self-conscious ruler. (1.14)

He "uprooted" (udbabarha), meaning he drew it forth. From what? From the *pradhāna*, which is his own cause (*ātmanaḥ kāraṇāt*). What is that mind (*manas*) and of what nature? It has been explained that it consists of both being and non-being (*sadasadātmaka*). And this shows the creation of the elements and the senses. Regarding the mind, it was previously stated that its cause is the *ahaṃkāra*. The phrase "in this way, then" (*evaṃ tarhi*) carries over. What is its property (*dharma*), such that it says: "In this regard, the conceiving subject (*abhimantṛ*) is merely a cognition; its activity is lordship (*īśvara*)"? Over what? Over its own transformations characterized by the elements and the senses. By the words "arisen" and "seizing," the *ahaṃkāra* is also established as preceding them.

And it continues: "He should cause that cause—which is the self itself, extending to the end of the mind—to emerge. The word *ātman* is a synonym for *tattva* (reality), or else it is called "great" (*mahān*) because it is the object of the self; likewise, the body is called "puruṣa" because it exists for the sake of the puruṣa, as are all things composed of the three guṇas.
The subtle elements (tanmātras) are now described. What he says regarding them is that they are the perceivers of objects gradually, in the sequence authorized by the logicians; this is the meaning.
And the five faculties. 1.15.
The five characteristics of the intellect together with the mind; by the word "and" (ca), the sense organs of action are also included—this is the meaning.
But having combined the subtle constituent parts of those six [gods] of immeasurable splendor with portions of himself, he fashioned all beings.

"Of the six" refers to the six specific principles: the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the ego (*ahaṃkāra*). By these, all this is created in succession. How so? From the subtle elements arise the gross elements; from the ego arise the sense organs. Others, however, explain "of the six" as referring to the sense organs with the mind as the sixth. Since these six rest upon the subtle constituent parts of form (*mūrti*), the wise call that [body] "form" (*mūrti*) because it is the body (*śarīra*). (1.17)

The etymological definition of "body" (*śarīra*) as "that which is based on the subtle elements" (*bhūtasūkṣmāśrayaṇāt*) is for the purpose of establishing the previously mentioned process. In that regard: "The great elements, together with their actions, enter [it], as does the mind with its subtle constituents; [thus] the imperishable creator of all beings [is established]. (1.18)

The subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) envelop the *liṅga*; it enters those great, gross elements together with their functions (*karma*) and their organs of action (*karmendriya*). It speaks of the collection of memory; by providing vast space through its own attributes, it [enters] the mind along with its subtle parts. The parts of the mind consist of mental resolves (*saṅkalpa*), and the mind’s determinations (*adhyavasāya*); these parts are infinite resolves, both auspicious and inauspicious. The mind is the creator of all beings, and that action which arises from auspicious and inauspicious resolves is the seed of the entire world. [11]
But from these seven immensely powerful persons,
the perishable arises from the imperishable through subtle material constituents.

Regarding the phrase "of the seven": here, the Great Principle (*mahat*) is understood as the seventh. For that purpose, there is a further mention of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and [the other principles], because from the subtle elements—which are general and unstable—this entire manifest world arises; from the imperishable, the perishable arises; from the eternal, the non-eternal arises. Furthermore, the term "person" (*puruṣa*) should be understood as applying to these [principles] because they exist for the sake of the person (*puruṣārthatva*). Alternatively, it has been stated that the term "person" refers to the non-specification of the seven elements and the six sense organs with the mind as the sixth, because they exist for the sake of the person.
Each subsequent one among them acquires the quality of each preceding one; whichever of these is the *n*-th in order, it is traditionally held to possess that many qualities. (1.20)

The sequence of the elements beginning with earth is not intended here; rather, it begins with space (*ākāśa*). For it will be stated: "From space [space] is born from that" (1.75), and so forth. Space is the first, and its quality is sound; beyond that is air, whose quality is touch, yet sound is also present in it as a result of contact. Thus, air possesses two qualities. In this manner, whichever specific element—whether the second, the third, or any other—is the *n*-th in the sequence and completes the series, that elemental essence possesses *n* qualities: two, three, four, or five. And thus, while each individual element possesses only one quality, the perception of multiple qualities is to be understood as arising from their combination and so forth.
Having explained the cessation of objects, he now describes the functioning of names and so forth:
"But at the beginning, he fashioned for all things their names and their various functions, as well as their distinct forms, from the words of the Veda alone. (1.21)

However, the names of all [beings]—such as "Brāhmaṇa," "Kṣatriya," and "Vaiśya"—possess scriptural authority (*śāstravat*), whereas others do not; these include those spoken by non-Aryans and those derived from their capacities, such as "Nābhi" and so forth, even though some of these are also spoken by Aryans. Furthermore, the various distinct and specific ritual actions, such as sacrifice and the like, along with their results (*sāmya*), he fashioned at the beginning of creation according to their respective natures, solely from Vedic words in the form of mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). And thus say the authors of the Purāṇas: "The names belonging to the Ṛṣis and the visions found in the Vedas..."
At the end of the night... [omitted] ...||

"The name-and-form of beings and the proliferation of their states—these indeed were fashioned by the Lord from words. Thus, his established conventions are either those recorded in the Smṛtis or those pertaining to worldly affairs—such as: "This must be done by this person," and "This must be protected by others through avoidance and so forth."
The Lord created the gods whose nature is action, as well as living beings;
he also created the subtle host of Sādhyas and the eternal sacrifice.

And the gods are the agents of action (*karmātman*); they are the deities of the limbs of action belonging to those who set the world in motion. Those [deities] belong to the class of living beings who are agents of action, as well as to the *sādhya*s. The term "agents of action" (*karmātman*) continues to apply here. The repetition is for the sake of emphasis. Thus he says "subtle. And "sacrifice" refers to both the external and the internal; the meaning is this. "Eternal" (*sanātana*) means perpetual due to its having proceeded from beginningless time. [13] From fire, wind, and the sun, he milked forth the threefold eternal Veda—characterized by the *Ṛg*, *Yajus*, and *Sāman*—for the sake of accomplishing sacrifice.

In the discourse on Brahman, the Ṛgveda is said to belong to Agni, the Yajurveda to Vāyu, and the Sāmaveda to Sūrya. It is said that the milking of the Vedas—abiding within these [deities]—occurs through a certain commonality of function. [He milked] time and the divisions of time, as well as the lunar mansions and the planets;
the rivers, the oceans, and the mountains; and the level and uneven terrains. (1.24)
Among time and the other [factors], some are to be understood as being for the sake of accomplishing sacrifice, some have the purpose of experiencing pleasure, and some serve both purposes.
Desiring to create these progeny, the Creator emitted this creation: austerity, speech, pleasure, desire, and anger. (1.25)

Austerity (*tapas*) consists of well-known practices such as the *ānayaṇa* (or *cāndrāyaṇa*); it is the function of the organs of action. Speech is that which takes the form of what is pleasant and beneficial; it is not the sense organ itself, because that has already been mentioned. Pleasure (*rati*) is delight in austerity, not sensual desire. And so he speaks again: "Desire (*kāma*) and anger (*krodha*)... This transmigrating self is the adversary of these [virtues]. He is to be seen in this creation as the cause for the basis of karma among those beings being created. And he brought forth creation—desiring such a form of creation, these progeny.
For the sake of distinguishing between karmas, he separated dharma and adharma;
and he joined these creatures with pairs such as pleasure and pain.

For the sake of distinguishing between actions inherent in the self (*ātmasamavāyin*) which are causes for prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and those for its opposite, *dharma* and *adharma*—and the two corresponding applications (*prayoga*) for their sake—are expressed by that word [“action”]. By implication (*sāmarthyāt*), he distinguishes them: "This application leads to *dharma*, and this one, on the contrary, leads to *adharma*. And through these two, he has joined these creatures with pleasure, pain, and so forth. Having discussed at length here, in connection with the context of the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest, this differentiation of the elements (*bhūtaviśeṣa*), he concludes that very point.
The minute, perishable particles which are said to belong to the five [elements]—with these together, all this comes into being in successive order. (1.27)

Now, since the cycle of existence is thus beginningless, the natural duty of every living being— which arises for the self wherever it may have been born due to previous habituation— is here prohibited. "Whatever action the Lord first assigned to each [being],
that very same [action] he performed spontaneously, being created again and again" (1.28).

When there is an obstruction to former habitual tendencies (*pūrvābhyāsa*), this person, by the power of the class of actions (*karmajāti*), acquires only the characteristics of the present birth, either through the influence of the actions that lead to that acquisition or by themselves alone. Just as a fish acquires the characteristics of another species—such as swimming, sleeping, giving birth, and blinking—even though these were previously practiced, so too should cattle and other animals be understood. What, then, is that action (*karman*) from which this elaborate exposition of the acquisition of those characteristics is set forth for the sake of illustration?
Violence and non-violence, gentleness and cruelty, righteousness and unrighteousness, truth and falsehood—
whatever each [being] was endowed with at creation, that very thing entered its own disposition.

Violence and non-violence, gentleness and cruelty, truth and falsehood—such pairs of actions as these, which are well known to exist in duality, share a common purpose and depend upon the various classes of living beings; they arise by taking *dharma* and *adharma* as their cause, and are not accidental. And so it is said: "The manifold practice of action among living beings is without seed. Thus, this verse is clarified by supplying ellipses (*adhyāhāra*) and rectifying the connection between the displaced words, so that there is no contradiction and the original meaning is upheld. What, then, is the illustration for this? It is stated as follows:
Just as the seasons themselves, at the change of seasons, assume their own respective characteristics according to the season, so too do the actions of embodied beings [bear fruit]. (1.30)

Just as the seasonal signs, such as mango blossoms and the like—the seasons being spring and so forth—occurring spontaneously in their sequence, each attains its own respective [characteristics], meaning that they produce their effects, the signs such as mango blossoms; even so, beings arising here and there from various classes of living creatures, by the power of karma, spontaneously assume their own roles as causes and effects, such as being violent or non-violent. Thus, immediately after the summary of the creation of the principles (*tattva-sṛṣṭi*), now, intending to demonstrate the creation whose nature consists of manifold purposes, he first states this creation of the castes (*varṇa-sṛṣṭi*) for the sake of what follows.
For the sake of the prosperity of the worlds, he brought forth from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.

"Vivṛddhi" means an abundance of rain. Both of these [increase] result from *karman*. And *karman* is both seen and unseen, residing in the Brāhmaṇas and the other [classes]. For this reason—whether by way of intending to express superiority and inferiority (*uttarādharya*), or by way of demonstrating a specific benefit through a connection, or by way of the relationship with Agni and others in relation to the mouth and so forth, or through the application of the *karman* of the mouth and so forth—their power is described as the manifestation of qualities (*guṇapravṛtti*). Having acted thus for the castes, they describe this creation by way of sexual union:
"Having divided his own body into two, he became a man with one half."
With the other half he became a woman, and in her the Lord created Virāj.

Because of their great assistance in matters of dharma, offspring, and wealth, women are entitled to a share; the statement that they are half of one's own body is a figurative praise (*guṇavāda*), as it is a restatement of established fact. If this Vedic tradition is not contradicted by either scripture (*āgama*) or reasoning (*upapatti*), then he created the resplendent and radiant Virāj together with the woman—Virāj who is indeed of his own nature.
[15] But that Virāj whom the Supreme Person himself created after performing austerities, know me, O best of the twice-born, to be the creator of all that belongs to him. (1.33)

After the venerable Manu had explained the origin of the entire world to those great seers (*maharṣi*), he further demonstrates himself as an example for their easy comprehension by saying, "Know me. Thus say the authors of the Purāṇas:
"Brahmā created Virāj; that Virāj created Puruṣa.
Know that Puruṣa to be Manu, from whom these human progenies (*mānavī*) are descended."
Desiring to create offspring, I performed most difficult austerities and first created ten great seers as the lords of creatures.
This verse serves to connect with the subsequent section:
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Prācetasa, Vasiṣṭha, Nārada, and Bhṛgu. (1.35)

These great seers (maharṣis) are designated by their specific names; for the purpose of the detailed ritual procedure, they should be honored during the worship of the seers by these very names. Thus it has been said regarding the libations to the gods, seers, and ancestors:
"These [seers], possessing immense splendor, created the other seven Manus, as well as the gods, the classes of gods, and the great seers of immeasurable power. (1.36)

The number seventy of mantras is stated because of the recollection of the names of the seven Manvantaras. As for the mantras that invoke the gods and others, those who are designated in groups such as the Vasus and so forth—he created these for the sake of accomplishing ritual acts (*karma*). Likewise, for the sake of accomplishing rites such as the offering of water, he created the gods known by the name of *ṛṣis*.
[He also created] the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas; the Gandharvas, Apsarases, and Asuras; the Nāgas, Sarpas, and Suparṇas; and the various classes of Pitṛs. (1.37)

He created these for the sake of ritual action and for the accomplishment of the self's enjoyments. Regarding the connection of Marīci and the others with Prajāpati, there is no further mention of their creation, nor is anything omitted.
(He created) lightnings, thunderbolts, and clouds; red-colored [clouds] and Indra’s bows;
meteors, thunderclaps, and comets; and various celestial bodies, high and low. (1.38)
Lightning and other such phenomena are intended to illustrate the workings of portents. Furthermore:
"Kinnaras, monkeys, fish, and various birds;
beasts, wild animals, humans, and fanged predators. (1.39)
[16] And worms, insects, and moths; lice, flies, and bedbugs; all gadflies and mosquitoes; and various kinds of stationary beings. 1.40.
This creation has been described for the aforementioned purposes.
Thus, by my command, all this—both the stationary and the moving—was created by those high-souled ones through the application of austerity, in accordance with their respective karma. 1.41.
And thus, saṃsāra is shown to be caused by karma. This verse serves as a summary of the creation of Prajāpati from the mirage and so forth:
"I shall now describe to you, according to their respective order, what kind of karma has been proclaimed here for each of these beings, as well as the sequence of their births. (1.42)
Domestic animals and wild beasts, as well as fanged predators, and Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and humans—these are the womb-born. (1.43)
Birds born from eggs, serpents, crocodiles, fish, and tortoises—whatever beings there are of such kinds, whether stationary or moving. 1.44.
The gadfly, the mosquito, the louse, the fly, and the bug are born from moisture;
and whatever else is of this kind arises from heat. (1.45)
All stationary beings are born from sprouts; they grow from seeds or from stems.
Herbs are those that perish at the ripening of their fruit and are endowed with many flowers and fruits. (1.46)

This follows from the very mention of their names in the passage previously cited and in this present section: "But for those beings whose kind of action has been proclaimed here... Action has been proclaimed; because their names are born of that action, they are designated accordingly. For example: they are *devas* because of shining (*dyotana*), or because of being in the celestial realm (*dyusthāna*). They are *ṛṣis* because of seeing (*darśana*). They are *yakṣas* because of sacrificing (*yakṣaṇa*). They are *piśācas* because of eating flesh (*piśitāśana*). They are *gandharvas* because of moving (*gamana*). They are *apsarases* because they are like water (*apa*) in their beauty (*surasa*), or because they are called *amṛta*, or because they are gods (*sura*). They are *asuras* because of non-attainment (*alābha*). They are *nāgas* because there is no going (*aga*) for them. They are *sarpas* because of crawling (*sarpana*). They are *suparṇas* because of beautiful flight (*śobhanapatanāt*). They are *pitṛs* because of being worthy of offerings (*pātratvāt*). They are *vidyuts* because of various shining (*nānādyotana*). They are *aśanis* because of excessive cutting (*atyarthaśātāt*). They are *meghas* because of sprinkling (*seka*). They are *rohitās* because of being red (*rohitatva*). They are *indradhanus* because of appearing according to Indra’s net-like power (*indrajālapadayathātthadarśana*). They are *ulkās* because of being cast upward (*ūrdhvakṛtatva*). They are *yūkās* because of mixing together (*miśrībhāva*). They are *matkuṇas* because of devouring the body (*śarīrabhakṣaṇa*). Such are the examples.
Those that bear fruit without flowers are known as *vanaspati*s;
those that bear both flowers and fruit are known as *vṛkṣa*s. || 1.47 ||

[17] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, in that regard, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the perfection of wisdom should train in the six perfections. Subhūti, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the perfection of wisdom train in the six perfections? Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of giving, gives gifts to all sentient beings, and while giving those gifts, he does not perceive a gift, nor does he perceive a recipient, nor does he perceive himself as the giver. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of giving. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of ethical discipline, observes the ethical discipline of restraint from taking life, and likewise observes the ethical discipline of restraint from taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view. He trains in this way: ‘I shall not abandon even a single precept of training. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of ethical discipline. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of patience, endures the abuse, insults, threats, and blows of others with a mind free from anger and resentment. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of patience. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of vigor, generates vigor for the sake of fully awakening to all dharmas; he does not become weary in body or mind. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of vigor. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of meditative concentration, enters and dwells in the various meditative concentrations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments, yet he does not realize the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) midway. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of meditative concentration. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, correctly discerns all dharmas as they truly are through the wisdom of insight, yet he does not fall into the level of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, it is in this manner that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the perfection of wisdom should train in the six perfections.”

The statement "trees are *vanaspatis*" is not said for the purpose of establishing a fixed definition. What then? Both terms apply to both; trees are *vanaspatis*, and *vanaspatis* are trees. This being the case, by the mention of "tree," the mention of "*vanaspati*" is intended to include all *vanaspatis* according to their actual nature, since the word "*vanaspati*" is observed to be applied to a tree. And this [author] will state: "The enjoyment of all *vanaspatis* [is determined] as it is" (8.285). Furthermore, in that context, it is impossible to understand an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of specific trees such as the mango, because there is no other scriptural authority to the contrary and because they perform the same function.

Furthermore, there are various kinds of shrubs and clusters, as well as species of grasses; likewise, there are those that grow from seeds or from stems, as well as spreading creepers and climbing vines.

For all these beings, whose nature is stationary such as trees and so forth, are indeed enveloped by manifold darkness caused by their past actions; they possess internal consciousness and are endowed with pleasure and pain. (1.49)

Enveloped by *tamas*—dharma that is multiform and of many kinds—and bound by the cause of unwholesome action consisting in the non-performance of what is prescribed and the performance of what is forbidden, all these stationary beings indeed possess internal consciousness. Just as the functions of the senses, though present in a person, do not manifest due to the influence of defects or for some other reason, even as a child [in the womb], so too the function of the senses and the function of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), though present in trees and the like, do not manifest because of their continuous state of birth. From karma, through both pleasure and pain, consciousness shines forth. And thus says the Śruti: "Whichever branch the living soul (*jīva*) leaves, that withers. Furthermore, it has been stated that a logical argument (*nyāya*) contrary to that [scriptural authority] is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). This being the case:
These destinies, beginning with Brahmā, are declared to end here within this terrible cycle of existence for living beings, which is eternal and continuously flowing.
Likewise: "The state of being caused by merit and demerit, as well as the state of being dependent upon saṃsāra, exists; and thus Vyāsa says:
'They call the imperishable Aśvattha tree one whose roots are above and branches below;
its leaves are the Vedas—he who knows it is a knower of the Vedas' (BhG 15.1)."

Having thus demonstrated the origin of the world through karma and so forth, he now shows its conclusion, known as dissolution: "Having thus created all this, including me, he of inconceivable prowess withdrew again into himself, subduing time by time. (1.51)

Disregarding the duration of his enjoyment by means of the time of withdrawal—just as a person here [in this world] disregards [the night] through the state of waking—so too, for the sake of the further cause of the one who is superior, it is said "by which": "When that god awakes, then this world stirs;
when he sleeps, his self being at peace, then everything closes its eyes. (1.52)

For in the world, the highest activity of a person is observed during the time of sleep. And so it is: while that [Self] sleeps in its own natural state, the embodied beings whose nature is action desist from their respective activities, and the mind falls into a state of exhaustion. (1.53)
Just so it is here as well:
"But when they dissolve simultaneously into that Great Self, then this Self of all beings sleeps happily and at peace. (1.54)
In the context of demonstrating the dissolution of the world into Hiraṇyagarbha, he now shows the departure (utkrānti) of the transmigrating self:
"But having resorted to this darkness, they remain for a long time with their senses;
when one no longer performs his own duty, then he departs from his body. (1.55)
When, having become as subtle as an atom, it enters in conjunction with the seed—both the stationary and the moving—it then casts off its form. (1.56)
Thus, through waking and dreaming, that immutable one incessantly brings this entire world of moving and non-moving beings to life and causes it to perish.

This verse serves to conclude the subject matter at hand. Having described the origin and dissolution of this world, he now introduces this [next] section for the purpose of demonstrating the period of its maintenance:
"Having composed this scripture himself from the beginning, he caused me alone to receive it according to the prescribed rule; and I, in turn, [taught it] to the sages Marīci and the others. (1.58)

By the indicative mark of "composing a treatise" (*śāstrakaraṇāt*), [the phrase] means "while composing a treatise. It does not mean "dharma," for if it were dharma, then even for Manu there would have to be an understanding of the dharma of tradition from some other source. Thus, he demonstrates the beginninglessness of this dharma; and in order to proclaim the excellence of the treatise, he cites Marīci and others as examples. Having thus shown this treatise of Svāyambhuva, the venerable Manu, with the intent of providing no further remainder, said this: "This Bhṛgu shall recite to you this treatise in its entirety; for this sage has learned all of this from me in its fullness. (1.59)
Then, having been addressed in that manner by Manu—meaning in substance, but not in the literal wording—the great seer Bhṛgu, with a joyful soul, spoke to all those seers: "Let it be heard. (1.60)

And his state of being filled with affection is appropriate due to the expectation of the Teacher’s power and because of the preceptor’s command; thus, the verse concerning the command of Bhṛgu was spoken in the presence of many disciples. Furthermore, Bhṛgu was chosen by the author out of affection for his own lineage, as in the case of the phrase "or the narrative of past events. With the intention of saying, "I shall now describe the period of the world's maintenance known as a Manvantara," he says this:
[19] "Six other high-souled and greatly powerful Manus of this Svāyambhuva Manu’s lineage have each created their own respective progeny. (1.61)
He indicates those sons of Manu by their specific names for the sake of conventional usage:
Svārociṣa, Uttama, Tāpasa, Raivata, Cākṣuṣa of great splendor, and the son of Vivasvat. (1.62)
He demonstrates their equality in power and majesty:
"These seven Manus, beginning with Svāyambhuva, possessed immense splendor;
within each of their respective intervals, they produced and sustained all this world, both moving and unmoving. (1.63)

They have protected [the world]. Thus, these Manus are to be understood as possessing equal strength and increase (*vṛddhi*). Those *manvantaras* are distinguished by their specific durations of time, and they are designated by these very names. Now, this is stated for the purpose of determining the measurement of time within a *manvantara*, beginning with Manu and others: Eighteen *nimeṣas* are a *kāṣṭhā*; thirty of those are a *kalā*.
Thirty *kalās* constitute a *muhūrta*, and a day and night (*ahorātra*) consists of that many [thirty *muhūrtas*]. (1.64)
In the human world, the sun divides day and night:
night is for the sleep of beings, and day is for the performance of actions. (1.65)
For the ancestors, a month constitutes a day and a night, divided into two fortnights;
the dark fortnight is their day for active duties, while the bright fortnight is their night for sleep. 1.66.
For the gods, a year consists of night and day; furthermore, their division is as follows:
the northern course [of the sun] is their day, and the southern course is their night. (1.67)
Now learn, in brief and in due order, the measure of a night and day of Brahmā, as well as that of each of the Yugas individually. 1.68.
They say that four thousand years constitute the Kṛta Yuga; its dawn (saṃdhyā) consists of four hundred years, and its twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa) is of the same duration.
In the other three [ages], together with their twilights and twilight-portions,
the thousands and hundreds decrease by one.
[20] This aforementioned cycle of four ages (*caturyuga*),
totaling twelve thousand [years], is called an age (*yuga*) of the gods.
A single day of Brahmā is to be known as consisting of a thousand divine yugas, and his night is of the same duration.
Those people who know day and night truly understand that the holy day of Brahmā lasts for a thousand yugas, and his night is of exactly the same duration. 1.73.

For praise is for the purpose of manifestation, since it is considered that praise proceeds spontaneously; at the end of that day and night, having fallen asleep, he awakens, and once awakened, Manu creates that which consists of both the existent and the non-existent. (1.74)

This instruction regarding the creation of the physical body is for Hiraṇyagarbha who has awakened immediately after the intermediate dissolution (*antarālapralaya*). Alternatively, it refers to the Supreme Self following the conclusion of the period of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*). As He will state: "Thus is their creation from the beginning" (1.78).
"The mind, being impelled by the desire to create, undergoes transformation.

In the view of Hiraṇyagarbha, "mind" refers to that internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) which undergoes transformation for the creation of the physical body. In the view of the Supreme Self, however, it is the Great Principle (*mahattattva*), the primordial mind; thus say the authors of the Purāṇas.
Intellect (buddhi), mind (manas), and consciousness (vijñāna)— these are proclaimed as synonymous terms for the first transformation of Mahat.

That mind, characterized by conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), undergoes transformation into the creation of the Great Principle (*mahat*), being impelled toward its own modification, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). By what [is it impelled]?
By the desire to create belonging to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
From that, space (*ākāśa*) is born; they know sound to be its quality. (1.75)
From ether, undergoing transformation, there arises the pure and powerful wind, which carries all fragrances; it is indeed considered to have the quality of touch. (1.76)
From ether also, as it undergoes transformation, there arises luminous light that dispels darkness; that radiant entity is said to have the quality of form.
And from light, undergoing transformation, water arises, whose nature is the quality of taste;
from water, earth arises, whose quality is smell—such is the creation from the beginning. 1.78.

Having described this creation of the great elements in general through these verses, he now explains it in detail. Furthermore, for the sake of a single thematic section, it should be understood that all of that, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), arises again in the same manner. Thus, having stated the initial [creation], this is said with reference to the process of creation, rather than as a supplement to the description of the original creation:
"That divine age (*yuga*) previously mentioned as consisting of twelve thousand [years] is here called a *manvantara* when multiplied by seventy-one. (1.79)

This verse is intended to determine the duration of the period of a Manvantara: "In this way, the Supreme Lord, as if in play, performs these countless Manvantaras, as well as creation and dissolution, again and again. (1.80)
The nature of the Kṛta Yuga and the other ages is now being described as it pertains to the present context:
"In the Kṛta age, Dharma is complete with its four quarters, and truth alone prevails;
no acquisition whatsoever comes about through unrighteousness for human beings. (1.81)

This fourfold duty of the social classes (*varṇadharma*), which consists of these four quarters—this entire and complete merit—is practiced by the qualified persons according to the instruction in the Kṛta Age. For what reason? Because of the statement, “In the Kṛta Age, truth alone,” where the word *eva* (alone) serves as a qualifier common to both [truth and faith]. The particle *ca* (and) is for the purpose of filling the meter, as there is no logical conjunction [of two distinct entities], or else it serves to conjoin [truth with] faith. The word *eva* has the sense of restriction. Truth alone, being accompanied by faith and possessing excellence, exists; it does not exist through its opposite. Therefore, this is so. And likewise, because of the contraction of Dharma in the Tretā and subsequent ages, he will later state the categories such as falsehood (*anṛta*) which bring about that contraction: “Through theft, falsehood, and deceit, Dharma departs quarter by quarter” (1.82). Since this is so, by virtue of faith and capacity, this four-quartered duty of the classes was then complete (*sakala*). Having established this, the separate mention of the cause for the non-existence [of falsehood] is appropriate. And since this is so, therefore: no determination of the Vedic scripture or Smṛti ever approaches human beings through unrighteousness (*adharma*). The second half of the verse is for the purpose of concluding the argument regarding the absence of a cause. Alternatively, the phrase *sa caiva* (and that very... is stated otherwise. How? For even though the practice of undertaking a vow is a quality (*guṇa*), it must be explained as a distinct category of matter; its demonstration is as follows: having undertaken, “I shall perform the Śrāddha for this month,” one performs it flawlessly at the time agreed upon. Other examples should be cited in the same way. Thus, this instruction is logically joined; it need not be mentioned separately from the previous [verse] because the entirety of truthful speech is included within the other. Likewise, in this view, the particle *ca* is appropriate for the purpose of conjoining the stated categories, and the word *eva* serves to restrict both. The rest is the same. Or rather, with the preceding [verse], the word *guṇa* (merit/quality) refers to this [duty]: this Dharma is “four-quartered” (*catuṣpād*) like a four-legged animal. In that age, just as in the world a corpse or similar object is said to be “four-quartered,” so too Dharma is designated as “four-quartered” due to its connection with those qualities. That connection with the qualities consists in its completeness and lack of deficiency, because at that time Dharma is such. Furthermore, even if it is called “four-quartered,” it is so because of the inherent nature of the Kṛta Age. The passage beginning “In the Kṛta Age, truth alone,” etc., is identical to the preceding. Others, however, say that the four quarters are austerity, knowledge, sacrifice, and charity, as will be stated in “Austerity is supreme in the Kṛta Age,” etc. That is incorrect, because there is no authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) for it, and because that statement is intended for another purpose and because they belong to the stages of life (*āśrama*). Since those [qualities] are merely a partial description of the duties of the Brāhmaṇa and other classes, that [interpretation] is incorrect, because the term “four-quartered” would then lack a complete cause and there is no evidence for it.
In the other [ages], Dharma exists by means of scripture, but it is diminished by one quarter at each stage;
through theft, falsehood, and deceit, Dharma departs quarter by quarter. (1.82)
