In the other ages, beginning with Tretā, that which was established as the system of Dharma through the *āgama*—that is, the scripture—is reduced quarter by quarter in each successive age. By what means? Through theft (*caurikā*), falsehood (*anṛta*), and deceit (*māyā*). Here, there is no one-to-one correspondence between these [vices] and the ages starting from Tretā, because such a view would contradict what is observed. What then? All of these, existing in Tretā and the subsequent ages, are taught as causes for the contraction of Dharma; they are differentiated according to their relative degree of intensity, whether great or small. This being the case, regarding the second mention of "Dharma" in the phrase "and Dharma departs quarter by quarter," this indicates the absence of the primary Dharma—the cause of prosperity—which consists in the establishment of order, due to the absence of its cause. And since this is so, therefore...
In the Kṛta age, people are free from disease, have all their goals accomplished, and live for four hundred years;
however, in the Tretā and subsequent ages, their lifespan decreases by one quarter [of its original duration].

They were free from disease because there was no occurrence of illness at that time, and because their desired actions were successful, they achieved all their goals and lived for four hundred years. Here, the word "hundred" (*śata*) has the sense of "many" and not a specific numerical count, as this would contradict the scriptures; we shall explain this later. Thus, humans with the longest possible lifespan—those living for four hundred years—possessed long lives compared to those of the present day due to the influence of *dharma* inherent in the nature of the Kṛta Yuga. Just as their age decreases by a quarter in each subsequent age such as Tretā and so on, so too do their spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*) and freedom from disease decrease. The mention of "age" (*vayas*) is intended to be illustrative. Furthermore, the inclusion of these two [accomplishments and health] is appropriate because they are relevant to the context, and not because they serve no purpose, since they likewise conform to the nature of the respective ages.
The lifespan of mortals declared in the Vedas, as well as the fruits of their ritual actions and the powers of embodied beings, bear fruit in the world according to each successive age. 1.84.

In this regard, the name mentioned in the Veda—such as "a thousand years" and so forth, which is undertaken for the sake of those performing that rite—is not [to be taken literally]. This is because it contradicts scriptural authorities such as "Man has a lifespan of a hundred years," and because, according to the Sūtra-writers, this too is impossible in terms of days [or the impossibility of such a duration]. Furthermore, when the primary assumption (pradhāna-kalpanā) is untenable, it is proper to resort to a secondary one (guṇa-ādi), just as the principle of obstructing the primary assumption is not applied. We shall explain this further. Now, regarding what is stated in Āyurveda, that ritual which brings about a lifespan of a thousand years is intended here; thus it is said by the learned: "Rāma ruled the kingdom for ten thousand years. In these cases of a thousand years and so forth, those possessing power (prabhāva-vantaḥ) are authorized by that ritual, just like the eligibility for the Aśvamedha sacrifice. Nor can one infer the incapacity of the Vedic scriptures simply because their meaning is not seen at once, as in the case of the Aśvamedha. Indeed, these blessings of the Vedic rites—which have purposes such as obtaining sons and so forth—are effective in the world age after age, provided there is no deficiency in the ritual due to the influence of the nature of the Kṛta and other ages. This is true because there is no obstruction to the production of its fruit, and there is power inherent in embodied beings. It is not the case that for men qualified for Śrauta and Smārta rituals, there is invisibility, possession, or the absence of spells, curses, and so forth. The phrase "they bear fruit in the world age after age" continues to apply. And this being so, this is stated with reference to the meaning of the aforementioned connection.
The duties for men in the Kṛta age are one way, in the Tretā and Dvāpara they are others,
and in the Kali age they are yet different, in accordance with the decline of the ages.

This other statement concerning the decrease of the *yugas* is merely a restatement of the meaning. In this context, the fact that the nature of the *yugas* conforms to their respective characteristics (*dharmas*) has already been explained; it does not remain as something further to be taught.
It is said: "Austerity is supreme in the Kṛta age; knowledge is said to be [supreme] in the Tretā;
they say that knowledge alone is [supreme] in the Dvāpara; and charity alone in the Kali age. (1.86)

In all ages, Dharma is found being practiced in every form. However, it has been stated that the predominance of these [ages] is intended according to their conformity with the nature (*svabhāva*) of each *yuga*. [12 syllables missing] ... by this person, their conduct is generally such. Having perceived from the *Manu-śāstra* this specific distinction of time, beginning with the Kṛta-yuga, which differs in its inherent nature, the Mīmāṃsaka, out of astonishment, raised this objection: "All of this is utterly untrustworthy because it is beyond direct perception (*atyantā-pratyakṣatvāt*). Therefore, just as there is no time for [beings] such as [those mentioned], likewise there are no divisions of time such as the Kṛta-yuga and their respective Dharmas. To this, it is said here: Even though this is not directly perceived, the divine year (*deva-saṃvatsara*), the four *yugas*, and so forth exist, because of the power of the traditional accounts (*smṛti-anvākhyāna*) regarding human time. Just as here the establishment of the practice of attaining merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) is understood to exist through the authority of this scripture (*śāstra*), so too here, even in the absence of [direct] means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the time consisting of the four *yugas* and so forth must be determined by the traditional scripture (*smṛti-śāstra*). Or rather, let it be granted. In that case, the distinction between what is to be done and what is not to be done should not be established on the basis of this [scripture] alone; or else, a specific distinction must be stated. For it is only the correctness of the arrangement of wholesome and unwholesome actions that is grasped through the capacity [of the scripture], and not otherwise. That single authoritative scripture is the sole indicator of the existence or non-existence of those two categories of things; a distinction [between them] is difficult to state. And without stating that distinction, it is not possible to correctly understand this division of the reality of action and time. Furthermore, a stubborn insistence on understanding that division without a cause would lead to the fallacy of error and arbitrariness, and since those are undesirable, they would obstruct one's own position. Because the arrangement of wholesome and unwholesome actions must necessarily be admitted, there is no restriction of [other] means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, the worldly arrangement of time beginning with the Kṛta-yuga comes to be. Likewise, just as there is a traditional account (*anvākhyāna*) of the perceived nature of time—characterized by days, nights, fortnights, months, seasons, solstices (*ayanā*), and years—so too, by tradition, there ought to be a description of the unperceived divine year, the four *yugas*, and so forth, even if they are not seen, but not of what does not exist. Nor can the existence or non-existence of time and the [scriptural] authority be imagined as equal when they are bound to the presence of a single source of knowledge (*ekāgama-pramāṇa*), provided there is no distinction. Nor do we perceive any specific means of knowledge within the scripture by which we might establish this. Nor is a distinction characterized by the favor of other means of knowledge, such as worldly consensus, capable of establishing a difference in this case, because the traditional scripture is independent in the cognition of supramundane matters. For just as this [scripture] does not depend on another means of knowledge in establishing the relationship of cause and effect for the means of attaining the supramundane Dharma and Adharma, so it is in all supramundane matters. Therefore, having granted this distinction through the traditional scripture, this specific point is stated. For if it were imagined in this way, then wherever the scripture is supported by logic (*nyāya*), it would possess authority there; and elsewhere, it would be capable of being dependent and so forth. [11 syllables missing] ... the attainment of Dharma and Adharma would follow. Nor is the arrangement of action intended to be reached through logical means of knowledge. And a scripture is meaningful when [its subject] is not already established [by other means], not when it is already established by another means of knowledge. Since nothing is equal to this, and because the explanatory scripture is favored by other means of knowledge such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is considered a statement of things as they are (*yathā-bhūta-artha-vacana*). In the same way, the scripture describing the divine year, the four *yugas*, and so forth, is also stated to be authoritative. Just as this category of the relationship between cause and effect for the means of attaining the utterly supramundane Dharma and Adharma is a matter not within the scope of the means of knowledge of direct perception and inference, yet is seen through the authority of the traditional scripture, so too both the unperceived time and the perceived [time] are described by the traditional scripture, which is capable of perceiving all supersensuous objects not otherwise prescribed. It is not reasonable to accept that it is authoritative in one part and non-authoritative in another, because there is no reason for such a view. And since this expansion of time, such as the division of days and nights, is seen to be consistent with the existence [of the system] supported by the means of knowledge of inference and scripture, it is not right to reject it due to contradiction. Nor are the Kṛta-yuga and others merely the conduct of kings; for they are established as real in the ultimate *yugas*. And when categories of things have equal scriptural authority, the proof of the unperceived is like the perceived; this is the analogy. For example, just as from the well-known expansion of the measurement of the Jambudvīpa mandala, or from the perspective of the expansion [of geography] to the east of the Himalayas, one understands from the Purāṇa scripture that the region beyond is also of the same nature according to the same scripture; or just as from a portion of the mass of categories taught in the Jyotiṣa-śāstra, such as lunar and solar eclipses, one infers the existence of the remainder, such as the auspicious times for journeys (*yātrā-lagna*) according to the scripture; and just as among Vedic categories, the inference of heaven and so forth—which are not directly perceived—is made from the son and other categories produced by the ritual injunctions of the Mantras; so too here, because the arrangements of perceived and unperceived time belong to the same scriptural authority, the unperceived must be established just like the perceived. If the existence of this were to contradict the authority of the Veda, the Śāstra, and the Smṛti, then I would not accept its non-existence. Just as the indifference of a person is not accepted when it contradicts the statement of agency, so it would be here. Nor is the Smṛti alone the authority for designating unperceived time, such that it could be doubted in the knowledge of ancient times. To explain the matter stated in detail: first, the Purāṇa scripture... *(Note: The final sentence is left incomplete as the source text ends abruptly.)*
Primary creation, secondary creation, the genealogies, the periods of the Manvantaras,
and the history of the dynasties— thus the Purāṇa has five characteristics.

And so forth. Furthermore, since there exists a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that conforms to multiple indicative marks (*liṅga*), it is impossible to conceive [the Purāṇas] as being devoid of truth. Those marks, or those *Atharvāṅgirasa* [mantras], declare this Itihāsa-Purāṇa; and it is said, "The Itihāsa-Purāṇa is the fifth among the Vedas. One should know that the second indicative mark of the Veda is the Itihāsa-Purāṇa, which is the Upaniṣad. Do not say so. First, the third [mark] is the knowledge of time (*kālajñāna*). Since it functions as an immediate auxiliary to the Vedic scriptures and its subject matter is thus established, the absence of any other well-known means of valid cognition is all the more easily set aside. This being the case, just as the distinction of the self-nature (*ātmasvabhāva*) based on the divisions of time characterized by the seasons is indeed perceived through the support of stationary bodies along with their specific effects, so too the division of the ages (*yuga*)—Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali—possessing the accepted nature of the ages, must exist according to the scriptures, supported by human beings and the like, because of the manifestation of health, lifespan, and activity, along with their specific effects. Thus, the triad of the Veda, the Kalpas, and the authoritative scriptures is established. You do not, however, admit the unseen time of the *devahotra* and *ātrātra* rites, which is the exclusive domain of the Vaiyākaraṇas. Is your understanding of that measure based on a means of valid cognition, or is it through reasoning? For a mere Mīmāṃsaka, it is possible for you to point out the nature of the ritual procedure (*prakriyā*) and its properties, such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, which fall within the scope of what has been stated in other scriptures. Just as this unseen time of the Kṛta-yuga and so forth is difficult to discern by students of Mīmāṃsā due to not being its proper object, so too, by not overstepping the established perception of its own domain, one should establish the multiplicity of scriptures—just as there is a multiplicity of sense organs—without rendering the demonstration of reality useless. And thus, one who knows everything ought to know everything; one who knows little cannot, just as one who lacks complete sensory faculties [cannot perceive everything]. Likewise, the Purāṇas and the teachings of the authors of the *Dharmasūtras* regarding the acquisition of all branches of knowledge (*sarvavidyādhigama*) appear without distinction in their respective treatises; and the *Smṛti* of the highly learned (*bahuśruta*) is the cause of those [teachings].
One should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas;
the Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, "He will strike me down."
Thus says a verse from the Purāṇas: "Likewise,
one should constantly study the scriptures that increase the intellect, which are auspicious and beneficial, as well as the Vedic Nigamas."
"For in whatever measure a person masters the scripture, in that same measure he understands it, and his specialized knowledge shines forth. (MDh 4.19–20)

"That person becomes highly learned (*bahuśruta*), whether he be one who knows the *Lokaveda* and the *Vedāṅgas*, or one skilled in *Vākovākya*, *Itihāsa*, and *Purāṇa*; he depends on that [knowledge] and subsists by means of it"—so says Gautama (GDh 8.4–7). Śaṅkha and Likhita explain this further: "The *Purāṇas*, the *Dharmaśāstras*, *Nyāya*, *Mīmāṃsā*, the four Vedas, and the six *Aṅgas*—these fourteen seats of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) pertain to the Brāhmaṇas. And thus, even though there is a difference of opinion among other philosophical systems (*darśanāntara*), it is indeed the case for our venerable teacher [Jaimini] that there is no perfect vision regarding the subject matter of perceptible time; rather, that which pertains to the domain authorized by those advanced in the threefold knowledge (*traividya*) is appropriate, especially where there is an absence of [other] means of proof. Had Jaimini’s section beginning with the refutation of the existence of the *Kṛtayuga* and other times been established in the *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtras*, we might have accepted that state of affairs—which would have resulted in a million-fold status of servitude caused by the absence [of such a teaching]. But since it does not exist, your practice based on non-authoritative sources is merely following a wrong path. Therefore, the time of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world, as well as the time of the divine year (*devasaṃvatsara*), exists exactly as described in the scriptures. Accordingly, there are indicative marks (*liṅga*) in the Mantras and Arthavādas: "That was then unmanifest; it was manifested from here. It was manifested through name and form... In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent (*asad*). Regarding that, they ask: 'What existed then? And the Brāhmaṇa-mantra begins: "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning," and so forth. Nor can the authority of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) be imagined [without support], for it has been stated that in cases of doubt, the determination of a specific meaning arises from the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), as in the example: "He places pebbles," and so on; likewise, it should be understood in other instances as well. Since this is so, the world is not spontaneous (*svābhāvika*). What then? Because it is produced by Hiraṇyagarbha and the multitude of living beings, this very arrangement of the world consisting of seven continents and oceans—which serves as the locus for the experience of the prosperity and adversity of all living beings—must arise from their very actions (*karman*), and not spontaneously. For one who does not accept this, it would follow that even the body and so forth, which serve as the locus for the experience of pleasure and pain, must be caused by action. To say "yes" [to spontaneity] would contradict inference and scripture. Furthermore, it is not reasonable to accept a "half-old woman" approach (*ardhajaratīya*). Since external and internal elements (*bhūta*) share the same characteristics insofar as they are subordinate to a person's experience of desired and undesired results, it is illogical to claim spontaneity in one case while claiming action as the material cause (*upādāna*) in another. Moreover, because both the egg (*aṇḍa*) and the great [universe] are impermanent, this gross sphere of great atoms must be capable of arising and perishing like a jar. Therefore, the day and night of Hiraṇyagarbha, which effect the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world, must exist according to the scriptures. This being the established state, the following is said concerning the subject at hand.
But for the sake of protecting this entire creation, that one of great splendor assigned distinct duties to those born from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet.

Creation (*sarga*) means the act of bringing forth; the world is said to possess "companionship" (*sahacarita*) because it exists in association with that act. Protection (*gupti*) means non-destruction. And for the sake of that protection—namely, stability (*sthiti*)—he ordained separate duties for the Brāhmaṇas and the other classes, intended for the purpose of righteous livelihood (*dharma-vṛtti*). And those [duties] were as follows:
"He ordained for the Brāhmaṇas teaching, studying, sacrificing for oneself, officiating at sacrifices for others, as well as giving and receiving gifts. (1.88)

He enjoined (or directed) the protection of subjects, the giving of gifts, the performance of sacrifice, the study of the Vedas, and non-attachment to sensual objects as the duties of a Kṣatriya. (1.89)
The protection of cattle, giving, sacrifice, study, trade, moneylending, and agriculture are the duties of the Vaiśya. (1.90)
But the Lord ordained only one duty for the Śūdra: to serve these very classes without malice. (1.91)

Because the stability and prosperity of the world depend upon the religious activities of the Brahmins—including the acceptance of gifts and so forth—and of the gods and others who constitute the components of sacrifice, through their mutual relationship of assistance via duties such as non-agricultural labor (*avṛtti*) and sacrifices (*ijyā*), the teaching concerning these is presented in this section. How so? First, the Brahmin, by accepting gifts from the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya, benefits them; and they [benefit] him. Those two [the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya] benefit the Brahmin. In this same manner, the application should be made for the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra. Likewise, the Brahmins and others [benefit] those who perform sacrifices and so forth; and the gods and others [benefit] the Brahmins and others. As he will state later:
An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun. (MDh 3.76)

And so forth. Thus, since the stability and growth of the world occur through the mutual assistance and connection of these [elements] based on the cause of karma (*karman*), their production occurs in the same manner. This is a praise of the *Śāstra* (treatise) intended to demonstrate its excellence by showing that it serves as the means for the performance of the teachings therein; for it is the virtuous action known as *dharma*, which is the very cause of the world's production, that results from such practice. This being the case, this instruction regarding actions is for the purpose of an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) and not for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhi*). The injunction, however, will be stated later. In this way, this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), caused by *dharma* and *adharma*, has been introduced by way of the world’s production and so forth, in order to demonstrate the efficacy of the commencement of the *Śāstra*. How so? Because this [treatise] is the means for attaining the goals and avoiding the non-goals of those *dharmas* and *adharmas* which are the causes of the prosperity and downfall of these persons; therefore, since it accomplishes the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), this *Dharmaśāstra* of Manu must be studied. Having studied it, it must be heard; and having heard it, out of compassion, it must be correctly expounded to seekers according to their eligibility. Now, by way of praising Brahman, this new section is commenced following the previous one in order to further demonstrate the excellence of the *Dharmaśāstra* in accomplishing the human goal.
The upper part of a person above the navel is proclaimed to be more pure;
therefore, his mouth has been declared by the Self-Existent One to be the most pure of all.

Even though this is a general description, the praise of the mouth of Prajāpati as being the most worthy of sacrifice (*medhya*), based on the divisions of time, is intended for the purpose of praising the subsequent origin of the Brāhmaṇas. And thus he shows:
"Because of his birth from the highest limb, because of his seniority, and because he maintains the Veda (*brahman*), the Brāhmaṇa is by right the lord of this entire creation. (1.93)

The fact of being born from the highest limb and the state of being the eldest are common to the Brāhmaṇa. He performs penance arising from that; for many thousands of years he remains beyond the inner gods, and so forth. And thus, among all beings—whether stationary, crawling, wild animals, domestic animals, or humans—the Brāhmaṇas are distinguished. What need is there for more? "The very birth of the Vipra is the eternal embodiment of Dharma;
for he was born for the sake of Dharma and is fit for becoming Brahman. [MDh 1.98]

The form of the Brāhmaṇa is eternal Dharma, consisting of mere origination even without ritual refinements (*saṃskāra*). Regarding the explanation of the term "refinement," although the "upholding" (*dhāraṇa*) of that which is called the Triple Veda (*trayī*) is common to all, it has been concluded through the two preceding reasons; thus, it becomes the cause for the praise of the Brāhmaṇa. With respect to the excellence of his teaching, the Veda becomes unique to him. Because he is the ruler of this entire creation by virtue of Dharma, the Brāhmaṇa is the lord, and not otherwise. Furthermore, we shall demonstrate at the end of the section that the purpose of the praise of the Brāhmaṇa is indeed this. Therefore: [The verse follows: *utpattimātram eva...* etc. (Note: The provided text contains a lacuna marked by "akṣ missing" regarding the term *saṃskāra*. The translation reflects the context of the surrounding argument.)

For the Self-Existent One, having performed austerities, first created him from his own mouth for the purpose of conveying the offerings to the gods and the ancestors, and for the protection of this entire world.

The commencement of this [work] is for the sake of showing respect by means of the qualification "born from the highest limb" (*uttamāṅgodbhavatva*). For the Self-born One, Hiraṇyagarbha—the Brahmin, and not any other Prajāpati—created him, authorized for the creation of progeny, from his own mouth. And he did so after performing austerity, not without self-restraint, nor out of contempt, because of the gravity of that state; and [he created him] from the beginning, not from another creation, and subsequently without disregard. Thus, these three qualifications, intended to demonstrate the production of respect, serve to praise the subject at hand. For what reason, then, did this Hiraṇyagarbha show such respect? Because in the creation of the Brahmin, the offering of *havya* (oblations to the gods) and *kavya* (offerings to the ancestors) is possible to perform directly, since the guests are perceptible; whereas the gods and ancestors are not perceptible, such that [offerings] cannot be given to them directly. Since those two [offerings] are the means of attaining those [deities], the creation of the Brahmin possesses great purpose. Furthermore, for the protection of all this [world], it has been said that the Brahmin, while offering oblations, becomes a benefactor of all the worlds through the satisfaction of the Sun (*Āditya*) resulting from the sacrifice. Therefore, since this [creation] is of great purpose, it is appropriate to produce such [respect]. And thus it is from this [reason].

That being by whose mouth the dwellers of heaven always consume the sacrificial offerings (havya), and the ancestors consume the ancestral offerings (kavya)—what creature could be greater than that? 1.95.

Since no other means of attainment is possible for the *havya* (offerings to the gods) and *kavya* (offerings to the ancestors), it is appropriate that the gods and ancestors should utter words of praise out of wonder, saying, "What being is greater than him? This praise may also be conceived as being offered by the gods and ancestors through the consumption of the food he has eaten; this constitutes one quarter of the verse. In this interpretation, these two subsequent verses are now commenced for the purpose of specifying the particular kind of Brāhmaṇa who is worthy of praise. Thus, the praise of the Brāhmaṇa in this context does not depend on birth alone; rather, this eulogy of the Brāhmaṇa depends on the specific qualities of the Brāhmaṇa which we shall describe.
Among beings, those with breath are the best; among those with breath, those who live by the intellect;
among the intelligent, men are the best; and among men, the Brāhmaṇas are traditionally held to be the best.
Among Brahmins, there are the learned; among the learned, those whose intellects are refined;
among those of refined intellect, the performers of duty; and among the performers, those who know Brahman.

And this praise of the Brāhmaṇa is not based on birth alone; rather, he attains [the status of] refinement (*saṃskāra*). Furthermore, having arisen for the sake of *dharma*, his body is the product of refinement.
Indeed, the very birth of a *vipra* is the eternal embodiment of *dharma*;
for he has arisen for the sake of *dharma* in order to attain the state of Brahman (*brahmabhūyāya*).
One is fit for the state of a Brahmā. || 1.98 ||
Since this is so, therefore:
"For a Brāhmaṇa, upon being born, is indeed born preeminent upon the earth;
he is the lord of all beings for the protection of the treasury of Dharma. (1.99)

"A Brāhmaṇa, at the very moment of birth... The word *hi* is used for emphasis. Where? "On the earth. How does he exist? "Above. Of whom? "Of all beings"—this connection with the distant term is to be understood through the force of the context. For what reason? Because he is not subordinate to anyone else. Do they possess sovereignty? No, he says. How then? Because he is the protector of the treasury of Dharma (*dharmakośa*). And this [protection] is to be understood as resulting from his teaching, reciting after, and officiating at sacrifices. Thus he will say later: "A Brāhmaṇa should know the means of livelihood for all [classes] within their own respective duties."
"He should proclaim it to others and act accordingly himself"—
thus for one who is such a protector of the treasury of Dharma:
"All this that exists in the world belongs to the Brāhmaṇa."
By virtue of his preeminence and noble lineage, the Brāhmaṇa deserves all this.

"All this is the property of the Brāhmaṇa. It is "property as it were" (*svam iva svam*). How is it understood that this contains an elided simile (*luptopamā*)? This is to be understood from the force of the context of praise (*stutiprakaraṇa*). Furthermore, this very meaning is understood from the force of the instructions regarding royal punishment and penance (*prāyaścitta*). For instance, due to the contradiction between what precedes and what follows, both systems of law would otherwise be undermined; thus, whatever exists in the world—even if belonging to another, such as gold and so forth—is included. This praise does not apply merely to wealth acquired through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, or receiving gifts, nor is it directed solely toward those who possess specific virtues. As he says: "By virtue of his preeminence, his noble lineage, and his birth from the mouth [of Brahmā]," and because of the association of these qualities with consciousness itself. Yet, it is by means of these very qualities that one becomes a distinguished Brāhmaṇa. And therefore, such a Brāhmaṇa deserves all this. From the use of the word "deserves" (*arhati*), we understand—as we have already stated—that this is intended as praise and not as an instruction regarding a formal relationship of owner and property. Since this is the case, it is entirely possible to speak in this way through praise and figurative application (*guṇavṛtti*).
A Brahmin eats only his own, wears his own, and gives away his own;
it is through the compassion of the Brahmin that other people eat at all. (1.101)

Just as one’s own property is enjoyed through action by a king, so too, by his very nature, a Brahmin enjoys his own property among his father and others; he accepts [gifts] at marriages and other ceremonies only after having taken hold [of them] as a guest. Furthermore, when instructing on the act of giving, he does not cause [others] to give like a master, because he causes them to give only by being employed for that purpose. Thus, figuratively, it is said: "By these means, the Brahmin enjoys his own, wears his own, and gives his own. And the statement in the preceding verse—"he eats his own, he clothes himself in his own, and he gives his own"—is introduced by the word *upa* (in the compound *upanyāsa*) for the sake of establishing the meaning of the term. This being the established rule, out of compassion (*mā...ānṛśaṃsyāt*), other people enjoy [the fruits] through the scripture of the Brahmin who studies the Vedas and Shastras along with their limbs and Upanishads, and who understands them, being authorized to instruct qualified persons. For when such a speaker, being authorized by the scripture, does not recite the text and its meaning to those who seek it according to their entitlement, the fruit of performing what is enjoined by the scripture—both seen and unseen—is lost. And thus says the Shruti: "He who, knowing the science, would not give to two seekers—he, through the failure of his duty, would shut the door to the highest good. One should teach; great is this glory. The wise say that in this yoga, all this is established. Those who know thus become immortal. In every way, by the force of the context, this must be understood as being solely for the praise of the Brahmin. And for this reason, he says: *(Note: The final sentence in the source text appears to be a fragment or a misplaced citation marker.)*
For the sake of discerning that karma, as well as for the sake of the remaining [topics], the wise Manu, son of the Self-Existent, composed this treatise in due order. (1.102)

[The objection is: "Because of the context of praise, this refers to the instruction of authorized persons by a Brahmin who has been instructed. But another says: "The purpose of the praise of the Brahmin is this one [point], since no other reason is taught and because such a purpose is impossible; furthermore, there is a verse regarding its purpose later on, and that is stated here: 'This should be studied with effort by a learned Brahmin, and it should be correctly expounded to disciples, and not by anyone else. (1.103)

In both cases, this [qualification]—being learned in one’s own and other treatises (*svaparaśāstra*)—is the reason for the study of the *Smṛti* scriptures by a learned Brāhmaṇa (*vidvad-brāhmaṇa*), because of the contradiction in meaning [otherwise] and because it is not seen elsewhere. Nor is it proper to assume that this [qualification] refers to the scripture itself, because no specific distinction is taught and because it is observed in the Vedic scriptures. Furthermore, the study by a learned Brāhmaṇa is not like a restrictive injunction (*niyama*), an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), or a praise (*stuti*), as we shall explain later. Therefore, by implication, this injunction for study should be understood as being for the purpose of hearing the treatise. How so? By supplying the ellipsis, the meaning is: "This must be studied and heard by a Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the sciences of words (*pada*), sentences (*vākya*), and logic (*pramāṇa*). Since injunctions, prohibitions, counter-exceptions (*pratiprasava*), restrictive rules (*niyama*), exclusive specifications (*parisaṃkhyā*), repetitions (*punarvacana*), and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are all causes that strike at the ultimate truth for a learned person who grasps the authority of what is heard, this *Smṛti* scripture must be understood by the wise in such a way due to its extreme difficulty of comprehension. Having understood this, the noble author made this qualification: "It must be studied and heard by a learned Brāhmaṇa. And "it must be properly expounded to disciples with effort"—in this very way, the two words "properly" (*samyak*) should be seen as appropriate expressions of respect for both qualifications. And so he will say later.
Whatever those who are shrouded in darkness and foolish declare to be the dharmas, that sin becomes tenfold and falls upon those speakers. (MDh 12.115)

In other treatises, there is a different statement by that same [author], because they are [independent] treatises. Therefore, no effort is made here, since the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) functions through immediate benefit for this [work]. Alternatively, because this is not a treatise concerning eligibility (*anadhikāra-śāstra*), its study is not mandatory. This being so, its instruction is for the sake of explaining the meaning of the teaching (*pravacana*). It should be explained as before, for the purpose of praising the treatise, even though it lacks specific qualifications. And having done so, it is said by some: "It should be correctly taught to disciples, and not by anyone else."

Thus [it is said]. To claim that this prohibition is connected with *pravacana* (teaching) and not with *adhyayana* (studying) is an unconsidered statement, since there is no injunction for studying in either of these two cases. And so it has been stated thus: This verse has the purpose of praising the Brāhmaṇa. Whether for the sake of distinguishing his duties (*karmaviveka*) or as a qualified [statement], this mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" here regarding the two activities of studying and teaching is not for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). This is because studying is already established for the three castes by virtue of their entitlement, and because teaching is already established by the rule: "A Brāhmaṇa should teach them" (MDh 10.1). For what purpose, then? It is for the praise of the Smṛti-śāstra. Just as in common usage, the mention of "kings" in the phrase "This pair of garments of such quality is to be worn by kings, and not by anyone else" serves to praise the pair of garments; so too here, the mention of the Brāhmaṇa restricts the king through association. Likewise, another example should be cited here: "This horse or elephant is fit for the king's riding. In this way, having praised the scripture—which is connected to the learned Brāhmaṇa—for the purpose of studying and so forth, he now praises it directly.
It has been stated that one who studies this treatise understands [the truth] by implication:
such a person is a Brāhmaṇa of firm vows.
By following the conduct of the learned and avoiding what is prohibited, one is never stained by the defects of action born of mind, speech, or body. (1.104)

Because there is an absence of such causes, he is eternally established in the teaching; he purifies his lineage and seven generations before and after him, and even this entire earth, though he be alone. (1.105)
The recipient is not defiled by the fault of receiving. This is primarily intended as a praise of the subject at hand; furthermore:
"This is the most excellent means of securing well-being; this increases the intellect; [31] this is always conducive to fame; this is the supreme state of ultimate bliss. (1.106)

"May there be well-being (*svasti*)"—this signifies excellence; this is the path (*ayana*), the way, for the sake of attaining that. One should proclaim this treatise. This supreme *niḥśreyasa* (ultimate good) is not [attained] merely through the performance of its meaning; rather, because it has the *niḥśreyasa* as its purpose, it is called *naiśreyasa*, using the secondary suffix (*taddhita*). What is this designation? It is intended to express that very meaning: "well-being" (*svasti*) means non-destruction; "path" (*ayana*) means a way. A path for the sake of well-being is the cessation of misfortune; the means to that is *svastyayana*. Excellence, prosperity, and liberation are called *niḥśreyasa*; the treatise concerning that takes on the word "that" (*tacchabda*). Even with the secondary suffix, the meaning remains the same. Now he states the reason for the subject matter taught in the three subsequent verses, beginning with "because": [The text continues: "Because..."
In this [work], Dharma has been declared in its entirety, as well as the virtues and faults of actions, and the eternal conduct of all four castes. 1.107.

In this [Dharmaśāstra], Dharma has been stated in its entirety; it must be practiced and avoided. However, it is not like the words of the Buddha and others, which depend upon the instruction of another because their meaning is incomplete; for here, this [work] is independent. Furthermore, the merits and defects of actions—the desirability or undesirability of their fruits—are stated for the purpose of inciting or deterring [people] from what is beneficial and prohibited. This is because [the duties] of all four castes have been declared through various expressions, and their conduct is eternal. Moreover, the Smṛti rules such as the eight types of action (*karma-aṣṭaka*) should be understood as being included within the category of "human duty" (*puruṣadharma*). Alternatively, although conduct (*ācāra*) is already subsumed under the word "action" (*karman*), it is mentioned separately for the sake of what follows. Thus, he says this:
"Conduct is the supreme duty, both that which is declared in the Śruti and that which is recorded in the Smṛti.

This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) for the purpose of praising [the subject] by means of an illustration. Just as the Agnihotra and other rites declared in the Śruti, and the Aṣṭakā and other rites recorded in the Smṛti, are the supreme duty, so too is conduct. Therefore, [the phrase] "one who is always intent upon this" refers to this very meaning. Alternatively, because of the unity [of the text] through the praise of worldly convention, when the reading is instead "conduct is the supreme duty, both that which is declared in the Śruti and that which is recorded in the Smṛti," then this reading is indeed appropriate.
Therefore, a self-possessed twice-born man should always be constantly devoted to this triad. || 1.108 ||

Thus it is said. Likewise, there is a verse by Vyāsa: "If one is unable to perform the rites prescribed in the Śruti, one should perform those prescribed in the Smṛti; if one is unable to perform even those, the wise person should maintain himself through right conduct."

Even when this is stated as a *bahuvrīhi* compound, namely, "Dharma has conduct as its supreme [element] (*ācāraparamo dharmaḥ*)," then too this very verse must be recited: "Therefore, a self-possessed twice-born man should always be constantly devoted to this [conduct]" (*tasmād asmin sadā yukto nityaṃ syād ātmavān dvijaḥ*). This is because conduct is heard of as being superior to other dharmas. And since this is so, it is known from the following: "A Brahmin fallen from conduct does not enjoy the fruit of the Veda. This is because conduct is the basis for the qualification (*adhikāra*) for performing rites prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis; for those rites do not bear fruit due to the deficiency of that [conduct].
But one who is endowed with right conduct becomes a partaker of the full fruit. (1.109)

[32] By this, moreover, it is established that even from an impermanent action that is deficient in its qualities, there exists a fruit. The wise ought to understand the significance of this, since the application of the analogy holds in both cases.
Thus, having observed the course of *dharma* through traditional practice, the sages [have declared it].
They took conduct to be the supreme root of all that has been born [from ascetic toil].

In what follows, the praise of conduct is intended to inspire one toward the performance of its injunctions; here, however, it should be understood as a restatement of what has already been said for the purpose of praising the scripture, according to the force of the context. Having thus stated this praise of the scripture—which was mediated by means of a praise of the Brāhmaṇas—he now begins the table of contents (anukramaṇī) for the sake of praising that very scripture: "The origin of the world, the rules for the sacraments, the practice of vows and observances, and the supreme rule for the ceremonial bath. (1.111)
The acquisition of a wife, the characteristics of marriages, the rules for the great sacrifices, and the eternal ritual for ancestral offerings (śrāddha). || 1.112 ||
The characteristics of the modes of livelihood, the vows of the Snātaka, the edible and non-edible, purification, and the cleansing of objects. (1.113)
The application of the duties of women, asceticism, liberation, and renunciation itself;
the entire duty of kings and the determination of legal cases. || 1.114 ||
The rules for examining witnesses, the law concerning husband and wife, the law of partition, gambling, and the removal of thorns [criminals]. 1.115.
He also described the conduct appropriate for Vaiśyas and Śūdras, the origin of the mixed castes, the duties of the social orders in times of distress, and likewise the rules for expiation.
The journey through saṃsāra, which arises from the threefold karma;
the supreme good resulting from actions; and the examination of the merits and defects of those actions. || 1.117 ||
In this treatise, Manu has declared the eternal laws of castes, the laws of families, the laws of countries, and the laws of heretical sects and guilds. (1.118)

Thus ends the first chapter of the *Smṛtimīmāṃsā*, a commentary on the *Manuśāstra* composed by Ānirnīya, the teacher of the venerable Smṛtisāyujya, in his work titled *Ṛjuvimalā*.
Śrī!

Thus, first was introduced the initial section consisting of three or four verses of explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), intended to demonstrate the efficacy of commencing the treatise; this pertains to the remainder of the scripture concerning the acts of study, comprehension, and recitation, beginning from the verse: "This [universe] was then enveloped in darkness" (MDh 1.5). Now, this [section] is commenced for the purpose of following the sequence of the subjects promised therein:
Understand that dharma which is practiced by the wise and the virtuous who are ever free from hatred and passion, and which is approved by the heart. 2.1.
(The fourth quarter of this verse was cited in the commentary on verse 2.1; there, the reading is "nibodhata varṇadharmān").

In this context, the learned ones such as Bhṛgu and others—who know the meaning of all the Vedas and Śāstras—are the *śiṣṭas* (cultured/authoritative persons). By virtue of that connection, they alone are the authorities; those who know other sciences are not, because of the lack of such a connection. As he will state later: "Whoever knows the Dharma of what has been done," "Even one who knows the Veda [knows] Dharma," and "Those who know the Veda should speak. That object which is practiced and performed by those learned ones—that is, the performance of the operations of the factors of action (*kārakas*) such as the agent—is *Dharma*, because it has Dharma as its purpose. Since this is so, one should determine what is to be stated by the entire treatise for the sake of that Dharma. The reading "nobodhateti" is an alternative; through the medium of the specific person who performs it, another qualification is stated by the word "by the good" (*sadbhiḥ*). Although the word *sat* is used in the sense of existence and goodness, here it should be understood in the sense of "goodness" (*sādhubhāva*) by implication. By those "good" ones—those who know the meaning of the entire Veda and Śāstras—the practice is seen in two ways: both the good and the bad. This inclusion of the qualification is for the sake of distinction. This "by the good" is another qualification. By the word "eternal" (*nityam*), he refers to those learned ones whose knowledge of the supreme truth is unassailable. This qualifies the action: that which is practiced eternally by the learned is *Dharma*; never is an improper thing fit to be practiced eternally by such great souls, even when there is an overwhelming of the senses by their objects. Or, the term "eternal" may qualify the nature of the being (*sattva*). It is practiced by the learned and by the "good"—those whose selves are restrained by the scriptures. The qualification regarding the absence of passion and hatred is primary here: "eternally free from hatred and passion. How so? Because the learned are eternal. And how do they become "good"? Eternal. And how do they practice? Eternal. Since this is the primary definition of the characteristics of Smṛti-Dharma, it is taken as a universal rule. It is enjoined: "eternally by those free from hatred and passion. For in a person characterized by the instruments of perception, passion and hatred arise from the experience of desirable and undesirable objects, rooted in pleasure and pain, because that person is for the sake of those objects. Thus says the Brāhmaṇa: "For one who possesses a body, there is no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant. Where there is the pleasant and the unpleasant, there passion and hatred necessarily arise; this is true. But in that case, someone is able to restrain those arisen passions and hatreds from improper action—one whose discriminative wisdom (*prasaṃkhyāna*) is cultivated by pure and profound insights into the supreme truth, whose inner self is favored by distinguished Dharma. Not everyone is capable of this. Therefore, because of the absence of the effects of passion and hatred, the qualification "eternally by those free from hatred and passion" is appropriate to employ due to its capacity. If this is so, then the treatises on Yoga and Liberation (*mokṣa*) become meaningful, and not otherwise. Therefore, this qualification "eternally by those free from hatred and passion" is logical. "Heaven-approved by the heart" (*hṛdayenābhyanujñātaḥ*) is another qualification of Smṛti-Dharma. How so? The heart is the region of the self where the cultivation of the Mantras, Brāhmaṇas, and so forth resides; it is said to be "approved" by the signs of that heart. Alternatively, the quality of the cultured person (*śiṣṭa*) known as "self-satisfaction" (*ātmatuṣṭi*), synonymous with faith and so forth, which acts as a cooperative factor in the performance of all rites, has its abode in the heart as before; it is the "heart" by which approval is granted. Or, for the cultured who are favored by distinguished Dharma, when they perform even highly censurable acts, their intuitive cognition (*pratibhā*)—which is like direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—is the "approval of the heart" based on the signs of the connection to that heart-approval. Or, for those who act with deliberation and possess knowledge of the scriptures, their conduct regarding matters of trust is the "approval of the heart. Thus, it is established: "Learn that Dharma which is approved by the heart. This has been explained. And just as in this world, when a person who knows the science of Āyurveda and acts with foresight, seeing that another person of a bilious temperament has rejected the use of bile-subduing substances but is nevertheless using other substances whose potency is unknown, [the wise man] concludes that those [other substances] are bile-subduing; so too here, since the cultured ones (*śiṣṭas*) such as Bhṛgu and others—who know the meaning of the Vedic scriptures, who have destroyed the faults of the expansion of passion and hatred, and who are entirely free from doubt and are virtuous—practice this Smṛti-Dharma, its excellence must be inferred directly from the Vedic scriptures even if it is not explicitly mentioned therein. How so? The recollection of Dharma pertains to human beings; for others, it is from custom (*ācāra*). Why, then, is this begun? To establish the general definition of all Smṛti-Dharmas. What is the purpose of establishing that? It is said: the purpose is the understanding of the distinction between human-authored and non-human-authored recollections. How so? Without this general definition of Smṛti, it would be difficult to discern whether a recollection pertains to humans or is mixed with something else. But when this exists, the distinction is easily known: "This is a non-human recollection of the Teacher, having an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭa*); and this is a human recollection not based on scripture, having a seen purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*). That human purpose exists; therefore, its commencement is justified, or rather, for the sake of ease of comprehension. Indeed, this treatise will proceed to demonstrate this general definition of all Smṛti-Dharmas.
To have desire as one's sole motive is not praised, yet here there is no such thing as being without desire;
for the study of the Vedas and the performance of Vedic ritual action are themselves objects of desire.

This introductory verse serves as a general rule (*paribhāṣā*): whatever action is taught by the scripture, that very action should be performed without desire for reward. Being "of the nature of desire" (*kāmātmatā*)—that is, performing obligatory rites with the intention of enjoying their fruits—is not praised; this is a censure of such an attitude. And since one should not practice what is censured, by the force of this implication, a prohibitive statement is inferred: "Of what kind of fruit should one perform an action with the intention of attaining it? Why? Because of the authority of the scriptural teaching and because [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of [obligatory rites] being non-obligatory (*anityatva*). For if the performer has the intention of attaining a specific fruit, the performance of the action as a means to that fruit belongs only to him, just as in worldly affairs; it does not belong to anyone else. Thus, the obligatory nature of the performance of action by one who is free from desire is established. Since this is the purpose of the rule, so too says another *Smṛti*: [36]...
Because the means are incomplete, because of the foolishness of the agent,
and because there is no connection with the fruit, it is traditionally known as a "defiled deception."

And Vyāsa has said thus: "Do not become motivated by the fruit of action" (BhG 2.47). Others, however, explain this as being for the purpose of prohibiting the connection with visible motives, saying, "To have desire as one's nature is not praised. For them, however, the fault of redundancy remains; for he will say later, "For those who are unattached to wealth and pleasure" (2.13). Therefore, the meaning is exactly as stated. And so, since it would follow that all scriptural activities are prohibited, this is commenced: "Moreover, there is no such thing as freedom from desire here. How is this understood? Because he says, "For the acquisition of the Vedas is desirable"; the acquisition of the Vedas (*vedādhigama*) is the attainment of the knowledge of Vedic study, and that is something to be sought after. Indeed, it cannot be acquired like fuel or like a discarded object, nor is it something that occurs by mere chance. "And the Vedic yoga of action"—the performance of rituals such as the *agnihotra*—is to be explained in the same way. And thus, since it is impossible to distinguish between performing and not performing those [actions], this is commenced for the purpose of cessation.
Desire indeed has its root in volition; sacrifices arise from volition;
vows, restraints, and duties—all are traditionally held to be born of volition. (2.3)

The root of desire (*kāma*), characterized by the longing for the enjoyment of the objects of the senses, is *saṃkalpa* (volition). What, then, is this? It is the naming of an object possessing qualities; however, that is not what is meant here. Rather, in this context, *saṃkalpa* is the determination of a task to be performed. That is the root of desire, which is the longing for what ought to be done. Thus, sacrifices (*yajña*)—whether Vedic or Smārta, consisting of ritual offerings and the like—are said to arise from *saṃkalpa* through the medium of the effort and longing to perform them. Likewise, sacrifices, conduct, and so forth, characterized by the performance of observances (*niyama*) and the duties of restraint (*niyamadharma*) in the form of cessation from worldly activity, are also included. And in this way, the fruit of action will no longer be volitionally pursued. Furthermore, due to the absence of such volition, and through the performance of obligatory duties (*nityakarman*), there will be no state of being driven by desire (*kāmātmatā*). And because of the [proper] volition regarding sacrifices and the like, through the medium of the longing and effort to perform them, the following applies: "For the acquisition of the Vedas and the application of Vedic rituals are [ordinarily] prompted by desire" (2.2)—this is the illustrative example.
No action whatsoever is seen here belonging to anyone who is free from desire;
for whatever one does, all that is the movement of desire. (2.4)

The word *kāma* refers to the volition (*saṃkalpa*) directed toward objects of desire. Precisely because of the force of this context, it is thus established that for one who is free from desire, no other action of will or activity is observed; this is logical. Then the Lord [concludes] with the summary of the subject at hand: "Whatever one does, all that is the movement of desire. And so it is said:
"Behaving rightly toward these, he goes to the world of the immortals, and here on earth he enjoys all desires exactly as they were willed" (2.5).

With joyful minds, the monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. This is the thirty-seventh discourse, titled “The Lion’s Roar. The third section is concluded. The fourth section follows. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dharma-discourse known as ‘The Lion’s Roar,’ so that I may learn it. The Blessed One then said: “Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? Here, Ānanda, some person dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [2] “Furthermore, Ānanda, there are four other kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four?
