And they dwell having attained the destruction of the taints, having realized for themselves with direct knowledge, in this very life, that unsurpassed liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, which is free from clinging and free from craving. These, Ānanda, are the four other kinds of persons found existing in the world. [7] “Furthermore, Ānanda, there are four other kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? Here, Ānanda, some person dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. And he understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. And he realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, that unsurpassed liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, which is free from clinging and free from craving. And he teaches the Dharma to others in detail as he has realized it. And those who follow him practice in accordance with the Dharma. And they dwell having attained the destruction of the taints, having realized for themselves with direct knowledge, in this very life, that unsurpassed liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, which is free from clinging and free from craving. And they teach the Dharma to others in detail as they have realized it. These, Ānanda, are the four other kinds of persons found existing in the world. [8] “Furthermore, Ānanda, there are four other kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? Here, Ānanda, some person dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. And he understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really

What, then, is the correct practice regarding those [actions]? It is the performance of obligatory rites (*nitya-karman*) by abandoning attachment to their fruits, and the renunciation of optional rites (*kāmya-karman*). This is because they are taught as such; furthermore, the application of ritual action for the attainment of the gods pertains only to optional rites, since they are not prohibited otherwise, and because [the goal] would be unattainable otherwise. Thus, the wise person who conducts himself according to the scriptures in these matters attains the state of the immortals. Due to the inherent nature of the meaning of the verbal roots of action, the teachers have stated that heaven is the fruit of actions whose specific results are not specified, based on the definition provided by the scripture. As it is said: "He enjoys here all desires exactly as he has intended. By this, the fact that action has the fulfillment of all desires as its purpose is directly perceived through the scripture; this concludes the further technical definition.
The entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as are the Smṛtis and the conduct of those who know it, as well as the practice of the virtuous and the satisfaction of one's own self. (2.6)

How is it established for the sake of its authority? Because the authority of Smṛti is rooted in the Veda. And so he will say: "The learned man, by virtue of the authority of Śruti, should indeed be established in his own duty" (2.8). This definition in the treatise is for the purpose of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*). Furthermore, this technical term (*paribhāṣā*) is intended to indicate other Smṛtis such as: "Even a single knower of the Veda [establishes] Dharma" (12.113), and so forth; for he will also say: "And the Smṛti and conduct of those who know that [Dharma]" (1.10). Now, it is explained: the root *vid* means "to know. That by which [the truth] is known through the instrument (*karaṇa*), or in which [the truth] is known through the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), namely those actions, duties, and excellences previously mentioned—that is the Veda. Alternatively, from the root *vid* in the sense of "to obtain" (*lābhe*): that in which the aforementioned actions are obtained, or that in which the existence of the ritual injunctions (*arthavāda*) and so forth is found—that is the Veda. How is it that there are many [meanings]? It is not logical for the existence of those actions and so forth to depend on the word alone, since they are established by the authority of the word itself. Therefore, it is said that they do exist. From the root *vid* in the sense of "investigation" (*vicāraṇe*): that by which the meaning and its auxiliary parts are investigated, or in which they are investigated—that is the Veda. By this much, the purpose is accomplished through what is called the Mantra and Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, it is of three kinds, characterized as Ṛk, Yajus, and Sāman. Why is the Atharvaveda not included? It is said: "Yes. Because the performance of rituals is completed within them; and thus says the Brāhmaṇa: "From the Ṛgveda [comes] *bhūḥ*, from the Yajurveda *bhuvaḥ*, and from the Sāmaveda *svar*. Thus, they perform the office of the Hotṛ with the Ṛgveda, the office of the Adhvaryu with the Yajurveda, and the office of the Udgātṛ with the Sāmaveda. If it is thus, then by that very knowledge [is attained] the purity and the status of a Brāhmaṇa. Likewise: "This is another Triad (*trayī*): indeed, the Ṛcs, the Sāmans, and the Yajuses. And because the status of the Brahman priest is heard of in connection with the three Vedas: "That which is performed as the office of the Hotṛ by the Ṛk, the office of the Adhvaryu by the Yajus, or the office of the Udgātṛ by the Sāman—then by what is the office of the Brahman performed? To this question, the answer "by the threefold knowledge" (*trayyā vidyayā*) is appropriate. Since there is activity in the Atharvaveda even regarding the office of the Brahman, it is not included under the word "Veda. Thus the author of the Sūtras, in the section concerning the office of the Brahman, states "and because of the connection with the three Vedas," thereby effecting an exclusion. Therefore, one should consult the Atharvanic [texts]. What is that Vedic rite? It is understood from the context. How then is the word "Veda" applied to the Atharvaveda? It is like the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Āyurveda. Because it is a collection of Ṛks alone, and because its application in rites such as *svastyayana* is not different from the other Vedas, the word "Veda" is used in the singular. The singular number refers to the unity of the collection, just as one speaks of "the Trayī" (the Threefold Knowledge) when referring to the purpose of the ritual. Even though there are many treatises teaching it, the singular is used with respect to the genus (*jāti*), as in the case of "Veda-like" (*vedavat*), because both [the individual and the genus] exist there. And since the meaning is expectant, it will be made complete by the compound word. How is the Veda the root of Dharma? He will show the connection with what is to be stated later. However, this is first undertaken for the purpose of qualifying the word "Veda. The entire (*akhila*) and complete [Veda] is declared to be the root of Dharma. Now, an objection: since only injunctive sentences teach the performance of actions that yield results, it is proper that they be the root of Dharma; but not so for Arthavādas, names (*nāmadheya*), and Mantras, because they are not of the nature of instruction. The rebuttal to this is: although Arthavādas are not injunctive, some state that they qualify the matter enjoined by an injunction; others state that they serve to direct one toward the performance of what has been enjoined. Thus, since the Arthavādas are supplementary to injunctive sentences and form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with the words of injunction, it is proper that they be the root of Dharma. As for names, since they are part of the injunction, they too are the root of Dharma. For example, "One should sacrifice with the Vājapeya in autumn": this is an injunction of the quality of the time "autumn" based on the name. Likewise, "One desiring food should sacrifice with the Vājapeya": this too is an instruction on the result of the action based precisely on the name. Thus, by way of being specific, these are indirectly the root of Dharma. As for the Mantras, since they are auxiliary parts of the ritual, their status as the root of Dharma is established without effort. In this way, there is no room for objection.

"Now, that which is called the 'root of Dharma' is being discussed. On this point, some say that the word *dharma* derives from the root *dā* (to give), based on the idea that 'it bestows pleasure upon man. However, Bhavadāsa, in his study of the Mīmāṃsā, explains it as arising from the action of 'holding' (*dhāraṇa*). The Vaiśeṣikas maintain that it is called *dharma* because the three worlds are supported by it, due to its connection with the nature of *dharma*. This [derivation] is based on the universal class (*jāti*). What is the use of this search for the etymological cause of the word? Let it be so, or let it not be so. In any case, the word 'root' (*mūla*) is a synonym for 'cause,' and it denotes a category of reality distinct from mere action—an entity that persists until the state of yielding fruit, serving as the cause for the performer’s worldly prosperity and ultimate liberation. Thus, it is stated that the 'root of Dharma' is the Veda. This is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound where the first member is predominant. Consequently, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between this and the word 'Veda,' which qualifies various specific entities: 'What is that root of Dharma? It is the Veda,' just as in the expressions 'the king's man' or 'the body of Udayana. Even though the root of Dharma is the action produced by the words of the Veda and not the Veda itself directly, it is stated in the context of the authoritative source (*adhikaraṇa*)—by way of representing the cause—that 'The entire Veda is the root of Dharma. Now, since the Agnihotra and other such rites are non-dharma when performed contrary to the rules, yet they are for the sake of Dharma and have the Veda as their root, this is logical. Because the Veda is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is spoken of by a word that depends on the action [it prescribes], due to their association. Since the Veda is the root of Dharma, this figurative application (*guṇavṛtti*) is appropriate; it is not a case of 'logical necessity' (*daṇḍāpūpikā*) where the primary meaning is abandoned. Furthermore, both the scripture (*śāstra*) and the study of actions such as the Agnihotra are involved. Therefore, by the injunction 'One's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied,' and according to this interpretation, when the entire Veda is taught as the root of Dharma in the statement 'The entire Veda is the root of Dharma,' it would follow that nothing else [is the root]; however, since there is no teaching to that effect, the status of other things as roots of Dharma is also accepted."

And since that [dharma] cannot be obtained without the effort of composing this treatise (*śāstra*), this work is commenced for that purpose: "The tradition (*smṛti*) and conduct (*śīla*) of those who know that [Veda]. The phrase "the root of dharma" (*dharmamūlam*) continues [from the previous verse]. Tradition (*smṛti*) is the dharma of cultured persons (*śiṣṭa*). It consists of the recollection of matters perceived through the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the conviction arising from the instructions of former cultured persons; its form is that of injunctions and prohibitions; it is the cause for the performance of rites such as the *Aṣṭakā*; it is the codification in treatises such as the *Mānava-śāstra* regarding the practice of ritual acts; and it functions as the agent of the recollection of things. Some, however, say: "It is called *smṛti* because it is remembered. And thus, the thing to be performed is established. For the performance of unregulated acts is indeed remembered by the cultured. Let it be so; what is the harm? But surely, if this is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then its performance follows. Now, if one considers the tradition to be the means of valid knowledge, then its performance is [established]; but if it is a property of persons (*puruṣadharma*), then that act is the recollection of the sacrifice (*kratusmaraṇa*)—an act being remembered by means of tradition. That is fivefold: for example, the performance of acts such as the *agnihotra* has the Veda as its authority, not the Veda itself. That performance of ritual conduct has tradition as its primary authority, not tradition itself. And they [the cultured] have distinguished that [tradition] according to their elders. Some consider tradition to be the cause for the understanding of ritual conduct and practices, such as the *Nṛtsaṅga*, *Śāpa*, and *Apūrika*. Nor are these [traditions] inferred from the mouth of the teachers like Āpastamba, nor from the absence of [direct] recitation or application. Others say they arise from the meaning of the mantras and from indicative marks (*liṅga*). Still others declare that tradition is independent, having an eternal purpose, with an unbroken lineage of transmission reaching back to the beginningless time. Even one exhausted by logic may accept it as it is. Let it be so in every way; for one who does not know the Veda, this [tradition] is among those who know the Veda. Others [say] that nothing other than the root of dharma exists; now, this tradition and conduct are said to be the abandonment of passion and hatred. One who is established in concentration (*samādhi*) has passion and hatred destroyed by conduct, or [it occurs] through firm rooting. A person free from passion and hatred is called "virtuous" (*śīlavat*); one possessing hatred and passion is "immoral" (*duḥśīla*). Therefore, these two—tradition and conduct—are the root of dharma. The word "and" (*ca*) is used for the conjunction of what has been stated: the Veda and tradition and conduct. Now, both of these—tradition and conduct—are the root of dharma, and nothing else.

Is this alone the root of Dharma? No, it is said: "And the conduct of the virtuous. Conduct (*ācāra*) consists of auspicious rites, blessings, and so forth, belonging to those who are virtuous and knowers of the Vedas (*vedavid*). But is not conduct simply Smṛti? Yes, it is said to be so. If that is so, why is it mentioned separately? It is appropriate to mention it separately from Smṛti according to the maxim of the "Brāhmaṇa and the wandering mendicant" (*brāhmaṇaparivrājaka-nyāya*), just as there is a separate instruction for the Kṣatriya and the Brāhmaṇa despite their lack of distinction in being twice-born. This is due to the special status of the wandering mendicant, whether because of his connection with the ascetic marks (*liṅga*), his specific qualification, or some other reason; thus, this must be explained by way of summary. For this is the reason for the separate instruction of conduct from Smṛti: Smṛti is that which is codified, whereas the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) is not codified. It is spoken of separately by this much distinction, namely, being codified or not codified. Furthermore, regarding the non-recollection [of everything]: first, because of the infinity of auspicious rites and blessings, it is impossible to codify them exhaustively, especially by an individual author, due to the infinity of the specific forms of local, caste, and family customs, as well as the recurrence of lunar days and so forth—since in verbal instructions there are counter-instructions, as in the case of various ways of looking back during a journey. Nor can these be taught in a book, because of the diversity of human dispositions. It might be argued: "But worldly conduct, which consists mostly of such counter-instructions, cannot be made known in the same way as 'this is your penance-house' and so forth; therefore, this is not Dharma. It is not so, because this statement is intended to satisfy [the listener], and its purpose is to prevent the appearance of results that have no unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). That [conduct] is indeed Smṛti. Just as one does not fall away from Dharma, or rather, because it does not depend on that [Smṛti] as its essence, it is codified according to what is primary and what is gross, while the opposite is not codified. Or rather, that which is not being taught is for the sake of prosperity through the influence of ritual action (*karma-pratyaya*), while that which is being taught is for prosperity; among those things that must necessarily be performed, that which is not being taught leads to transgression, whereas that which is being taught leads only to prosperity. Just as standing with arms raised and so forth is something that must necessarily be performed, conduct is mentioned separately from Smṛti by this single qualification, because it is character (*śīla*), because it has the form of action, and because it serves all purposes.

Self-praise (*ātma-stuti*) is a synonym for clarity of disposition (*bhāva-prasāda*) and faith (*śraddhā*). Others maintain that self-satisfaction (*ātma-tuṣṭi*) is the performance of actions beyond those prescribed, provided they are not contrary to the *Smṛti*. In this way, because it consists of the essence of conduct (*śīla*), both the recollection of the *Smṛti* and self-satisfaction should be regarded as such. Thus, the section on the *Veda* and *Smṛti* is supported, as well as the fact that the *Smṛti*, conduct (*śīla*), custom (*ācāra*), and self-satisfaction are the roots of Dharma. This should be understood as having the same resolution as the *Veda*. The statement regarding the application of the expansion of the *Smṛti*—"this is to be done, this is not to be done"—demonstrates that the purpose of the *Smṛti* is its practical application, and because its nature is that of knowledge (*vijñāna*).

Another reading is *śabdasya* [instead of *śīlasya*], and the meaning is: "The entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as are the Smṛti and the conduct (*śīla*) of those who know it. Here, "conduct" (*artha*) refers to the performance of rites such as the Aṣṭakā; that which is the recollection of the performance of these by those who know the Veda is also a root of Dharma, as is the Veda itself. Furthermore: "And also the conduct of the virtuous. Conduct is the collection of restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*). The recollection of their performance is a root of Dharma, as is what was previously mentioned. Therefore, precisely because of the power of this instruction on conduct, by the word "conduct" (*śīla*) only the specific rites such as the Aṣṭakā are understood, and not the entire collection of restraints and observances, nor all the duties of the Smṛti, nor self-satisfaction (*ātmatuṣṭi*), nor perhaps faith (*āstikya*), nor the desire for a home, nor the clarity resulting from the state of being an auxiliary to the performance of all rites, nor self-praise, nor the recollection of its performance by those who know the Veda—though that too is a root of Dharma along with what was previously mentioned. Thus, since the Smṛti serves as a qualification of conduct, the recollection of Dharma in the form of conduct, behavior, and self-satisfaction is to be enjoined.
But why is it stated that the Smṛti has its root in Dharma through its connection with those who know the Veda? [It is because:
"Whatever dharma has been proclaimed by Manu for anyone, all that is declared in the Veda; for he consists of all knowledge. (2.7)

Therefore, it is logical that its authority arises from its connection with those who know the Veda, rather than from human authorship. If that is so, let the Smṛti not be a separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) from the Veda; what is the harm? No, for its authority cannot be stated as being due to a connection with those who know the Veda, but only through the authority of the Veda itself.

[Objection: But surely its authority is established because there is no other source for its subject matter. [Response: To this we reply: We say that all of it is stated in the Veda by way of being an inferential mark (*liṅga*) of the Veda. [Question: How is the objection thus resolved? [Answer: It is said: "Yes. [Question: How so? [Answer: Just as ritual items such as the *agnihotra* are directly taught by the Veda, so too are those prescribed in the Smṛtis. What then? They are indeed inferred from inferential marks (*liṅga*). And thus, the Smṛti is a distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just like common worldly experience. Just as the cognition of fire—which is not perceived—arising from smoke which is perceived is a distinct means of knowledge called inference (*anumāna*), so too the Smṛti scripture is a means of knowledge for the cognition of rites, restraints, and observances such as the *Aṣṭakā*, which are not perceived, arising from the inferential marks of the Veda which are perceived. Like an object of inference being a distinct entity from the object of perception, the Smṛti scripture ought to be a distinct entity from the perceived Vedic scripture. And thus, when we said, "All of that is stated in the Veda," we meant it is stated through the Vedic inferential mark and not through direct perception, unlike the *agnihotra* and other rites. An example of this connection between what is to be remembered as to be done and what is to be remembered as not to be done, both originating from Vedic inferential marks, is stated: "In the desert, you are like a water-station" (*dhanvan iva prapā asi*). This refers to the Smṛti regarding the duty to provide a water-station. How indeed could it be otherwise? Because it is possible due to his being a progenitor; thus, even that which was never performed before becomes possible. This should be understood everywhere in this manner. [Objection: If it is argued that the claim that the Smṛti originates from Vedic inferential marks is incorrect because it is not observed in every case, then let an effort be made to observe it. For while one can infer the unperceived from the perceived and the unperceived, one cannot infer the unperceived from that which is itself unperceived. Nor is there a loss of the perceived simply because something is unperceived. Furthermore, the Vedic inferential mark for all the duties in the Smṛtis is perceptible even to one who has studied the three Vedas, let alone to one who has studied only one Veda. Thus it is said: "For he consists of all the Vedas. [Question: Who is this "Veda"? [Answer: Manu, who is composed of all-knowing wisdom cultivated by the knowledge of the meaning of all Vedic scriptures, is able to declare all the duties in the Smṛtis. There is no one else equal to him.
And how so? Having examined all this in its entirety with the eye of knowledge, the learned man should indeed abide in his own duty according to the authority of the sacred revelation. (2.8)

Having fully considered all this entire *smārta* ritual action—the word "entire" (*nikhila*) demonstrates that the word "all" (*sarva*) expresses its primary meaning, as both are seen to serve the same purpose—one should consider it with the eye of knowledge, namely the Veda. How so? As we stated in the preceding verse. This being so, a learned man who knows and understands through the authority of the *śruti*—one who is conversant with the Vedic scriptures—should abide in his own respective duty (*dharma*), and not by the authority of human beings. For, having declared his connection to the Veda, it cannot derive its authority from anything else. And thus it has been said: "Practiced by the wise and the virtuous" (MDh 2.1).
And thus, regarding the authority of Smṛti, this is stated for the purpose of its praise:
"For a human being who practices the dharma declared in Śruti and Smṛti attains fame in this world and the unsurpassed state after death" (2.9).

The mention of *śruti* here is for the purpose of praising *smṛti*. How so? Just as one who performs the duties declared by *śruti* is endowed with fame, so too is one who performs those declared by *smṛti*; this is to be understood through the force of the context of praising the subject at hand by means of a statement of fact (*bhūtārthavāda*). And thus, the *śruti* does not provide instruction regarding its own primary meaning; rather, it is for the purpose of praising *smṛti*.
"The *śruti* is to be known as the Veda, while the *smṛti* is indeed the Dharmaśāstra. These two are not to be questioned in any matter, for from them Dharma has emerged" (2.10).

This [section] is commenced for the purpose of removing doubt regarding Agni, and it continues for the sake of praise. Whatever means of accomplishing Dharma is not perceived through a Smṛti whose words are fixed in the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), all that is Smṛti without distinction; there is no difference between these two. For since both the fixed and the unfixed possess authority, it has been stated that the very remembrance of the learned (*śiṣṭasmaraṇa*) and the composition of the Vedas in accordance with them serve the purpose of Smṛti. All such matters are to be respected and are not to be prohibited. Just as the distinction between pure and impure things established by the Vedic Smṛti scriptures is not questioned by those belonging to other systems, so too the slaughter of animals and the like in the context of enjoined rites is not to be scrutinized here. This is because "Dharma indeed shone forth from those two. How so? Just as Dharma, when not obtained through other means of knowledge, attains its own nature in the Vedas—such as the *agnihotra* and so on—so too does it do so through Smṛti, such as the *aṣṭakā* rites. Thus, another meaning of the sentence is that Smṛti, like Śruti, is not to be prohibited in the case of the *aṣṭakā*. This Smṛti is thus praised in both ways, and this is seen as the supreme [authority] due to the context of praising Smṛti.
That twice-born man who, relying on the treatises of logic, would despise both of these—he is an atheist and a reviler of the Veda, and he should be excluded by the virtuous. (2.11)

[42] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by virtue of his great compassion, beheld those who were suffering and heard their cries for help. Then, while traveling through the perilous path of the five hundred yojanas in the realm of Śrāvastī, he saw the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā being pursued by five hundred robbers. Seeing this, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara extended his right hand and touched the crown of her head. At that moment, the five hundred robbers were struck with fear and, trembling, fell to the ground. Having seen this, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: "O Noble One, these five hundred robbers are pursuing me; please protect me. Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara spoke to the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā: "Do not fear, sister. I shall protect you from these five hundred robbers. Having said this, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara emitted a great light from his body, which illuminated the entire realm of Śrāvastī. At that time, the five hundred robbers, having seen that great light, were filled with wonder and approached the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Having arrived, they prostrated at his feet and sat to one side. Sitting there, they addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: "Noble One, what is the cause, what is the reason, for this great light? Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara spoke to the five hundred robbers: "Sons of good family, this great light is emitted by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, out of compassion for all beings, so that they may hear the Dharma. Hearing this, the five hundred robbers were filled with joy and addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: "Noble One, we too wish to go forth into the religious life under the Tathāgata. Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara led the five hundred robbers to the presence of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni. Having arrived, they prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side. Sitting there, the five hundred robbers addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, we wish to go forth into the religious life under the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, out of compassion for them, granted them the going-forth and the full ordination. Having been ordained, the five hundred bhikṣus, through diligent application, secluded dwelling, and right effort, in no long time realized for themselves with direct knowledge, in this very life, the unsurpassed goal of the holy life, and having attained it, they dwelt therein, saying: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, and there is no further state of existence after this. Thus, the five hundred bhikṣus became arhats. This is the second chapter on the manifestation of the power of Avalokiteśvara. [42]

Because it is not based on direct revelation (*aśabdatvāt*), there is a suspicion that it lacks authority; therefore, by means of the Vedic text, [the author] equates it [with the Veda]: "And I think that you, though a twice-born (*dvija*) instructed in the Vedic scriptures, are rejecting both [the Veda and Smṛti] by relying on the science of logic (*hetuśāstra*). This is a censure of that person who, being an adherent of the science of logic—which contradicts the Veda, Smṛti, and Āgama—is obstructed [by fallacy] and practices a pseudo-logical system (*nyāyābhāsa*). He is to be excluded by the virtuous from rites such as hospitality, because he is an atheist (*nāstika*) due to his reviling of the Veda. For the status of a twice-born consists in having the threefold scripture (*trayīśāstra*) as its authority; thus, for one established therein, reviling is improper. Precisely because a twice-born person is engaged in asserting contradictions to the meaning of the three Vedas, he is censured. Furthermore, the mention of the "Veda" here should be understood to include the *Smṛti* as well, by virtue of the force of the stated reasoning. And this being so, just as the Veda is not to be rejected because it is the root of Dharma when one relies on the science of logic, so too is the *Smṛti*; thus, by the force of the context, this section is explained as being primarily concerned with the *Smṛti*.
"The Veda, the Smṛti, the conduct of the virtuous, and what is pleasing to oneself—they say that this fourfold is the direct definition of Dharma. (2.12)

This verse as well is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*) by way of another method. How so? Just as the Veda is the direct root of *dharma* even when it is not explicitly present, so too the *Smṛti*, which consists of injunctive sentences (*codanāvākya*), is the direct root of the *dharma* to be performed; it is not, however, something additional to that which arises from the Veda. Alternatively, this verse is intended as a concluding summary (*upasaṃhāra*) for the praise of *Smṛti*. This conclusion aims at introducing a different technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) by way of excluding the previous method, and is intended to show another opinion. Some consider the *Smṛti* to be threefold through the non-recitation of the Vedic sentence of one who possesses that character (*tacchīla*). With the recitation of that together, it is fourfold, as it has been said: "The *Smṛti* and conduct (*śīla*) of those who know it, and also the practice (*ācāra*) of the virtuous" (MDh 2.6). Gautama, however, says it is twofold: "And the *Smṛti* and conduct of those who know it" (GDh 1.2). Thus, this enumeration of the divisions of *Smṛti* was indeed intended by both Gautama Ācārya and Manu. Regarding the distinction in the meaning of the term *Smṛti*, there is only one *Smṛti*. And so it has been stated by him elsewhere: "The *Dharmaśāstra* is indeed *Smṛti*" (MDh 2.10), and "the *dharma* declared in *Śruti* and *Smṛti*" (MDh 2.9). He spoke of *Smṛti* as being one and the same, whereby he makes this known. This division of *Smṛti* is not primary. What then? It is secondary (*gauṇa*) due to other causes. Now, since the Veda and *Smṛti* are the roots of *dharma*, the relationship between the entity and the act of performance—whether the person performing its meaning is motivated or unmotivated—is observed directly in the case of the prohibition of illness and the arising of prosperity when medical treatment is applied. And so he will say: "Performing their own duties... (MDh 8.42); the scripture is commenced for the purpose of regulating the yoga.
For those who are unattached to wealth and sensual desires, knowledge of Dharma is prescribed;
for those seeking to understand Dharma, the Śruti is the supreme authority. (2.13)

For a person who is an agent of the performance of the scriptures, the sequence of purpose (arthakrama) inherent in the act of performance is perceived through direct observation as having a visible human goal. And so it will be said: "Even when they are far away, men performing their own duties... (MDh 8.42). Likewise, the Vājasaneyaka Brāhmaṇa, having stated the visible purpose of the practice of Vedic study for one living in the world, says: "The world, while being sustained, nourishes the Brāhmaṇa with four virtues: with honor, with gifts, with knowledge, and likewise with immunity from harm. (43) And similarly, another Smṛti states:
"Just as water sprinkled here for the sake of sugarcane also waters the grasses and creepers, so too a person walking upon the paths of Dharma enjoys fame, desires, and wealth. Thus it is said.

For those practitioners who perform the purpose of the scripture by abandoning the pursuit of wealth and desire, there is enjoined the knowledge of Dharma (*dharmajñāna*), which is merely a restatement of an existing fact (*bhūtārthānuvāda*). How is the scripture known to be the source of the knowledge of Dharma? [The answer is] "by that," meaning that the statement of the authoritative person (*deśavākya*) is the root of knowledge. Alternatively, *dharmajñāna* means the knowledge of Dharma; or it is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*) because the application for its sake is known therein. Thus, by a figurative usage (*guṇavṛttyā*), the causal function of the scripture—the knowledge of Dharma—is expressed by the term *dharmajñāna*. In this way, that scripture, or rather the knowledge of Dharma, is enjoined or taught. By whom? By the cultured (*śiṣṭa*) or by the scripture. For what reason? Because one who desires the knowledge of Dharma asks, "By what means does Dharma come to be? To this, [it is said]: "The supreme authority is the Veda (*śruti*). Why? From inference (*anumāna*). And that has been stated: even if that Veda is not directly perceived, it must be sought in this matter through the Smṛti, which originates from signs (*liṅga*) derived from the cultured, and not by mere conjecture.
They say that for one whose purpose here is action, knowledge, or austerity, but not for the sake of the next world, [that effort] is fruitless;
yet that divine fruit which lasts for infinite kalpas has been lost to others through greed. And likewise, there is a statement by Bhṛgu:
This follows from the restatement of the scriptures concerning the rules for the performance and application of all ritual acts:
because of the abandonment of what is seen, when there is no visible purpose, the application [of these rules] leads to prosperity.

Thus, in this way, just as not all human actions constitute *dharma*—but rather only those taught in the scripture (*śāstra*)—so too, not every follower of the scripture possesses *dharma*, nor does the scripture belong to one who is without [the necessary] substratum (*nirupadha*). And in this manner, the inherent nature of the relationship between action and its object, which leads to the production of *dharma*, is abandoned for a follower of the scripture who remains in any state whatsoever. Because of the contradiction with this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*), he begins another technical rule in order to exclude the performance of actions that are impossible to combine, whether they be these or others.
Where there is a conflict between two Vedic texts, both are traditionally held to be Dharma;
both of them have been correctly declared as Dharma by the wise. (2.14)

The mention of *śruti* here is for the purpose of establishing an option when there is a conflict with the *smṛti* under discussion; it is not for its own sake, as it is not the subject of the context (*aprakaraṇāt*). In this regard, there is a verse stating the meaning of the example:
"Whether at sunrise, at sunset, or likewise during the twilight (*samayādhyuṣita*), the sacrifice proceeds in every way"—this is the Vedic *śruti*. (2.15)

And just as in the case of Vedic word-meanings that are mutually contradictory yet capable of being combined, the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled by the performance of either one of them—just as the study [of the Veda] is performed when there is no contradiction—so too should it be understood in the case of Smṛti. An example is: Gautama says, "Food contaminated by hair or insects is always unfit to be eaten," whereas Manu says, "It is fit to be eaten after the purificatory rite known as the scattering of earth. Thus, when there is a mutual contradiction between Smṛti authorities of equal strength, an option (*vikalpa*) is to be understood; that is, the performance of either one is to be recognized, just as in the Vedic injunction "one offers with the *juhū*," which is an inference.

He for whom the ritual procedure beginning with the impregnation and ending at the cremation ground has been prescribed by means of mantras—only he is to be known as qualified for this scripture, and no one else whatsoever. (2.16)

This verse establishes the eligibility of the twice-born (*dvijāti*) for the study of the *Smṛti*. How so? By mentioning the first and last sacraments—namely, conception (*niṣeka*) and the funeral rites at the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*)—the inclusion of all the sacraments falling between them is understood by implication; this is done for the purpose of defining the twice-born. Furthermore, the definition of the twice-born serves to establish their eligibility for the study of the *Smṛti*. Thus, that ritual action which pertains to a person within this context of eligibility for the *Smṛti-śāstra* should be understood as applying to them, but not to a *Śūdra*, for whom there is no study. Nor does he possess the sacraments of the twice-born. Therefore, the prohibition of his eligibility for the study of the *Smṛti* follows from the force of that specific instruction. It is not logical to grant him eligibility to study that *śāstra* merely because of his eligibility for ritual acts (*karma*), as is the case with women or with the *Aśvamedha* and other such rituals, where an option might exist. Alternatively, based on the authority of the *śāstra*, the understanding of the *śāstra*'s meaning occurs exactly according to the instruction, and not through mere logic. Moreover, the eligibility for the study of the *Smṛti* has already been stated in the verse: "This should be studied with effort by a learned Brāhmaṇa" (MDh 1.103). The phrase "of the twice-born" (*dvijātīnām*) thus serves in both ways: either as praise for the *Smṛti-śāstra* itself, or as a statement that this eligibility for the *Smṛti* does not apply to those [who are not twice-born]. Furthermore, the verse "The three castes should study" (MDh 10.1) is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the injunction regarding Vedic study prescribed through the method of initiation (*upanayana*) and so forth; it is not an injunction for the eligibility to study the *Smṛti*. Some, however, say: "In this *śāstra*, the primary subject is the Veda, while the *Smṛti* is included through the force of the context and the remainder. That is incorrect. For in the section concerning initiation, after the performance of the initiation and the observance of Vedic vows, the rule for the acquisition of the Veda immediately following attendance upon the teacher is set forth in the sequence of the text. And thus, this very point is stated in that same context: "A Brāhmaṇa should always place the *praṇava* at the beginning and at the end" (2.74).
The three imperishable great utterances preceded by the syllable *oṃ*, together with the three-footed *sāvitrī*, should be known as the mouth of Brahman. [MDh 2.81]

And so forth. Therefore, this is not an entitlement to the Veda; rather, it is an entitlement to the *Smṛti* alone. But surely, whether the action of speaking or the root *kṛdhi* preceded by *adhi*—as in the aforementioned qualification—is involved, this entitlement to study (*adhyayana*) would be contradicted in the *Smṛti*. Thus, this entitlement might apply to a work intended for the purpose of memorization, as in the case of "the duties of those like us. Another, however, says: "Because of the statement, 'For the sake of distinguishing his duties, and of the others in due order' (MDh 1.102), the entitlement to study the *Smṛti* belongs to the Śūdra himself. He [the opponent] understands the meaning of this scripture thus: "The purpose of distinguishing duties has been stated at the beginning of the treatise; here there is no entitlement to study. But how then is this to be understood: "All men on earth should learn their respective conduct" (MDh 2.20)? Here, the inclusion of the word "all" is the refutation of what was stated. Furthermore, who is this person standing outside [the community] who, through instruction, would have no entitlement to study? Likewise, regarding the statement, "A teacher of Dharma to a king may never be a Śūdra" (MDh 8.20), we shall explain that this is for the purpose of providing a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) for the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya in the absence of a Brāhmaṇa. Since this is not an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the attainment of a prohibition, and it has been said here: "Of him who, out of pride, gives instruction in Dharma to Brāhmaṇas" (MDh 8.272)—this also is not an indicative mark for the attainment of the scripture. What then? It is for the attainment of the sense (*artha*). An indicative mark serves to illuminate what is already attained, not to bring about what is unattained. We shall clarify this in the verse: "One should not give counsel to a Śūdra" (MDh 4.80). Therefore, there is no entitlement for an uninitiated Śūdra to study the *Smṛti*. [45]
The region between the two divine rivers, the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī, that land created by the gods, they call Brahmāvarta. (2.17)

Because it is embraced by the gods and fashioned by the gods, and because the Veda (*brahman*)—which had arisen [there]—is said to have been revealed here to the great seers (*maharṣi*), the region is praised under the name "Brahmāvarta. Regarding that country: "Whatever conduct has come down through traditional succession among the social classes (*varṇa*) and the intermediate castes (*antarāla*) in a particular country, that is called 'right conduct' (*sadācāra*). (2.18)
This verse also serves to praise the region. Thus, it is not as if improper conduct is said to exist elsewhere.
"Kurukṣetra, the Matsyas, the Pañcālas, and the Śūrasenakas—this is indeed the land of the Brahman-sages, immediately following Brahmāvarta. (2.19)

"The region of the Brahman-sages is immediately adjacent to Brahmāvarta"—this designation of the region is likewise for the purpose of praising the land. "Immediately adjacent to Brahmāvarta" means slightly inferior in praise. And this mention of "immediately adjacent" applies to every subsequent region; compared to each preceding region, each succeeding one is slightly inferior. In this way, the sequential description of the regions is upheld.
From the presence of a twice-born man born in these regions, all men on earth should learn their respective proper conduct. (2.20)

This too is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) concerning the region of the Brahmanical seers (brahmarṣi). And thus, there is no prohibition against learning proper conduct from anyone other than those of the first-born caste (agrajanman).
The region between the Himālaya and the Vindhya mountains, extending eastward from Vinaśana and westward from Prayāga, is proclaimed as Madhyadeśa (the Middle Country). (2.21)

This [definition] is stated here as a commendatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) for the sake of praising the region; however, it should be understood according to the context. This same principle is to be understood for the subsequent verses as well. Furthermore, because it is mentioned in the midst of a section describing an excellent region, this [region] should be seen as the "Middle Country" (*madhyadeśa*), which is significant in its literal meaning.
From the eastern ocean to the western ocean, And between those very two mountains, The wise declare this to be Āryāvarta. (2.22)
"Because noble ones (ārya) dwell in this place, it is praised as a land by that very designation [of being 'Āryāvarta'].
"But wherever the black antelope roams by its own nature, that should be known as the land fit for sacrifice; beyond that is the land of the barbarians (mleccha). (2.23)

The term *mlecchadeśa* means a country inhabited by people who are not entitled [to Vedic rites]; the meaning is that such a place is unfit to serve as a locus for sacrifices. Thus, the prohibition against residing there should be understood as having been stated for this very reason. "Twice-born men should diligently seek refuge in these countries;
but a Śūdra, distressed for a livelihood, may dwell in any [place whatsoever]. (2.24)

Because of the specific description of various regions and foreign lands, one should dwell according to rule in each preceding [region] mentioned. This is shown so that a specific result may arise from a specific effort, and for the purpose of abandoning uncivilized regions. Even for a Śūdra who serves the twice-born, this restriction regarding residence in these regions is established by implication through association with them, even though the term "twice-born" is used [in the verse]. And this is his distinction from them: a Śūdra, distressed by the lack of means of livelihood, may reside anywhere at all; whereas the twice-born, even when their livelihood is exhausted, should not reside elsewhere [than the prescribed regions], because residing elsewhere is prohibited except in times of distress. Their travel to other countries for the sake of livelihood is sometimes not forbidden, but permanent residence there does not exist.
This source of Dharma has been proclaimed in brief, as well as the origin of all this; now learn the duties of the social classes (varṇas). 2.25.

This system of castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramavyavasthā*), which is the primary source and cause for the prosperity of Dharma—the Dharma that persists until the granting of its fruit—has been briefly stated by me to you in this context, within the verse beginning with "Practiced by the wise and the good" (MDh 2.1). Nor does this refer merely to the technical definitions of the scriptures, such as "being motivated by desire is not praised" (MDh 2.2), and so forth. Rather, since this verse [2.1] deals with the origin of this entire world along with its maintenance and dissolution, other passages of similar meaning—including those praising the Brahmin found in the introductory sections of the first chapter which were spoken for the purpose of demonstrating the capacity for the commencement of the treatise—are also included here even though they were not mentioned previously. This summary is intended to introduce the forthcoming sections; and the purpose of that summary is to prevent confusion in the listener. That, moreover, is a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Having thus summarized this, the Teacher speaks the following with the desire to state the subject matter he has promised: "Learn the duties of the castes" (*varṇadharmān nibodhata*). Why are the duties of the stages of life (*āśramadharma*) not mentioned? Because they too are indeed duties of the castes, since they are enjoined by the same authoritative injunctions. Thus, whatever duties of the castes exist in all conditions, such as sipping water (*ācamana*) and so forth, and the duties of the stages of life—which are distinguished from the duties of other conditions—all the duties spoken of here are duties of the castes, insofar as they persist as long as the caste exists, because birth (*jāti*) is never lost.

The purifying refinement of the body for the twice-born, beginning with the rite of impregnation, must be performed through meritorious Vedic rites; it is sanctifying both in this world and after death.

To this extent, those who have received full ordination (*upasampanna*) consider the *Aṣṭakā* and other rites to be preceded by Vedic revelation (*śruti*). According to that view, it is indeed appropriate for the sacramental acts (*saṃskārakarma*), beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*), to possess a Vedic character. Even for those whose authority is based on Smṛti, their Vedic nature is not merely figurative, because they are accomplished through Vedic mantras. Alternatively, their Vedic character consists in being subsidiary to Vedic rituals. This "Vedic character" is intended as praise; it means they are like Vedic rituals, such as conception and the rest. The phrase "by meritorious [acts]" is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). "That body-sacrament of the twice-born, beginning with impregnation (*niṣeka*), must be performed"—this is the instruction of the father. For what reason? Because he becomes purified after death (*pretya*) for the sake of excellence, and because of the non-obstruction of Dharma here in this world, by preventing the causes of bodily afflictions such as leprosy. Thus, this is an explanatory praise for both purposes. "The body-sacrament must be performed through a connection with merit and by way of purification"—this is the injunction (*vidhi*). Furthermore, this other point—that all general sacramental acts are duties to be performed according to the Smṛti—is merely a subsidiary part of that same injunction.

By means of oblations performed during pregnancy, and by the rites of birth, the tonsure, and the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass, the taint derived from the seed and that derived from the womb are wiped away from the twice-born. (2.27)

The venerable [author] states that the purpose is the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the embryo (*garbha*) by means of those "embryonic" (*gārbha*) oblations (*homa*). The mention of *homa* is for the sake of illustration. Of what? Of the applications of mantras, ritual acts (*kriyā*), and medicinal herbs (*auṣadha*) prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*. Having established this, the following explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) arises: "by means of the applications of mantras, ritual acts, and medicinal herbs, and by means of oblations. Why? If it is asked why this mention of *homa* is merely illustrative, it is because of the following arrangement: of the three [sacraments], namely *garbhādhāna*, *puṃsavana*, and *sīmantonnayana*, the first two are sacraments consisting only of the application of mantras and herbs; they are performed with oblations for each conception (*pratigarbham*). However, the third (*sīmantonnayana*) is accompanied by an oblation. Here, *sīmantonnayana* is a sacrament pertaining only to the first conception and does not occur for every subsequent conception like the previous ones; therefore, the mention of *homa* is postulated for the sake of illustration. Alternatively, one should understand that the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) has been elided here; thus, "by means of oblations and so forth," where the mention of *homa* serves as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*). Regarding the sacramental rite of the embryo (*garbhasaṃskārakarman*) which involves specific actions: the sacraments of birth (*jātakarma*), tonsure (*caula*), and the tying of the girdle (*mauñjīnibandhana*) have already been mentioned; thus they are directly taught through the use of compounds and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*). Alternatively, the mention of *homa* should be understood as applying even to the individual items [of the list], not only to the preceding context. Consequently, [the phrase refers to] "by means of the embryonic oblations, the birth-oblations, the tonsure-oblations, and the girdle-tying oblations. As for their [impurity]: the blood of this [woman] becomes defiled by the man's thoughts when he is overcome by lust. As it will be said: "That which my mother longed for... (MDh 9.20). And for the father, the habitual practice of forbidden sexual intentions likewise defiles the semen. Thus, whatever sin (*enas*) belongs to the embryo on account of those [semen and blood] is "seminal" (*baijika*). Alternatively, even without unwholesome thoughts, the blood and semen of the parents are impure by their very nature. Since the sin of the embryo is caused by connection with those [impurities], it is called "seminal" (*baijika*) and also "embryonic" (*gārbhika*) due to its location in the womb. That sin is wiped away from the seeds by the sacraments beginning with *garbhādhāna*. Having established this, this explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) is in some way intended to praise the rule under discussion; it is not an instruction regarding a causal origin, as that would contradict authoritative scriptures (*pramāṇaśāstra*). And thus, another [explanation] is that this explanatory statement is merely a supplement (*śeṣa*) to that [rule].

Through private study of the Vedas, through vows, through burnt offerings, through the knowledge of the three Vedas, through sacrifices, through sons, and through the great sacrifices and other rites, this body is made fit for Brahman. (2.28)

"By private recitation" (*svādhyāyena*) means by the study of the *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *sāvitrī* as a supplement to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). Why? Because one who has not been instructed in the Vedic observances (*vedavrata*) lacks the qualification for Vedic study. As he will state later: "For one who has undergone initiation, the instruction in the observances and the acquisition of the Veda (*brahman*) are required in due order according to the rule" (MDh 2.173).

Regarding the phrase “by vows” (*vrataiḥ*), this refers to those vows prescribed for each Veda—such as those pertaining to the *Ṛgveda* and others—or alternatively, to the fire-rites (*agnikārya*) such as the *sāvitra* oblations consisting of the placing of fuel-sticks (*samidādhāna*) and so forth. By “knowledge” (*vidyayā*) is meant the study of the three Vedas; thus, the vow of the Veda (*vedavrata*) is performed through sacrifice (*ijyā*). As for those who serve their teacher and those who practice austerity, their austerity is to be understood as being accomplished precisely through service to the teacher. Although bathing (*snāna*) is not explicitly mentioned here, it is implied by the instruction on the duties of the religious student (*brahmacārin*), such as study and the like, which are associated with it. Marriage (*udvāha*) is to be understood from the mention of “sons” (*sutaiḥ*), since sons are produced through the performance of Dharma. By the five great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) prescribed in the *Smṛtis*, and by the sacrifices such as the *huta-yajña* and others, as well as the Śrauta sacrifices such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, this body is made “Brahmic” (*brāhmī*). This “Brahmic” state is said to be the culmination of the purification resulting from the discernment of the *Smārta* sacraments (*saṃskāra*), intended for the attainment of Brahman. It serves as a praise of all *Smārta* duties. One might ask: how can there be such greatness in these *Smārta* sacramental rites that this body—which is inherently extremely impure—is rendered fit for the attainment of Brahman? If that were the case, it would be illogical to mention Śrauta sacrifices, for the body is made Brahmic by Śrauta sacrifices like the *Jyotiṣṭoma* just as much as by all the *Smārta* sacramental rites. Thus, the supreme human goal—the attainment of Brahman—is established as being accomplished through the combination (*samuccaya*) of both Śrauta and *Smārta* acts, rather than being accomplished by the mere performance of Śrauta injunctions alone. In this way, the praise of the *Smṛti* scriptures remains intact through the force of the context. Another, however, says: “By these three verses, the purification beginning from conception is stated. This is for the sake of obtaining the sacraments for one born of an outcaste (*patita*), for his purification is purposeful, whereas for another it is not. To this it is replied: if that were so, the birth of an outcaste would be the occasioning cause (*prayojaka*) for the sacraments of the embryo. Consequently, because they would be contingent upon a specific occasion (*naimittika*), they would become non-obligatory (*anitya*), and they would also serve the purpose of expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Neither of these is desired, because these sacraments are not part of a specific context (*aprakaraṇatvāt*) and are obligatory (*nitya*). As for the claim that the praise of his purification is meaningful while for another it is not, it has already been stated: the statement “the purification of the body must be performed” (*kāryaḥ śarīrasaṃskāraḥ*) is a commendation (*prarocanā*) for the performance of what is enjoined; it is not meaningless. Likewise, it is for the purpose of praising the performance of all enjoined acts, including the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). Furthermore, if he were excluded from these due to a cause of degradation (*patanīya*), then this [text] would have to be addressed to him. But rather, you yourself have stated in these three verses that purification from conception onwards is taught. Therefore, the meaning of the three verses is exactly as explained above.
For a male child, the birth-rite (jātakarma) is prescribed before the cutting of the umbilical cord;
it includes the ritual feeding of him with gold, honey, and clarified butter, accompanied by sacred mantras.

"Before the cutting of the umbilical cord"—this is an indication of the time for the *jātakarma* (birth-rite) as previously described. The mention of "male" (*pum*), however, is for the purpose of excluding the neuter. For females, he will state that the rite is performed without mantras. Alternatively, the mention of "male" is not intended to be restrictive, because the context refers to the human species (*jāti*). [The phrase] "one who has been feverish" means one who has suffered from fever. "At the end of the day, one should feed the man. Or rather, "mantric" (*mantravat*) means that which is worthy of mantras. What is that? It is the "feeding" (*prāśana*). Of whom? Of the boy (*kumāra*). Of what things? Of gold, honey, and clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Some say it is of clarified butter alone. From this point forward, a general enumeration of the rules stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtras* is intended for the sake of establishing authority and for the sake of including those [rules] already recited; thus, the inclusion of additional injunctions—provided they do not contradict other Vedic branches—is accepted here as if they were direct revelation (*śruti*).
One should have his naming ceremony performed on the tenth or the twelfth day,
on an auspicious lunar day, at a favorable moment, or under a constellation endowed with excellent qualities.

[49] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Great Collection. It should be learned, Ānanda, and it should be taught extensively to others. This is what the Blessed One said. Delighted, the Venerable Ānanda and the monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken. 106. The Chapter on the Great Collection is concluded. 107. The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how many kinds of bodhisattvas are there? The Blessed One replied: “Śāriputra, there are two kinds of bodhisattvas. “What are these two? “They are the bodhisattvas who have newly entered the vehicle and the bodhisattvas who have long practiced the vehicle. “Blessed One, what is the cause and condition for a bodhisattva to become one who has newly entered the vehicle? “Śāriputra, it is because they do not hear this Dharma-discourse, do not see it, do not understand it, and do not practice it. “Blessed One, what is the cause and condition for a bodhisattva to become one who has long practiced the vehicle? “Śāriputra, it is because they hear this Dharma-discourse, see it, understand it, and practice it. “Blessed One, what is the cause and condition for a bodhisattva to become one who has newly entered the vehicle? The suffix *-dheya* is used in the sense of the base word itself; thus, *nāmadheya* means simply "name. One should cause the name of the child under discussion to be given. This is an instruction for the father, or rather, for whoever has authority over the matter. At what time? On the tenth day. The context refers to birth; therefore, the tenth day should be understood as starting from that very moment of birth, not the lunar date (*tithi*), because of the contextual force of the passage. By this, the twelfth day is also explained. The word "auspicious" (*puṇya*) qualifies both [the lunar date and the hour]; here there is a conjunction of an auspicious lunar date and an auspicious hour, not an option between them. Furthermore, the strength of the moon and stars, praised through its connection with the qualities of the asterism (*nakṣatra*), is also included. This being the case, if on the tenth lunar day the name cannot be given because it is afflicted by defects such as planetary opposition (*viṣkambha*), the conjunction (*vyatīpāta*), the *vaidhṛta* yoga, or unfavorable positions of the stars and moon, then on the twelfth day—which is free from such defects—the naming may optionally take place at a later time, depending on the excellence of the lunar date and other factors, due to the necessity of the situation. Furthermore, [Note: The final sentence fragment "punar" indicates that more text follows.]
The name of a Brāhmaṇa should be auspicious; that of a Kṣatriya, endowed with power;
that of a Vaiśya, associated with wealth and prosperity; but that of a Śūdra, contemptible. (2.31)

A name for a Brāhmaṇa should be auspicious (*maṅgalya*), meaning it should signify the Dharma or its purpose. Examples include Śatāyu, Nandana, Dharma, Deva, Yajña, Satya, Śānti, and so forth. For a Kṣatriya, the name should be endowed with power (*balānvita*). Examples include Śatruṃtapa, Dviṣantapa, Paraṃtapa, Bhīṣma, Yudhiṣṭhira, Vijaya, Duryodhana, and so forth. For a Vaiśya, the name should be connected with wealth (*dhanasaṃyukta*). Examples include Aśvapati, Dhanapati, Gopati, Paśupati, and so forth. For a Śūdra, however, the name should be contemptible (*jugupsita*). Examples include Karmakāra, Śabaraka, Lubdhaka, Dhīvaraka, Niṣāda, Kaivartika, and so forth—these being names associated with the inverse castes (*pratiloma-varṇa*). Furthermore, such [contemptible] names are inauspicious (*amaṅgalya*).
The name of a Brāhmaṇa should end in a word meaning "shelter" (śarman).

Names such as Viṣṇuśarman, Yajñaśarman, Somaśarman, and so forth, are like the word *śarman*. Alternatively, the word *śarman* may be auspicious (*maṅgalya*). Why is this? Because of the force of the initial statement [of the rule]. Otherwise, it would follow that [the name] is merely for the purpose of identifying a person. Since this is already established by the rule, "The name of a Brāhmaṇa should be auspicious" (MDh 2.31), the present rule serves another purpose. Furthermore, that which is inauspicious is of two kinds: that which does not serve an auspicious purpose, and that which has an inauspicious meaning. For example, Kapila, Piṅgala, and so forth. As for the phrase "it should be like *śarman*," this is the inclusion of the sense [of auspiciousness] because of the force of the initial statement; or rather, this is the literal mention of the word itself, as he will explain further below.
Or, as stated, it is endowed with strength;
or it is provided with protection for the king.
Or, as in the case of *pālaka* (protector), *rakṣaka* (guardian), *śaraṇya* (refuge), *trātṛka* (savior), *nāthaka* (lord), and so forth.
Likewise, it may be associated with wealth as previously described, or for a Vaiśya, it may be associated with prosperity;
such as "owner," "wealthy," "lord," "possessor of cattle," and so forth.
Or perhaps it is called "despised," as in the case of a Śūdra.
As it has been stated:
"Accompanied by a servant."
Or, for example, like a slave, a servant, or a laborer.

In this context, regarding names of Brāhmaṇas, there is the inclusion of the meaning (*artha*) in the preceding verse and the inclusion of the word-form (*śabda*) in the subsequent one, such as [the suffix] *śarman*. This is because in that case there is an optional conjunction (*pākṣika-samuccaya*), and thus it has been described accordingly. For Kṣatriyas and others, however, there is only the inclusion of the meaning in the two previously mentioned verses; therefore, no such conjunction exists there. Furthermore, in names such as *parantapaḥ*, *dviṣantapaḥ*, and *śatruṃtapaḥ*, there would be a conjunction [of both meaning and form], which would result in a contradiction with the Gṛhya-smṛti scriptures. For it is stated therein: "The father gives a name consisting of two or four syllables. But this is not the case here. Therefore, this [interpretation] is meaningless. Nor is a conjunction possible in all names. Or, even for the sake of protection, since it possesses a name, it is not as there is a plurality among those who speak of strength, so it is in other cases. Therefore, the meaning is exactly as stated. This same principle should be understood to apply to the names of Vaiśyas and Śūdras. As for those who say, "The name of a Brāhmaṇa should be auspicious or possess the suffix *śarman*," for them, since an option is impossible, this [conjunction] is untenable; and that impossibility should be understood by implication. For if the word *dharma* were spoken even as an optional alternative, there would be an absence of practical usage (*vyavahāra*).

Alternatively, there is another interpretation of the verse. The statement that "the name of a Brāhmaṇa should contain the word *śarman*" is explained here as being endowed with protection (*rakṣā*), as previously stated for a king. This is now explained as applying to the names of Brāhmaṇas. How so? *Varman* means protection; thus, by including the word *varman*, one should understand the inclusion of the word *tat* (that), referring to one who possesses that protection, namely the protector. This is because the literal meaning [of the action] is impossible, either through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) or because the word and its meaning are treated as one. Thus, since the word *varman* includes the word *rakṣā*, that which was previously stated as the Kṣatriya's name being "endowed with strength" should be seen here as being like *varman*. By this logic of "Bhīma," examples such as *Bhīmavarman* or *Bhīṣmavarman* follow. Likewise, for a Vaiśya, the name should be "connected with prosperity" (*puṣṭi*). Prosperity means growth; the word *puṣṭi* refers to protection (*gupti*) for that purpose, and because of the connection with the state of being protected. By including the word *puṣṭi*, one should understand the inclusion of the one who is protected. Just as, due to the connection with cooking (*pāka*), the word *pakva* (cooked) implies the past tense, so too, what was previously stated as the Vaiśya’s name being "connected with wealth" should be seen here as being like the word *gupta* (protected). Examples include *Dhanagupta* or *Jñānagupta*. Or rather, according to the rule of the twice-born (*dvijāti*), the adoption of *śarman* and *varman* is prescribed for the names of the twice-born in the *Gṛhya-smṛtis*. Just as in the context of time, the word *datta* implies the inclusion of words like *ādi* (and so forth) in names, so it is here as well. And so he will say: "Whatever is desired and auspicious in the family" (MDh 2.34). But if this is so, does it not contradict this Smṛti by implying the inclusion of *datta* and others? If that is the case, why then is this technical rule meaningful: "When there is a conflict between two rules of equal force, there is an option"? Therefore, both are the intended meaning of the Smṛti, and because of their conflict, there is an option. Thus, the name of a Śūdra should be explained as being connected with his service (*preṣya*).

Having stated the names of men, this is now said regarding women: [their names] should be easy to pronounce, not harsh, clear in meaning, and captivating; they should be auspicious, end in a long vowel, and consist of words expressing a blessing. (2.33)

*Su-khodyam* means easy to pronounce and easy to utter. For example: *Sunāthā*, *Vasunāthā*, *Vasudā*, *Vasumatī*, *Yaśodā*, and so forth—these are easy to utter. *Kṣmā*, *Kṣoṇī*, *Vṛṣākapāyī*. *Akūrārtham* means not having a cruel meaning; as cruelty has been illustrated [previously]. *Sumālinī*, *Gandhamālinī*, *Pāpabhayaṅkarī*. *Vispaṣṭārtham* means whose meaning is clear and does not require explanation. *Rākā*, *Sinīvālī*, *Kuhūḥ*. *Manoharam* means pleasing to the ear. *Cārumatī*, *Candralekhā*, and so forth. But what is truly captivating is that which is [unclear syllable] and so on. *Maṅgalyam* means expressing an auspicious sense. For example: *Viśavdinī*, *Svastimatī*, *Puṇyodayā*. He will state the opposite [case] as established in the scriptures: "One should have a name derived from a constellation, a tree, or a river" (MDh 3.9). Alternatively, [names like] *Dāsī* or *Gaṇikā*. That name at the end of which there is a long vowel is called *dīrghavarṇāntam*. An example has been stated. The opposite, however, is as follows: according to custom (*yathācāra*), names such as *Prakṛtiśānti* and others are used. This is the consensus of the learned (*śiṣṭo vādaḥ*). That name in which there exists a designation containing a benediction is called *āśīrvādābhidhānavat*. Examples are: *Dhanadā*, *Yaśodā*, *Dharmadā*. The opposite, however, would be names like *Kṛṣṇā*, *Hrasvā*, *Dīrghā*, and so forth. Thus, these seven qualifiers have been stated as applicable qualifiers for the names of women.

Now, since the departure from the house (*niṣkramaṇa*) and the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*) would otherwise be subject to uncertainty—depending on the child’s capacity or the intention of the parents—the treatise begins by establishing a rule:
The departure from the house for the infant should be performed in the fourth month;
the first feeding of solid food should take place in the sixth month, or whenever an auspicious occasion is desired by the family. (2.34)

Since the complete procedure for the rites of departure (*niṣkrāmaṇa*) and the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*) has been prescribed in specialized treatises or the *Gṛhya-smṛtis*, their mention here—despite this work being a general *smṛti*—is intended as an auspicious benediction (*maṅgala*). This should be understood as a supplementary element throughout the entire section on sacraments (*saṃskāra*), both preceding and following them. For this very reason, names such as "Datta" and others are to be adopted; furthermore, family customs (*kuladharma*) that do not contradict the scriptures are established as valid.
"The tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākarma*) for all twice-born (*dvija*) classes is indeed a duty according to the law."
It should be performed in the first or the third year, as enjoined by the sacred revelation (śruti). || 2.35 ||

He states this for the sake of restriction regarding that which was previously established by implication: the *cūḍā-saṃskāra* and the *cūḍā-karman* are of the same nature as those prescribed in the *Gṛhya-śāstras*. That is not explained here for fear of excessive length. Furthermore, there is only one purpose for all these purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) when the entire rule of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) is not explained. And it has been stated in this regard that this is because it is a general *smṛti*. The difference in location is recorded according to specific lineages (*gotra*): the tuft of hair (*cūḍā*) is left on the right side for the Dakṣiṇas; on the left for the Bharadvājas; on both sides for the Kāśyapas; upwards for the Gālavas; and five tufts for the Aṅgirases. It is also said, "the Bhṛgus are like the Ṛddhas" (or "the Vṛddhas are among the Bhṛgus"). And the mention of the "twice-born" (*dvijāti*) is for the purpose of excluding the Śūdra. Thus, its time should be understood as unrestricted, as in the alternative: "in the first year or the third," which is an option depending on the child's capacity, or depending on the auspiciousness of the stars and planets, or depending on family custom (*kuladharma*). "It should be performed" is the injunction (*vidhi*), because it is impelled by the *Śruti* and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the *Śruti*. That indicative mark is known from the verse, "the boys like arrows" (RV 6.75.17), which shows that all *dharma*s of the *Smṛtis* originate from the indicative marks of the *Mantras* and *Brāhmaṇas*. [52]
One should perform the initiation ceremony for a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception;
for a Kṣatriya, in the eleventh year from conception; and for a Vaiśya, in the twelfth year from conception. (2.36)

For what purpose is this? This is undertaken so that for the twice-born, the calculation of the years for initiation (*upanayana*) shall begin from the year of conception, and not, as might occur in common worldly usage, from the time of birth.

The year that accompanies the pregnancy is designated by the word *garbha*. The eighth is that which completes eight. He whose pregnancy is the eighth is called *garbhāṣṭama*; this is the meaning of the compound. One should perform [the rite] in that year. What is it? It is the *upanayana* (initiation). Its etymology is as follows: that sacrament (*saṃskāra*) by which one is led (*nīyate*) into the presence of the teacher (*guru*), of the groups (*vrāta*), of the Brāhmaṇas, of the restraints and observances (*yama-niyama*), or of the deities—that is the *upanayana*. It is a *karaṇa*-kāraka (instrumental case). *Aupanāyanam* is derived from *upanayana*; the secondary suffix (*taddhita-pratyaya*) is used here in its own sense for the sake of metrical completion. In the *Gṛhya-sūtras*, however, being the eighth from conception is optional; therefore, it is specifically the eighth year. For he states an indicative mark (*liṅga*): "One initiates the Brāhmaṇa with the *gāyatrī* metre; the *gāyatrī* indeed has eight syllables; Agni is its deity. Therefore, the first alternative sacrament here is the *upanayana*. By using the term "Brāhmaṇa" [in the rule], he shows that Brāhmaṇahood does not arise from the sacraments of initiation and the rest, because that would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). What then? He will state later: "Among wives of all castes who are equal and whose wombs are unviolated... (*MDh* 10.5). Thus, it is logical that caste (*jāti*) is the basis for eligibility for the sacraments, and not Brāhmaṇahood resulting from the sacraments. Similarly, for a Kṣatriya it is the eleventh year from conception, with the *triṣṭubh* metre. For a Vaiśya it is the twelfth year from conception, with the *jagatī* metre. What is the subject under discussion? The author of the *Gṛhya-sūtras* says: "For all, the *upanayana* is indeed the *gāyatrī* by way of option."
The time for the obligatory initiation has been stated. Now the optional [initiation] is described: for a Brahmin desiring spiritual luster, the optional initiation is in the fifth year;
for a Kṣatriya seeking power, in the sixth; and for a Vaiśya desiring success in this world, in the eighth. (2.37)

The counting of years begins from conception (*garbha*). That splendor (*tejas*) of a Brāhmaṇa which arises from the excellence of study, knowledge, conduct, and the performance of duties is *brahmavarcasa*. One who desires that is a *brahmavarcasakāma*. Because there is no specific knowledge regarding the splendor of a child (*bālavarca*), this instruction is given by the father. At a distinguished time and place, through the application of the primary ritual act, visible strength (*bala*) is bound [to the person]. *Brahmavarcasa* has its cause in connection with qualities; and that is understood through the authority of the scripture (*śāstra*). As in: "One desiring a village [should sacrifice] with barley-gruel (*yavāgū*)," "one desiring strength with rice-grains (*taṇḍula*)," "one desiring sense-power with cow-dung (*gudgha*)," and "one desiring a variegated [result] with *mādira*. But the external treasury and army consist of the body—attained through excellence in the practice of weapons and missiles—and the ministers and other constituent elements (*prakṛti*). "One who desires that" is explained in the same way as before. "One seeking the effort of a Vaiśya" means one seeking the acquisition of wealth; that is the accumulation resulting from the success of agriculture and so forth. "One who desires that" is the explanation. Now, some Brāhmaṇas desire this initiation (*upanayana*) to be a *saṃskāra* (purificatory rite). Since after obtaining that [initiation], there is the study of the *praṇava*, *vyāhṛtis*, *sāvitrī*, and so forth—beginning with the Veda—and since the vows of studentship (*brahmacarya*) are distinct, the lying down [of the child] like a vow would also be for the sake of the Vedic *saṃskāra*. Others, however, say this is for the sake of the purification of the person (*puruṣasaṃskāra*) alone, [stating] "the vows and so forth. This is understood in the study of the sacrifice (*yajña*); likewise, Gautama places this among the purifications of the person. According to logic, it pertains to both in the two positions. We, however, say: in every respect, this is for the purification of the person alone. And thus, the Veda, having been purified by this [initiation], purifies the person. Since study is for the sake of the person, even though there is an interval, it is said to be for that purpose. And thus, the person, purified by it, becomes capable of studying the Veda. Just as a jar, through contact with fire, is qualified for [use] by examples and the like—even in the position that both are purified, there is no fault. It has been stated [that this applies] whether there is an interval or not.
