The Sāvitrī does not expire for a Brāhmaṇa until the sixteenth year, for a Kṣatriya until the twenty-second, and for a Vaiśya until the twenty-fourth. (2.38)

For what purpose is this desired? Why is it maintained that this [initiation] does not apply to these [classes] at any time other than during the period of the first aeon (*prāthamakalpika*)? This is the beginning of the inquiry. Is this prefix *ā* used in the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*) or in the sense of exclusion (*maryādā*)? And what is the distinction here? If it is in the sense of inclusion, then [the age limit] includes the sixteenth year from conception. If, however, it is in the sense of exclusion, then by excluding that [sixteenth year], the attainment of the double [age] for a Brāhmaṇa—due to following the *gāyatrī* metre—is accomplished in the sixteenth year; thus, the *sāvitrī* does not exceed that point. Initiation is called *sāvitrī* because it is the means for the recitation of the *sāvitrī*. Numerically, this [period] does not abandon that time; it declares [the person] fit for entitlement. Similarly, for the Kṣatriya, [the limit] reaches twenty-two, though it is not explicitly recited for fear of exceeding the metrical foot. However, its meaning is understood through the force of the context. Even regarding the statement "for the Vaiśya until the twenty-fourth," the repetition of the prefix *ā* is for the sake of completing the metrical foot.
Beyond this time, all three of these, if they remain uninitiated according to the proper season, become Vrātyas who have fallen from the Sāvitrī and are censured by the Āryas. (2.39)

Beyond this—beyond this initial period (*prāthamikakalpa*) and the subsequent period (*ānukalpika*)—all three of these, having remained uninitiated at the appropriate time, become fallen from the *Sāvitrī* due to the failure to undergo the *Sāvitrī*-consecration, that is, the initiation (*upanayana*). They do not exist as [members of] the social order by name; this is a designation of their status. And thus, for the sake of worldly convention, they become those who are censured by the distressed. Since this is so: "One should never, even in times of distress, [perform rites] with these who have not been purified according to the rule."
He should maintain connections with Brahmins through both spiritual and matrimonial ties.

One should perform [the rite] together with Brāhmaṇas, either through a Vedic (śrauta) or a traditional (smārta) expiation, or even through a connection with Brāhmaṇas; performing it thus, the mention of "Brāhmaṇas" is intended to include the relationship [of kinship]. The term "acceptance of gifts" (pratigraha) may also serve to indicate relationships such as birth and so forth.
The time for the initiation (upanayana) of Brāhmaṇas and the others has been stated. Now, this [section] is commenced in order to explain the rules regarding relationships, materials, and forms.
The skins of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, and the goat are for the religious student (brahmacārin).
They should wear, in due order, garments made of hemp, flax, and wool.

[44] That skins serve as upper garments (*uttarīya*) for students (*brahmacārin*) is understood from the *Gṛhya-śāstra*, even though there is no specific mention [of them]. And thus, by implication, the sequence of wearing [the garments]—namely, those made of hemp, linen, and wool—is to be understood as intended for the sake of what follows. Now, one might object: since this is established by the number [of garments], as it is stated in the *Gṛhya-smṛti* that "the garment of a Brāhmaṇa is made of hemp or linen," and since there is a difference in number, let it not be the case that all [garments] belong to all [classes]; therefore, the mention of the sequence is for the purpose of removing that doubt regarding the obligatory rule. How so?
The girdle of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of Muñja grass, triple-stranded, even, and smooth;
that of a Kṣatriya should be a bowstring made of Murvā fibers; and that of a Vaiśya should be made of hempen threads.

The term "made of muñja grass" is a qualification; "triple-stranded" means consisting of three strands that are equal and of uniform quality. "Smooth" means possessing the quality of being thin through rubbing. The mention of the "bowstring" (jyā) is for the purpose of qualifying the girdle of a Kṣatriya. And thus, the triple-stranding of the Brahmin’s girdle does not apply here due to contradiction; rather, it applies only to the Vaiśya, because there is no contradiction regarding the qualities of the hemp (balaja) fibers, and the possibility of [the girdle] being triple-stranded and so forth exists for him.
However, in the absence of muñja grass, it should be made from kuśa, aśmantaka, or balvaja grasses, triple-stranded with one, three, or five knots. (2.43)

[The mention of] the absence of *muñja* grass is either for the purpose of indicating that the other two [types of grass] are also to be understood as the means of grasping, or it is due to the elision of the word "etc. (*ādi*). In the absence of *muñja* and the others, there is an option based on their respective absences according to the sequence: "But in the absence of *muñja*, it should be made with *kuśa*, *aśmantaka*, and *balvaja*. In the phrase "with three-fold knots," the state of being three-fold (*trivṛttva*) is an attribute of the knots. However, regarding the single [girdle], the previously stated rule—"either with three or with five"—does not apply to the knots in the girdles of the various castes by virtue of the force of the statement according to the sequence. What then? It applies as an option to all of them. And this attribute, which is indicated as optional in the case of absences, should be understood to apply to the preceding ones as well.
The sacred thread of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of cotton, twisted upward and triple-stranded; that of a Kṣatriya should be made of hempen threads, and that of a Vaiśya of woolen threads. 2.44.

The term *upavīta* means that which is worn like the *yajñopavīta*. And so he will say: "when the right hand has been raised" (MDh 2.63). It is wound upwards, triple-folded, and wound to the right; it is sewn with three strands. This specific description of the Brāhmaṇa’s *upavīta* should be understood as applying without contradiction to the *upavītas* of the other castes as well.
"A Brāhmaṇa deserves staffs made of Bilva or Palāśa wood; a Kṣatriya, of Vaṭa or Khadira; and a Vaiśya, of Pīlu or Udumbara—this is the rule according to dharma. (2.45)

The meaning is "according to the treatises" (*śāstrataḥ*). The plural number is used because the term refers to the collection [of staffs]. However, for each individual caste (*varṇa*), there are two staffs, which are presented as alternatives (*vikalpena*) through secondary derivation (*taddhita*). Nor can it be argued that this refers to a *dvandva* compound where both members are primary, because such a construction would have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatvāt*). Just as there is a restriction regarding the material [of the staff], so too, according to the literal text, there would be two staffs for each caste. Here, the dual form is employed by following the rules of grammar (*chandaḥ*). How is this understood? From the *Gṛhya-smṛti*, traditional practice (*sadācāra*), and logical necessity (*sāmarthya*). There may be an option (*vikalpa*) based on other scriptural authorities. Thus, it should be seen that "darkness" (*tamaḥ*) and its absence refer respectively to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and the teacher (*ācārya*), and like the restrictive rule, this has an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭatva*). Even when carrying only one staff, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, in the subsequent injunctions regarding the qualities of the staff, the use of the singular number indicates an option.
The staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be made according to the measurement reaching to the hairline; that of a Kṣatriya should reach the forehead, and that of a Vaiśya should reach the nose. (2.46)

Regarding the rule for the fixed measurement of the staff: when the measurement is obtained by implication and its limit is not explicitly taught, the staff of a Kṣatriya should be understood by its capacity to reach as far as his forehead.
Furthermore, all those staves should be straight, without blemishes, pleasant to behold, not causing alarm to men, possessed of their bark, and not damaged by fire. (2.47)

Although the word "all" (sarva) follows from the quality of straightness (*ṛjutva*), it should be understood through the force of the context as qualifying the specific qualities of the staff, such as being free from flaws and so forth.
Having taken the desired staff and having approached the sun, he should circumambulate the fire to the right and go for alms according to the rule. (2.48)

This practice of begging alms is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), because it occurs within that context and because the initiate is required to beg only after having eaten; it is not for the purpose of livelihood. Therefore, having taken cooked or uncooked food, he should present it to the teacher according to the rule. Since this has been stated, the procedure for that is now being declared: "The best of the twice-born who has been initiated should go about begging his alms with the word *bhavat* at the beginning; a Kṣatriya, however, with the word *bhavat* in the middle; and a Vaiśya, with the word *bhavat* at the end. (2.49)

That which has the word *bhavati* preceding it is called *bhavatpūrva*; this is the meaning of the *bahuvrīhi* compound. Why is the term *caraṇa* (begging) used? It is because the request for alms (*bhikṣāprārthanā*) is understood by implication from the context. What is the grammatical characteristic? It is the form "dehi idam" (give this). At the time of its usage, the shortening of the vowel in the word *bhavati* is to be understood by the rule "ambārthanadyor hrasvaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.107). Furthermore, by the mention of the base form (*prakṛti*), the inclusion of the suffix is implied; the word *bhavat* is uttered without a suffix in accordance with the *anuṣṭubh* meter. And as long as one should beg with the word *bhavat* preceding it—whatever is for the sake of alms, the act of begging, is denoted by the word *bhikṣā*. Because it is for that purpose, the sentence requesting alms is also called *bhaikṣa*. That by which something exists in alms, or is for the sake of alms in terms of quality—that is what is meant. Thus, the *Gṛhyaśāstra* provides the instruction on its purpose: "A Brāhmaṇa should recite 'let him beg with the word *bhavat* preceding it. And since the rule for begging as part of the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) is stated in the passage "the best of the twice-born, having been initiated," it should be understood by implication as being universally applicable. By this, the usage of the word *bhavat* at the middle or end of the request "give alms" for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas is explained. Even though the male is the primary referent, one should beg by addressing a woman—whether present or absent—using the word *bhavati*, and not a man; thus, this instruction is intended for them alone. [56]
He should first beg for alms from his mother, or his sister, or his own maternal aunt—whichever of these would not treat him with contempt. (2.50)

And because of the fear of being refused or insulted, the instruction for a religious student (*brahmacārin*) to beg first from his mother and others is for the sake of prosperity; this is known from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the Veda, as they say: "He should beg from her. This [begging] is worldly. And for this very reason, it is inferred that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) if one is refused at the first instance of begging.
But having collected that food, as much as required, without guile, he should announce it to his teacher and eat, having sipped water, facing the east, and being pure. (2.51)

Regarding the phrase “as much as needed” (*yāvadartham*): this refers to the measure of satiety; one should refuse food that exceeds that by means of deceit (*māyā*), which is to say, by abandoning any hypocrisy (*upadhā*) such as saying, “I am ill,” or “I am hungry,” and so forth, when inferior food is being offered. This is for the sake of what follows. Having offered it to the teacher without deceit, one should eat after sipping water (*ācamya*). The instruction to hide the alms from the sight of others is due to the fear of violating the rule of facing east (*prāṅmukha*). However, the offering to the teacher is for the purpose of consecration (*saṃskāra*) and not for the purpose of giving, since that [offering] is for the sake of subsistence (*vṛtti*). Thus, the text shows this: “Having offered to the teacher, one should eat”; the mention of “after sipping water” is a restatement of the rule to be stated later. Furthermore, because of the statement, “The restriction of facing east is for the sake of merit (*dharma*); otherwise, he may eat with permission,” there is the giving of alms at the teacher’s will according to another Smṛti. And in the case where the teacher himself receives the alms, they should be begged again, because of the statement “as much as needed. It is true that this is so; however, if eating with permission were considered to have only a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), then in the absence of that [permission], it would have no invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Therefore, nothing [would follow]. Thus, the restriction of facing east is stated for the sake of merit when connected with desire (*kāma*); that is optional (*kāmya*).
One who eats facing the east gains long life; facing the south, one gains fame;
facing the west, one gains prosperity; and facing the north, one eats the truth.

Some maintain that the mere act of bathing is purposeless, since this injunction is intended for one who desires a specific result (*kāmya*). Others, however, hold that because it is prescribed in a manner that does not constitute a formal instruction, it is merely a praise of the general direction for the purpose of prohibiting [eating] during the intervening times. Furthermore, if eating alms-food were a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the rite, one would have stated, "One should eat this alms-food facing east," using a different verbal form such as *bhuṅkte*. But he did not say so; therefore, I have sought to understand that this is not a subordinate part of eating alms-food. From this, it is understood that this injunction is universal. For it has been said: "Having offered it to the teacher, one should eat" (MDh 2.51); thus, that injunction is being taught.
Having sipped water, a twice-born man should always eat his food with a concentrated mind;
and having eaten, he should sip water properly and touch the cavities of the head with water.

The mention of "twice-born" (*dvija*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of those already under discussion, used here for the sake of completing the meter. The mention of "constantly" (*nitya*) indicates that this is a duty of the caste (*jāti-dharma*) that follows one through all conditions of life. Others, however, state that the purpose of the mention of "twice-born" is as follows, and they interpret the mention of "constantly" as being for the sake of showing respect. Still others, however, consider this mention of "composed" (*samāhita*) to be redundant; it shows that one who is eating must exercise restraint over the senses, or else abandon the unwholesome qualities of base men such as anger. Thus, this state of mental clarity (*prasāda*) is prescribed for him while he is eating. [57]
One should always honor food and eat it without disparaging it;
upon seeing it, one should rejoice, be gracious, and always welcome it. (2.54)
Regarding food, because it is the specific deity [of this rite], it is not for the sake of worship or for the sake of life-force. Thus says the scripture:
"The twice-born who, knowing the scriptures, eats while biting me for the sake of his life-force, meditating on my being for that purpose—he always worships me."

Thus it is heard that food indeed spoke thus. One should eat this today without disparaging it with speech or mind; and even while eating, one should take pleasure in the mind upon seeing those [foods], thinking, "These [are good]. Having understood that food is the cause of sustenance and the destroyer of the suffering of hunger, one should be contented. The word "having seen" carries over [from the previous context]. Furthermore, even when anger arises for other reasons, one should welcome and praise it by means of renunciation, [regarding] the censurable food as a narrative concerning the hosts of beings and the mountains. And because these are grasped as constant, they too are the very duties of her [the woman’s] caste; this is the praise for the sake of its performance.
For food that is always honored bestows strength and vigor;
but when eaten unhonored, it destroys both of these. (2.55)

The word "honored" (*pūjita*) is used for the sake of indicating the others as well—such as "not contemptuous" (*akutsita*) and so forth—by virtue of their association. Thus, when those [qualities] have been established, the praise by way of their fruit applies without distinction in both ways, due to the nature of the sentence. For the student (*brahmacārin*), who has obtained [food] from one who is eating, that which is [already] reached is prohibited:
"He shall not give his leavings to anyone, nor shall he eat between [meals]. He shall not overeat, nor shall he go anywhere while still impure from food. (2.56)

Since there is a prohibition stating, "One should not give the leavings of anyone," this injunction being undertaken serves to provide a specific qualification. And thus, for the sake of not contradicting the Vedic revelation, the author will state a prohibition against giving non-leavings to a Śūdra: "He should not eat this, nor likewise in between. Because the matter is drawn out by implication, one who is not yet satiated might sometimes proceed even during that interval; therefore, it is commenced in order to prohibit that. He who says this [argues] that because of the rule regarding eating in the evening and morning, this [interval-eating] must be stated as a purposeful restriction. What, then, is its scope? It is not the case that leavings are inedible even when they have not lost their measure. Or rather, by the prohibition against [eating] in between, it brings about the eating of alms even in the evening for the religious student (*brahmacārin*). Is that not already established? It is not established because of the absence of a scriptural rule. Since eating—even if for the sake of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*)—is meaningful according to the scripture, and since there is a visible purpose, the statement "nor should he go anywhere with leavings" is a deprecatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended to censure what is prohibited as a duty of the social classes (*varṇadharma*). This is for the purpose of creating aversion.
Excessive eating is detrimental to health, detrimental to longevity, and detrimental to rebirth in heaven;
it is non-meritorious and loathed by the world; therefore, one should avoid it. (2.57)

When there is a prohibition regarding "bhūḥ," the gravity of eating is understood through an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) of censure. Because it is a cause of ill health, over-eating is non-beneficial for longevity and non-conducive to heaven due to its lack of merit. How so? Because it involves the transgression of the rules of merit and, due to incapacity in matters such as ritual purity, results in the abandonment of those rules. Thus, even for those prohibited acts taught in conjunction with over-eating, an explanatory eulogy of censure is to be inferred, since this [text] is intended for the purpose of showing extremes. Now, an instruction regarding the sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*) based on caste is provided for students (*brahmacārin*), in order to prevent them from engaging in [prohibited] activities.
A Brahmin should always perform the ritual sipping (upaspṛśet) using the Brāhma tīrtha;
or he may use the Kāya or Traidaśika tīrthas, but never the Pitrya. (2.58)

The phrase "by means of the Brāhma [tīrtha]" is a praise of the *tīrtha* by way of its connection with a specific deity. Because of the context of "for the sake of honoring others" (*paropacārārthān*), this rule regarding the *tīrtha* belongs specifically to that [Brahmin]; and by the inclusion of the word "regularly" (*nitya*), it is inferred that the same ritual procedure applies to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas as well. Others also explain that the mention of the twice-born is for the purpose of indicating the [other] castes (*varṇa*) due to the context. Furthermore, the inclusion of the word "regularly" is not intended to mean that the Prājāpatya rite is to be performed as a duty of the castes; rather, the Traidaśika is divine (*daiva*), and these two are to be understood as optional alternatives to the Brāhma. The prohibition of the Pitrya is a restatement of what is constant (*nityānuvāda*), which serves as their defining characteristic.
They declare that the Brāhma tīrtha is at the base of the thumb;
the Kāya is at the base of the fingers, the Daiva at their tips, and the Pitrya below those two. (2.59)

This is the instruction regarding the characteristics of the *tīrtha* for the purpose of sipping water (*ācamana*). Thus, when this occasion arises, one should sip water three times; first, having wiped [the mouth] twice, one should then wipe the face.
One should touch the cavities with water, as well as the self and the head. (2.60)

This verse has the purpose of explaining the rule for sipping water (*ācamana*). Now, since the term "Self" (*ātman*) is established through its own inherent nature, the metaphorical designation of the "Self" (*ātmopacāra*) in the Brāhmaṇa discourses is intended to establish its specific qualities; it is for this reason that the following is taught:

"One who knows the Dharma and desires purity should always sip water with [water] that is neither hot nor frothy, using the proper part of the hand (*tīrtha*), in a secluded place, facing either the east or the north. (2.61)

"Not hot" (*anuṣṇābhiḥ*) means not heated; they are said to be unboiled, not warmed by the sun, such as in the case of naturally warm winds or water, according to another Smṛti. Śaṅkha and Likhita said: "If that [water] is unmixed, not hot, and without foam. This is also established by the force of the instruction itself; otherwise, this would be impossible in cases such as approaching women during their courses or in the context of ascetic heat and water. The prohibition regarding these two—[the rule on] "by the *tīrtha*" and "desiring purity"—is for the purpose of a collective reference (*gaṇārtha*). One who desires purity is one who desires self-purification (*ātmasaṃskāra*); thus it is stated that there is no religious merit (*dharma*) from the mere act of sipping water (*upasparśana*). What then? It is merely a self-purification of an unseen nature (*adṛṣṭa*), just as with other ritual groups. When the self has been purified through the performance of rituals involving clarified butter and so forth, religious merit necessarily arises from the performance of subsequent rites due to that capacity; therefore, the rule "one should sip water" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of a previous injunction regarding the duty of the castes (*varṇadharma*), intended to connect it with a secondary injunction (*guṇavidhi*), just as in the cases "he offers with curds" or "he offers with milk," which involve a specific restriction. The phrase "facing east or north" is for the sake of providing an option. Regarding the rule "one should sip three times," even from the word "water" (*apaḥ*), the remainder [of the rule] implies that the water for sipping is not optional; it is desired as the cause of purification for the sense organs and so forth. This measurement is the cause of their purification individually. And that is established without a separate treatise on purification. For this purpose, this [text] is commenced.
A Brahmin is purified by water that reaches the heart; a Kṣatriya, by water reaching the throat; a Vaiśya, by water that has been sipped; and a Śūdra, by water merely touched at the extremity. 2.62.

The specification of the heart and other parts as limits is for the purpose of indicating the quantity of water for sipping (*ācamana*). Thus, even though it was not previously established, the connection of the defects [of insufficient water] should be understood through the force of the sequence. Regarding the phrase "by a Śūdra with [water] touched at the end," this does not mean by the hand; rather, it means by the tongue and lips. This is because, based on the force of the statement that the water for sipping enters the interior of the heart and so forth for Brāhmaṇas and others by that [tongue/lips] alone, and because of the scriptural injunction "by [water] touched at the end," its consumption is also inferred for him. Since the characteristics prescribed according to the division of castes have been stated for the twice-born in general, but not for their specific arrangements, he begins this [section] for that purpose.
When the right hand is raised, a twice-born man is called *upavītin*;
when it is on the left, he is *prācīnāvītī*; and when it hangs from the neck, he is *nivītī*. (2.63)

The incidental mention of the *nivīta* is for the purpose of indicating the other two modes of wearing the garment. How so? When the cord hanging from the neck is raised up through the middle of the right arm, that mode of wearing—characterized by the holding of the hand—is designated as the *upavīta*; it is the name for that specific arrangement. One who possesses this [arrangement] is called *upavītī*. When the word *upavīta* refers to the cord itself rather than the arrangement—as in the passage, "the *upavīta* and the water-pot" (MDh 2.64)—then, according to this principle, the suffix *a* here functions in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), either through the elision of the *matup* suffix or by association with the term. Thus, by virtue of its quality, the mere cord is called *upavīta*, just like the *upavīta* arrangement; it acquires a different designation when it serves as a requisite for sacrifice. For the sake of sacrifice, it is the *yajñopavīta*. These [two modes] apply to rites for the gods. By this same logic, the *prācīnāvītī* is explained. Regarding rites for the ancestors, one is *nivītī*, and in sorcery, one is likewise [so designated]. Thus, the wearing of the girdle and other items has been taught. And so, even if these are lost, they are not considered non-existent, since this [text] is commenced to prohibit their loss and to prescribe the rules for their restoration.
Having thrown the girdle, the skin, the staff, the sacrificial thread, and the water-pot into the water when they are worn out, he should take others with the appropriate mantras. (2.64)

I shall describe the ritual acquisition (*grahaṇa*) of these items according to their respective possibilities. When only those two [the skin and the girdle] are acquired, the essence of the mantra is contained within them; even though there may be specific injunctions regarding the skin (*ajina*) and the sacrificial thread (*upavīta*), it is taught that the destruction of the girdle (*mekhalā*) and the other items occurs along with their constituent parts. In the case of destruction without remainder (*niranvayavināśa*), because the purpose is lost, both would be useless in their respective places. Since the rules for disposal (*pratipatti*) are taught together with the scriptural acquisitions of the girdle, skin, staff, and sacrificial thread, the application of the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*)—both its acquisition and its maintenance—is also to be understood solely from scripture. It is not determined by mere worldly purpose, as there is no specific reason [for it otherwise]; and thus there is the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Vyāsa. [The following section is unclear.]

"One who is unskilled in ritual ablutions obtains fortune; there is no doubt in this. Furthermore, we do not examine [this further]. Regarding the rule, "And a water-pot with water" (MDh 4.36), for one who has performed the initiation (*upanayana*) and is observing the Vedic vows, this occurs after the time of the ceremonial bath (*snāna*).
The tonsure of the hair (*keśānta*) is ordained for a Brāhmaṇa in the sixteenth year;
for a member of the royal caste (*rājanyabandhu*), in the twenty-second; and for a Vaiśya, two years beyond that. (2.65)

The *keśānta* is a Smṛti rite; its refinement (*saṃskāra*), which is slightly different from the *cūḍākaraṇa* and other rites, has been taught by the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras. And that [rite] is appropriate at this time for one who has been a student of a single Veda and has bathed after his vow (*vratasnāta*). As for the rule "for as long as [the Veda] is being mastered," this applies only to those students who are intelligent, not to others; nor can it be said that this [rite] does not exist for others because of its obligatory nature (*nityatva*). By this logic, the end of the sacraments (*saṃskārānta*) must necessarily occur even for these students after their formal return home (*samāvartana*), though its specific timing should be understood as something to be determined. However, for those for whom this [rite] does not exist at all, there would be a contradiction with other Smṛtis; thus, these are the forty sacraments. Regarding the statement, "prior to the cutting of the umbilical cord for a male" (MDh 2.29), the mention of "male" is stated for the purpose of excluding females and neuters. And so, since women would otherwise have no entitlement to the sacraments such as the birth-rite (*jātakarma*) and others, this [text] is commenced for the sake of granting them that entitlement.
This entire series of rites for women must be performed without omission, for the sake of purifying the body at the proper time and in the proper order. (2.66)

Since the birth-rites (*jātakarman*) and so forth follow a temporal sequence for a male, this same [sequence] should be understood to apply to females as well, though it is devoid of mantras. By this, the following is demonstrated: it is not the case that both the mantra and the ritual action together possess the capacity for consecration (*saṃskāra*). Rather, by virtue of the authority of the instruction, even the mere sequence (*āvṛt*) alone is applicable to females without mantras. However, there is no entitlement at all for a neuter. This is because of the statement: "This sequence for women should be performed without mantras until they reach sixteen years of age. Since, based on this, one might conclude—just as with the birth-rites and so forth—that those below the [age limit] are entitled to the rite without mantras, that [conclusion] is here prohibited.

For women, the marriage rite is considered equivalent to the initiation ceremony; service to the husband is their residence with the teacher, household duties are their sacred fire-maintenance, and [the care of] the domestic fire is their ritual obligation. (2.67)

The very rite of marriage for women should be regarded as their *upanayana* (initiation), just as it is for men. Thus, their initiation is without mantras; their service to the husband is equivalent to service to the household, and they possess a form of worship. They are to be understood as equal to those who follow the duties of a *brahmacārin* through service to the teacher and the performance of fire-rites. In this way, they are considered "equal" (*samāḥ*). These women are not excluded from the connection with the initiation involving mantras. And when that [initiation] has been performed, even though there is an absence of the other vows and so forth associated with initiation, the absence of formal Vedic study is established. Furthermore, in stating that marriage is equal to initiation, the further purpose is that, like men, women also have freedom of action, speech, and eating prior to marriage, while after this [marriage], they are subject to restraints and observances (*yama-niyama*). This is for the sake of the concluding summary and for the purpose of introducing the application of ritual action (*karmayoga*). Now, this [following] is stated regarding the *brahmacārin*.
This has been declared the sacred rite of initiation for the twice-born, which manifests their true birth; now learn the application of their duties.

The inclusion of the term *aupanāyika* is for the sake of illustration; or rather, there is an elision of the word *ādi* here. Thus, *aupanāyanika-ādiḥ* becomes *aupanāyanikaḥ*. The word *ādi* is intended to indicate that class [of persons]. Furthermore, this word is a qualifier used in the sense of "one who has been initiated. He is the one who manifests the birth, the motherly folk, or the one who bestows capacity upon the Vedic birth (*brahmajanman*). For this reason, he is called "meritorious" (*puṇya*). However, the application of ritual action (*karmayoga*) belongs to the teacher, the student, or both; as he will state later: "For one who has performed the initiation (*upanayana*), the instruction in the vows (*vratādeśana*) is prescribed" (MDh 2.173).

And thus, immediately after the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), during the instruction on the vows (*vratādeśa*), this is commenced: "Having initiated the pupil, the teacher should first instruct him in purity (*śauca*), as well as in proper conduct (*ācāra*), the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), and the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*). (2.69)

For one who has mastered cleanliness, conduct, the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), and the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) is capable of Vedic study; it is for that purpose that he is qualified for the observances (*vrata*) upon the instruction [of the teacher], and not immediately after the initiation (*upanayana*). This statement is appropriate for the sake of showing respect, and this repeated mention of respect is justified because cleanliness is a constant accompaniment. Indeed, the fire-rituals and other duties occur only at their own proper times. Furthermore, when the praise of the subject at hand is possible, it is not right to assume something unprecedented (*apūrva*); for in that way, the subject at hand would be fulfilled—this is the instruction of the Guru. And thus, the student must be taught by the Guru according to the rule and not by anyone else; and being a religious student (*brahmacārī*) who has mastered cleanliness, conduct, the fire-ritual, and the twilight worship, and being qualified for Vedic study because he has undertaken the Vedic observances as instructed, [he proceeds].

But when about to be taught, having sipped water according to the scriptures, facing north, with palms joined in the *brahmāñjali* gesture, wearing light clothing, and with senses subdued, he should be instructed. (2.70)

One who has not been instructed in the various Vedic vows [is not qualified]. For he will state: "For one whose initiation (*upanayana*) has been performed, the instruction in the vows is prescribed" (MDh 2.173), and "having sipped water according to the scriptures"—this is a restatement (*anuvāda*), because it is for the sake of the primary act. The instructions from the teacher regarding facing north, forming the *brahmāñjali* gesture, wearing light clothing, and having the senses subdued are the ancillaries (*aṅga*) of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). This is another rule concerning the approach to the teacher (*upasadana*) and the acquisition of the Veda (*brahmagrahaṇa*):
"At the beginning and at the end of Vedic study, the feet of the teacher should always be clasped."
Having joined the two hands together, one should study; for that is known as the *brahmāñjali*.

The meaning of the subsequent verse is intended to explain the ritual salutation to Brahman (*brahmāñjali*) mentioned in the preceding verse. Because this act is extraordinary, it is appropriate that it be characterized by scriptural injunction. It has been stated that one should clasp the feet at the beginning and conclusion of the study of the Veda; now, this specific rule regarding the teacher is being declared: "The clasping of the feet must always be performed with crossed hands:
the left [foot] should be touched with the left [hand], and the right [foot] with the right [hand]. (2.72)

[62] Here, the inclusion of the word "always" (sadā) is for the sake of the rules regarding the recitation of the Veda; furthermore, for one who has set out to study, the permission granted by the teacher is stated as being subordinate to the rules when in the presence of the teacher, since it is an auxiliary to the private recitation (*svādhyāya*).
However, he should always, without weariness, attend upon the teacher while the latter is engaged in teaching.
One should say, "Please, recite!
When permitted by him, one should say, "May you recite.
And one should conclude with, "May there be a pause. (2.73)

When [the teacher] says [this], then he should cease from his study. And in this way, even while running after you, he must not interrupt the study of the Veda for the sake of attending upon the teacher. Having said, "Teach me," and having ceased [his study], and having himself performed the ritual approach (*upasada*) and salutation (*abhivādana*), he—being permitted by the teacher—is instructed to utter the syllable *oṃ*. "One should always place the *praṇava* of Brahman at the beginning and at the end.
What is not preceded by *oṃ* flows away; what is [not followed] by it at the end falls apart. (2.74)

The inclusion of the phrase "even after the period of studentship" (brahmacaryottarakālam api) implies that [the rules apply] at all times; this is for the purpose of prescribing the duties of study as ordained. This [verse] is commenced for the purpose of prescribing the proper time for the syllable *oṃ*.

"Sitting upon grass-blades with their tips pointing eastward, purified by means of purifiers (*pavitra*), and cleansed by three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), one then becomes worthy of the syllable *oṃ*. (2.75)

The word *kūla* is a synonym for *graha* (the tip). Those whose *kūlas* are directed toward the east are called *prākkūlāḥ*, meaning those with their tips facing east. What, then, are they? They are *darbha* grasses. How is this known? From another *smṛti* text. For in this very context, Gautama, having stated, "Touching the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) with *darbhas*" (GDh 1.54), says, "And the seat upon those with tips facing east" (GDh 1.56). By virtue of the context, these [tips] must be *darbha* grasses. Such is the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭas*). Therefore, seated upon them and purified by the purifying *darbhas* themselves—which touch the exterior of the heart—Gautama likewise says, "Touching the vital breaths with *darbhas*. Since sprinkling and other such acts are here impossible by their very nature, [the text specifies] "purified by three breath-restraints" (*prāṇāyāmaiḥ*); the mention of "three" is for the purpose of excluding one or two, and not more than that, because of the inherent capacity [of the rite]. Immediately after that, one is entitled to perform the utterance of the syllable *oṃ*, which has been prescribed; the sequence of performing these duties is established precisely from the textual recitation. This is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) to the injunction: "One should make the *praṇava* of the Veda" (MDh 2.74).
Prajāpati milked from the three Vedas the syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m*, as well as the words *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*. (2.76)
It was not merely the syllable *oṃ* and the *vyāhṛtis*. What else?
From the three Vedas alone, he milked out one quarter from each;
[63] that which is "Tat" is the foot of this Sāvitrī verse, and Prajāpati Parameṣṭhin [milked it]. 2.77.

Since it should be understood in this way—that this triad known as the *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *sāvitrī* constitutes the extracted essence—therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should utter the *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *sāvitrī* at the beginning of his study and at all times at its conclusion. Thus, the mention of the *praṇava* is for the sake of illustration; or else, there is an elision of the word "beginning" (*ādi*). This being so, the previous verse [is explained]: "Reciting this syllable and this [Sāvitrī] preceded by the *vyāhṛtis*, a Brāhmaṇa who knows the Vedas becomes endowed with the merit of the Vedas during the two twilights. (2.78)

This is a restatement of the *saṃdhyopāsana* (twilight worship) that is about to be described, intended as a praise for the previously established rule. As it has been said: "A Brahmin who knows the Veda is endowed with the merit of the Veda. This refers to the extraction of the essence of the three Vedas. He who knows this very [essence] is here called a "knower of the Veda," by virtue of the context. Regarding the phrase "is endowed with the merit of the Veda": through the study of the three Vedas, he is joined with the merit of the Veda—this is what is meant. And thus, this is not an original injunction (*vidhi*) for *saṃdhyopāsana*. For if it were, there would be an obstruction to the subject matter at hand; moreover, introducing a topic outside of its proper context is not appropriate because it would obstruct the context. That which shares the same characteristics will be explained further below, and it is stated again precisely because of the recollection of that [previous rule].
But by practicing this triad externally a thousand times,
a twice-born man is released from even great sin within a month, just as a snake is freed from its skin.

This restatement of expiation outside of the aforementioned time for practice is intended solely as a praise for the rule under discussion. And because that has already been stated, this is neither a praise for the performance of the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*) outside [of their proper time], nor is it a rule for expiation, since that is not the subject matter of the context. This is another praise:
"Deprived of this worship and of his own ritual action at the proper time, one born of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya castes incurs reproach among the virtuous. (2.80)

One who is devoid of the Sāvitrī—that is, one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*) and for whom the ritual instruction of the vows (*vratādeśana*) was not performed at the proper time—though being a twice-born (*dvijāti*), incurs reproach among the virtuous. Alternatively, since the Sāvitrī is an integral part of Vedic study (*adhyayana*), this [person], being destitute of it, is said to be "destitute of study," according to the context. The rest is the same. This is a praise of the triad in another manner; and this is as before. Another [verse]:
"The three imperishable Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*) preceded by the syllable *Oṃ*, and the Sāvitrī consisting of three feet, should be known as the mouth of Brahman. (2.81)

In another way, this too is merely a supplement to what precedes it, and not a supplement to the *saṃdhyopāsana* under discussion. "The mouth of Brahman" is the gateway for the acquisition of the Vedas. And so he will state later:
"Knowing this, the learned daily practice the essence of the threefold Veda; having first studied that [the *Purāṇas*, etc. in sequence, they afterwards study the Veda" (MDh 4.125).

Alternatively, "mukhya" refers to the leading breath (*prāṇa*). It is called "mouth" (*mukha*) because it is like a mouth; this is an elided simile (*luptopamā*). What is the purpose of the comparison? It is purity, excellence, or preeminence. And this is another greatness of the one authorized for the performance of the recitation (*japa*):
[64] "He who studies this day after day for three years without weariness..."
Becoming like the wind and possessing the form of space, he attains the supreme Brahman.

Having established [the subject] through the statement of the actual fact (*bhūtārthavāda*) that he has become like the wind, there follows a praise of the topic at hand by way of a restatement of the optional injunction (*kāmyavidhi*). Thus, he recites the *Sāvitrī* together with the *Vyāhṛtis* and the *Praṇava*. For three years—or even for a long time prior—this very [mantra] is taught as a prescription for the fruit of its recitation (*japa-stuti-phala-vidhāna*) by means of a commendatory statement of results (*phalārthavāda*), namely: "He attains the supreme Brahman. By this, his dissolution (*apya-ya*) into the Supreme Brahman is declared because of his identity with its nature; yet, like the Supreme Self, the enjoyment of a body occurs through the possession of all powers according to his previous intention. And this is appropriate through the ritual act of reciting the *Praṇava* and so forth, since this greatness of yours is such.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the highest austerity;
there is nothing superior to the Sāvitrī; and truth excels silence. (2.83)

The *svara* (vowel) alone is the *akṣara* (syllable), as well as that which consists of consonants (*vyañjana*). Because this is a collection of vowels and consonants, the *praṇava*, consisting of a single syllable, is designated here. It is the Supreme Brahman because it is extracted from the Brahman characterized by the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas—which share the same genus as its creator—and because it is the Supreme Brahman and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). Thus says Brahmānandi: "‘Om’ is the Self; for those of evil deeds, it serves as their goal. This is inferior to *prāṇāyāma* (breath control). It is a praise of the three prescribed *prāṇāyāmas* or a praise of the *Oṃkāra* compared to austerities such as the *Cāndrāyaṇa*. [The phrase] *raṃ dṛśonam* (? [refers to] this *Oṃkāra*; it has been stated that it ought to be performed by means of these three *prāṇāyāmas*. "There is nothing higher than the *Sāvitrī*"—this refers to the *Brahman* to be recited, such as the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn. And so says the Śruti: "Just as the *Gāyatrī*—which is the extraction of the three Vedas—is exhausted in its course through that which is called the *nicchandas* (?), [so too is this]. This is stated as an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) to serve as an illustration for all cases, just as it is said: "Truth is superior to silence. The *praṇava* and others are also [superior] to their own kind. But how is truth superior to silence? For one who observes silence, there is no transgression (*pratyavāya*), whereas from speaking the truth, there is no possibility of spiritual advancement (*abhyudaya*). In the case of truth, however, there is neither that [transgression] nor [the lack of] advancement; rather, both [advancement and the absence of transgression] necessarily occur due to the force of scriptural injunction. If this is so, then the praise of the other [silence] would be useless. It is not improper, however, because it does not contradict perceived reality. In that case, in silence there is restraint in every respect, whereas in truth there is restraint in only one part. From partial restraint, there must be total restraint, so that the great effort of the scripture may be meaningful. Thus, since there is no contradiction with perceived reality, the production of a eulogy is logical for what is appropriate. Alternatively, from this very [statement], the superiority of truthful speech over silence is established by the scripture; the word "atha" (now/then) indicates its [truth's] preeminence. When the *Oṃkāra* and *Sāvitrī* are mentioned, the mention of the *Vyāhṛtis* should be understood, due to their association. Just as elsewhere, in the passage "he who studies this day after day" (MDh 2.82), the mention of the *Sāvitrī* implies the inclusion of the *praṇava* and *Vyāhṛtis*, so it is here as well. Or rather, this is not an illustration at all; what then? It is a eulogy of the *Vyāhṛtis*, like the *praṇava* and others. How so? In another Smṛti, the *Vyāhṛtis* beginning with *bhūr* are taught together with Truth and the *Vyāhṛtis*. This being the case, by virtue of that association, the mention of them by that [demonstrative] pronoun should be understood even in terms of their qualities, as is common in the world. And thus says Gautama: "The five *Vyāhṛtis* preceded by *Oṃ* and ending with Truth. This [objection] is incorrect; for this very [interpretation] must be accepted due to the force of establishing the association with the eulogy of the *praṇava* and others. Furthermore, this greatness of the fruit of this act of recitation is justified by the fact that—
All Vedic rites of offering oblations and chanting perish;
but the Imperishable (akṣara) should be known as the imperishable, as Brahman itself, and as Prajāpati.

Because the qualification for that [state] is difficult to attain, it is said that these [merits] flow away (*kṣaranti*). Thus says the treatise on qualification: "It belongs to the sacrificer and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); among the priests, the one who is most inwardly restrained, who acts rightly, whose speech is [controlled], who is neither deficient-limbed nor has an extra limb, who is not excessively white—such a person is to be sacrificed for. It is explained by three qualities: [the horse, the chariot, and the merits]. The learned one sacrifices; the learned one sacrifices—thus one should observe. These [merits] flow away. And here the proof is: "When the material cause is exhausted, that which was produced from it perishes first, as is seen in the world. Likewise, the *Brāhmaṇa* says: "He who performs the sacrifice once, he falls; he who performs it twice, he falls. [Objection: But isn't there also consciousness (*caitanya*) there? [In the passage] "He falls from that world who is devoted to women," this should be understood as being for the sake of praise, with the intent of illustrating the excellence of the fruit of action. How is this known? From the statement regarding the falling of those who sacrifice once or twice, and because of the exhaustion of what has been performed, as is observed. Furthermore, it shows: "These stars are indeed the lights of good deeds; they are brought low when merit is exhausted. And it is not only for one who has performed mere action. What then? Even for one who practices the combination of knowledge and action, the exhaustion is the same, because the means of knowledge are equal, as in the case of the single syllable (*ekākṣara*). The triad is to be known as the imperishable (*akṣara*), because it is the sole means to the Self. Since even for the ignorant there is qualification through recitation (*japa*), and since Prajāpati is Brahman characterized as the ultimate reality, and because He is designated by that name, therefore its recitation should be constant; it is enjoined as having an immediate fruit. Nor should this be called unutterable due to the equality of faults in its causal nature. Therefore, by censuring ritual actions, the act of recitation—which is the means for the three categories of things qualified—is praised, according to the nature of the sentence, as is common in the world. Otherwise, for those who accept the authority exactly as heard, there would be contradiction with the scripture and with logical reasoning. And those two are not desired. Therefore, this is the meaning: since this is so, therefore... *(Note: The final sentence is left incomplete in the source text.)*
The sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) is ten times superior to the ritual sacrifice (vidhiyajña);
the whispered recitation (upāṃśu) is a hundredfold more effective, and the mental recitation (mānasa) is declared to be a thousandfold.

The *vidhi-yajña* (prescribed ritual sacrifice), such as the *jyotiṣṭoma* and others, was authorized in the preceding verse as a *karma-yajña* (action-sacrifice). Therefore, the *japa-yajña* (recitation-sacrifice) beginning with the syllable *Oṃ* is ten times superior to that. For in this case, there is no violence characterized by weapons, nor is there any characteristic of the meaning of the term "prescribed ritual" (*vidhi-yajña*), nor is there the defect mentioned in the previous verse regarding the deficiency of means (*sādhana-vaiṣamya*) and so forth; it is for these reasons that its superiority exists. Even compared to that audible recitation (*śrāvya*), the whispered recitation (*upāṃśu-japa*) is superior. And what is that like? It is that which another person does not hear. That very recitation is the prior duty (*dharma*), which consists in the restraint of the self (*ātma-nigraha*). Compared even to this, the mental recitation (*mānasa*) is a thousandfold superior, due to the excellence of mental restraint and because of the internal application of those qualities; furthermore, a distinction in the fruit arises from a distinction in effort, as is inferable from the authority of the scriptures, just as in the case of worldly and Vedic matters. This being so, just as a particular action is postulated by implication through the force of context despite bypassing the immediate topic, so too the two qualities of whispered and mental recitation should be understood as the common characteristics (*dharma*) of all recitation. However, the specific injunction for that [mental recitation] is intended to subsist upon the context of praise (*stuti-prakaraṇa*). Alternatively, its purpose may be to provide a counter-example for the praise of the subject at hand, or for the sake of an illustration. Or rather, its purpose is precisely the injunction of the two qualities of whispered and mental recitation, and because of the context of that [injunction], this is an extreme praise of the act of recitation.
The four types of cooked sacrifices (pākayajña), together with the ritual sacrifices (vidhiyajña), are all not worth even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña). || 2.86 ||

This entire passage, though appearing to be a censure of Śrauta and Smārta rites, is actually a praise intended to encourage the study and performance of the Vedas; it is an "exaggerated praise" (*ati-stuti*) due to the inherent nature of the statement. Since there is no contradiction here—just as in the case of worldly and Vedic matters—the Smṛti scripture is authoritative. And this being so, with reference to the two qualities of the whispered and mental [recitation], it is said:
"A Brāhmaṇa may achieve perfection through muttered recitation alone; of this there is no doubt. He may perform other rites or not; he who is friendly [to all] is called a Brāhmaṇa. (2.87)

One may indeed attain perfection through recitation alone, never through ritual acts. This praise of recitation occurs precisely because of the context of abandoning the rites prescribed by the *Śruti* and the *Smṛti*. This being so, one should perform it according to one’s desire. Why [perform] anything other than recitation? What is that [other thing], and why should one not perform it? For what reason is he called a "friendly" (*maitra*) Brāhmaṇa by the learned, and not another? He is "friendly" (*maitra*) because he exists in friendliness, or because his actions are for the sake of non-injury (*ahiṃsā*). But one who is established in [worldly] action is injurious, because his actions are means for harming others; thus, in both ways, his action is flawed. Having understood this, one should either not perform such action, or rather, one should perform only recitation because it is free from harm. This praise is for the purpose of the study of the Veda; it is a praise of the *praṇava* and so forth, occurring through the abandonment of the performance of Vedic rituals. Otherwise, there would be an inconsistency and contradiction with the scriptures—this is the logic already stated. Furthermore, in this section on the praise of the *praṇava* and so forth, this praise of the recitation under discussion should be understood as pertaining to all Brāhmaṇas by virtue of the context, and not merely for the purpose of praising the injunction regarding the [student's] mode of life (*prakṛti*). Thus have been described the duties of the student (*brahmacārin*) regarding the study of the Veda; now follows his duty regarding the observances (*vrata*).
A wise man should exert effort in restraining the senses as they roam among alluring objects, just as a charioteer restrains his horses. 2.88

The purpose of the statement is the equality of all the sense organs. This verse is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) to that. Furthermore, although this is not the primary topic (*aprakaraṇa*), the enumeration and essential nature of the sense organs are introduced here for the purpose of demonstrating the means of their conquest.
"The eleven sense organs which the ancient sages have spoken of—I shall explain them correctly, in due order and as they truly are. (2.89)
And this is the demonstration of the essential nature of those [faculties] mentioned by number:
"The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth; the anus, the generative organ, the hands and feet, and speech is recorded as the tenth. (2.90)
Furthermore, due to the difference in their functions, this division of them into two groups remains:
among these, the five beginning with hearing are, in their respective order, the sense organs of cognition (buddhīndriya).
The five organs of action among these are said to be the anus and so forth. (2.91)
And all objects are their domain.
The eleventh, the mind, should be known as being of both natures by its own quality;
when it is conquered, these two groups of five become conquered. (2.92)

One's own group (*svagaṇa*) is the volition (*saṃkalpa*) of the mind. By what [means] is it "of a dual nature"? It is the cause of the volitions of both the auspicious and the inauspicious, which are the causes for the activity of the senses; furthermore, it is "of a dual nature" because it is the cause of those two types of volitions that lead to the activity of the senses. Having established this, the following is said for the sake of emphasis: "When that one is conquered, these two groups of five become conquered. Thus, the purpose of restraining the senses has been stated. Now, it is stated for the sake of an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*): "Because that is twofold, through attachment to the senses, one undoubtedly incurs evil."
But by fully restraining those very [senses], one then attains perfection. || 2.93 ||

Why? Because restraint of the senses is to be honored due to its exceedingly great purpose. Why? Because it is not intended that their cessation occurs through the mere satisfaction of hunger by means of the enjoyment (or tasting) of sense objects; rather, it is for the sake of maintaining the capacity for the performance of ritual action.
For desire is never appeased by the enjoyment of desired objects;
indeed, like a fire fed with clarified butter, it only increases all the more. (2.94)
And here is another enumeration, distinguished by its prior particulars:
"He who should attain all these [objects] and he who should abandon them entirely—the renunciation of all desires is superior to their attainment. (2.95)

Therefore, one who seeks the goal of the dharma of the bliss of tranquility should be devoted to *prasaṃkhyāna*. For when restraint is taught by means of the non-proximity of objects—which is characterized by the absence of attachment—the goal is accomplished. And so, why resort to the hardship of *prasaṃkhyāna*? It is for this reason that the following is undertaken: "These [senses], corrupted by objects, cannot be restrained in such a way through mere non-association as they can be constantly restrained through knowledge. (2.96)

The phrase "by means of the enumeration according to the instruction" is a praise of the enumeration under discussion. Thus, by this praise, it is understood that the enumeration is indeed purposeful; and this being so, one should understand that the instruction on enumeration is also purposeful when acting as an auxiliary to the instruction on the restraint of the senses. But why is such great effort made here? Because the restraint of the senses does not, by the power of the scripture alone, directly result in the unseen goal (*adṛṣṭa*). What then? It accomplishes the aim of the person (*puruṣārtha*) through the channel of the performance of prescribed duties and meditative concentration (*samādhi*). And he shows this as follows:
The Vedas, renunciation, sacrifices, observances, and austerities never lead to perfection for one whose disposition is corrupted. 2.97
Because it is seized by non-concentration, this [practice] must be respected for the sake of that concentration; thus, restraint is for one's own benefit. Now he defines the sense organ:
That man who, having heard, touched, seen, tasted, and smelled, neither rejoices nor desponds—he should be known as one who has conquered his senses. (2.98)

The exposition of the objects of restraint regarding those [senses] should be understood as pertaining to all the senses, and not merely to the well-known objects of the individual senses. And having established this, it is said:
"For if even one among all the senses leaks, by that [leakage] his wisdom flows away, like water from the foot of a leather water-skin. (2.99)

This explanatory passage (arthavāda) is to be understood as intended for the purpose of praising the restraint of all the senses, as established by the force of the context. Furthermore, that restraint is concluded with its previously stated purpose: "Thus, having attained concentration through the restraint of the senses, the student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī), having brought the collection of senses under control and likewise restrained the mind, should accomplish all his goals through yoga without wasting his body. (2.100)
This is the conclusion regarding the purpose of restraint of the senses; furthermore, this is another duty within the section on the duties of a religious student (*brahmacārin*):
"One should stand reciting the *Sāvitrī* during the morning twilight until the sun appears; but one should sit during the evening twilight until the stars are clearly visible. (2.101)

The phrase “the morning twilight” (*pūrvāṃ saṃdhyām*) is a qualification. However, regarding the rule “one should stand while reciting during the evening,” the act of recitation (*japa*) is the primary element because its fruit is heard [in scripture]. This is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) for the rules concerning the study of the Vedas and their duties. In this verse, the connection with the qualities is such that one stands; thus, the act of recitation is taught here for the sake of the result, and not otherwise. Furthermore, the form of the sentence here is as follows: “one should recite while standing. Why was it not stated simply as “one should recite standing”? The objector might say that this very point is stated in the prose section (*gadyagrantha*). That is incorrect, for this is a metrical work (*padyagrantha*). Therefore, it was not read in that way for fear of violating the meter. The mention of the *Sāvitrī* is an instruction regarding the specific ritual act, intended to exclude others. Although there are many forms of verses dedicated to the deity Savitṛ—such as those beginning with *tat-sad-iti*, those consisting of three feet, and so forth—it is this specific *Sāvitrī* under discussion that is understood here. If another were taken, then the mention of the “three” [feet] would have to be understood here; as it has been said in the verse summarizing the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*): “this syllable and this [verse]” (MDh 2.78). Now, the rule for the time of that recitation is stated: “until the sight of the sun” (*arkadarśanāt*). Since “sight of the sun” is not a mandatory injunction, by this being the case, the commencement of the rite is established before sunrise. Although this [time limit] is unexpressed, it should be understood as specified in another Smṛti: “as long as the light [of dawn] exists, until the light [of the sun] appears. Regarding the evening, this is a restatement of what is already well-established. As for the word “always” (*sadā*), let that be for now. While the phrase “reciting this” is present, it is said “he should sit”; thus, he should sit while reciting. Here too, as before, the expansion of the syntactical inversion should be understood: “seated, he should recite. This is also a rule regarding the time and quality of this act of recitation. Because of the proper arrangement of the verses (*ṛk*), the word “properly” (*samyak*)—just like the word “always”—let that be for now. The word “always” from the second half of the previous verse is carried over here. Thus, the phrase “until the sight of the sun” indicates the limit for its cessation and the time for its commencement as being prior to that; this is established by implication. It has been stated that this unexpressed [limit] is to be qualified by another Smṛti. The words “always” and “twilight” (*saṃdhyā*) here should be seen as referring to both twilights. This demonstration of the performance of the rule is general; it is not a rule for a specific fruit. For if it were a rule for a fruit, this would entail a penance (*prāyaścitta*), which is improper because it is not the context and because it would lead to the non-permanence of the rite. By this, the second half of the following verse is explained. Moreover, what else?
"Standing while reciting during the morning twilight, one removes the sin committed at night;
but sitting during the evening twilight, one destroys the impurity created by day.
However, he who does not stand for the morning [twilight] and does not sit for the evening [twilight],"
He should be excluded from all the duties of the twice-born, like a Śūdra. || 2.103 ||

This is another explanatory passage (arthavāda) intended to praise the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana) by means of censuring its non-performance. It should be understood as being like worldly usage, for the purpose of strengthening one's resolve toward the performance of prescribed duties. Furthermore, that which is another duty of the religious student (brahmacārin) is stated: "Having gone to the forest, self-controlled and composed, he should recite the Sāvitrī, remaining constant and established in the daily rule near water. (2.104)

It has been stated that the mention of the *sāvitrī* is for the purpose of indicating others as well. This injunction for the *brahmayajña* should be understood as having the same rules (*sadharmaka*). Is this not also the rule regarding the location for the *saṃdhyopāsana* under discussion? [This is so] because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the phrase "the *sāvitrī* also," and because of the force of the context (*prakaraṇa*) to be mentioned later. Furthermore, this injunction called the *brahmayajña* is a daily obligatory rite (*naityaka*). Why? Because:
"And also in the study of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*vedopakaraṇa*), and in the daily recitation of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*). (70)
For there is no restriction regarding recitation on forbidden days (anadhyāya) with respect to the oblation-mantras. || 2.105 ||

Regarding the statement, "The entire Veda is to be mastered" (MDh 2.165), since the study of the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) is enjoined together with the study of the Veda, one might conclude that the prohibition against studying on days unfit for study (*anadhyāya*) applies to them as well. However, this is not so; for this prohibition is either refuted within this very section at the beginning of the *Kalpa* or in the context of the *Brahmayajña*. Alternatively, this is an illustrative explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the *Brahmayajña*, and its own specific meaning is established through inference. Others, however, say that there is no fault in the study of the "auxiliaries of the Veda" (*vedopakaraṇa*). They argue that the author will later state regarding the suspension of study (*anadhyāya*): "At the commencement (*upākarma*) and the conclusion (*utsarga*), a three-night cessation is prescribed" (MDh 4.119). Even then, they claim, one should indeed continue to study these. That is incorrect, because the point is already established by what follows: "And also during the daily recitation of the *Svādhyāya*. The term *naityaka* refers to the obligatory *Brahmayajña*; there is no restriction regarding days unfit for study here. This rule is prescribed because it does not apply to other forms of study—namely, those intended for acquisition and retention, nor to the *vedopakaraṇa* and the *Brahmayajña*. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and in the case of sacrificial mantras" (*homamantreṣu*), the mention of "sacrificial mantras" is for the sake of illustration, including all specific types of mantras used in oblations, offerings, sacrifices, silent recitations (*japa*), purifications (*mārjana*), and so forth. Why, then, was this stated? Because the general prohibition against studying on unfit days applies to all forms of study, and thus this specific exception is made for the *Brahmayajña* and similar rites.
In the daily rite there is no omission,
for it is remembered as the "Brahma-sacrifice."

This name is provided as an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). For it is said that [the study] is "constant" (*satata*), or that it occurs "therein" (*tatra-bhava*). And thus, there is no suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) in this case.

Furthermore, because it is said that "merit is offered as a *brahmāhuti*," and since the supreme praise is itself the *brahmāhuti*—either because it serves the purpose of an oblation or by association with it—in this way, the merit of what has been studied becomes an offering made as a *brahmāhuti*.
That which is consecrated with the *vaṣaṭ* call during a time unfit for study. || 2.106 ||

The *vaṣaṭkāra* is indeed a non-study period (*anadhyāya*); this is a conceptual construction for the purpose of praising it. Therefore, there is a connection with that: "that which is consecrated by the *vaṣaṭkāra* during a non-study period" means that even during a non-study period, one must certainly study [the Veda]. The purpose [of the statement] regarding the *brahmāhuti* is to establish its connection with the *vaṣaṭkāra*. For one who desires an excellence of merit, that very [study] should be performed together with oneself. Thus, this is solely for the purpose of praising the *brahmayajña*: "He who studies his own portion of the Veda for a year..."

Moreover, in that context, it should be understood as "omitted by implication" (*uktalupta*) due to the force of the circumstances. Even for a year, and certainly not for the duration of one's entire life, because this is the nature of the *jāti-dharma* (the duty of one's caste). [71] The study [of the Veda] achieves its purpose even in a single year; thus, there is also praise for the *brahmayajña*.
According to the rule as previously stated.
The term *dvija* is a restatement (*anuvāda*), used for the purpose of completing the meter;
its constant occurrence [in this context] is as follows.
The sacrifice to Brahman consists of milk, curd, ghee, and honey. || 2.107 ||

[The items] beginning with milk: this is an injunction regarding the fruit, which is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) of the fruit, intended as a commendation for an injunction that has been set aside. Others, however, say: "Milk is prescribed because of its commonality with purity; ghee because it shares the nature of being a cause of nourishment; honey because of its similarity to oiliness; and [the meat of] the cow alone because it is the essence of the food of cows. It is accepted that those duties taught in the section on the religious student (*brahmacārin*) do not apply elsewhere by virtue of the power of that specific context. Yet, without some effort to initiate a new scriptural treatment, certain of those duties would not be established in other contexts; therefore, this [section] is commenced for this purpose.

Having undergone the initiation ceremony, a twice-born man should maintain the sacred fire, practice begging for alms, sleep on the ground, and perform what is beneficial for his teacher until his formal return home (samāvartana). (2.108)

Since [the duties] such as kindling the fire are already established as being subordinate to the primary requirement of being cultivated through lifelong celibacy (*brahmacarya*), this new undertaking is for the purpose of extending those duties—such as kindling the fire—to other related practices like ritual ablutions (*upasparśana*). Regarding the question of what is beneficial for the teacher even after the period following the student's bath (*snāna*) and during his residence, such as the fetching of sacrificial fuel, *kuśa* grass, wood, and water-jars: the text will state later that the student should perform these until the end of his life, and that this applies even beyond the formal gift of the final fee (*samāvartana*). Thus, the present rule serves to ensure the continuation of these specific duties.
"One should always do what is pleasing to those two and to the teacher at all times" (MDh 2.228).

And likewise, another Smṛti states: "And this applies to the subsequent [stages] provided it is not inconsistent. This pertains to the religious student (*brahmacārin*) in the context of study; however, for others, the teaching of students is prescribed. [The teacher's son should be: devoted to service, a giver of knowledge, righteous, and pure.
One who is capable, a giver of wealth, a seeker of knowledge, one's own kin, and a virtuous person—these ten are to be taught according to the Dharma. || 2.109 ||

The treatise on polity (*arthaśāstra*) is regulated. Among these, teaching one who bestows wealth and one who is desirous of hearing is for the sake of *dharma*, because it is established as a single statement through the acceptance of the underlying cause; thus it is designated as "according to *dharma*. In the reading where it says, "one who is capable, a giver of wealth, and virtuous" (verse 72), the mention of the teacher (*ācārya*) is independent. However, in the previous reading, the mention of the teacher should be understood as being for the purpose of qualifying the son. Alternatively, this is called the duty of teaching them, which consists of favoring them by means of the ten [qualities].
One should not speak to anyone unless asked, nor to one who asks improperly;
for even though he knows, the wise man should conduct himself among the world like one who is dull-witted. 2.110

One should speak to these [persons] only when asked, and not unasked; even when asked, one should not do so improperly. This is the restrictive purpose for the commencement of the treatise. [The verse: "He who asks me by an unlawful method, and he who answers him by an unlawful method—of these two, one incurs either displeasure or hatred. This is intended as a censure of the transgression of the prescribed rules for studying and teaching unlawfully, and as a praise of their proper observance. Thus, there is a praise of those authorized according to their respective capacities. Where neither dharma nor artha exists, nor even a corresponding desire to learn—that [method] is likewise [condemned].
Knowledge should not be sown there, just as a wholesome seed is not sown in salt-waste.

Nor is this person a teacher for hire, as is well known from the verse [MDh 3.156]: "He who teaches for a fixed amount, saying 'so much, so much'... This being the case, a teacher for hire is to be understood as one who produces [the pupil] through instruction; otherwise, he would have taught only the one seeking service and the one providing wealth, for fear of contradiction. Furthermore, he will not state that the teacher’s fee (*gurvartha*) is for this reason. Teaching is for the purpose of an injunction. As it is said: "Of the six duties, three are his means of livelihood" (MDh 10.76).
And thus, by this teacher, there is no non-existence [of the duty].
A knower of Brahman should die together with his knowledge at his own will;
for even in the midst of dire calamity, he must never sow it upon barren soil.

For in times of distress, there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) if one does not impart knowledge to one who is worthy; therefore, this statement is indeed appropriate: "One may even die together with one's knowledge. Likewise in common worldly usage: "One may eat poison at will, but do not eat in his house. And so says the *Brāhmaṇa*: "He who, having studied the knowledge, does not bestow it upon one who asks for it, shall be deprived of his purpose. One should teach [it]; for that which the sages call the 'great transformation of speech'—in this yoga all this is established. Those who know thus become immortal. And thus, this *Smṛti* is merely a restatement of the meaning of the *Śruti*.
Knowledge approached a Brahmin and said: "I am your treasure; protect me.
Do not give me to one who is envious, so that I may remain most powerful. (2.114)
The mention of "the censorious" (asūyaka) is for the purpose of illustrating all the causes that render one unworthy (apātrīkaraṇa). Where, then, should this [knowledge] be given?
[72] But to him whom you know to be pure, self-restrained, and a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin)—to that Brahmin, who is a guardian of the treasure and is vigilant, teach me. (2.115)

This [instruction] should not be given merely because the aforementioned defects are absent; rather, it is for the purpose that those in whom a regard for purity and other such qualities must be expected. Even without this formal approach, inquiry, and acceptance, [the rule applies]:
"He who, without permission, should acquire the Veda from one who is studying it, is joined with the theft of Brahman and falls into hell. (2.116)

Therefore, one should indeed act with questions at the outset in order to avoid the transgression arising from doubt and other such uncertainties; the following verses are for the purpose of praising the injunction regarding teaching. Having concluded this section, there is this other [rule]:
"Whether it be secular or Vedic, or likewise pertaining to the inner self (adhyātmika), he from whom one receives knowledge, him one should first salute. (2.117)

Worldly knowledge is that which is human in origin; Vedic knowledge is that which consists of the *mantras* and *brāhmaṇas*. "Spiritual" (*ādhyātmika*) refers to that which pertains to the inner self, like the silence of a sage; it is mentioned separately for the sake of showing respect for the truth. Alternatively, "spiritual" refers to any knowledge existing within sciences other than the Vedas, such as the science of Ayurveda; one who would receive such knowledge for the sake of his welfare should first salute him. Why? Because [the rule applies] specifically to those who are teachers of one's own lineage; thus, this scripture is to be understood as meaningful only in the presence of a teacher of one's own lineage or a teacher of one's own field of knowledge. Otherwise, by way of prohibiting study from others, improper study is established through the verse beginning with "he who is a thief... (*yat stenaḥ*).
