A Brahmin who is well-restrained is better, even if his essence consists only of the Sāvitrī mantra;
one who is unrestrained is not better, even if he knows the three Vedas, if he eats all things and sells all things.

One should be satisfied even with the mere study of the *Sāvitrī* according to the rule; for even if he has the capacity to study more, the religious student (*brahmacārin*) should not study anything else by which he might master even the three Vedas. Thus, this is a praise of systematic study and not an instruction for the study of the *Sāvitrī* alone, because there is a traditional legal authority (*smṛti*) determining the study of the entire Veda. Accordingly, he will state later: "The entire Veda is to be mastered" (MDh 2.165). The mention of the *Sāvitrī* is stated for the purpose of illustration regarding the others. And it is said that having completed this triad, one has [mastered] the mouth of Brahman. Having thus declared the duty of study, he now instructs upon the duties of the religious student.
One should not occupy a bed or seat already used by a superior;
rather, while remaining on one's own bed or seat, one should rise to meet him and offer salutation. 2.119.

One should occupy a bed or seat that does not conflict with one's vows, either with a superior elder, one equal to him, or another person. Why? Because it is understood from the rule "one should not speak of oneself" that this applies to others. Wherever one might sit, upon seeing someone approaching or already seated on that very bed or seat, one should rise and salute them. Thus, two rules are established here for the sake of spiritual excellence (*śreyaḥ*); for he will later explain the relative strength and weakness of these cases. This is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for this rule:
"For when an elder approaches, the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) of the youth rise upward."
One regains them again by rising to meet them and by saluting them. || 2.120 ||
This is another praise for the performance of intermediate injunctions, seen through the observation that there is transgression when what is prescribed is not performed:
"For one who is habitually respectful and constantly serves the elders, four things increase properly: life-span, wisdom, fame, and strength. (2.121)

This is either a praise of seniority (*sthāvirya*) as a cause of excellence; or rather, it is understood that even when other causes of excellence exist, one must salute this [teacher] because of his seniority. For it has been stated: "Having risen, one should salute" (MDh 2.119). Since that rule has thus come to be expressed, it is now enjoined:
"A Brahmin, after saluting an elder, should announce his own name, saying: 'I am so-and-so by name. (MDh 2.122)

One should greet an elder and then utter one's own name beyond that, saying, "I am so-and-so by name. In place of all names, one's own name [is used] as "I am so-and-so," which indicates a specific name. This instruction regarding the name for the purpose of greeting is an alternative to the [standard] greeting. Now, since the utterance of one's own name would generally apply in the presence of anyone to be greeted, it is set aside by another reason:
those who do not understand the greeting of a person by his name.
A wise man should say "I am he" to them, and likewise to all women. (2.123)

The meaning is that having taken up the name, those who are worthy of salutation should be saluted; this is because of the association with the return-greeting (*pratyabhivāda*). Here, by implication, the word *abhivāda* does not denote the return-greeting itself—it refers to the person toward whom the return-greeting is directed. To those who do not know how to employ the return-greeting according to the scriptures—that is, those incapable of performing the return-greeting—one should say "I am [Name]. Who? The wise man. Thus, the instruction regarding the pronunciation of the word is for the purpose of avoiding the utterance of one's own name at the end of the salutation; otherwise, the statement of the rule would be redundant. And this applies to women whether they are skilled in the return-greeting or not. Why is there the inclusion of "all"? Because the word *abhivāda* (salutation) is used here by implication. Otherwise, this would be equivalent to not beginning at all, as it would already be covered by the preceding rule. And thus says the author of the *Cūrṇikā*: "In the return-greeting, at the end of the name, those who know the prescribed form—among them, even a Brahmin may, if he wishes, say 'This is I' to those who are not women. But another says: "Since [Manu] will state that even a Śūdra who has reached his tenth decade is worthy of salutation (MDh 2.137), and since he might sometimes, due to lack of wisdom, not understand the Sanskrit being spoken, one should say 'I am' in that case. Or else, even a non-Śūdra might not understand the mention of a well-known personal name when it is being grasped through a title such as 'Vākyair-vartamāna'; therefore this is said. Thus, in both cases—whether the name is uttered or not—this is for the purpose of prescribing the remainder of the name for the one returning the salutation.
In greeting, one should utter the word "bhoḥ" at the end of one's own name;
for the sages have declared that the nature of the word "bhoḥ" is the very essence of names. (2.124)

According to the treatises, it is improper to utter the name of those who are to be saluted. Furthermore, for one who is to be saluted, there can be no turning toward the greeting if their name has not been grasped; nor is the practice of returning the greeting possible without that [name]. Therefore, this is said: by the rule "one should utter the word *bhoḥ*," both the fault of omitting the name of the person to be saluted will be avoided, and the state of being turned toward the address will be accomplished. However, the meaning of the subsequent verse must be explained as being for the purpose of praising the preceding rule.
The rule for salutation is completed. Now, the rule for the response to a salutation is stated:
"O long-lived one! O gentle one!"—thus should a Brahmin be addressed in response to a salutation;
and at the end of his name, the vowel *a* should be made protracted (*pluta*), with the preceding syllable [also protracted]. (2.125)

The term *āyuṣman* is intended here as the grasping of the meaning; others, however, say it is the grasping of the word itself. The form *bhavet* is the second-person singular imperative (*loṭ*) used in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*). And the address *saumya* is a qualification [of the person] because of their being long-lived (*āyuṣmat*), for the sake of showing affection. Thus, the rule for returning a greeting consists in using the word itself or its meaning as the object of expression. The mention of the *vipra* (Brahmin) is for the purpose of illustration, since no other [caste] is taught regarding the return of a greeting, and because a greeting is necessarily required [from them] just as it is from a Brahmin. Accordingly, the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) states: "In returning a greeting, except for a Śūdra" (Pāṇini 8.2.83). By this, the verse concerning the greeting is concluded. The mention of the *vipra* has been explained. Regarding the phrase "after the greeting, the Brahmin": thus the Brahmin should be addressed. The remainder of the sentence is: "when the greeting has been performed. Furthermore, the mention of the vowel *a* at the end of his name is to be understood as an indication of vowels such as *i*, etc. The word *ca* (and), which expresses the absence of a restrictive rule, serves a conjunctive purpose: that which was stated previously and what we shall state here [should both be applied]. The genitive case in *asya* is a possessive qualifier. Of what? Of the name of the one who greets. The mention of "the end" is for the purpose of excluding the beginning and the middle. For it is said: "Of each [syllable] of the teacher's [name], the final one should be pronounced. Thus, the final *i*-vowel of the name is to be pronounced. In what manner? Because this is said: a protracted vowel (*pluta*) consists of three morae (*mātrā*), not one or two. And so, by connection with the qualification of the vowel *a*, this [rule] is to be understood as a restatement (*anuvāda*). But this is another qualification of the vowel *a*: "preceded by a syllable" (*pūrvākṣara*). Why? From the contextually relevant vowel *a*; what then is the consonant? And this is called a "syllable" (*akṣara*) by virtue of its quality. Due to its association with the vowel *a*, the word "syllable" is used for a consonant. However, this word "syllable" qualified by the word "preceding" does not apply to the vowel *a*, because there is no other rule [for it] following it. Therefore, by general analogy, the word "syllable" should be understood as applied to a consonant through figurative usage (*guṇavṛtti*). This being the case, the vowel *a* situated before the "preceding syllable" is treated metaphorically as if it were the "preceding syllable" itself, like the letter *m*. And having done so, this is what is meant: this vowel *a* followed by a consonant should be pronounced protracted (*pluta*), not otherwise—neither separately nor as anything else—even when a preceding consonant exists, or when combined with the preceding syllable, it is called the "preceding syllable. In that view, the elision of the result expressed by the word "combined" (*samaveta*) is to be understood. The rest is the same. And so it has been said: "In returning a greeting, except for a Śūdra" (Pāṇini 8.2.83). By Manu, [the rule] for the protracted lengthening of the final vowel of the name is indicated.

**The manuscript contains folios 231–241 here before 126 and the subsequent pages. I follow the standard sequence of Manu here:** "A Brahmin who does not know the proper form of returning a salutation should not be saluted by a learned man; he is exactly like a Śūdra. (2.126)

When one faces someone who is about to offer a salutation, that response from the saluter is called a "return-salutation" (*pratyabhivāda*), whose specific form has been stated. If one does not know how to employ those two according to their grammatical rules, it is not a valid salutation. Is this, then, a prohibition of the act of saluting? No, it is said. What is it then? This is a praise of the return-salutation. This is understood from the illustrative example, not from the literal power of the words themselves. It is not said that for one incapable of returning a salutation, there is an absolute prohibition against saluting at all. And so it has been said:
To those who do not know how to address one by name, a wise man should say "I am he," and the same applies to all women. (MDh 2.123)

Thus [it is said]. Yet, one should not become entirely unworthy of salutation merely on account of this fault, like a Śūdra, because the Brāhmaṇa caste is held in absolute honor. Alternatively, there is an absolute prohibition regarding women, as indicated by the force of the mention of the Śūdra as an example. This being the case, since there is both a rule and a prohibition, there is an option (*vikalpa*). Or, one who is unable to return a formal greeting may be saluted by the mention of his own name, as we have already stated; or [there is] an absolute [prohibition]. And this is a restricted option (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*): one who is superior to oneself in terms of birth and so forth should be saluted in this manner without mentioning his name, but another [inferior person] should never [be saluted] even without his name—this has been explained by the preceding discussion. In connection with the topic of returning a greeting, this other rule for conversation is now enjoined: he who is to be saluted by someone else [should address] that saluter...
Upon meeting a Brāhmaṇa, one should inquire after his welfare; a Kṣatriya, after his freedom from illness; a Vaiśya, after his prosperity; and a Śūdra, after his health alone. (2.127)

How, then, is it understood that this rule regarding salutation pertains to the one being saluted and not to the one saluting? This is understood from the force of the instruction given in the context of the *pratyabhivāda* (the formal response to a salutation); for this is a rule concerning the act of saluting. Otherwise, due to redundancy, this would be unnecessary; furthermore, in the absence of such a rule, the scripture would be rendered invalid. The term "having approached" (*samāgamya*) applies as a supplement to all [the subsequent rules]. Alternatively, the previous rule concerns those who are superior (*śreyas*), whereas this one is stated for those who are equals, such as "one should ask a Brāhmaṇa about his welfare," and so forth. This meaning is also understood from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the word "having approached. And because this leads to a discussion on the rules for conversation, this other matter is now stated.
One who knows the Dharma should address an initiated person by name only if he is younger; otherwise, he should address him using the honorifics "bhoḥ" or "bhavat" placed before his name. (2.128)

The prohibition [against addressing a teacher by name] applies to one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*) as the cause, even if he is younger, according to the statement "even a junior," which—by the logic of the "stick and cake" (*daṇḍāpūpika*)—prohibits the mention of the name of a teacher who has been initiated, even if he is senior by birth.
One should always behave toward those who are superior exactly as toward a teacher: *śreyaḥsu guruvad vṛttiṃ nityam eva samācaret* (MDh 2.207).

By this [statement], some interpret the word *api* as having the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*): "Even one who is younger [should not be addressed thus], let alone an elder. This must be carefully examined as to whether it is correct or not. A twice-born person who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*) should not be addressed by name by other twice-born persons, because of the context; however, by the logic of the "stick and cake" (*daṇḍāpūpika*), he may be so addressed even by a Śūdra. Now, since there was previously no restriction regarding names in other cases, this [sūtra] is commenced for the purpose of establishing a rule: "But one should address him preceded by *bhoḥ* or *bhavat*" [80]. That speech in which the word *bhoḥ* or the word *bhavat* comes first—this pair of words, *bhoḥ* and *bhavat*, is prescribed by the learned (*śiṣṭas*) for the sake of showing respect, as is traditionally handed down. And so it has been said:
For the word "bhoḥ" is remembered by the seers as the very essence of names. (MDh 2.124)

Furthermore, this is stated repeatedly in the *Patañjali-bhāṣya*: "In the address to the venerable Pāṇini. And in the address to a consecrated sacrificer (*dīkṣita*), the word *bhobhavat* is to be understood because it serves the purpose of addressing. An example of this is: "O consecrated one (*bho dīkṣita*), O sacrificer (*yajamāna*), O performer of the Soma-pressing (*sunvan*), [you] are constantly engaged in the sacrificial session (*satram*). Because the word *dīkṣita* functions here as a term of reference, words preceded by *bhoḥ* are understood through the force of the context. How is it that the mention of the consecrated one’s name is prohibited here? Elsewhere, no subsequent word for *bhobhavat* is taught; yet here he says, "and him preceded by *bhobhavat*," and the word *dīkṣita* is heard here. This alone is understood, as we have said: because the addresses to that venerable consecrated one occur here both in his presence and in his absence, such as "of the venerable consecrated one" (*tatrabhavato dīkṣitasya*). Alternatively, this word *bhavat* is to be understood through its capacity in the address to a consecrated one and elsewhere: "You, O consecrated one, are wise, faithful, and observant of the rules"—thus it is stated in the address to him. The usage of both the words *bhoḥ* and *bhavat* together in the address to a consecrated one is also to be understood: "O you, the venerable consecrated one, are wise," and so forth. And this is an inclusion of the base form (*prakṛti*); when the base form is included, the inclusion of the suffix is established by implication, since it is analyzed in this very way and according to the context. This rule for addressing women is stated elsewhere with reference to the student (*brahmacārin*) under discussion.
But toward a woman who is another's wife and not related by birth, he should address her as "Lady," "Fortunate One," or "Sister. (2.129)

Now, regarding the woman who is another's wife: what kind of woman? He explains her: "And one who is unrelated by birth. She should be understood here as the wife of someone other than one’s mother or father. The rule for addressing her is that he should speak to her in this manner; thus, the specific form of address is prescribed. What are the characteristics of the religious student (*brahmacārī*)? It is of such a nature [as follows]: "O fortunate lady" (*subhage*) or "sister" (*bhagini*). As for the particle *iti* used here, which is indicated as being closely joined [to the words], that word should be understood as signifying the actual object and as standing in apposition to each term. Furthermore, the subsequent term "sister" is intended to include the other categories, such as "mother" and so forth. And such is the common usage in the world. This rule for addressing women and oneself should be understood according to the appropriateness of their respective ages. Others, however, describe an alternative based on designation: a woman taken by another should be addressed as "fortunate lady," while one's own wife of noble family should be addressed as "sister"; [otherwise] she becomes a doubtful [case]. But this [distinction] would be for a specific purpose according to the context. This is another duty of the religious student.
Upon rising, one should address maternal uncles, paternal uncles, fathers-in-law, officiating priests, and teachers who are younger than oneself, saying, "I am so-and-so. (2.130)

In this context, the word *guru* (teacher/elder) should be understood as including those not explicitly mentioned, such as maternal aunts and others—excluding, however, those who are teachers of sacred knowledge (*vidyā-guru*). For, because he is a supreme elder, one must rise to greet him even if he is younger in age, though without performing a formal salutation (*abhivādana*), as this would contradict other scriptures. Thus, the author will state regarding childhood: "We teach our fathers," and so forth. Furthermore, the mention of the "afflicted" (*ātura*) here does not refer to maternal uncles and the like, for that would result in a redundant inclusion of those already covered by the term *guru*. Moreover, if it were intended as an illustrative example, mentioning many others would be purposeless; thus, the word *guru* does not apply to maternal uncles and the rest. If, however, by implication the term somehow serves to indicate many others, then this use of the word *guru* is appropriate as a reference (*anuvāda*) to maternal uncles and so on for the sake of praise: "How is it that these, though younger, are to be risen for upon by one capable of treating them as elders? Furthermore, the pronoun *asau* (he) refers to the aforementioned rule: "He should say, 'I am so-and-so. What then? It is intended to prohibit the use of the honorific *bhavat*. Accordingly, Gautama states: "But in the case of officiating priests, fathers-in-law, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles who are younger in age, there is merely rising to meet them, but no formal salutation. This very point is understood from the force of the definition of a formal salutation.
A mother’s sister, a maternal uncle’s wife, a mother-in-law, and a father’s sister are to be honored like the wife of one’s guru; they are equal to the wife of a guru. (2.131)

Regarding the statement, "She is to be honored like the wife of one's guru," since this meaning is already established by the rule "They [the wives] are equal to the guru’s wife," it is stated again for the sake of emphasizing the point (*arthavādārtham*). Just as, according to tradition, even though they are younger, these [wives] must be honored by their elder husbands; because of this instruction, they are to be saluted with rising from one's seat. And so the author will say: "And also toward an elder sister" (MDh 2.133). From this indicative mark (*liṅga*), it follows that this wife of the guru is to be saluted regardless of her seniority. It is also stated in another Smṛti: "The wives of one’s husband’s friends. As for the elder wives, rising from one's seat is established just as it is toward a maternal uncle; however, for the wives of elder brothers, both [rising and saluting] are established by the logic of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpikayā*). Alternatively, this is the reason for the rule: "She is to be honored like the wife of one’s guru. For what reason? Because "they are equal to the guru’s wife. Furthermore, in the context of honoring, this [rule regarding the guru’s wife] is more than merely rising and saluting. For other women, the clasping of the feet is specifically prescribed as the cause of honor.
The wife of one's brother of the same caste may be saluted day after day;
however, upon returning from a journey, the wives of kinsmen and maternal relatives must be saluted. (2.132)

In the presence of a female relative, this word "brother" refers to one who shares the same mother; this indicates another textual context. According to other Smṛtis and established custom, the wife of a brother should be clasped by the feet. Even within the section on elders, this qualification applies specifically to a younger brother; furthermore, for a kinswoman or a female relative, the rule of rising and salutation applies only when she returns from a journey, as it is an optional alternative rather than a constant duty. This also applies to the father’s sister and to an elder sister of the mother.
One should maintain a conduct toward them like that toward a mother; yet the mother is more venerable than they. (2.133)

Since the instruction regarding conduct toward paternal aunts, maternal aunts, and elder sisters is taught to be like that toward one's mother, the clasping of their feet is prescribed here as being without alternative (nirvikalpaka), just as with the wife of an elder brother; it is not, however, optional (savikalpaka) like the case of women who are merely relatives or connected by marriage. Now, since this is already established by the sense of the matter, for what purpose is it stated that "the mother is more venerable than they"? It is said: for the sake of providing an option. Thus, it should be understood that the aforementioned clasping of the feet for these women is to be performed optionally. Alternatively, while for those who are relatives or connected by marriage, the clasping of the feet occurs only after returning from a journey, or perhaps daily; for the wives of elder brothers, it occurs daily provided they are present. Or else, since the rule "one should maintain conduct toward them as toward a mother" would imply that the entire conduct due to a mother applies to all of them—including the performance of every command—this statement is begun for the purpose of restriction: "The mother is more venerable than they. This is intended to restrict the full extension of the rule.
Friendship with fellow citizens is established after ten years; that with artists after five years;
that with Vedic scholars after three years; and even with those of one's own kin, it is formed after a very short time.

That which is described as being ten years older than oneself is called *daśākhya-abda* (ten-year-elder). What is that? It is *paurasakhyam*. One who exists in the city (*pura*) is a *paura*; his friendship is *paurasakhyam*. The mention of "city" is for the sake of illustration. As for friendship, it refers to one of an earlier age, because of the scriptural injunction: "One should rise and salute [an elder]" (MDh 2.119). Therefore, rising to greet and so forth in the morning is prohibited here. And thus says Gautama: "O sir, O venerable one—thus [should one address] a peer" (GDh 6.14). Because of their status as friends, one should speak in this manner; however, one who is worthy of honor should not be addressed thus. This should be understood to apply to those of the same caste who lack [other] qualities, since qualities will be taught later and caste has already been praised. Thus, regarding those who possess arts (*kalābhṛt*), there may be one younger by more than ten years due to an abundance of qualities. The phrase "three years senior among those learned in the Vedas" (*tryabdapūrvaṃ śrotriyāṇām*) uses the mention of "those learned in the Vedas" (*śrotriya*) as a mark of the twice-born (*dvijāti*); this serves to indicate the inclusion of the twice-born and, subsequently, the Śūdra. Even with a small difference, one who is established in a very small [difference] and established in a common origin (*samānayoniṣṭha*) is established in caste (*jāti*). It is the same as the previous [rule].
One should recognize a ten-year-old Brahmin and a hundred-year-old king as father and son; yet of these two, the Brahmin is the father.

Since it was not mentioned [among the factors] such as the father and so forth when [a person] is born, the status of being an object of respect for that [birth] is now stated. This should be understood in the same way regarding Kṣatriyas and others as well. Furthermore, because birth is stated to be predominant over age, its predominance is also inferred over wealth and kinship. However, birth does not possess predominance over action or learning. Thus, the previous verse should be understood as applying only to those of the same caste. And since it is supplementary to that, birth is mentioned here separately from wealth and the other factors; it is not that birth alone is the ground for respect. And these—
Wealth, kinship, age, action, and learning as the fifth—these are the grounds for respect; each subsequent one is weightier than the preceding. (2.136)

That which is to be honored (*mānya*) because it is worthy of worship (*pūjā*) in these three [categories] is a "station of honor" (*mānyasthāna*). These are those very stations of honor for them. And thus, the honorability of wealth and the rest is stated by implication. Their relative strength and weakness is now being declared. Between each pair, that which is "heavier" (*garīyaḥ*), meaning more important, is to be understood on account of their commonality. What is that station of honor? Whatever follows is established as superior to each preceding one; this repetition is understood even though not explicitly heard due to the force of the context. Among the five, there are many [stations of honor] within the three castes, and they are possessed of qualities.
Wherever such persons may be found, even a Śūdra who has reached his tenth decade of life is worthy of honor there. [2.137]

This [verse] is commenced for the purpose of praising those who are entitled [to respect] by connecting them with two qualifying attributes. Regarding wealth and the other [factors], that twice-born person in whom these—wealth and the rest—are most numerous and excellent, he is to be known as the one most worthy of honor here in this world among the four castes. By implication, even a Śūdra may be preeminent in age; or, in this context, even a Vaiśya from the former [category], or even a Kṣatriya from the former, or even one of the same caste who is superior, [is to be honored]. The statement "having reached the tenth decade" is to be understood as intended to demonstrate the excellence of wealth and the other factors. This being so, in the phrase "even a Śūdra," the particle *api* is used in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvanā*); the other [usage of *api*] is for conjunction (*samuccaya*). Why? Because of the rule regarding the prohibition of saluting a Śūdra: "He who has reached the tenth decade [of life] is not to be saluted by a learned man" (MDh 2.126), which shows that even a Brāhmaṇa of ten years [is not to be saluted] based on the extreme venerability of his birth-place or region. Thus, what some say—that this is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) to prevent the instruction from being restricted to the subject of inferior castes—is incorrect. For if it were so, the teaching would be construed as applying only to those of lower birth, such that a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya possessing such qualities would be considered honorable. This is untenable. Therefore, this is commenced to teach that birth, wealth, and the rest are the causes of honor, and that even a partial claim to honor is not desired for those devoid of them, even if they are set aside. Thus, this is begun.
The way must be yielded to one who holds a wheel, to one who has reached his tenth decade, to a sick man, to one carrying a burden, to a woman, to a *snātaka*, to a king, and to a bridegroom. (2.138)

And for one who makes a vehicle like a chariot, even if he is of low birth and so forth, the path must be yielded because he is a "charioteer" (*cakrin*), by way of metaphorical treatment (*upacāra*) like a bed. The same applies hereafter. Why is this? Because there is equality in the commencement [of the rule], as required by the sense. This applies even to one who stands in the tenth stage (*daśamīstha*) though he is not a charioteer; to one who is ill, even if he is neither a charioteer nor in the tenth stage; to one who is carrying a burden, even if he is not such a person; and to a woman who is about to give birth, because she is moving very slowly due to her advanced state of pregnancy, she is to be favored. This is because the mere mention of the "vehicle" and "woman" is taught together with those who are to be favored, such as the sick and others. Furthermore, the mention of the *snātaka* refers specifically to the Brāhmaṇa, due to the force of proximity to the King. And this king, being endowed with qualities such as sovereignty, is a Kṣatriya by virtue of his caste, not merely any Kṣatriya. [Objection: But in this case, the mention of the *snātaka* is redundant, since it has already been stated and because he is equal to the sick and others. [Response: True, this is so. However, this should be understood as being for the sake of providing an illustration (*dṛṣṭāntārtha*), not for the purpose of enjoining what was not previously established. How so? Just as the *snātaka* is to be honored, so too is another who deserves honor as described; and for the sake of what follows, he will indeed say: "Among those gathered together, the *snātaka* and the king are to be honored" (MDh 2.139), and so forth. By doing so, the mention of the "king" here also becomes appropriate. And the mention of the "other" (*para*) is to be explained as before. And because he is heard separately from all the others—such as the charioteer and the rest—his preeminence is understood to be beyond exception. Since there is no fixed rule regarding the order of honor among these, such as the charioteer and others, one may proceed according to one's wish in other cases. Having thus established the necessity of the honorability of these—the charioteer and others—in relation to the person worthy of honor, this [distinction] is now begun with the desire to explain their specific differences.
Among those gathered together, however, the *snātaka* and the king are to be honored;
and between the king and the *snātaka*, it is the *snātaka* who receives the honor due to a king. [84] 2.139

When those entitled to the same honor are encountered together, it is a rule that the Snātaka and the King must be honored according to their respective status; however, in cases other than these two, an option (*vikalpa*) must be adopted regarding the grounds for honoring the Cakrin and others. But when a King and a Snātaka meet, "the Snātaka receives the honor due to a king. For [Manu] will say:
"Because of his specific excellence, because he maintains the primacy of the original source, and because of the distinction of his sacraments, the Brāhmaṇa is the lord of all castes" (MDh 10.3).

Therefore, it is appropriate that the status of the *snātaka* as a person worthy of honor is taught in relation to the king by such statements as, "Because he was born from the highest limb [of Brahmā] and because of his seniority" (MDh 1.96).
"But that twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda along with the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) and the secret doctrines (*rahasya*), him they call an *ācārya*. (2.140)

"With the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) and with the secret doctrines (*rahasya*)" means that these are for the purpose of practicing the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*) through ritual acts. Alternatively, the mention of *kalpa* is intended to indicate all the auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*) [of the Veda], and the mention of *rahasya* is intended to indicate the comprehension of the meaning of the Vedas. Thus, because he imparts both the text and its meaning, the teacher (*ācārya*) is superior to all other gurus. Furthermore, the designation of the teacher as "one who calls out from childhood" (*śaiśava*) is for the sake of conventional usage regarding his ease of address. And so he will say later: "The teacher is ten times more venerable than the sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*)" (MDh 2.145), and so forth. By this, the designations of the *upādhyāya* and others are explained.
Alternatively, one may study a single portion of the Veda—
consisting merely of the mantras or merely the Brāhmaṇas,
or even its constituent parts, the Vedāṅgas.

[These are] devoid of the Vedas. Why? Because of the force of this very undertaking: whether he teaches them all, individually, or a portion thereof, for the sake of livelihood and not for the sake of dharma. And thus, in the scripture, the superiority of the *ācārya* is taught through his teaching of the complete Veda and its dharma, while the inferiority of the other [the *upādhyāya*] is taught through his teaching of the complete Veda for the sake of livelihood.
He is called an upādhyāya. || 2.141 ||

Thus has been stated the purpose of the instruction on designations. That Brahmin who performs the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony according to the rules, and who supports [the child] with food, is called a guru. (2.142)

Not by initiation (*upanayana*) or teaching (*adhyāpana*). This is understood from the force of the context and from the mention of the *niṣeka* (conception rite). Thus, this father is understood to be devoid of the assistance provided by initiation and teaching. And so, he shows merely the assistance beginning with the *niṣeka*, together with nourishment, in the words: "and he provides for him with food. He is thus one who has performed the *aśloka-kāra* (?). The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is for the sake of illustration; the "teacher" (*guru*) is what is being discussed. However, some say that this is indeed a general designation. But this is a specific designation for the one described as "the teacher is the best among gurus. As Vyāsa says:

"The father is the lord, the source of the body, the doer of what is pleasing, the provider of livelihood, the teacher, the instructor of beneficial things, and a visible deity. This very same [principle] regarding the mother should be understood as having been meaningfully indicated by Śaṅkara. For he will say: "But the mother [is worth] a thousand fathers" (MDh 2.145). Alternatively, this [father] is also a *guru*; how much more so are the two preceding ones who assist with the Veda—this is the praise of the *ācārya* and the *upādhyāya*.

He who, being chosen by someone, performs for him the establishment of the sacred fires (āgnyādheya), the cooked sacrifices (pākayajñas), and the soma-sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma and others, is called his officiating priest (ṛtvij) in this world. (2.143)

In this section concerning teachers (*guru-prakaraṇa*), the designation "officiant" (*ṛtvij*) is used as a synonym for the purpose of making known their status as teachers. It is said that for teachers there are duties such as rising to meet them and saluting them; [this term is used] so that these same duties may apply to them as well. Now, this praise is intended to demonstrate the superior excellence of the *ācārya* over all other types of teachers:
"He who truly covers both ears with the Veda—he should be known as mother and father; one should never act treacherously toward him. (2.144)

He covers, that is, he conceals. How? By means of truth. What does he conceal? By means of *brahman*—that is, by teaching the Veda, by explaining its meaning, or by both. What is that? Both ears. Of whom? Of the disciple. "He is to be known as mother and father"—having established this through such a specific benefit, this praise of the teacher is to be understood as being equal to virtuous parents, by virtue of his capacity for instruction in the third stage of life (the *smṛti*). It is not [equal] to those devoid of virtue. Therefore, one should never bear malice toward him; the meaning is that even when one has achieved one's purpose (*kṛtārtha*), at no time whatsoever. Others, however, say: This is a praise of both the *ācārya* and the *upādhyāya*, intended to show that the *ācārya* alone is superior in what follows. But that is incorrect because it would contradict the [grammatical] incapacity [of the singular form]. Therefore, in the passage "He is to be known as mother and father," the praise of the *ācārya*—who possesses greater benefit—is made over against the parents, who possess lesser benefit due to [their role in] the *niṣeka* ceremony and so forth, and who are inferior [to him]. It is said: Because... [text continues].
An Ācārya is ten times more venerable than an Upādhyāya; a father is a hundred times more venerable than an Ācārya; and a mother exceeds even a father a thousandfold in respect. (2.145)

"He who possesses all virtues—since the mother exceeds the father a thousandfold in dignity on account of being the cause of the purificatory rites such as initiation (*upanayana*) and instruction"—this too has been explained. And having established this, it is appropriate to praise the teacher (*ācārya*) as being equal to virtuous parents; however, a father devoid of virtue is merely the cause of procreation and not the cause of the purificatory rites such as initiation. In that regard:

[86] Between the father who begets and the father who gives the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is the more venerable; for the birth through the Veda is eternal for a Brahmin, both after death and in this world. 2.146.
The mention of "Brahmin" is for the sake of illustration, since all three [classes] are under discussion. Furthermore:
One should know that the production of him which occurs when his mother and father unite is merely his birth from a womb. (2.147)

This praise of the teacher and censure of the parents should be understood from the context of the section; and this [verse] is immediately preceding. "But that birth which the teacher, having mastered the Vedas, produces for him according to rule with the Sāvitrī—that is true, that is free from old age and death. (2.148)
By means of a different context, this is another praise of the subject at hand:
"Whether it be little or much, whoever benefits another through sacred learning—know that person here to be a teacher by virtue of that assistance rendered through the learning. (2.149)

If even one who provides only partial assistance is designated as an *upādhyāya*, how much more so the *ācārya* who provides great assistance? Thus, while this praise of the *ācārya* is indeed valid, since praise is not given without cause, it serves to demonstrate the weightiness of this *upādhyāya* as well. Now, this verse is commenced as an introduction to the work of another author (*parakṛti*), for the purpose of praising the subject at hand:
"The creator of the Vedic birth (*brāhma-janman*) and the instructor of one's own duty—by virtue of the Law (*dharma*), even a young Brahmin becomes the father of an elder. (2.150)
And [fatherhood] does not arise from birth. What then? Regarding this meaning—that "the giver of the Veda is the father"—an ancient precedent is cited:
"The young Kavi, son of Aṅgiras, taught his ancestors;
having encompassed them with knowledge, he said to them, 'O little sons! (2.151).
Filled with indignation, they questioned the gods regarding that matter;
and the gods, having assembled, said to them, "The child has spoken what is right for you. (2.152)
For this is the praise given here:
"The ignorant one is indeed a child; he who imparts the mantras is a father.
For they call the ignorant one a 'child,' but the imparter of mantras a 'father. (2.153)
And this being so:
"Neither by years, nor by grey hair, nor by wealth, nor by kinsmen."
The sages established this law: "He who is learned in the Vedas is great among us. (2.154)
And this being so:
"The seniority of Brahmins is by knowledge, that of Kṣatriyas by valor, that of Vaiśyas by grain and wealth, and that of Śūdras alone by birth. (2.155)

The mention of the *vīrya* (valor) and other qualities of the Kṣatriyas and others is for the purpose of praising the subject at hand; since valor and the rest are not the immediate topic, they are cited as examples. This being the established sense of the context, it is said: "One does not become venerable (*sthavira*) merely because one's head is grey.
Even if he is young, the gods know him to be venerable who is devoted to study. (2.156)
And this being so:
"Just as an elephant made of wood, just as a deer made of leather, and a Brahmin who has not studied—these three merely bear the name. (2.157)
Moreover:

Just as a eunuch is fruitless with women, just as a cow is fruitless with a cow, just as a gift given to an ignorant person is fruitless, so too is a Brahmin who knows not the Rigveda fruitless. (2.158)
It appears that this commentary should be connected with verse 2.149—or perhaps 145?

By virtue of the context, even those scriptural citations (*śruti*), though existing for other purposes, serve to praise the Teacher (*ācārya*). This should be understood as consisting of an excellence of praise through the power of the statement, following the example of the exceptional benefit and the respect accorded to teachers, which surpasses even that shown to parents. Because both types of instruction are purposeful, when there is a concurrence of the sacrificial teacher, the father, and the mother, the [respect due to] the Teacher is optionally substituted for that due to the father and mother in matters of salutation and worship.
Now, even for a religious student (*brahmacārin*), this rule for the teacher is stated regarding study with a serene mind:
"By non-injury alone toward living beings"—
by virtue of the context, this refers to the students.

Instruction regarding what is beneficial is a duty; it is connected with the teaching of the Vedic scriptures, word by word and without interruption. This is a prohibition against unrighteous acts such as violence that might otherwise follow from worldly motives. [88] And speech that is sweet and gentle should be employed by one who desires righteousness. 2.159.
And from this rule of instruction, it follows that there is Dharma, as in: "He for whom all these rules [apply] to everyone. And thus is this praise of the subject at hand:
"He whose speech and mind are pure and always perfectly guarded, he indeed attains the entire fruit realized through the Vedānta. (2.160)
And this being so:

even when distressed, one should not be a wounder of others; one should not have a mind intent on acts of malice toward others; nor should one utter that speech by which another is agitated, for such speech does not lead to the higher worlds. (2.161)

Furthermore, if someone out of pride or arrogance should fail to honor the teacher or even treat him with contempt, the teacher should nevertheless avoid mental agitation through this reflection and means:
"A Brahmin should always tremble at honor as if it were poison;
he should desire contempt from all sides as if it were nectar. (2.162)
For what reason?
Because he who is held in contempt sleeps in happiness and wakes in happiness;
he moves through this world in happiness, while the one who holds others in contempt perishes. 2.163

The following two verses are intended to show how one might approach the teacher in a way that causes agitation of his mind. Alternatively, this may be understood as a general rule taught in another context, mentioned here for the purpose of praising the student (*adhyāpya*) and the religious student (*brahmacārin*), rather than being a new injunction. Why is such an extensive discourse on restraints and observances prescribed for the religious student? [It is asked: "How so? [The answer is: "By name. By this sequence of practices, the twice-born man, having purified his self, while dwelling with his teacher, should gradually accumulate the austerity conducive to the acquisition of the Veda. (2.164)

This verse serves to conclude the subject matter at hand: "And this being so, by this very student who has thus purified his self—through various specific austerities and vows enjoined by rule—the entire Veda, together with its secret portions (Upanishads), must be mastered by the twice-born. (2.165)

By various kinds of specific austerities (*tapoviśeṣa*)—such as maintaining the sacred fires, kindling the fire, and wandering for alms—as well as by those already mentioned and those yet to be mentioned, namely the duties (*dharma*) of the student (*brahmacārin*) known as restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), through their teaching in this particular section; and by vows (*vrata*) prescribed in the *Gṛhya-śāstras* for each Veda, the Veda—consisting of the *Mantra* and *Brāhmaṇa* portions—is to be mastered by the student whose self has been refined. This is a synonym for the acquisition of the Veda. Its qualification is "entire" (*kṛtsna*), meaning together with its auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga*). How, then, is this understood? It is said that this entirety refers to the Veda, and not merely to the *Mantra* portion in relation to the *Brāhmaṇa*. Since both *Mantra* and *Brāhmaṇa* are names for the Veda, it is appropriate to designate them as parts when the word "Veda" lacks sufficient power [to denote the whole]. Furthermore, it is understood that the collection called "Veda," consisting of *Mantra* and *Brāhmaṇa* along with the auxiliaries, possesses the capacity for accomplishing human goals (*puruṣārtha*), but not the *Mantra* alone. Therefore, it is stated to be "entire" because it is independent when accompanied by its auxiliaries. Likewise, this word-commentary (*padabhāṣya*) is indeed a compendium of Smṛti: "The Veda with its six auxiliaries (*ṣaḍaṅga*) must be studied by a Brāhmaṇa without [any worldly] motive. "Together with the secret portion" (*sarahasya*) is a qualification of that very same thing. But what is that "secret portion"? It is the knowledge of the performance of the Veda’s purpose. Why, then, is this knowledge the meaning of the word "Upaniṣad"? Because of its capacity and because the *Rahasya-brāhmaṇa* is included under the term "Veda. Again, its separate mention is improper, since there is no contradiction with the inclusion of the auxiliaries as "entire," and because it would not be the subject matter of the treatise (*śāstra*), as another meaning is possible. It is improper to claim that the word "secret" (*rahasya*) has a different scope, since its meaning is precisely as stated. [Objection: Is this not already established by the instruction on the acquisition of the auxiliaries, such that "together with the secret portion" is proven? [Response: No, because the acquisition of that knowledge is not established by the mere study of the words themselves. Therefore, this instruction is for the sake of a further effort. Or, this instruction is given by way of permission regarding a different scope, using the phrase "together with the secret portion" to show respect. This is because of the capacity for eligibility for ritual acts (*karmādhikāra*), and because of the indicative marks of the Śruti, such as: "The learned one sacrifices; the learned one causes [others] to sacrifice. Thus, this Smṛti rule regarding the study of the entire Veda applies to a student who has accomplished his purpose by studying only one Veda. Accordingly, the singular number is used in the word "Veda. And so he will say:
Having studied the Vedas— either all of them, or two of them, or even one— in the proper order,
and having remained inviolate in his student discipline (*brahmacarya*), he should enter the stage of the householder (*gṛhasthāśrama*).

Thus it is said. Another *smṛti* likewise states: "Having studied one branch (*śākhā*) of the Veda, one becomes a *śrotriya*. And it is logical that a specific result should follow from a specific effort. However, this rule applies specifically to one who studies the three Vedas; only one who has studied the three Vedas is a *śrotriya*, not one who has studied only a single Veda. As for the claim made by some that the literal meaning of the word [in the rule] implies the study of two Vedas because of the mention of "the whole" (*kṛtsna*), that is improper. Furthermore, as for what is said regarding the form of the sentence-meaning: the claim by some that the term "Veda" refers to the *mantra*, "the whole" refers to the ritual action (*karman*), "Brāhmaṇa" refers to a collection of *mantras*, and "secret portion" (*rahasya*) refers to the *Upaniṣads*—this too should be understood as mere attention [to specific details]. And having established this:
A twice-born man of the highest order, desiring to perform austerity, should always practice the Veda;
for the study of the Veda is declared here to be the supreme austerity for a Brahmin. (2.166)

The statement "the entire Veda is to be mastered" (MDh 2.165) is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for the injunction that has been heard. And because of the context, this instruction pertains to the religious student (*brahmacārin*); however, due to the inclusion of the word "always," it should be understood as a duty specifically for the twice-born. Alternatively, the inclusion of the word "always" is intended to refer to the obligatory expiatory rite (*nityaprāyaścitta*). Accordingly, the *Vājasaneyaka* Brāhmaṇa reiterates this very point: "Even if he is adorned with garlands, that twice-born man performs the highest austerity unto his very fingernails, who studies his own Vedic lesson daily to the best of his ability" (2.167).

The word *ā* (or *āśabda*) has no connection with the term *nakhāgra* (the tips of the nails). The word *ha* signifies tradition (*aitihya*). The word *eva* is used for emphasis. We shall state the meaning of the sentence: "From the tips of the nails, this person performs austerity who studies his own Veda (*svādhyāya*). The meaning is that he practices the Veda. For thus it is heard in the section praising *svādhyāya*: "Even if one is anointed, adorned, and lying on his bed, if he studies his *svādhyāya*, he indeed performs austerity from the tips of his nails. He who, knowing this, studies his *svādhyāya*—therefore, the *svādhyāya* must be studied. This should be understood as an excellence of praise for the practice of the Veda under discussion. By this, it is shown that even one who is "wearing garlands" (*sragvī*)—meaning one who, due to being an organ [of sense], lacks [proper conduct] at the tips of his nails—is still performing austerity. This statement, "the Veda must be studied even by one whose conduct is contradictory," is intended primarily as praise; it is not intended as an instruction for a mandatory injunction. And this mention of "wearing garlands" should be understood as applying to all transgressions of the rules of study. Thus, the Brāhmaṇa has been cited: "The entire Veda is to be mastered" (MDh 2.165). By this, the sequence of studying the Veda along with its auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga-veda*), which follows naturally from the context, is here restricted.
The twice-born man who, without having studied the Veda, exerts himself in other pursuits, quickly sinks to the status of a Śūdra while still alive, along with his descendants. (2.168)

This rule is stated for one who has been initiated (*upanīta*). This being the case, some say that there is no prohibition against studying the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) prior to initiation. We, however, believe that this rule is undertaken because, by the force of such statements as "by specific austerities" (MDh 2.165) and by the context, the study of the Veda along with its auxiliaries necessarily applies to one who is already initiated; thus, this restriction is commenced. And so, this censure of transgression—"he quickly falls to the state of a Śūdra while still alive, together with his lineage"—is intended to praise the study [of the Veda]. In this treatise, as in common worldly practice, one should understand that injunctions and prohibitions are inferred from praise and censure. Furthermore, because of the commonality of eligibility for Vedic study, it is said that "he quickly falls to the state of a Śūdra. The phrase "together with his lineage" serves to intensify the censure, and for the purpose of further intensifying the praise of the subject at hand. This [verse] praises this "birth as a Brahmin" (*brahmajanman*), which is the purpose of the eligibility for Vedic study.

The first birth of a twice-born man is from his mother; the second is at the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass; the third is at the initiation for sacrifice, as ordained by the rule (or, according to the injunction of the Śruti). 2.169.

The statement, "First, birth from a mother," is not a word of censure regarding birth from a womb, because it serves to demonstrate the mother by way of its occurrence; rather, it is for the purpose of praising the birth from Brahman (*brahmajanman*), since that is the subject at hand here. Furthermore, praise is appropriate here because this [birth] is the cause for the study of the Veda. Regarding this, he provides an illustration: just as the initiation for a sacrifice (*yajñadīkṣā*) has the purpose of elevating one's birth and is not merely a matter of existing, so too is this birth from Brahman. Thus, through this indirect means, there is praise of the subject under discussion. Birth is observed to be caused by a mother and father; therefore, even in the case of birth from Brahman, he figuratively designates a mother and father for the sake of praising either the immediate or the remote subject. In that regard—
In that regard, as for his birth from Brahman ordained by the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass, in that [birth] Sāvitrī is said to be his mother and the teacher his father. (2.170)
First, he states the cause:
[91] Because of imparting the Veda, they call the teacher "father."
And likewise for the *sāvitrī*, which is the mother of the religious student (*brahmacārin*) and constitutes his preparatory rite:
"Indeed, no ritual act whatsoever is enjoined for him prior to the tying of the girdle of muñja grass. (2.171)

[This refers to] the study [of the Veda] and so forth. This is a praise of the subject at hand by way of another method. Thus it says: "In this case—that being so—one should not utter the *brahman* [formula] except for the purpose of the counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) regarding the utterance of *svadhā*. "One should not utter the *brahman* except for the pouring of *svadhā* (*svadhā-ninayana*). That by which the *svadhā* is poured into the ancestral rite (*pitrya-karman*), such as the rising [of the vessel], is called "pouring" (*ninayana*); thus, this mantra is understood through the power of the counter-exception. And having established it thus, this restatement (*anuvāda*) is made for the purpose of praising the enjoined matter.
For he remains equal to a Śūdra as long as he is not born into the Veda. || 2.172 ||

And so another *smṛti* states: "Prior to initiation (*upanayana*), one may act, speak, and eat according to one's desire" (GDh 2.1). Others read the root *harati* with the prefix *pra-* in the sense of "not to utter," as in "he should not utter [the Veda]. That is incorrect, because of the force of another *smṛti*: "He should not utter the *brahman* [Veda], except for the offering of the *svadhā*" (GDh 2.9). Therefore, the root *harati* is stated here with the causative suffix (*ṇi*). This instruction is for the father, not for the boy. Or, even if it were for the boy, there would be no fault in the scripture if the root were used in its primitive form (*prakṛti*). Now, since the study of the Veda by this student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) is established as following initiation—based on such indicative marks as "In that regard, his birth as a Brahmin is marked by the tying of the girdle of muñja grass" (MDh 2.170)—this [section] is commenced for the purpose of prescribing the sequence of its performance.

For one who has undergone the initiation ceremony (upanayana), the instruction in the observances (vratādeśana) is prescribed, as well as the formal acquisition of the Veda (brahmagrahaṇa), in due order according to the rules. (2.173)
[Editor’s note: This verse is cited in the commentary on verse 4.80. There, in the first quarter, where the reading is "kṛtopanayanasyāsya," the variant reading is "na cāpy anupanītasya."]

Immediately after the initiation (*upanayana*), there is the instruction regarding the observances (*vratādeśana*). For one who has been instructed in the Veda and its associated vows, the practice of those Vedic vows follows this sequence or procedure for those studying the *brahma* (the Veda) according to the rule; this is for the purpose of establishing that regulation. Now, since it is established that the student (*brahmacārin*) must wear the skin, the sacred thread (*sūtra*), the girdle (*mekhalā*), the staff (*daṇḍa*), and the garment—those items prescribed at the initiation—for as long as his studentship lasts, the following is commenced:
"Whatever skin, whatever thread, and whatever girdle is prescribed for each."
Whatever staff he has and whatever garment he wears, that very same [staff and garment] he carries even during his religious observances. (2.174)

And thus, in the instruction on the vows, having performed the relinquishment (*utsarga*) of the former ones, those [vows] are to be adopted by him; however, those very same [objects] are not to be retained. For their rule of practice has already been established: "The girdle, the skin, the staff," and so forth. And because of the context, this other [set of rules] for the religious student (*brahmacārin*) is stated for the purpose of teaching the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*): "But the religious student, dwelling with his teacher, should observe these observances, having fully restrained the collection of his senses, for the sake of increasing his own ascetic merit. (2.175)
The mention of "observances" (*niyama*) is for the sake of illustration; for he will speak of those as well: "First, these are his observances:
having bathed daily, being pure, he should perform the libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors, as well as the worship of the deities and the placing of fuel on the sacred fire" (2.176).

The inclusion of the word "always" (*nitya*) is for the purpose of reiterating out of respect, or for the purpose of establishing it as a general rule (*jāti-dharma*); and the mention of the placing of fuel-sticks (*samid-ādhāna*) is for the sake of the proper sequence, not for the purpose of an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*). As for the restrictive rules (*niyama*):
"He should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, savory flavors, women, all fermented acids, and the harming of living beings. (2.177)

Is the consumption of honey and other such things here intended for the purpose of praise? "Sour" (*śukta*) refers to harsh speech. And because violence is prohibited in this context regarding that which is parched and devoid of essence, these words are directed toward [such speech]; for there is a prohibition regarding the five flavors because they serve a specific purpose. And thus says the Śrauta Sūtra: "Sour words" (GDh 2.19). Furthermore: Anointing the body, applying collyrium to the eyes, wearing shoes and carrying an umbrella, as well as lust, anger, greed, dancing, singing, and playing musical instruments. (2.178)

This prohibition of ointments for the body follows from the prohibition of [cosmetic] eye-ointment by implication. From the prohibition of women follows the prohibition of sexual desire. Furthermore, it is for another purpose: namely, the prohibition of those things which would otherwise be undertaken.
Gambling, idle gossip, slander, and likewise falsehood; gazing at and touching women, and injury to others. (2.179)

Regarding women, looking at them and touching them are forbidden for him whose eye of inner disposition (*bhāva-cakṣus*) is free from transgression; the purpose for undertaking this has been stated. He should always sleep alone—why? Because [otherwise] he might somehow smell [the scent of] a woman.
He shall not spill his semen anywhere.
The explanatory passage for this is: "For by spilling his semen out of desire, he destroys his own vow. (2.180)
[93] Even though this transgression is not part of the current topic, the penance for it is stated here for the sake of emphasis:
"If a twice-born student of sacred knowledge should involuntarily emit semen during sleep,"
Having bathed and worshipped the sun, he should then mutter three times the verse beginning with "mām". (2.181)

The mention of the *brahmacārin* (celibate student) is due to the context; therefore, this expiation applies to him alone in the event of a transgression, and not to others. His specific rules are as follows:
"He should fetch a water-pot, flowers, cow-dung, earth, and *kuśa* grass, as much as required; he should eat his food every day. (2.182)

The instruction for collecting alms daily is for the sake of the teacher, for one's own sake, or for the sake of both; it is intended to prohibit the practice of eating alms-food stored over time and to introduce what follows. From those houses, however, he should collect alms every day, being self-restrained: from those who are not deficient in Vedic study and sacrifices, who are eminent in their own duties, the student, being pure, should fetch alms (2.183).
Restrained in mind, speech, and sight—this is the primary rule for the twice-born regarding the practice of begging for alms. Its specific qualification is as follows:
"He should not beg from the family of his teacher, nor from the families of his paternal or maternal kin.
But if houses of others are unavailable, he should avoid each preceding one [in the list of forbidden relatives] in favor of the next. (2.184)

The prohibition of the teacher’s family (*gurukulapratiṣedha*) implies that begging even from the teacher’s family is established by the sense of the rule. Alternatively, the term *gurukula* refers to the teacher’s household itself, whereas the *jñātikula* (the family of kinsmen) belongs to the student (*brahmacārin*). Or, the *gurukula* may refer to the teacher’s own lineage (*sagotra*), provided that there is no failure to find houses belonging to those related through the mother or father or through the *tṛpya* degree of kinship. In the absence of such [related] houses, one should seek the houses of unrelated *śrotriyas*. This is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) for what is otherwise permitted by the scriptures. Furthermore, this is a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*) to be used when the primary option is unavailable. Indeed, one may wander through the entire village if the aforementioned [houses] are not available.
Having restrained his speech, he should set out, but he must avoid those who have been cursed.

From the word *sarva* ("all"), and because of the prohibition [of certain individuals], it is taught that alms may be accepted from all four castes (*varṇas*). And so says Gautama: "The wandering for alms is from all castes, with the exception of those accused of crimes and those who have fallen [from their status]" (GDh 2.35). An accusation (*abhiśaṃsana*) constitutes a minor offense (*upapātaka*); since there is a prohibition regarding those mentioned, by the logic of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpikayā*), [the prohibition applies] to those guilty of major sins (*mahāpātakin*), and not to others who are lighter offenders. Having fetched fuel-sticks from afar, he should place them in the open air.
He should, unwearied, offer oblations with those [verses] into the fire every evening and morning. (2.186)

[94] The word *dūra* (far) has its meaning understood by implication. The phrase *saṃnidadhyād vihāyasi* (he should place it in the air) is for the purpose of prohibiting contact with the ground. Because fuel (*samidh*) is the abode of many minute living beings, [the rule] "lest there be a mass of living beings moving upon the earth" is intended. Without having gone for alms and without having kindled the fire...
If he is not ill, he shall observe the vow of the Avakīrṇin for seven nights.

Having failed to go out for alms, having risen repeatedly [to perform his duties] for seven nights without interruption, and likewise having failed to kindle the sacred fire—provided he is not in a state of illness. What then? When there is a transgression of either of these two—failing to kindle the fire or failing to go for alms—he, being healthy, shall perform the vow of the *avakīrṇin*. Some say this applies even when the omission is done intentionally (*cittena*). This point is considered, as it is not well-established: is this sentence intended to prescribe an expiation for the transgression, as it is heard [in the text], or is it for the purpose of indicating the gravity of the offense? On this matter, it is said: This is not a prescription for an expiation. What then? This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) regarding the rule of the seven nights, because an expiation is not the subject under discussion (*aprakaraṇāt*). These two transgressions are not listed among the minor offenses (*upapātaka*). Nor can an expiation for these be somehow inferred from another source. And this being so, the mention of the *avakīrṇin* is for the purpose of making known the gravity of this act—that such is this improper deed that the expiation of an *avakīrṇin* must be performed here. Even in the view that this is an expiation, this instruction should be understood as being outside the immediate context (*aprakaraṇa*), like the instruction on expiations for transgressing the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and so forth; it is for the sake of showing respect. Regarding this view, some say: "There is a general expiation prescribed for one who is ill. For if there were no expiation whatsoever for the ill, then [the rule] regarding eating meat and so forth would not apply to them. Nor is this desired, since everyone is always authorized by the fixed Smṛti rules. An authorization excluding the ill is not tenable. Furthermore, one cannot establish a contingent (*pākṣika*) obligation by looking at an occasional (*anitya*) exemption for the ill, especially since there is no accidental Smṛti rule stating that there is no fault for the ill regarding the mere kindling of the fire and going for alms. To this we reply: Since authorization is defined by the scriptural injunction (*śastra-lakṣaṇatvāt*), authorization should be understood according to the scripture, not by inference. For where there is a scriptural prohibition of authorization for the ill, there they are not authorized at first, as in other cases: "Neither the ill nor at midnight" (MDh 4.129), and "The healthy man [should close] his own sense-orifices" (MDh 4.144). Moreover, where such a prohibition does not exist, one should know that the person is authorized there precisely by virtue of the general rule of authorization. This being so, there is no room for the aforementioned logic here. And since this is the case: [The verse follows: *Akṛtvā bhaikṣacaraṇam utthāyotthāyāvyavahitaṃ saptarātram asamidhya ca pāvakam / na sarvāvasthaḥ / kiṃ tarhi / anāturaḥ sann anayor anindhanabhakṣacaraṇayoḥ pratyekavyatikrame saty ayam avakīrṇivrataṃ caret / cittenāpy anākṛta iti kecit / tad etad aprasiddhaṃ vicāryate / kim idaṃ vyatikramaprāyaścittopadeśaparaṃ vākyam, yathā śrūyate, āho svid ayaṃ gauravopadeśanārtham / atrocyate / nedaṃ prāyaścittavidhānam / kiṃ tarhi / saptarātravidhyarho 'yam arthavādaḥ, aprakaraṇāt prāyaścittasya / naitau vyatikramāv upapātakamadhyapaṭhitau / naitāsām anyād idam atra prāyaścittaṃ kathaṃcit kalpyeta / evaṃ ca saty avakīrṇigrahaṇam asya gurutvajñāpanārtham īdṛśam etad akāryaṃ yenāvakīrṇiprāyaścittam atra caritavyam iti prāyaścittapakṣe 'pi saṃdhyopāsanādipratikramaprāyaścittopadeśavad ayam aprakaraṇo 'pi ca tadupadeśo 'yaṃ vijñeyaḥ ādarārthaḥ / asmiṃś ca pakṣe yat kaiścid ucyate – "āturasya sāmānyavihitaṃ prāyaścittam asti / yadi hy ātursaya na kiṃcit prāyaścittaṃ bhaven māṃsabhakṣaṇādiṣv anyatamaṃ (? na syāt / na caitad iṣṭaṃ niyatasmṛtyā sarvasya sarvadādhikṛtatvāt / nāturavarjam adhikāra upapadyate / na ca nityo 'dhikāram anityam āturaraṃ prekṣya (? pākṣikaḥ sādhayitum (? / na cāgnīndhanabhaikṣyacaraṇayoḥ kevalayor āturasyādoṣasmṛtir ākasmikī yuktā" iti / atra brūmaḥ / śastralakṣaṇatvād adhikārasya yathāśāstram adhikāro vijñeyaḥ, nānumānataḥ / yatra hy āturasyādhikārapratiṣedhaśāstram asti, tatrādau nādhikriyate yathānyatra "nāturo na mahāniśi" (MDh 4.129), "anāturaḥ svāni khāni" (MDh 4.144) / kiṃ ca yatra tv asya tan nāsti tatrāsāv adhikāraśāstrād eva tasminn adhikṛto veditavyaḥ / evaṃ ca saty atra nāsti yathoktanyāyāvakāśaḥ / yataś caitad evam ataḥ –* [The verse follows: *Anāturaḥ samidhaḥ pāṇinā juhuyād ākāṣṭhād bhaikṣacaryāṃ ca caran / saptarātram akṛtvaitad avakīrṇivrataṃ caret //* One who is not ill should offer fuel-sticks with his hand until wood is available, while practicing the life of a mendicant. If he fails to do this for seven nights, he should perform the vow of the *avakīrṇin*. [Commentary: The phrase "until wood is available" (*ākāṣṭhāt*) means until wood is obtained. The term "hand" (*pāṇinā*) is used to exclude the use of ladles and other implements. The phrase "while practicing the life of a mendicant" (*bhaikṣacaryāṃ ca caran*) indicates that the offering of fuel-sticks and the begging for alms are both required. It is not the case that one may simply choose between them. The word "and" (*ca*) implies that both are necessary. The mention of "seven nights" is for the purpose of praising the rule, as it is not the subject of the current context. The mention of the *avakīrṇin* is to indicate the gravity of the act, signifying that such a failure is a serious misdeed for which the specific expiation of an *avakīrṇin* must be performed. Even in the view that this is an expiation, this instruction should be understood as being outside the immediate context, like the instruction on expiations for transgressing the twilight prayers; it is for the sake of showing respect. Regarding this view, what some say—"There is a general expiation prescribed for the ill. For if there were no expiation for the ill, then [the
One who observes the vow should always subsist on alms and must not eat the food of a single person;
for it is traditionally taught that the livelihood of a vow-observer sustained by alms is equal to fasting.

To this it is replied: regarding the statement, “He should go for alms every day” (MDh 2.182), the injunction for alms is not for the purpose of establishing a means of livelihood, since that is already established by the general rule of conduct (*vṛtti*). [Objection: But then this [specific rule] is redundant. [Reply: Its commencement is for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyama*). How so? So that even when food is available, the student’s livelihood shall be by alms alone. This commencement serves as a restriction against accepting gifts and other such means; for while the general rule might apply in the absence of [other options], there is no such restriction when those [other means] are present. Alternatively, the repetition is for the sake of an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*): “The livelihood of one observing a vow through alms is declared to be equal to fasting. Or, this is a concluding summary of the practice of living on alms. Or, the repetition is intended to make known the greater weight of alms-gathering compared to the kindling of the sacred fires. Or, this repeated mention is for the purpose of providing an exception (*pratiprasava*) to the prohibition against eating the food of a single person. And thus it is said: [95] Or, this is the commencement [of the section] from the kindling of the fire onwards, for the purpose of making known the gravity of alms-gathering. Or, this repeated statement is for the purpose of counteracting the eating of food from a single source, which has been prohibited. And so it is stated in the *Rabhe* [text].
In a rite dedicated to the gods, one should eat like one observing a vow; in a rite for the ancestors, one may eat like a seer (ṛṣi).
At will, one may eat at the invitation of a guest; his vow is not thereby violated. (2.189)

"One who possesses a vow (*vratavān*) is so called because he is worthy of a vow. What then? He should eat food that is devoid of honey and meat. At what time? At a *daivadaivatyam* [rite]; that is, at a *abhyudaya-śrāddha* (prosperity rite) for which the gods are the deities. Being invited to such a rite, even if he is observing a vow, the scripture states: "One may, at will, engage a daughter's son (*dauhitra*) who is standing in a vow at a *śrāddha*" (MDh 3.234). Thus, for him while eating, even a single meal of that [forbidden] food does not destroy his vow; therefore, the eating of village food from the beginning of the cycle [of rites] is to be understood as occurring here, since forest food is taught later on. That which has the ancestors as its deities is *pitrya*; this refers to the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* and other *śrāddhas*. Here, "forest food" (*āraṇya*) means the food of sages (*munyanna*), characterized as previously described. This being the case, this regulation regarding the giving of village or forest food and so forth does not apply to the student (*brahmacārin*) with respect to *daiva* and *pitrya* *śrāddhas*, such that the phrase "that" would be inappropriate. Nor is this a qualification of the food of ascetics (*tāpasa*) under this teaching. From this also, it is known that this qualification cannot possibly be for the purpose of teaching forest food. And having established this, whatever is not contrary to his vow—whether village or forest food—he should eat when invited at those two [types of] *śrāddhas* alone for one day, and not elsewhere. In this way, the mention of *daiva* and *pitrya* becomes meaningful. Some, however, explain the eating of village and forest food in the context of *daiva* and *pitrya* according to the aforementioned qualifications by way of a division of scope: village food for the *daiva* [rite] like one observing a vow, and sage-food for the *pitrya* [rite]. This matter of the student's threefold conduct has been deliberated. Now, since the eating of a single meal at a *śrāddha* might apply to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas just as it does to Brāhmaṇas, this [text] is commenced to prohibit that."
This duty has been taught by the wise as belonging solely to the Brāhmaṇa;
however, for the Rājanya and the Vaiśya, this duty is not prescribed in such a manner. (2.190)

Nor is this already established by the preceding [verses], such as "he whose mouth they always eat from" (MDh 1.95). For that [verse] must be understood as dependent upon this, because this [present verse] is an injunction of prohibition, and because of the force of its instruction within the context of praising the Brāhmaṇa. Having concluded that [section] with the word "of him" (*tasya*), another rule regarding the conduct of the religious student (*brahmacārin*) is stated in that very same context: "Whether urged by his teacher or even without being urged, he should constantly apply himself to his studies and to the welfare of his teacher. (2.191)
The undertaking is for the sake of the objects [of experience]:
namely, the body, speech, the faculties of perception, and the mind.
Restraining himself, he should stand with palms joined in reverence, gazing at the face of his teacher.
[96] This is the rule for the time of study and at other times when in the presence of the teacher; this is another [rule] for that occasion:
"One should always have the hand uplifted, be of virtuous conduct, and well-restrained."
And when told, "Be seated," he should sit facing the teacher.

The meaning is that he should sit down only when permitted. This rule, moreover, is universal. And this is another [point]: because of the use of the word "always" (*sadā*), the duty of the vow (*vratadharma*) should be understood as lasting for the duration of one's life.
He should always have inferior food, clothing, and appearance in the presence of the teacher; he should rise before him and go to bed after him. (2.194)
Except when about to sleep, this is another rule of conduct for him:
he should not engage in answering a call or in conversation while lying down, nor while sitting, nor while eating, nor while standing, nor with his face turned away. (2.195)
What then?

One standing should perform [the service] for one who is seated; but for one who is approaching, one should go forward; for one who is coming toward oneself, one should go out to meet him; and for one who is running, one should run behind him. (2.196)
Facing one who has turned away, approaching the presence of one who is far off, bowing to one who is lying down, and likewise standing before one who is staying in a foreign land. (2.197)
In the presence of his teacher, his bed and seat should always be low; within the range of the teacher's vision, he should not sit as he pleases. (2.198)
One should not utter his name alone, even in his absence;
nor should one imitate his gait, speech, or gestures. (2.199)
Even though these [rules] have been taught in the section concerning the religious student (*brahmacārin*), they are to be observed for as long as one lives:
"Wherever censure or even reproach of the teacher occurs,
there the ears should be covered, or one should depart from that place to another" (2.200).

This [injunction] regarding the non-hearing and non-instruction of slander and censure directed toward one's teacher is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to the preceding rule: "And one should not imitate his gait, speech, or gestures" (2.199). How so? For where even the hearing of slander against the teacher is not permitted, how much less the imitation of his gait and so forth performed by oneself? What, then, is the distinction between these two—slander (*parivāda*) and censure (*nindā*)? Slander is the recounting of the actual physical actions of the person concerned.
