This being so, this becomes a separate sentence due to the difference in meaning. The word *sadā* ("always") is a supplement to both of those. How so? Even though the censure of the birth of a second or subsequent son for one who already has a son is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*)—"they know the others to be born of desire" (MDh 9.107)—nevertheless, the meaning is: "Even one who has a son should be devoted to his own wife. Thus says the Vedic mantra: "Place ten sons in her; make the husband the eleventh. The phrase "avoiding the wives of others, always" applies even to the view of appointing a widow, by the words "or from one of the same caste" (MDh 9.59). But another says: approaching during the *ṛtukāla* is appropriate only toward a woman of the same caste (*sajātīya*) and of the same class (*savarṇā*), because of the possibility of propriety (*yuktatva*); whereas toward others, it is merely the natural state. That, moreover, must be deliberated upon as to whether it is right or not. Now, by the words "avoiding the forbidden days," he prevents approaching during the first seven nights of the *ṛtu*, which would otherwise be established by the previous scriptural rule. And so he will say.
On the new moon day, the eighth, the full moon, and the fourteenth,
a twice-born *snātaka* should always remain celibate, even during the fertile period.

If this were the case, there would be the fault of tautology (*punaruktadoṣa*). I shall demonstrate right there how tautology does not occur between these two [rules]. Alternatively, this is a restatement for the sake of what follows. From the force of the initial statement, it is understood that one should approach her even outside the fertile period (*anṛtu*), with the exception of the forbidden lunar days (*parvan*). But surely, since this has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) and because such a purpose is possible, the initial statement is made. And if there were no initial statement, let there be a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) in the form: "one should approach her with the exception of the *parvan*. There is no need for two separate sentences. [The opponent asks: "One should approach her during the fertile period" and "one should approach her with the exception of the *parvan"—if the initial statement exists, then even though the act serves the purpose of obtaining offspring, those two [rules] remain. Regarding the phrase "being devoted to her" (*tadvrataḥ*): the remainder of the sentence is "having become devoted to her. What is that devotion? It is the vow (*vrata*) of not intending [sexual union] with another man; he who possesses that vow is "devoted to her" (*tadvrataḥ*). By the logic of the "camel-faced" compound (*uṣṭramukhanyāya*), one of the two words *vrata* is elided. Or, he whose vow is toward her is "devoted to her"; his vow consists in protecting her. And he becomes such if he approaches her according to his desire out of a wish for her pleasure, and not out of a desire for self-indulgence. Rather, it is out of regard for his wife. Furthermore, the letter *a* here should be understood as a *sāṃhittika* (phonetic combination). Thus, by restraining the mind through non-obstruction of her pleasure, he becomes "devoted to her. And so the author will say later: *na ca tatkāmitāyāṃ strī gamyānyā tu kāmataḥ |* *anṛtāv api gacchaṃs tu tāṃ sa rakṣitum arhati ||* *(MDh 4.40)* "And a woman should not be approached by another at her own desire; however, she may be approached by him at his own desire. Even when not in season, he who approaches her is able to protect her. And: *ṛtukālābhigāmī syādyāvat putro 'bhi jāyate |* *ṛtāv upeyāt sarvatra vā pratiṣiddhavarjam ||* *(MDh 3.45–46)* "One should approach her during the fertile period until a son is born. Or he should approach her during the fertile period, or at all times except on the forbidden days. And: *strīṇām āliṅganādhāni kāmatas tāni kurvataḥ |* *ahorātram upāsīta prajāpatyam akāmataḥ ||* *(MDh 11.178)* "For one who performs acts such as embracing women out of desire, he should perform a *prājāpatya* penance for a day and a night if it was unintentional. And: *paradārābhimaśaṃ tu kṛtvā kāmād dvijottamaḥ |* *kṛcchrātikṛcchrau kurvīta cāndrāyaṇam athāpi vā ||* *(MDh 11.176)* "But having intentionally touched another's wife, the best of the twice-born should perform a *kṛcchra*, an *atikṛcchra*, or even a *cāndrāyaṇa*. And: *yo 'kāmāṃ dūṣayet kanyāṃ sa kṛcchraṃ sāntapanaṃ caret |* *kāmatas tu parākaṃ vai tathā kṛcchrābdaṃ eva vā ||* *(MDh 11.173)* "He who defiles an unwilling maiden should perform a *sāntapana-kṛcchra*; but if intentionally, a *parāka* or even a year-long *kṛcchra*. And: *parivittiḥ parivettā yayā ca parividyate |* *paryādhātā tadādhāyī ca te sarve patitāḥ smṛtāḥ ||* *(MDh 3.172)* "The elder brother whose younger brother marries before him, the younger brother who marries before him, the woman who is so married, the younger brother who gives her away, and the elder brother who accepts her—all these are declared fallen (*patita*). And: *parivettā parivittiś ca yayā ca parividyate |* *sarve te narakaṃ yānti dātṛ-yājaka-pañcamāḥ ||* *(MDh 3.171)* "The younger brother who marries before the elder, the elder brother so superseded, the woman who is superseded, the giver, and the officiating priest as the fifth—they all go to hell. And: *parivettā parivittiś ca saṃskartā caiva yaḥ pumān |* *kṛcchrātikṛcchrau kurvīraṃs teṣāṃ pāpaviśuddhaye ||* *(MDh 3.173)* "The younger brother who marries before the elder, the elder brother so superseded, and the man who performs the marriage ceremony—these should perform the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances for the purification of their sin. And: *parivettā parivittiś ca saṃskartā caiva yo naraḥ |* *kuryur ete tathā kṛcchraṃ māsaṃ cāndrāyaṇaṃ tathā ||* *(MDh 3.174)* "The younger brother who marries before the elder, the elder brother so superseded, and the man who performs the rite—these should likewise perform a *kṛcchra* and a *cāndrāyaṇa* for a month. And: *parivettā prayuñjīta kṛcchraṃ cāndrāyaṇottaram |* *parivittis tathā kuryāt kṛcchraṃ sāntapanaṃ tathā ||* *(MDh 3.175)* "The younger brother who marries before the elder should perform a *kṛcchra* followed by a *cāndrāyaṇa*; the elder brother so superseded should likewise perform a *kṛcchra* and a *sāntapana*. And: *parivittiḥ parivettā yayā ca parividyate |* *careyuḥ sarve kṛcchrārdhaṃ svasthair iṣṭaṃ vivarjayet ||* *(MDh 3.176)* "The elder brother so superseded, the younger brother who marries before him, and the woman who is superseded—all these should perform half a *kṛcchra*. Those who are healthy should avoid performing a sacrifice [for them]. And: *parivittiḥ parivettā dātā yaś caiva yājakaḥ |* *te sarve narakaṃ yānti dātṛ-yājaka-pañcamāḥ ||* *(MDh 3.171)* "The elder brother so superseded, the younger brother who marries before him, the giver, and the officiating priest—they all go to hell, with the giver and the priest as the fifth. And: *parivittiḥ parivettā ca saṃskartā caiva yo naraḥ |* *kṛcchraṃ cāndrāyaṇaṃ caiva careyus te
[117] By protecting his wife, he indeed protects his offspring, his conduct, his lineage, himself, and his own dharma; therefore, he should guard her with great effort. [MDh 9.7]

Thus [it is said]. And Gautama likewise says: "The duty (*dharma*) consists in the protection of offspring and the avoidance of confusion" (GDh 8.3). Alternatively, there is another reading: "One who observes that vow out of a desire for pleasure," which refers to the husband alone and not to himself. Or rather, it pertains to both; the word "that" (*tat*) must be supplied. Thus, "one who observes that vow out of a desire for that pleasure. In all three readings, the engagement prompted by the wife may occur even outside the fertile period (*ṛtu*), but not for his own enjoyment or by mere whim. In this way, there is no restriction for subsequent occasions. However, one must certainly go during the fertile period. This continues until the fulfillment of the duty regarding progeny; thereafter, if he has no son, he should proceed according to the rule for the sake of obtaining a son. But for one who already has a son, there is a transgression in procreating a second or subsequent son. From the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the verse, "They know others to be born of desire" (MDh 9.107), it follows that there is spiritual merit (*abhyudaya*) in not procreating [further]. Because of the statement, "But cessation yields great fruit" (MDh 5.56), this is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) by implication. Regarding "They know others to be born of desire" (MDh 9.107), from that it should be understood that this is a constant rule. And so says another Smṛti: "When one's wife is endowed with virtue and progeny, one should not take another."

The natural fertile period of women is said to consist of sixteen nights; observing the prescribed vow, he may approach her during that time for the sake of sexual pleasure, avoiding the forbidden days. (3.46)

The natural season (*ṛtu*) of women is that which occurs without being influenced by substances, passion, or disease—these being the first four [factors] along with the other impure ones, which are rightly censured; this is a deprecatory explanatory statement intended for the purpose of avoidance.
Of those, the first four days, as well as the eleventh and the thirteenth, are condemned; the remaining ten nights, however, are praised. (3.47)

Of those [women], sixteen nights beginning from the onset of menstruation are recommended; among them, the eleventh and thirteenth are to be known as excluded. However, ten lunar days (tithis) are not recommended for them.
Sons are born on even nights, and daughters on odd nights. Therefore, one desiring a son should approach his wife during her season on an even night. (3.48)
This creation is for the sake of the son’s entitlement to the Vedic dharma and for the sake of his own purification; but for another [purpose], it is for the sake of refuting [the opponent].

A male is born when the male seed is in excess, a female when the female seed is in excess; when they are equal, a neuter is born, or both a male and a female; and when the seed is diminished or scant, the opposite occurs. (3.49)

A male is born when, at the time of the male's [conception], the male seed exceeds the female seed; likewise, a female is born when, even at the time of the male, the female seed exceeds the male seed from their union. How is this understood? This refers to the time of birth for a male or female; it would be effective at the start [of conception]. If they are equal, there is a non-male (*apumān*); if the male and female seeds differ, then by the power of the wind, whether the lunar day (*tithi*) is even or odd, or in the case of a difference in the inequality of the two, or in the simultaneous difference of the seeds, twins—either two females or two males—are born through the power of destiny. "When diminished, [the seed is] small"—this means that both are small. If this is the instruction, it is due to the requirement of the *anuṣṭubh* meter; otherwise, it is a restatement of what was said regarding the birth of a neuter, or it signifies an absence. Alternatively, it is a reversal of the embryo; or "diminished" refers to being small in quantity and lacking essence. Now, the presentation of a second traditional authority (*smṛti*) is made for the sake of this [verse], namely: "The ten nights are recommended" (MDh 3.47).
Avoiding women on the eight censured nights and the other [inauspicious] nights, he remains a celibate student (brahmacārī) regardless of which stage of life (āśrama) he inhabits. (3.50)

By this [verse], the entitlement to approach [one’s wife] on all nights—whether sequentially or otherwise—is prohibited during the six censurable nights and the eight non-censurable nights. By implication, even while approaching her on the remaining two nights, one remains a *brahmacārī* (celibate student). [Objection: Even a husband who has entered another stage of life (*avasthāntara*) from that of a householder, residing in whichever stage of life he may be, would still incur sin if there is an interruption in the production of a distinguished lineage of sons. Furthermore, if he is already possessed of sons, since no ritual act is seen for him, or according to the view of the appointment of a widow (*vidhavā-niyoga*), by the scriptural injunction "he who does not beget a son is to be shunned" (MDh 8.170), one who—like Vyāsa—has restrained his self through the word of his guru and approaches her for the sake of a son, remains a *brahmacārī*. Some say this applies regardless of which stage of life he resides in. However, both of these views are incorrect, because of the absolute instruction regarding celibacy, and because of the specific instructions for penance distinct from that [period], such as: "Thus disciplined and with senses conquered, he attains the world of Brahmā. Therefore, this [statement] regarding the approach on two nights is intended as praise. How so? Because this time for approaching is so highly praised that, even though he enters another stage of life, the celibacy of one who was previously an absolute *brahmacārī* is not violated. Thus, the instruction on celibacy remains consistent with the context, and no contradiction with other scriptures is imagined. Others, however, maintain that this applies to one who, residing in the householder stage, remains constantly among any of the social classes (*varṇas*). This is an explanation of those ignorant of the meaning of the sentence and should be disregarded. The reading "on the eight censurable or other [nights]" is un-Vedic (*anārṣa*), because it would obstruct the instruction on celibacy during the sacred festival days (*parvan*). Thus, of the ten nights, eight are set aside at will, and two are retained. Of these two, for one desiring a son, the instruction for the other [night] is appropriate because it is not for the sake of a son; and for one desiring a daughter, the instruction for the daughter is also appropriate, since the scripture prescribes rules for her giving and bestowal. Moreover, the sacrifice in the *Viśvajit* is of great fruit; the giving of a daughter is of great fruit, as it is said: "Neither the maintainer of the sacred fire (*agnicit*), nor the father of a virtuous son, nor the giver of a daughter goes to hell. And in the Upaniṣads of the Vājasaneyins, a ritual act is prescribed for one desiring a daughter. If it is argued that this would not have been prescribed had the birth of a daughter been unintended, we reply: a statement is appropriate when there is no contradiction. Here, the scripture would not have mentioned "ten" if it were not so; thus, it would have spoken of those very [nights] for the sake of a son. In the case of the absence of a son, they would be completed by means of a daughter. Accordingly, it will later praise the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā-putra*), saying: "For even a daughter's son saves him in the hereafter," and "by whom he crosses over. Thus, because the rule for the giving of a daughter is optional, it will not be mandatory. Therefore, activity for the sake of a daughter also serves the purpose of Dharma. And so, only the two [nights] for the sake of a son are permitted. Nor is only one night permitted for the sake of a son, because both are heard in the scripture. There is, however, this distinction: for one who has already produced a son, since he has the capacity for religious duties (*dharma-adhikāra*) and the capacity for his own [spiritual] duties, it is proper that his initial activity be regulated for the sake of a son through various connections to the production of a son. He is regulated for the sake of a son. It has already been stated that activity for the sake of a daughter is also desired. Some, however, say: "This is not another Smṛti text stating 'ten or two nights'; therefore, the connection of the sentences is that of the ten [nights], or 'whichever one'. That is incorrect. If there were no difference in the sentences, the commendatory statement "the ten nights are praised" (MDh 3.47) would be inappropriate. Therefore, these are two separate Smṛti texts. How? Because of the difference in sentences: "Ten are praised, or two are more highly praised" due to the capacity for self-restraint. This being so, the first Smṛti is for one who has not yet achieved his purpose, while the latter should be understood as a reiteration for one who has achieved his purpose. Some, however, read this verse differently: *(Note: The original text ends abruptly here with the phrase "kecit tv anyathemaṃ ślokaṃ paṭhanti".)*

"By avoiding women on all censurable nights, one remains a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) regardless of which stage of life (*āśrama*) one dwells in. This is what they explain as the meaning of the other [text]. Even those nights such as those following a death or a birth are included by the term "all. And this is a concluding statement intended to prohibit the six [specific types of nights]. Whether this is logical or not must be investigated. Now, that which pertains to marriage is being discussed.
A wise father should not accept even the slightest bride-price for his daughter;
for by accepting a bride-price out of greed, a man becomes a seller of his offspring. (3.51)
This is a prohibition against the Asuras taking an optional bride-price (*śulka*):
"But those kinsmen who, out of delusion, subsist upon a woman’s property—whether it be her vehicles or her clothing—are sinners who go to a downward state. (3.52)

If even those related to her would incur a fault, how much more so the father? This is a praise for the non-acceptance of a bride-price (*śulka*), intended as a basis for rejecting its acceptance. Furthermore, from this mention of "relatives" (*bandhu*) for the sake of praise, it is understood that nothing at all should be received even from the relatives.
Some say that in the *ārṣa* marriage a pair of cattle is the bride-price; that is indeed false.
Whether it be small or large, it is just as much a sale. (3.53)

This is another verse intended as praise for the taking [of the bride], occurring in the context of the rules for marriage: "When the kinsmen do not take a fee (śulka) for the girls, that is not a sale; it is merely a token of honor for the maidens and an act of pure benevolence. (3.54)

Because they are not one, there is a fault in taking a bride-price solely for the sake of the girl after she has been given away; therefore, these women should be honored and adorned by fathers, brothers, husbands, and brothers-in-law who desire much prosperity. [120] 3.55.

This is a praise of the means for accepting the gift of a daughter as taught by the ancestors. Therefore, that wealth must be accepted without reservation for the sake of the daughter. For it is said: "But where women are honored, there the gods rejoice;
but where they are not honored, all rites there are fruitless. (3.56)
There is another [verse] censuring the transgression of prescribed means:
"In that family where female relatives (jāmayah) grieve, that family quickly perishes; yet, when they are favored, its ornaments, wealth, and property flourish."
But where these do not grieve, there indeed everything always prospers.
Those houses which female relatives, not being duly honored by their fathers-in-law or kinsmen, curse, perish on all sides as if struck by a magical spell (*kṛtyā*). (3.58)
Therefore, by increasing their lack of worldly conditioning,
these [women] should always be honored with ornaments, clothing, and food by men desiring prosperity, both at times of hospitality and during festivals. (3.59)
Because of the word "ca" (and), this should especially be done during marriages. How so? So that the husband may be satisfied with his wife, and likewise the wife with her husband.
From the giving [of the bride], joy arises for the girl; and for the husband, it arises when the wife is adorned with ornaments. And this being so—
In whatever family one is born, there will certainly be constant prosperity.
Just as it occurs between husband and wife through their mutual concern for one another:
"For if the woman does not find pleasure, she will not delight the man; and from the lack of delight on the part of the man, procreation does not proceed. (3.61)

A woman who does not take pleasure in being adorned will certainly not delight her husband; from a lack of delight comes a failure of procreation. Therefore, she is that which binds the mind and the eyes of another. Thus, the praise of the maiden’s adornment—by means of the adornments for giving and so forth—is intended to convey the sense of an unavoidable comparison: namely, that a lack of interest arises toward those who provide no benefit. Consequently, effort should be exerted so that there may be no lack of interest in the *agnihotra* and other rites performed together with her. This is a praise of a desirable marriage; by connection with that, this is now stated. [121]
When a woman is pleasing, the entire family is pleased;
but when she is displeasing, nothing at all is pleasing. (3.62)
Families perish through ill-arranged marriages, the omission of sacred rites, the failure to study the Vedas, and by showing disrespect toward Brahmins. (3.63)
By means of crafts, commerce, and the exclusive offspring of Śūdra women;
by means of cattle, horses, vehicles, agriculture, and service to the king. (3.64)

Through officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, through atheism regarding ritual acts, and through neglecting the sacred mantras, even noble lineages fall into a state of ignobility. (3.65)
But through the power of mantras, families—even those with little wealth—become prosperous; they attain the status of noble lineages and draw forth great renown. (3.66)

These four verses concern the rules for the preservation of the family lineage (*kula*). Since the rule for preserving the lineage is also violated when these [other rules] are transgressed, they are prohibited here once again. In the phrase "prosperous through mantras," the mention of "mantras" is for the sake of illustration; one should understand that this applies to ritual acts (*kriyā*) and so forth as well. Thus, it should be explained as "prosperous through mantras and the like. This same principle applies here as well. Furthermore, regarding the verse "those which are deficient in mantras" (65), this same principle applies there too. Alternatively, because this is a section praising the rules for marriage, it implies that for other types of bad marriages—such as those involving the omission of rites—just as families fall into a state of non-lineage (*akulatā*) through the omission of rites and so forth, so too do they fall into a state of non-lineage through bad marriages. Therefore, that which is ordained by the authoritative scriptures of rules must be respected; this is the meaning of the section. Now, the sequence for one who has already performed the marriage is being set forth. If—
In the nuptial fire, the householder should perform the domestic rites according to the rules,
as well as the performance of the five sacrifices and the daily cooking.

Marriage is its purpose; thus, it is "pertaining to marriage" (*vaivāhika*). For some authors of the *Gṛhyasūtras*, it has been established (*āhita*), while for others, it has not. This procedure applies to both groups: one should perform therein the domestic rites such as the *Aṣṭakā* and the *Pārvaṇa*, the procedure for the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) which will be described hereafter, whatever is intended for the *Vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, the *Aṣṭakā*, and the daily reception of guests from the first day onwards. Therein begins the performance of the *Smārta* (tradition-based) rites. What is the reason? Because these very rites are to be performed thus every day. Therefore: "The householder has five slaughter-houses: the hearth, the grinding stone, the broom, the mortar and pestle, and the water-jar."
The mortar and the water-jar are bound [to him] for those whom he causes to carry. (3.68)
And since these are thus, therefore— [122] for the sake of the sequential expiation of all of them, by the great seers...
Five great sacrifices have been ordained for householders to be performed every day.

These two verses are for the purpose of praising the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*); the mention of the "slaughterhouse" (*sūnā*) is likewise for the sake of praise. This is a glorification of the duties of the householder. It is not, however, merely an expiation (*niṣkṛti*), as the force of the scriptural statement implies that this is primarily an instruction on ritual action; furthermore, because these duties are obligatory, they do not serve the purpose of expiation. The five great sacrifices are defined by their essential nature as follows:

Teaching is the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*); the libation to ancestors is the sacrifice to the manes (*pitṛyajña*); the burnt offering is the sacrifice to the gods (*daivayajña*); the food offering is the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*); and the honoring of guests is the sacrifice to men (*nṛyajña*). (3.70)

By the word "teaching," study is also included under the name of the *brahmayajña* through figurative usage. Giving to the ancestors and the libation (*tarpaṇa*) constitute the *pitṛyajña*. The oblation of food (*annahoma*) is the *devayajña*; other than that, the offering of portions (*baliharaṇa*) is the *bhūtayajña*. Giving food to guests is the *manuṣyayajña*. Because of the context, these—the *brahmayajña* and the others—are part of the *vaiśvadeva* ritual.
"He who does not neglect these five great sacrifices according to his ability, even while living constantly in the house, is not defiled by the faults of the kitchen. (3.71)

For the sake of conclusion, they have also stated at the end of this verse: "Furthermore, for the sake of non-return [to rebirth], those who are deficient [in merit] should recite [the mantra] according to their ability; [this is achieved] solely through the great practice that must be performed daily. Thus, for what reason is there the mention of "according to one's ability" (*śaktitaḥ*) here? Because of this:
"He who does not offer [oblations] to these five—the gods, guests, servants, ancestors, and himself—does not truly live, though he breathes. (3.72)

This verse should be recited with the sense of the dative case (*saṃpradāna*). The *bhṛtyas* and the *ātman* are not to be understood as being included within the *viśvedevas*, for they are [separate] deities. Thus, because of their connection with the offering of the *bali*, they are designated as "beings" (*bhūta*); therefore, since they are already included by the mention of the "deities," the beings are not mentioned separately at the end. Even though the phrase "he does not live who does not breathe" is heard [elsewhere], it should be understood here through the force of the praise. Furthermore, giving to the deities and others is called a "disinterested gift" (*nirvyāpa*). And the gift to the sages is traditionally taught as a "gift of Brahman" (*brahmadāna*); this repetition is for the purpose of enjoining that very rule for them.
The unoffered sacrifice (ahuta), the offered sacrifice (huta), the likewise well-offered sacrifice (prahuta),
the sacrifice to Brahman (brāhmya-huta), and the consumed sacrifice (prāśita)— these they declare to be the five sacrifices.

The repetition of these very great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) is for the purpose of showing them under different names and for the purpose of stating the remaining rules; this following verse is intended as an explanation of that [preceding] verse:

Recitation (*japa*) is the *ahuta* sacrifice; the fire-oblation (*homa*) is the *huta*; the offering of food (*bhaikṣika*) is the *prahuta*; the *bali* offering is the *brahmya-huta*; the honoring of the foremost of the twice-born is the *prāśita*; and the libation to the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*) is the *prāśita*. (3.74)

[123] At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus: “Bhikṣus, in the past, there was a king named Mahādeva who ruled over Jambudvīpa. He possessed great wealth and power, and his dominion extended over the four continents. He had a son named Śūradatta, who was handsome, virtuous, and beloved by the people. One day, King Mahādeva, accompanied by his ministers and retinue, went out from the city to a pleasure grove. There, he saw a great forest fire spreading across the woods. Fearing for his life, the king fled toward the city. However, as he was fleeing, he encountered a large river in his path. The river was deep and swift, and there was no bridge or boat to cross it. The king thought to himself: ‘If I do not find a way to cross this river, I shall perish in the fire. Just then, he saw a young man standing on the bank, holding a leather bag. The king asked him: ‘Young man, can you help me cross this river? The youth replied: ‘Great King, I am indeed able to help you. However, I have one condition: you must give me your son, Prince Śūradatta, to serve as my servant. The king, fearing for his own life, agreed to the youth’s request. The youth then placed the king upon his back and carried him across the river. Once they reached the other side, the youth set the king down and said: ‘Great King, your son is now yours to keep. As for me, I have fulfilled my promise. The king, having escaped the fire and the river, returned to his palace. He searched everywhere for his son but could not find him. Meanwhile, the youth took the prince to a remote mountain hermitage and raised him there. When the prince grew up, he became wise and compassionate. One day, while wandering through the forest, he encountered a starving tigress. Moved by compassion, he offered his own body to feed the tigress so that she would not devour her cubs. Upon hearing of this, King Mahādeva was overcome with grief and remorse. He realized the true nature of impermanence and renounced the world to become a monk. Later, he attained arhatship. The youth who had saved the king was none other than myself. And the prince Śūradatta was the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī. Thus, bhikṣus, you should know that the Bodhisattvas practice such acts of great compassion and self-sacrifice for the sake of all sentient beings.”

Regarding the term *japa*: because of the context, it refers to the *brahmayajña* (sacrifice to Brahman). That is designated as *vākyam*. The offering into the fire (*agnau homaḥ*) that has occurred is called the *devayajña* (sacrifice to the gods). The presentation of food offerings (*baliharaṇa*) is the *prahuta*; that indeed is declared to be the *bhūtayajña* (sacrifice to beings). Giving to a Brāhmaṇa is the *brāhmya-huta*; the honoring of the foremost of the twice-born is declared to be the worship of guests (*atithipūjā*). What is consumed (*prāśita*) is the libation to the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*), such as the giving of water and the *śrāddha* ceremony. Thus, these very five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajñāḥ*) belonging to the *vaiśvadeva* rite are designated by the term *pākayajña*. Its purpose is of this nature. Other rules (*vidhayaḥ*) should also be understood as being included by the word *pāka*. For the sake of obtaining the rules for the *pākayajña*, even one who lacks the means should diligently perform the triad [of daily duties] as a householder.
He should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*) and to the rites directed toward the gods (*daiva-karman*) here in this world.

This demonstrates that the purpose of the householder is the sustenance of the entire world; for it is he who, engaged in the rites directed toward the gods, supports this universe of moving and unmoving beings. (3.75)
And thus, even from the performance of a single part of the great sacrifice, there is benefit for all the worlds, because:
"The oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings. (3.76)

This is a praise of the fire-sacrifice (homa-yajña) because of the context; moreover, there is nothing else [intended]. Just as all living beings exist depending upon their mother, so too do the other stages of life (āśramas) exist depending upon the householder. (3.77)
"Just as all living beings depend upon the wind for their life,
so do the other stages of life depend upon the householder.
This being the case,
Since members of all three other stages of life are daily supported by the householder alone with both knowledge and food, therefore the householder’s stage is the most excellent. (3.78)

This should be understood from the context of the praise for the performance of the duties prescribed [for it], since this very stage of the householder (*gṛhasthāśrama*) possesses great purpose due to its capacity to benefit all the worlds. Therefore:

"It should be maintained with effort by one who desires imperishable heaven, and by one who desires ultimate happiness in this world—even though it is difficult to maintain for those with weak senses. (3.79)
The praise of the performance of the five great sacrifices is by way of stating their results:
"Sages, ancestors, gods, spirits, and likewise guests—these expect [offerings] from householders; therefore, one who understands his duty should act toward them. (3.80)
[124] What is this that is being said?
One should honor the sages through the private recitation of the Vedas and the gods with burnt offerings according to the prescribed rule.
One should satisfy the ancestors with śrāddha offerings, men with food, and the spirits with the bali ritual.
This verse is intended to demonstrate the constituent elements of the sacrifice (*ijyā*). However, it depends upon the means for the performance of the prescribed rites. Furthermore:
"He should perform the *śrāddha* ceremony day after day with food and drink, or even with milk, roots, and fruits, thereby bringing satisfaction to the ancestors. (3.82)
Thus, having performed the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, the householder should feed even a single Brāhmaṇa for the sake of the ancestors during the fivefold sacrifice;
however, he should not, in this regard, rely upon any Brāhmaṇa for the Vaiśvadeva rite itself. (3.83)

This rite of *śrāddha* is described in two verses as being superior to the *vaiśvadeva*. He will also state that its performance may be optional. "A Brāhmaṇa should daily perform an oblation (*homa*) in the domestic fire (*gṛhya-agni*) according to the prescribed rule for these deities from the cooked food of the *vaiśvadeva*. (3.84)

By the word *vaiśvadeva*, the cooked offering (*pāka*) is here indicated. Because of the statement "of that which is prepared" (*siddhasya*), this *vaiśvadeva*—that whose deities are the Viśvedevas—is called the cooked offering intended for all the gods.
[The offering is made] first to Agni and Soma, then to those two together, then to the Viśvedevas, and also to Dhanvantari. (3.85)
To Kuhū and to Anumati, and to Prajāpati, and likewise to Dyāvāpṛthivī together, and finally to Sviṣṭakṛt. || 3.86 ||

Having thus properly offered the oblation, he should present the sacrificial offering (bali) to Indra, Antaka, Appati, and Indu, together with their followers, while circumambulating in a clockwise direction toward all quarters.
One should throw [food] at the door with the words, "To the Maruts," and likewise into the water with the words, "To the Waters";
one should offer [food] upon the pestle and mortar with the words, "To the Forest Trees."
One should offer to Śrī at the head of the bed and to Bhadrakālī at the foot;
one should present the bali offering to Brahmā and Vāstoṣpati in the middle of the dwelling.
And he should cast an offering into the air for all the gods,
as well as for the beings that roam by day and those that roam by night.
One should offer a bali-oblation on the back part of the house for the prosperity of all food;
however, one should carry all the remainder of the bali toward the south for the ancestors.
One should slowly place [the food] on the ground for dogs, outcasts, dog-cookers, those afflicted with foul diseases, crows, and worms. (3.92)
Thus, the Brahmin who constantly honors all beings goes by a straight path to the supreme abode, his very form consisting of light.
The *vaiśvadeva* [offering] is performed with three verses for the purpose of ensuring the correct application of the ritual procedure.
Having thus performed this *bali* rite, one should first feed the guest and give alms according to the rule to a mendicant and a student (*brahmacārin*). (3.94)
Whatever merit one obtains by giving a cow to a preceptor according to the prescribed rule, that same fruit of merit a twice-born householder obtains by giving alms. (3.95)
The two verses have a straightforward meaning:
Even alms or a vessel of water, having honored them according to the prescribed rule, one should present them to a Brāhmaṇa who knows the true meaning of the Vedas. (3.96)
The offerings to the gods and ancestors of ignorant men perish when they are given out of delusion to Brahmins who have become like ashes. (3.97)
An oblation offered into the fires of the mouths of Brahmins who are enriched by their knowledge rescues one from misfortune and even from great sin. (3.98)
The definition of a guest and the definition of a mendicant are to be understood through these three verses, along with their explanatory praise:
"When a guest has arrived, one should offer him a seat and water, as well as food according to one's ability, having honored him in accordance with the prescribed rule. (3.99)
Even if one constantly gathers grains by gleaning and offers oblations in the five fires, a Brāhmaṇa who dwells unhonored takes away all that merit. (3.100)
Grass for a seat, ground for resting, water, and fourthly, kind speech—these things are never lacking in the homes of the virtuous. (3.101)
A Brāhmaṇa staying for only one night is traditionally known as a guest (atithi);
because he stays for a non-permanent duration, he is therefore called a guest. [3.102]

This etymological definition of "guest" (atithi) should be understood as a traditional rule (niyamasmṛti) concerning a Brāhmaṇa who stays for only one day and night. This being the case, there is no transgression of the aforementioned rule for one who does not extend hospitality on the second day and subsequent days. However, this etymological definition was stated so that, when hospitality is extended, the aforementioned spiritual merit (abhyudaya) may accrue as demonstrated. "One should know that a Brāhmaṇa from the same village, as well as a kinsman, is not a guest when he arrives at the house where his wife or even the sacred fires are located. (3.103)

According to the *Śāstra*, one should not consider a guest to be present in the house if a virtuous Brahmin, though a resident of the same village, has arrived from another region and stays beyond the proper time, having bypassed his own home. This prohibition applies specifically to the offering of a formal meal (*niyama-dāna*) and not to other forms of hospitality. A companion (*sāṅgatika*) is defined as follows: even if he does not live in the same village, one who comes along with a friend on a journey for the sake of meeting or visiting is a companion. One who lives by means of various stories and jests, through whom a graduate (*snātaka*) maintains his livelihood, is not prohibited; for it is said: "One should never follow the ways of the world for the sake of a livelihood" (MDh 4.11). In this context, a mere friend (*sakhi*) is not considered a companion (*sāṅgatika*), because he is prohibited later in the text: "A Vaiśya, a Śūdra, and a friend" (MDh 3.110). Furthermore, there can be no mutual recognition between a householder and someone who has gone to another village; therefore, the author says: "Wherever his wife or fires are located," there hospitality must be provided. Another, however, reads: "His wife, sons, or even the fires. In this reading, the meaning is as follows: not only is a resident of the same village not a guest in this quarter-verse, but wherever the wife and sons are being led, even if they are residents of another village and have arrived first in that village, he should be known as not a guest. This point is already stated redundantly by the rule: "One should not [consider] a resident of the same village a guest. Now, this deprecatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is stated for the purpose of prohibiting travel abroad by guests for the sake of eating another's cooked food.
Those foolish householders who subsist on the food cooked by others, upon departing this life, enter the state of cattle for those who provided them with food and other gifts. (3.104)
This [verse] is either a statement of the fruit [of the action] or a commendatory eulogy (arthavāda) regarding the fruit. Now, however, this is stated for the sake of a specific rule:
"A guest brought by the setting sun in the evening must not be turned away by the householder;
whether he arrives at the proper time or at an improper time, he must not remain in the house without eating. (3.105)

This undertaking is prohibited for him; how, then, is it understood that he should dwell there? It is understood from the force of the context (*ārambhasāmarthyāt*) that this is so. Otherwise, since the guest (*atithi*) defined by the characteristics previously mentioned would—just as in the morning—be subject to the rule of not being sent away (*apraṇodya*), and since the householder has the vow of performing the *vaiśvadeva* twice, the non-undertaking of this [evening rite] would follow as a consequence. But this [rule] is necessary. Therefore, the meaning of the verse is exactly as stated. Now it is explained: "The guest is not to be sent away in the evening," even if he is a resident of the same village (*ekagrāmanivāsī*). Even if he is a fellow traveler (*sāṅgatika*), because he is destitute, he is "borne by the sun" (*sūryoḍha*)—that is, he is brought or reached by the setting sun—and because of the prohibition [of sending him away] in due order, he is not to be sent away by the householder at this time. A "householder" (*gṛhamedhī*) is one who possesses the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*); when such a person arrives at the proper time, whether during the mealtime or after the meal, or even if the sun has not yet set, whether his food is deficient, slightly qualified, or fully qualified, he is a guest (*atithi*)—whether he be a village-resident or a fellow-traveler—and he must not stay in the house of the householder without having eaten. Regarding the phrase "even if he is prohibited": this is because of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) concerning Vaiśvānara. For when a guest arrives at night in a secluded place, he becomes Vaiśvānara; therefore, unless permitted by him, one should not offer even a small amount [of food], for he is his supreme deity (*parādevatā*). Now, although the giving of hospitality to guests exists, this [next section] is undertaken for the purpose of prohibiting the householder’s irregular eating at both times.
"One should certainly not eat that food oneself which one does not offer to a guest.

This explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) is composed for the purpose of encouraging the performance of this duty by means of its connection to both visible and invisible benefits, due to the inherent nature of the matter:
"Feeding a guest brings wealth, fame, long life, and leads to heaven" (3.106).
As previously specified:
"In this manner, one should provide a seat, lodging, a bed, attendance while walking behind, and respectful service;
toward those who are superior, one should act with excellence; toward those who are inferior, with inferiority; and toward equals, with equality. (3.107)
Based on the context, it is stated that for guests—whether low or high—one should provide food exceeding the meal [of the household] in accordance with one's own capacity and merit.
But if another guest should arrive after the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice has been completed, one should give him food according to one's ability, but one must not perform the Bali offering again. (3.108)

And thus, this offering of oblations known as the *vaiśvadeva* is not a consecration of the cooked food; what then? It is for the purpose of purifying the self. For otherwise, it would have to be repeated at every meal, since there is a prohibition against that which is already established by scripture. Now, the proclamation of one's own qualities for the sake of receiving food from a guest is forbidden: "A Brahmin should not announce his own family or lineage for the sake of a meal;
for he who praises himself for the sake of a meal is called a 'vomiter-eater' by the wise. (3.109)

And thus, the mention of "receiving food" is intended to illustrate the acceptance of all [gifts]; and by analogy, it should be understood that one should not accept the mention of family or lineage, nor any personal qualities of the self.
"But for a Brāhmaṇa, a guest in his house is not said to be a Kṣatriya; nor a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, nor even a friend, nor kinsmen, nor a teacher. (3.110)

The word *tu* (but) serves the purpose of restriction. For a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are not guests (*anatithi*). However, for Kṣatriyas and the others, those of their own or higher castes—given the absence of [guests] from lower castes—are indeed guests. Furthermore, in this context, the "friend" (*sakhi*) must be understood as a Brāhmaṇa alone, due to the force of the commencement [of the rule]. Likewise, among Kṣatriyas and others, the status of being a Brāhmaṇa is established through effort in the case of kinsmen and teachers; yet, because of the statement that they are not guests, their non-guest status does not arise from the same causes. For Kṣatriyas and the rest, [non-guest status] arises from being of a lower caste; for the friend and the kinsman, it arises from being trusted like a son and so forth; and for the teacher, the householder’s lack of guest-status arises from his being attached to another [the teacher]. Regarding him—
But if a Kṣatriya should come to the house in the manner of a guest, one may, if desired, feed him as well after the Brahmins have finished eating. (3.111)

If one has arrived in this manner according to the duty of a guest—being unknown from afar, possessing no offspring or wealth, and having come at the proper time—one should feed him after the Brahmins have eaten; for this is an exception to the previous rule. Even a Vaiśya or a Śūdra who have reached the household as guests according to the duty of a guest, he should feed along with his dependents, practicing compassion toward them. (3.112)

"By the rite for guests" means according to the duty toward a guest; that has already been explained. The rest is straightforward. This [rule] applies only to a Brāhmaṇa donor, because it is taught as a cause for compassion toward the other castes (*varṇas*) when it is time for them to eat. This too is an exception to the rule regarding the sacred festival days (*parvan*), being based on a specific cause.
He should also feed his friends and others who have come to his house out of affection, providing food according to his ability, together with his wife. (3.113)

Even for the sake of affection or as a reason for kinship, one may give instruction regarding the time for a wife’s meal; however, this is not said to apply to the teacher of sacred knowledge (*vidyā-guru*). This is because he possesses independence regarding the time of his own meals and because he is superior; for it has been said: “One should act with the highest [respect] toward those who are superior” (MDh 3.107).
One should feed the following after the guests, without hesitation: smiling young maidens, the sick, and likewise pregnant women. (3.114)

If there is a desire for them, those such as the unmarried women (*suvāsinī*) and others should eat immediately after; if there is no desire on their part, or if they are unavailable, the boys and others may eat according to their wish. However, it is recorded in the tradition that this fault of violating the rule applies to that unwise person who eats before these [others]: "And thus, there is this statement of censure."
While eating, he does not know that he is being devoured by dogs and vultures. (3.115)

In whatever way possible, I shall censure the prohibited matter, not for the sake of its cessation [by mere avoidance], but because that [cessation] serves the purpose of man; therefore, this instruction is appropriate for its accomplishment. "When the Brahmins, as well as his own servants, have finished eating, the husband and wife should then eat what remains" (3.116).

One's own slaves and so forth, as well as servants and wage-earners, are directed [to this]. For what reason? It is said that such an extensive section is composed to provide instruction on self-restraint for the householder. How so? "Not by this alone is one a knower of self-restraint;
having honored the gods, the seers, humans, the ancestors, and the household deities, only thereafter should the householder be an eater of the remains. (3.117)

This practice of the householder eating after [others], though already mentioned in the preceding verse, is stated again so that even when he is away from home (*proṣita*), he might not eat at that time having omitted the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*). Alternatively, this verse serves to conclude the section, whereas the previous one was intended for the purpose of prescribing the eating of leftovers. This being the case, it is logical that this entire statement of censure—which says, "He who cooks for his own sake eats only sin"—is dependent upon the conclusion of the section. He who cooks for his own sake eats only sin.
For this food of the virtuous is ordained as that which remains from the sacrifice. (3.118)
In this section concerning guests, the means for an exceptionally distinguished form of worship is prescribed even for certain individuals who would otherwise not be objects of such honor:

"One should honor with the *madhuparka* offering a king, an officiating priest, a *snātaka*, a teacher, one's beloved, a father-in-law, and a maternal uncle, provided it has been a full year since they were last honored. (3.119)

The word *rājan* is seen to apply to any Kṣatriya, as stated in the rule: "For a king seeking strength, [the guest-offering is] on the sixth [day]" (MDh 2.37). However, for one who is a Kṣatriya and possesses the qualities of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), protection, sovereignty, and majesty, the word *rājan* is also seen to apply to a non-Kṣatriya due to his actions and qualities, as in the rules: "A king should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha," and "A king should sacrifice with the Rājasūya. [This is also seen in the prohibition: "One should not dwell in the kingdom of a Śūdra king" (MDh 4.61). To whom, then, does this [term] refer? It refers to a Kṣatriya who is connected with the qualities of consecration and so forth, by virtue of the context. Therefore, the phrase "one should honor with the Madhuparka" (which was introduced earlier) prescribes the time for re-honoring one who has been previously accepted, after a year has passed (*parisaṃvatsarāt*). The meaning is: after more than a year. Some, however, read "parisaṃvatsarān"; for them, the meaning is as follows: those for whom a year has elapsed are *parivatsarāḥ*, etc.; such [persons], namely the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) about to be mentioned, "one should honor with the Madhuparka"—this is the same as before. And the *snātaka*—the teacher (*ācārya*) and the disciple who has returned home immediately after completion of studies—as in the rule: "Him, being well-known, according to his own duty" (MDh 3.3), and so forth. Otherwise, since all these—the priests and others—are already *snātakas*, a separate mention of the priests and others would be improper. And the pupil [should honor] the teacher; the father-in-law [should honor] the beloved son-in-law who has come for the daughter's wedding. Others hold that the word "beloved" (*priya*) is an adjective qualifying the father-in-law and the maternal uncle (*mātula*), [interpreting it as] "the beloved father-in-law and maternal uncle. For them, there is no evidence for this. [130] Furthermore, the worship with Madhuparka for the son-in-law would not have been mentioned [separately], yet it is well-established in all the Smṛti scriptures. Gautama, however, does not mention "beloved," but reads the paternal uncle (*pitṛvya*) additionally: "Upon the arrival of the officiating priest, the teacher, the father-in-law, the paternal uncle, and the maternal uncle, there is the Madhuparka" (GDh 5.27). In the Gṛhya-sūtra, however, the word "beloved" refers specifically to the son-in-law, and the word "one to be wedded" (*vivāhya*) refers to the father-in-law. Thus, the son-in-law should honor the father-in-law, and the sister's son should honor the maternal uncle. The inclusion of the paternal uncle is established because the maternal uncle, though not explicitly mentioned here, is included elsewhere, due to the similarity of relationship and the context. This mutual connection of giving and receiving the Madhuparka pertains only to the twice-born (*dvijāti*). Others, however, maintain that it applies to all castes (*varṇa*). They cite the statement of Vyāsa: "He himself should offer to that Blessed One a seat worthy of him, and likewise the Madhuparka and a cow"—meaning Vidura offered this to Vāsudeva. That, moreover, is without mantras. Whether the Madhuparka for the twice-born is accompanied by mantras or not, the Blessed Ones, the gods of the earth, are the ones who ought to know.
Editor’s note:
In the *Sabhāparvan* of the *Mahābhārata*, the presentation of the *madhuparka* by Yudhiṣṭhira to Nārada is described as follows:
"Then, bowing low with humility, he greeted him with affection."
Having offered him a seat worthy of him according to the prescribed rite, [he said:]
Having presented a cow, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and the guest-offering (arghya),
as well as jewels and all desirable things, he who knew the dharma paid him honor.

These two verses belong to the fifth chapter. According to Nīlakaṇṭha’s commentary, they are numbered 14–15, whereas according to Kṛṣṇamācārya’s edition, they are numbered 17–18. If Vidura had offered the *madhuparka* to Kṛṣṇa, that incident would certainly have occurred in the *Udyogaparvan*; however, these two verses do not appear anywhere there. As for how this discrepancy is to be reconciled, only those who possess knowledge of the flaws [of the tradition] can be the authority. "The king and the learned *śrotriya* when a sacrificial rite has arrived..."
They are to be honored with the honey-mixture (madhuparka), but not if it is not a sacrifice; such is the established rule.

Therefore, the reading *yajña* is another [variant], because of the prohibition against giving gifts to one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*). By that, the reading “*rājā ca śrotriyaś caiva yajñe prāptau vidhānataḥ*” should also be understood as refuted; likewise, this reading “*yajñakarmaṇy upasthitau*” [is refuted]. What then is the correct reading here? It is: “*rājā ca śrotriyaś caiva yajñakarmaṇy upasthite | madhuparkeṇa saṃpūjyau na tv ajajña iti sthitiḥ*. Because of the force of the commencement [of the sacrifice] even before a year has passed for the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), and since such commencement does occur, the word *śrotriya* includes every officiating priest. Consequently, there is an exception for the king and for him. Thus it has been said: “Even if he should sacrifice with Soma more than once a year, [the guest] must have the *arghya* offered to him; one should not cause him to sacrifice if the *arghya* has not been offered”—this is the meaning of the scripture. By the word *śrotriya*, all officiating priests and others are included. Therefore, on account of the sacrifice being the occasion, there would be a renewed offering of *madhuparka* for everyone even before a year has passed; thus, it would be an exception to all [the previous rules]. And so says Gautama: “Upon the arrival of officiating priests and others, there is the *madhuparka*; again after a year; and before [that], at a sacrifice or a wedding. The offering of the *bali* oblations in the evening and morning has already been stated. Now, this [section] is commenced for the sake of its specific details.
In the evening, when food has been prepared, the wife should offer a Bali oblation without reciting mantras;
for this is called the Vaiśvadeva, which is prescribed for both morning and evening.

[131] The *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, characterized by the *homa* oblation, is prescribed for both evening and morning. However, as for the offering of the *bali*, the householder’s wife alone shall perform it in the evening, without fire and without mantras; such is the manner of the *bali*-offering observed in the world. Another [author] states the purpose of its commencement: since some householders have traditionally taught the *vaiśvadeva* for both evening and morning, this is now prescribed so that one may instruct them regarding this monthly rite, which is distinct from the *śrāddha* mentioned among the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*). Thus he speaks now.
Having performed the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires should, at the waning of the moon,
perform the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka Śrāddha monthly.

The monthly *śrāddha* performed for those who have not yet attained *sapinda* status should be understood [as distinct]. Why is this called *anvāhārya*? Because it is derived from the root *adhi-vas* [in the sense of "to place upon" or "to perform"]. How is it to be brought (*āhārya*)? The meaning is "subsequently" (*anu-paścāt*). Of what? Of the *piṇḍas*. That which is brought to its conclusion is called *anvāhārya*. And thus, because it is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of that [funeral rite], this too—like the *piṇḍas*—is established as occurring every month. This instruction regarding the recommended raw meat (*āmamiṣa*) is for the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). In that regard, [it concerns] those best of the twice-born who are to be fed and those who are to be avoided: *tatra ye bhojanīyāḥ syur ye ca varjyā dvijottamāḥ* || 1.249 || [The following verses list those to be invited and those to be rejected. ... caivātra śucir nityaṃ na caivātra śucir bhavet* || 3.294 || *na caivātra śucir nityaṃ na
I shall describe, without omission, exactly how many there are and by which foods they are sustained. || 3.124 ||
This verse is for the purpose of introduction:
"At a rite for the gods, he should feed two; at a rite for the ancestors, three; or one at each of the two.
Even if he is very wealthy, he should not be overly attached to a large company. (3.125)

Two [should be fed] at the rite for the gods (*daiva*), because that is the context; one should feed three at the rite for the ancestors (*pitrya*). This is the injunction regarding the feeding of Brāhmaṇas qualified by a specific number. The statement, "Or one may feed one at each of the two," is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). Furthermore, the prohibition, "Even if very prosperous, one should not indulge in abundance," will be stated later: "One should invite at least three" (MDh 3.187). And Gautama says: "One should feed more than three" (GDh 15.21). It is also stated in another Smṛti: "But not just one for all. This being the case, since this is an *arthavāda*, its praise remains appropriate even when there is a greater number. One might wish to treat "one at each of the two" as an injunction regarding the number; however, one should not indulge in abundance, and thus the feeding of only one at each of the two is not authorized. Just as in common parlance, "You may eat poison if you wish, but do not eat in his house"—this does not mean that eating poison is being enjoined. By this, the verse "even a single learned man" (MDh 3.129) is explained. Since this is intended as praise of the learned, no specific number is being enjoined. Therefore, at least three Brāhmaṇas should be understood as required for the ancestral rite (*pitṛkarman*). Some, having construed this as an *arthavāda* and considering this to be a different injunction from the optional rule of "at least three," feed the Brāhmaṇas accordingly. Others, however, say: "The number of Brāhmaṇas is not enjoined here; where then? It is in the passage 'one should invite at least three' (MDh 3.187). That is incorrect, because of the instruction "one should feed. Because of the statement, "Even if very prosperous, one should not indulge in abundance," this very injunction regarding the Brāhmaṇas qualified by number must be considered an *arthavāda*. And that sentence is for the purpose of invitation, not for the purpose of enjoining a number. Therefore, this [verse] states the reason why, due to the requirement of a minimum (*avaratva*), "even if very prosperous, one should not indulge in abundance."
Hospitality, proper place and time, purity, and the excellence of the Brahmins—these five are destroyed by excessive elaboration; therefore, one should not seek elaboration. (3.126)

"Hospitality" (*satkriyā*) refers to the honoring of invited Brahmins through such acts as following their instructions. "Place and time" (*deśakālau*) refer to those factors that constitute the constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the *śrāddha*. "Purity" (*śauca*) refers to food that possesses its proper qualities. "Perfection of the Brahmins" (*brāhmaṇasaṃpad*) is that which is prescribed according to the scriptures. Since "excessive elaboration" (*vistara*) destroys [the merit] for all householders, the statement "therefore one should not seek elaboration" is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). Its purpose is to indicate that at any given time, many qualified individuals are difficult to find. This description of the qualities of the ritual actions and so forth is not for its own sake, as it does not belong to the immediate context. Furthermore, while prohibiting elaboration on account of the aforementioned reasons, the text permits elaboration when there is the capacity [to perform it]. Thus says Gautama: "An odd number [of Brahmins], according to one's enthusiasm" (GDh 15.78). This [passage] is commenced for the purpose of praising the injunction: "One should perform the monthly *māsānumāsika* rite" (MDh 3.122).
This rite for the deceased, known as the *pitrya*, is celebrated at the waning of the moon;

it is renowned among all householders as the sacrifice for the ancestors, a rule famous simply as the *pitrya* intended primarily for the praise of the funeral rites (*preta-kartavya*) performed by the householder when his ritual duties have concluded, and not for one engaged in other stages of life (*āśrama*).
Out of devotion to their father, they themselves always go at the proper time;
what is that?

He distinguishes that [ancestral worship] by means of the *śrāddha* rite, which is the honoring of the ancestors through the state of having many sons and grandsons for one who has gone to the other world; this is the worldly *pretakṛtyā*. (3.127)

Therefore, the meaning is that this [state] is indeed based on the Smṛti. And thus, by means of this praise, it is understood through implication that those deceased persons who performed śrāddha rites reside there, having been born in whatever state they were reborn according to the power of their Smārta duties; there, due to the absence of any cause for the cessation of the *kavya* (food for ancestors) provided by their sons and grandsons in accordance with the injunctions, they remain enjoying uninterrupted happiness. Otherwise, this praise of their ritual action would be accidental and groundless. Moreover, this is undesirable, because it has been taught in the authoritative scriptures that "those who are to be fed therein... (MDh 3.124). For this reason, they are called "these."
Sacrificial offerings to the gods and the ancestors must be given by donors only to one learned in the Vedas;
what is given to such a most worthy Brahmin yields great fruit.

In this context, the term *śrotriya* does not restrict [the recipient] to one who has merely studied the Vedic meters (*chandas*). What then? It restricts [the recipient] to one who studies both the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas. And the word *eva* (only/precisely) serves to exclude those who are not *śrotriyas*. Even though he possesses Brāhmaṇa-hood, that by which this becomes the cause for his entitlement to eat at a Brāhmaṇa’s *śrāddha*—namely, being a *śrotriya*—is expressed by the phrase "to the most worthy" (*arhattamāya*). By the term *arhattama*, the author indicates one whose excellence of qualities is well-known. Thus he shows: "One should feed even a single learned man at the rite for the gods and at the rite for the ancestors."
One obtains abundant fruit, even from many who do not know the mantras.

This [verse] is intended primarily as praise for learned men, not as an injunction; thus, this verse has already been explained: "One should examine from afar a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas; he is a sacred ford for the offering of *havya* and *kavya*, and he is declared to be a guest. (3.130)
This verse is intended to demonstrate the attainment of the qualities of noble birth.
For a wise man who knows the mantras, being pleased, rightfully deserves all those thousands upon thousands of people who eat where he himself does not recite the Ṛgveda. (3.131)

This is a praise of those who know the meaning of the *aparā* [portion of the Veda]. This being the case, let it not be thought that this applies to those who do not recite the *ṛc*s; rather, it should be understood as "those who know the *ṛc*s. Furthermore, the term *mantravit* (knower of mantras) refers to one who knows the collection of the meanings of the Vedas. And this being the case—oblations for the ancestors (*kavya*) and sacrificial offerings (*havis*) are to be given to one distinguished by knowledge.
The explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) provides an illustration of this.
For hands smeared with blood are not cleansed by blood alone. (3.132)

Just as only one who knows the method of washing is capable of cleansing hands smeared with blood, and no other, so too only one who knows the meaning is capable of delivering both himself and others, and not another. As many morsels of food as one who is ignorant of the mantras consumes at offerings to the gods and ancestors, so many glowing spikes, spears, and iron balls shall he consume after death. (3.133)

In this case, the fault lies with the one who causes [the Brahmins] to eat, not with the one who eats, because the latter possesses the qualification for the scriptures that instruct on the giving of *śrāddha* offerings. This being so, the statement, "As many lumps as the giver of the *piṇḍas* causes to be eaten during the *śrāddha* rite by those ignorant of the mantras regarding the *havya* and *kavya* offerings"—this very point is to be understood through the force of these words. Alternatively, the fault of the one who causes [them] to eat is to be understood as being "ignorant of the mantras. As for what kind of affliction (*raṅkuśa*—or perhaps *kleśa*) the one who causes [them] to eat suffers, it is as follows:
"Some twice-born ones are devoted to knowledge, while others are devoted to austerity."
Some are devoted to austerity and Vedic study, while others are devoted to ritual action.
This is for the purpose of distributing the offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*). Thus it has been said:
"Offerings to the ancestors (*kavya*) should be diligently established among those devoted to knowledge (*jñāna-niṣṭha*);
however, offerings to the gods (*havya*) should be given according to the rule to all four [classes] alike. (3.135)
If one's father is unlearned in the Vedas, but his son has mastered the Vedas; or if the son is unlearned in the Vedas, but the father has mastered the Vedas. (3.136)
Regarding a conflict of opinion between these two teachers, the blessed Manu said:
"One should know the elder of the two to be he whose father is a Vedic scholar;
the other, however, deserves honor for the sake of honoring the sacred mantras. (3.137)

The father of a *śrotriya* son, because of his refinement (*saṃskṛtatva*), should be understood as being intended primarily to praise the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*). The perfection of conduct (*ācārasaṃpat*) is for the purpose of illustrating [the suitability of] the recipient of the meal. Because of the statement, "Only to a *śrotriya* should divine offerings be given" (MDh 3.128), it should be understood that the censure of the other [type of person] has that very [lack of learning] as its primary focus. And thus says the mantra:
"What is the use of asking about the Brahmin’s father, or what is the use of asking about his mother?
If the sacred learning (*śruta*) exists, those two—father and mother—are traditionally defined by their submissiveness (or, by their seniority)."

Others say that this refers to praise from outsiders; however, that is incorrect, because it has already been stated: "One should examine [the guest] from afar" (MDh 3.130). Therefore, it is exactly as previously explained. And it has been said in this regard: "When [the guest] possesses Vedic learning (*śrotriyatva*), [one should give] to the most worthy" (MDh 3.128). The purpose here is the gathering together of all qualities; thus, the logical connection (*hetumadbhāva*) should be applied here. If the son of one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) is superior, then one should examine him from afar. This is the result: "One should not feed a friend at a *śrāddha*; his [friend's] acquisition should be made through wealth."
One should feed at a śrāddha that twice-born man whom one knows to be neither an enemy nor a friend. || 3.138 ||

This is for the purpose of prohibiting the performance of *śrāddha* rites and the giving of gifts to both enemies and friends; it is a prohibition against what would otherwise be permitted by the scriptures. This serves as an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) regarding one who possesses the excellence of qualities such as being a master of the Vedas (*śrotriya*).

"For him whose *śrāddhas* and sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*) are primarily directed toward friends, there is no fruit after death, neither from the *śrāddhas* nor from the sacrificial offerings. (3.139)

And this is the prohibition regarding both of these. Furthermore, there is a specific statement in the preceding verse: "That twice-born man whom one knows to be neither an enemy nor a friend, him one should feed at a *śrāddha*" (MDh 3.138). The mention of "him" (*tam*) in that context is for the purpose of indicating the enemy, because the enemy is the subject under discussion here. This other [verse] is commenced with a view toward augmenting the deprecatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) found in the previous verse:
"The man who, out of delusion, forms alliances through a *śrāddha*, that lowest of the twice-born, a 'friend' by means of a *śrāddha', falls from the heavenly worlds. (MDh 3.140)
That which is called a communal feast is declared by the twice-born to be a *paiśācī* sacrificial gift;
it remains in this very world like a blind cow in a single house.
Just as one who sows seed in barren soil does not obtain fruit, so too the giver who offers an oblation to one ignorant of the Ṛgveda does not obtain the fruit. 3.142

This verse is intended to provide an exception regarding a virtuous friend. It shows that such [giving] may occur in the absence of another virtuous person; as the author demonstrates in the following verse:
"By giving a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to the rule to a learned man, one makes both the giver and the recipient partakers of the fruit, both in this world and after death. (3.143)

On account of the context, [the guest] must be a learned friend; since [offering to] another learned person has been prescribed elsewhere, [a friend] is impossible here. This being so, in the absence of one possessing qualities such as Vedic learning (*śrotriya*), one may at will honor a qualified friend at a *śrāddha*, but not an enemy, even if he is otherwise worthy. The meaning is: in the absence of a qualified Brāhmaṇa. This is the explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for this.
For an oblation consumed by one who harbors hatred becomes fruitless after death.

Regarding the statement, "One should not know [him] as either an enemy or a friend" (MDh 3.138), since both enemies and friends have been prohibited, one might fear that this exception (*pratiprasava*)—which applies to a virtuous person like a friend—might also apply to a virtuous enemy. To prevent this, and because there may be an absence of virtuous Brahmins, the following is undertaken for the purpose of further prohibition: "The *havya* and *kavya* offerings must be given only to a *śrotriya*" (MDh 3.128). Since he qualifies them with the word "only," it is for the purpose of excluding those who study merely the *chandas* (the Vedic meters).
Therefore, it is said: "With effort, one should feed at a *śrāddha* a Bahvṛca who has mastered the Veda."
Then, [he should approach] the Adhvaryu priest who has reached the end of his branch, or the Chandoga who has completed his recitation. || 3.145 ||

All of these, having completed their study of the Veda, are designated by various terms. This being so, just as one who recites the *Bahvṛca* (the Ṛgveda) is called a "Vedapāṭhaga," so too is the *Adhvaryu* (Yajurvedin) described in that same way through his mastery of another branch (*śākhā*), and likewise the *Chandoga* (Sāmavedin) through his completion [of his study]. One should know the "Three-Thousandfold Knowledge" (*trisahasravidyā*). Even in the context of sacrifice, there are those sciences characterized by the science of the Self (*sādhyātmavidyā*); they are indicated by the thousandfold path, hence they are the "thousandfold" (*sahasravartman*). These belong to the thousand-fold Sāmaveda; thus, he who possesses these three thousandfold sciences is "one who possesses the Three-Thousandfold Knowledge" (*trisahasravidya*).
If one should partake of the honored funeral offering (*śrāddha*) of any one of these,
there shall be eternal satisfaction for the ancestors extending through seven generations. [3.146]

This mention of the Bahvṛcas and others is not for the sake of establishing a sequence based on their non-existence or as mere alternatives. What then? It is that for these *śrotriyas*, instruction has been given constantly in this specific order. This is because the Vedas begin with the Ṛgveda in the mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavādas*). Thus it is said: "Whosever [of these] should eat the honored *śrāddha* feast... This is indeed the primary rule regarding the offering of *havya* and *kavya*. This statement of praise refers to the exclusion of those Brāhmaṇas who are otherwise qualified. But in their absence, however—
But this secondary rule (anukalpa) should be known as that which is always practiced by the virtuous.

The secondary option (*anukalpa*) will be explained [later]. When one deliberates regarding the secondary option, it is indeed praiseworthy because it is always practiced by the virtuous; that very point is now stated:

"One should feed the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, the sister’s son, the father-in-law, the teacher, the daughter’s son, the husband of a daughter, a kinsman, the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), and the person for whom one sacrifices (*yājya*). (3.148)

In this context, the mention of the *guru* is for the sake of including the teachers of sacred knowledge (*vidyā-guru*). Some, however, say that the phrase "one who is dear in this place" is intended as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) regarding friends. That is incorrect, because the counter-exception regarding friends has already been stated: "One may, if one wishes, honor a friend at a *śrāddha*" (MDh 3.144). The term *viṭpati* refers to the son-in-law (*jāmātṛ*), because the word *viś* denotes progeny, and because he is heard of in proximity to the daughter's son (*dauhitra*). He is not merely a guest among relatives and kinsmen; rather, he is a relative. As for what some have said—that the *viṭpati* is a guest because he is the lord of all people (*sarva-viśāmpati*) and because he is mentioned as being close by, thus constituting the primary option (*prathamakalpa*)—that is not the case. Furthermore, the instruction regarding the mother’s brother (*mātula*) and others is an alternative rule (*anukalpa*); it should be understood otherwise through the implication of the word "or" (*atha vā*).
One who knows the Dharma should not examine a Brahmin for a rite dedicated to the gods;
however, when a rite dedicated to the ancestors is at hand, he should examine him with great care. (3.149)

One should respond in such a way that the world understands this prohibition. However, regarding the ancestral rite (*pitrya*), one must apply effort toward the mastery of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). Alternatively, although those such as the one-eyed (*kāṇa*) and the club-footed (*ślīpadin*) may have a corrupt recitation (*durācāra-pāṭha*), they do not possess the status of being "of corrupt conduct" (*durācāratā*); thus, the prohibition against examination is intended to permit them for divine rites (*daiva*). In the case of the recitation by others, the phrase "those whose conduct is censured by the virtuous" becomes meaningful there as a description of censurable conduct. Since the context concerns prohibited Brāhmaṇas, one should avoid those who possess censurable conduct in both types of rites. For those here, such as the one-eyed and the club-footed, [the rule applies] "in the ancestral rite. Accordingly, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) prohibiting [such persons] from the sacrificial oblation (*havya*)—which will be stated later as, "For a Brāhmaṇa who does not study is extinguished like a fire of straw" (MDh 3.168)—is appropriate. The term "not studying" implies: "A Brāhmaṇa deserves exclusion; is he one of corrupt conduct, or is he one who studies? This latter case does not include the club-footed and others. Alternatively, this statement regarding the effort of examination—"But when the ancestral rite has arrived, one should examine [them] with care"—serves to introduce the subject matter of the subsequent section. And so he says:

Those who are thieves, outcasts, or eunuchs, and those who follow the lifestyle of nihilists—Manu has declared that such Brahmins are unworthy of offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya). 3.150.

A thief is one who steals gold and other such valuables, as indicated by the separate mention [in the list]. A eunuch (*klība*) is one who is impotent or whose semen has been stolen. One of "thievish livelihood" (*nāstikavṛtti*) is one who, while being a non-believer (*anāstika*), lacks a means of subsistence from those [other sources], or who, despite having manhood, lacks a livelihood due to his state of atheism; he is one of no faith. These, first of all, are prohibited in both cases; this is a prohibition regarding those things prescribed by the scriptures. The same applies to the subsequent [categories] as well:
"One with matted hair who does not study, one who is weak, and likewise a gambler."
