And one should not feed at a śrāddha those who officiate as priests for groups of people. (3.151)

A religious student (*brahmacārin*) is characterized by his matted locks (*jaṭā*). Since there is no possibility at all for one who has not studied [the Veda], it follows by implication that one who has not completed the study of the Veda in some other manner is understood here as "one whose Veda is incomplete" (*asamāptaveda*), or "one who has not formally accepted the Veda" (*asvīkṛtaveda*). By this, a prohibition is implied; for while there is a possibility of a slight study [of the Veda] in rites for the gods (*daiva*), there is none in rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*). Alternatively, this is a prohibition against one who has only slightly studied [the Veda] while remaining fixed in asceticism (*tapas*). Thus it has been said: "Likewise others are devoted to asceticism. Or perhaps it refers to one who has merely been initiated (*upanītamātra*), because he has not yet undertaken the Vedic vows (*vedavrata*); thus, there is a prohibition of the "one who has not studied," even though such a person might be included under the rule: "Even a daughter's son who is established in a vow" (MDh 3.234). The three terms "weak," "bald," and "red-haired," along with "one with impaired senses," are here used in a disordered sequence, like those fallen from their status. As it will be said: "Evil-minded men undergo a transformation of form" (MDh 11.48). A "gambler" (*kitava*) is a professional player. Regarding the phrase "and likewise a gambler," some explain the text by reading "a woman" (*striyam*) in place of the word "likewise" (*tathā*), stating that one should not feed a woman. This excludes a woman who might otherwise be included due to the context of the *śrāddha*. For it is said that those offerings are especially appropriate for mothers and the like, since they are rooted in water and consist of vegetables and cakes. One might argue: "One should feed Brāhmaṇa women endowed with good conduct to the mothers"—but we reply to this: since a woman is seen in the context of the *śrāddha*, there is no prohibition there; and since a human being is not [normally] included in the *śrāddha*, the prohibition of an unsuitable woman is improper. Furthermore, the word "likewise" (*tathā*) is used either for the purpose of beginning the description of those to be gratified or as an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) regarding women. This is the reading. Others, however, say that because a female Vedic scholar (*brahmavādinī*) possesses the status of a learned Brāhmaṇa (*śrotriya*), she is subject to the prohibition; but whether that is logical or illogical must be investigated. "And those who officiate for groups" refers to priests who obtain wealth from a collective group. They perform the *vrātyastoma* sacrifices which will be mentioned later. Because of the injunction "having separately taken up the fires," their sacrifice for a group is heard of in scripture; and this is known to be an improper act through the penance prescribed. For it will be said: "Having performed the sacrifice for *vrātyas*" (MDh 11.198). Since these are prohibited from the *śrāddha*, it implies permission for them to partake in rites for the gods (*daiva*). And because of this permission, it is understood that they are not performers of absolutely forbidden acts.
Physicians, temple-priests, meat-sellers, and those who live by trade— these should be avoided at offerings to the gods and the ancestors. [3.152]

Because the separate prohibition of physicians and temple-priests (*devālaka*) is meaningful, it is understood by implication that the prohibition applies to those who engage in these as a means of livelihood. Furthermore, regarding meat-sellers—even if they do so only once—the text states, "They fall immediately through meat" (MDh 10.92). Therefore, in both cases, those who live by selling even minor goods, provided such trade has become habitual, are to be avoided. A servant of a village or of the king, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one who opposes his teacher, one who has abandoned the sacred fires, and likewise a usurer; 3.153.

The prohibition regarding a village headman and a royal servant applies solely on account of their connection with their respective duties. Regarding a man with deformed nails and one with black teeth, the prohibition is due to the persistence of the results of past actions. One who opposes his guru is one who acts against the king; "pratiroddhā" is an alternative reading for "pratikūlam. He is one who harms [the guru] by facing him directly. One who has abandoned the sacred fires is included because there is no specific exception. And a usurer is one who lives by forbidden interest. A consumptive, a cattle-herder, a younger brother who marries before his elder, a Nirākṛti, a hater of the Veda, an elder brother whose younger brother marries first, and one who belongs to a multitude (gaṇa)—these are excluded from the Śrāddha. (3.154)

A *yakṣmī* is one suffering from consumption (*kṣaya*). The prohibition regarding the cattle-herder (*paśupāla*) is based on his connection to a non-livelihood [for a Brahmin]. There, another reading is *gorakṣaḥ paśupālaś ca*; and that should be explained according to the maxim of the cow and the bull (*gobalīvardanyāya*). He will later mention both the *parivettṛ* (the younger brother who marries before the elder) and the *parivitti* (the elder brother so superseded). A *nirākṛti* is one who neglects the gods, sages, and men; the meaning is an "untrue man" (*anaddhā puruṣaḥ*), i.e., one who does not support [them]. And thus is the Śruti of the Vājasaneyins: "Those for whom a man is 'untrue'—he who does not bow to the gods, nor to the ancestors, nor to men. And Gautama prescribes an expiation for him: "The same applies to those who extinguish the sacred fires, to the *nirākṛti*, and to those who commit minor offenses" (GDh 22.34). A *brahmadviṭ* is a hater of Brahmins (*brāhmaṇadviṭ*), because the words *brahman* and *brāhmaṇa* have the same meaning. And thus is the usage of the learned: "Why do you not study, O Brahmin? However, a hater of the [Vedic] words is specifically a reviler of the Vedas, because of the rule given later: "and also the reviler of the Vedas" (MDh 3.161). A member of a *gaṇa* is one who stands within the conventions of a group. Alternatively, *gaṇas* are associations of people of various castes who live by their physical labor and follow specific rules; a member of such a group is meant here.

One who is of bad character, one who has broken his vow of chastity, the husband of a low-caste woman, the son of a remarried woman, one who is one-eyed, and he in whose house lives a paramour—these are excluded. (3.155)

One who dwells in a palace while being the husband of a *vṛṣalī* should be known as a *kevala*. He has been mentioned; furthermore, these two—the *nauravimāhiṣaka*—have been explained. The *paunarbhava* will be described later. A *jāra* is a paramour, depending on the context of his qualities.
One who teaches for wages, one who has been taught by such a teacher, a *śūdra* disciple, and likewise a teacher of a *śūdra*, one who is corrupt in speech, and the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* sons. (3.156)

If a teacher who teaches for a fee or a teacher who teaches for wages were to exert himself as a true *guru*, this would be well-known among those who receive payment. If indeed this were the case, then scriptural injunctions such as "ten should be taught according to the law" (MDh 2.109), "where neither dharma nor wealth exists" (MDh 2.112), "one about to perform the ceremonial bath, being commanded by the *guru*, should provide for the *guru*'s sake according to his ability" (MDh 2.245), and "three activities constitute a livelihood" (MDh 10.76) would be meaningful; otherwise, they would not. As for the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, they will be explained later.
Those who have abandoned, without cause, their mother, father, or teacher; and those who have entered into association with outcasts through Brahmanical or matrimonial connections; 3.157.

He will state the reason for the abandonment of one's mother and the others; therefore, whoever abandons them without such a reason is a person with whom one must not eat. The rest is straightforward.

An incendiary of houses, a poisoner, one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa*, a seller of Soma, one who travels by sea, a bard, an oil-presser, and a forger [are persons with whom one must not eat]. (3.158)

An arsonist is one who sets fire to a dwelling; a poisoner is well known; a "kuṇḍāśī" (one who eats from a broken vessel) will be described later; a seller of *soma* is one who sells the *soma* creeper used in the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice; a royal priest (*sthāpaka*) is one who establishes kings with hymns of praise joined with the *prasthānas*; an oil-presser and a forger are included even in the absence of an arsonist; a *śmaśānodarī* (one who lives in a cremation ground) is well known. And one disputing with his father, a gambler, a drinker of intoxicants, one afflicted by a foul disease, one accused of a crime, a hypocrite, and a seller of liquids—(these are also excluded). 3.159.

The gambler (*kitava*) has already been mentioned in the verse beginning with "and one with matted hair" (*jaṭilaṃ ca*, MDh 3.151) as one who quarrels with his father regarding matters of law or worldly affairs. Why, then, is he mentioned again here? The former [gambler] is the direct agent of the gambling, and thus is primary; this one, however, is the instigator of that act and is therefore secondary. Since between the primary and the secondary, the primary is understood first, this [latter] is also secondary. Furthermore, he must be mentioned because he belongs to the category of those who are to be designated among the four [types of gamblers]. Because he must necessarily be stated, he is mentioned again as a distinct category, just as milk from another scripture is included among the modifications [of food]. Or, as in Gautama’s rule, the mention of the drinker of intoxicants (*madyapa*) is for the purpose of qualifying the gambler; or perhaps this person is not a gambler at all. But why is the former called a gambler (*akṣititapaḥ*)? Why, then, is only the drinker of intoxicants (*madyapa*) mentioned here? What is the point of imagining such a relationship of qualifier and qualified? The word *ha* is used merely to fill out the meter of the verse. Others, fearing redundancy, read *kekara* here instead: "One who quarrels with his father, and likewise a squint-eyed man (*kekara*), a drinker of intoxicants. The meaning is that a squint-eyed man is cruel toward what he sees, and is therefore to be avoided. A drinker of intoxicants, however, is one who drinks other substances such as *ariṣṭa*; whereas a drinker of *surā* has already been mentioned. For in another scripture, the drinker of *surā* is distinguished as someone else, and it is said that for drinking *surā* or intoxicants, one should practice the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance. He will also say later: "Water standing in a vessel for *surā*" and so forth. [This refers to the numbered verse: "Having drunk water that has stood in a vessel for *surā* or in a vessel for intoxicants, one should drink milk boiled with *Śaṅkhapuṣpī* for five nights" (MDh 11.147)]. And the specific penance for intoxicants is also stated by him in that context. A person afflicted by a foul disease is one suffering from leprosy (*kuṣṭhī*). An accused person (*abhiśasta*) is well known. A hypocrite (*ḍāmbhika*) is one who sells flavors or poisons under the guise of practicing dharma. This designation is seen in the arrangement of meanings. Likewise, in the case of secret killing, the employment of poison is mentioned.

One who makes bows and arrows, one who is the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister remains unmarried, one who betrays a friend, one who lives by gambling, and likewise one who is a teacher to his own son. (3.160)

In the phrase *agredidhiṣūpati*, two individuals are excluded: the *agredidhiṣū* and the *didhiṣūpati*. Among these, the *agredidhiṣū* is one who, while his elder brother remains unmarried, marries a maiden; the *didhiṣūpati* is the husband of that [younger sister]. Thus Gautama recites this pair at the beginning: "The *didhiṣū* and the *didhiṣūpati*" (GDh 15.16). Furthermore, one should know that the defiler of a maiden is also included among these, for even another [type of offender] incurs sin; however, this [specific category] is for the purpose of excluding those such as a betrayer of friends (*mitradruh*), a gambler (*dyūtavṛtti*), or a procurer (*karayitṛ*). From this very [text], it is inferred that the act itself is forbidden. By this, the performer of gambling is also explained. A "teacher of a son" (*putrācārya*) is one from whom the son has studied.

One suffering from epilepsy, one with scrofulous swellings, one with vitiligo, as well as a slanderer, one who is insane, one who is blind, and likewise a reviler of the Vedas—these should be avoided. (3.161)
One suffering from epilepsy; those afflicted with *gaṇḍamālā* and other such diseases are well known [as excluded].
Also, one who trains elephants, cattle, horses, or camels; one who lives by the stars (an astrologer); a breeder of birds; and likewise a teacher of warfare. (3.162)
A military preceptor skilled in weaponry, one who diverts the courses of rivers and stands to block them, a builder of houses, a messenger, and likewise a planter of trees. (3.163)

A messenger may sometimes be a servant sent by a king, or even one dependent on a king, yet he is considered neutral; however, a planter of trees is excluded from this [category] because he is prohibited from planting for another due to his capacity for instruction. A dog-keeper, a falconer, a defiler of maidens, a violent man, the son of an unmarried woman, and a priest for guilds—[these are also excluded]. (3.164)

It has been stated that one who defiles a maiden is such; the other, however, is explained as the *agredidhiṣū*. A "cruel man" (*hiṃsra*) is one by whom [others] are harmed through the killing of small creatures and so forth; the other [type] has already been mentioned. A "son of a *vṛṣala*" is said to be the son of a Śūdra woman when no other wife’s son has been born. An "officiant for groups" (*gaṇānāṃ yājakaḥ*) is one who officiates for many patrons, or for a worldly group through such activities as reciting prayers and the like. In the verse, "And those who cause groups to sacrifice" (MDh 3.151), the officiant for *vrātyas* is mentioned. Alternatively, the repetition may be due to the distinction between worldly and non-worldly groups. Others, however, fearing redundancy, read it differently as "and the divider of men" (*nṛṇāṃ caiva vyeṣakaḥ*). This means one who looks on with indifference at the initiation of a *sāman* singer who is supported by his family.
One devoid of proper conduct, a eunuch, one who is constantly begging, one who lives by agriculture, and one with elephantiasis are indeed censured by the virtuous. (3.165)

One who is deficient in conduct, such as the performance of the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and so forth, should also be known as one who commits transgressions. A *klība* (eunuch/impotent), however, is defined as one who has studied the Vedas but lacks vigor; even if he possesses a wife with discernment, his enthusiasm for the performance of domestic duties is broken. Being qualified [for ritual action], yet being lazy, he is called a *klība*. Just as Arjuna, whose enthusiasm was broken in battle, was told by Vāsudeva: "O Pārtha, do not yield to unmanliness" (*BhG* 2.3). Alternatively, a *napuṃsaka* (neuter) is one in one sense, while a *klība* is one whose life-force is impaired in another; this is because, despite possessing masculinity, he is mentioned again for the sake of emphasis. One who is constantly begging, even though he possesses wealth, is called a beggar even without a specific cause. But as for the one who lives by agriculture—who performs it merely for livelihood and not for the sake of dharma, being intent on various censurable and useless sensual enjoyments—he is thus censured. A *ślīpadī* (one with elephantiasis) is well-known. And one who is censured even for a slight transgression is blameworthy because of his ill-will toward that [transgression].
The butcher of sheep, the keeper of buffaloes, the husband of a woman previously married to another, and likewise the one who carries out the dead—these must be avoided with great effort. (3.166)

The [slaughter] of sheep and buffaloes has been explained. Some say that one who sells the exudations of trees (preta-niryāsa) is a performer of the rite of cursing; that is incorrect, because there is a prohibition against performing funeral rites for disciples, kinsmen, and others. In that case, it refers to a non-kinsman out of compassion for the person or for the sake of dharma. And thus says the Śruti: "This indeed is the supreme austerity: that they lead the deceased to the forest.

A learned man, the best among the twice-born, should avoid these lowest of the twice-born, who follow censurable conduct and are unworthy of the company at meals, in both cases (regarding marriage and dining). (3.167)

If those who are blind, lame, and so forth—who, despite being described as having reprehensible conduct—were actually of irreproachable conduct, it would be appropriate for them to have access to the sacrificial offerings according to this treatise. But if even they have no place there despite their irreproachable conduct, then the mention of "reprehensible conduct" becomes meaningless. Alternatively, it would be logical that they have no place there because they are not *śrotriya*s; that is the reason.
For a Brahmin who has not studied the Veda is extinguished like a fire of straw; one should not give him a sacrificial offering, for nothing is poured into ashes. (3.168)

For it is stated in the scripture that a Brāhmaṇa who does not study deserves exclusion. However, even one who studies but is of bad conduct—such as one who is one-eyed, has elephantiasis, or the like—is fit for a place at the meal during a rite for the gods (*daiva*). Thus, the prohibition against feeding those with one eye and so forth at a rite for the ancestors (*kavya*) becomes meaningful when applied to those of bad conduct who are reciters of the Vedas. By means of the grounds of being one-eyed and so forth, as well as being a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) despite his bad conduct, their eligibility for eating at a rite for the gods is established through the force of the contrast. Regarding the fruit that accrues to the giver after giving to those unworthy of the row (*apāṅktya*):
I shall explain that in its entirety, whether it pertains to rites for the gods or to rites for the ancestors.
This verse is introduced for the purpose of presenting a deprecatory explanatory passage (arthavāda) regarding this prohibition:

"Whatever is eaten by twice-born men who have not observed their vows, or likewise by those such as a younger brother who marries before his elder, and by others excluded from the company at meals—that indeed the Rākṣasas consume. (3.170)

"Whoever performs an improper act is all unfit for the company (*apāṅktya*). This explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—"In eating from the vessels of these [unfit persons], one eats indeed the *rakṣas* demons"—is intended as a censure. How so? It is so that one might avoid all those unfit for the company. This being the case, this passage does not authorize giving to those unfit for the company as a censurable alternative to giving to *rakṣas* demons; for giving to *rakṣas* demons is unrefined and is not mentioned in the context of the treatise. Therefore, this is an explanatory passage intended to prohibit, in general, feeding all those who are unfit for the company.
He who enters into marriage and the performance of the *agnihotra* while his elder brother remains [unmarried] is to be known as a *parivettṛ*; the elder brother, however, is a *parivitti*. (3.171)

Here, by the word *agnihotra*, the *āvasatha* (domestic fire) is also included by virtue of its capacity, since both are constituent parts of the ritual action (*karmāṅga*). Accordingly, they will be referred to by the term *svāgnihotra*. As it is said: "Neither a maiden, nor a young woman, nor one of little learning, nor a fool shall be the *hotṛ* priest for the *agnihotra*" (MDh 11.36). Thus, the designation of both is expressed through the scripture itself; this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) of censure regarding this transgression is intended for the purpose of avoidance: "The elder brother who remains unmarried (*parivitti*), the younger brother who marries before him (*parivettṛ*), and she with whom he marries (*yayā parividyate*)—all these go to hell, with the giver and the officiating priest making five. (3.172)

First, the *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder brother) falls due to the transgression of the scriptures, and the *parivitti* (the elder brother so superseded) falls because he becomes an obstacle [to the younger brother’s duty]. Furthermore, when the younger brother performs his rites, both the girl and the giver [of the girl] become causes of sin (*pratyavāya*), by which [the elder brother] indeed falls. Likewise, the giver and the officiating priest (*yājaka*) fall through their cooperation in the performance of a forbidden act; from the mention of the "giver and the priest" as the fifth [along with the four], it is inferred that there is a prohibition against acting in concert in all such matters. This being the case, this is precisely the traditional censure of the learned (*śiṣṭa*): "Whatever men are present at an assembly for a foul deed or for the accumulation of merit, the inner self (*antarātman*) perceives them, and those men certainly partake in a portion of that [result]."
He who, out of lust, becomes attached to the wife of his deceased brother—even if she has been appointed according to the sacred law—is to be known as a *didhiṣūpati*. (3.173)

[143] Some read this [verse], though it is not recited in the traditional scripture (*āmnāya*). This "husband of a *didhiṣū*" (*didhiṣūpati*) has been explained here by the force of another Smṛti text as being the same as the previously mentioned "elder brother whose younger brother marries first" (*āgredidhiṣū*). Now, regarding the husband of a *didhiṣū* and the husband of an *āgredidhiṣū*, the author points out the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* in this verse which is intent upon a prohibition: "Two sons born of the wives of others are the *kuṇḍa* and the *golaka*."
If he begets a son while the husband is alive, he is a *kuṇḍa*; if the husband is dead, he is a *golaka*.

And thus, one who eats from such a vessel would not be known as a "kuṇḍāśin" (one who eats from a *kuṇḍa*). The mention of the *kuṇḍa* may also include the *golaka*, because they are taught together in the prohibition.
Regarding that, those two born in the field of another—living beings—destroy the offerings of *havya* and *kavya* given by the donors, both in this world and after death. (3.175)
And here is another statement concerning specific distinctions:
"As many as those in the row whom an unworthy person looks upon while they are eating, for that many [members] the foolish donor does not obtain the fruit there. (3.176)
An eyeless man destroys the merit of ninety [gifts], a one-eyed man that of sixty, a leper that of a hundred, and one afflicted with a foul disease that of a thousand given by a donor. (3.177)

The meaning is that even those who are included in the row (paṅktigata) are [excluded] despite seeing. And thus, the statement "the blind man, having seen ninety, becomes one-eyed" becomes meaningful, because of his lack of vision and because of the mention of sixty and so forth. In some way, this is a deprecatory explanatory passage (arthavāda) where the specific number is not intended to be emphasized; rather, its purpose is to permit a higher specific number. When these [persons] are present: "As many Brahmins as a priest for Śūdras may touch with his limbs, for that many [gifts] the donor shall not obtain the fruit of the gift pertaining to the Pitṛs. (3.178)

In this context, the word *aṅga* should be understood as "limb" (*dṛṣṭa*), according to the subject matter. Alternatively, these [limbs] are situated in a row, and because they are not joined in a single line, they appear as if touching one another; it is on account of this commonality that this is called "contact.
And even a Brahmin learned in the Vedas, by accepting a gift out of greed for this [king], goes quickly to destruction, like an unbaked clay vessel in water. (3.179)

It should be understood that this applies even to one who knows the Vedas; furthermore, this prohibition should be known from the indicative mark [of the text] to apply specifically to the acceptance of gifts from unworthy persons:
"The food of a seller of Soma is ordure; that of a physician is pus and blood;
that of a usurer has no foundation; and that of a temple-priest (devalaka) is lost. (3.180)
Whatever is given in any way for the sake of one's livelihood, but what is given to a merchant— that shall bear fruit neither in this world nor in the next.
Just as an oblation poured into ashes, so too [is an offering] made to a twice-born man who is a paunarbhava.
But regarding other unworthy persons who are not fit to sit in the company of the virtuous, as previously specified, the wise declare that their food is fat, blood, flesh, marrow, and bone. (3.182)

This is a deprecatory explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) concerning all [unworthy recipients] without distinction. This is the intended meaning: not only does what is given to those who are censured become fruitless, but it further produces harm. And the production of such harm is appropriate, since it occurs in the context of a verse that prohibits [giving to] those who are forbidden. Since interpreting the text according to its literal hearing would contradict logical principle—given the incapacity of one who is shaven-headed—it must be understood that this [act] has the purpose of bringing about demerit (*pratyavāya*).
"By which best of the twice-born is a row defiled by those unworthy of the row purified?"
Learn of them in their entirety, those foremost of the twice-born who purify the company at the meal.

[Objection: Surely, since those unworthy of the company (*apaṅktya*) are prohibited, it would be purposeless to mention those who purify the company (*paṅktipāvana*) when their appointment [to the rite] is impossible. [Response: In that case, even for those possessed of noble lineage, Vedic study, and specialized knowledge, but whose faults are unknown, their appointment occurs by chance at the point of the ritual performance as a matter of course. How so? By the effortful selection of those intended to purify the company, they teach—by their own greatness—that there is no fault in feeding those unworthy of the company at that time, according to the verse: "But when the ancestral rite has arrived, one should examine [the guests] with great care" (MDh 3.149). Otherwise, they would either cause a deficiency in the *śrāddha* itself. Why is this so? Because of the force of the instruction regarding the appointment of those who purify the company; otherwise, that instruction would be purposeless. Alternatively, this mention of those who purify the company is for the sake of praising the Brāhmaṇas who are about to be described. How so?
Those who are foremost in all the Vedas and in all the expositions [of the scriptures], and who are born of a lineage of Vedic scholars, should be known as the purifiers of the assembly. 3.184

Just as these previously mentioned Brahmins—possessing the perfection of qualities such as noble birth and being born in the primary or secondary kalpas—are purifiers of the row (*paṅktipāvana*), so too are these who are about to be described, beginning with those who have kindled the *triṇāciketa* fire. Why, then, is this verse stated for the sake of an illustration? Because it was spoken for the benefit of others and not for one's own sake; otherwise, their repetition here would be purposeless if they were merely examples, for the *triṇāciketa*s and others have not been mentioned [previously] because they do not possess the aforementioned qualities. Therefore, this instruction in this verse is for the purpose of praising those previously mentioned [Brahmins], and it does not describe various types of material substances.

One who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, one who maintains the five sacred fires, one who knows the Trisuparṇa hymns, one who is learned in the six Vedāṅgas, one born of a lineage where the daughter was given in marriage according to the Brahma rite, and one who chants the Jyeṣṭhasāman. (3.185)

The study of the *triṇāciketa* is mentioned here because of its association with the vow (*vrata*); that too is recited. A *brāhmaṇa* is described by the *bahuvrīhi* compound as one who maintains the five fires (*pañcāgni*). Through the two terms *savya* and *apasavya*, there is the attainment of the forest-dweller’s practice; by the rule "he should perform the five-fold heat on his head," the *trisuparṇa* vow of the *Bahvṛca* is indicated, and because of its association with that, the possessor of it is said to be recited. Others, however, say that because it is read as a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), it is called *sauparṇa* due to its presence therein. Even though these are minor studies, they are included here for reasons such as the *triṇāciketa* and others, since this [text] cannot be undertaken without them; thus, this consists of six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). One who has completed his study is a giver of the *brahmadeya* (the gift of a daughter in marriage), born of a *brāhma* wedding. A *jyeṣṭhasāmika* is one who possesses the *jyeṣṭhasāman* of the *Chandoga*s; others, however, read it as *jyeṣṭhasāmaga*. For them as well, the etymological derivation should be stated according to their specific qualities.

One who knows the meaning of the Vedas, an expounder of them, a celibate student, one who bestows a thousand gifts, and one who lives for a hundred years—these Brāhmaṇas should be known as purifiers of the assembly. (3.186)

Even without the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), [one may know] the meaning of the Veda through tradition (*āgama*). And so say the etymologists (*nairukta*): "For there is no direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of these [meanings] for one who is not a seer (*ṛṣi*); or else, such persons are unworthy of the row (*apāṅkteya*). The term "teacher" (*pravaktṛ*) refers to those of other treatises, such as the *Smṛtis*, and not to those outside the Veda. For he will say: "The study of false scriptures" (MDh 11.66) and "those scriptural traditions which are outside the Veda" (MDh 12.95). Thus, the word "teacher" must be explained as having a different meaning from the phrase "knower of the six auxiliaries" (*ṣaḍaṅgavit*). And the student (*brahmacārin*) is to be discussed as before. We shall also resolve the prohibition against his eating at a *śrāddha*. One who knows a thousand [verses] is enjoined; disregarding these groups [of qualities], one whose defects have matured over time attains concentration (*samādhi*) and thus becomes a purifier of the row (*paṅktipāvana*). From the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the alternative—that the row is defiled by one unworthy of the row—it is inferred that there is sin in eating in the same row with these [unworthy persons]. In this way, the statement regarding the defilement of the row becomes meaningful here, since elsewhere one should neither eat nor sit together with them. However, the excellence of the "purifiers of the row" is stated by this means. Alternatively, by eating in the same row with them, there is either prosperity or merely the non-occurrence of sin; thus, because they do not defile the row, there is prosperity and no sin when eating in the same row with them. And likewise, the examination of Brāhmaṇas mentioned in connection with the *śrāddha* meal should be understood to apply elsewhere as well, because the reason is the same and because of established custom. Furthermore, the invocation of the gods (*daiva-saṃkīrtana*) should be understood to apply even to rites dedicated solely to the gods, because there is no difference in the purpose and because of the general reference in the rule: "those who have bathed after completing their Vedic studies and vows" (MDh 4.31). Thus has been described the procedure for examining Brāhmaṇas. This, however, is stated with a view toward ritual action (*karman*).
On the day before or on the very day when the śrāddha rite is to take place, he should properly invite at least three Brahmins who possess the qualities previously described. (3.187)

"On the previous day" means on the day before the *śrāddha*; this invitation for a future time is intended to prevent the suspicion of sexual intercourse. Furthermore, since sexual intercourse is forbidden on festival days (*parvan*), and because the monthly *śrāddha* is performed on such days, this [invitation] is rendered purposeful; or, because that day is difficult to obtain, it may be done on the very same day as the Brahmins, even if it is on the following day, provided it falls on a single day. In the absence of these two reasons, the rule "at least three" has already been considered. The rest is straightforward. [146] A twice-born man who has been invited to a rite for the ancestors (*pitrya*) should always remain self-restrained.
And one should not recite the Vedic hymns for whom that śrāddha is being performed. (3.188)

And for this reason, it is proper that those who eat at a *śrāddha* be invited for the future; the purpose of this instruction regarding celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is for that day and night. This rule of celibacy applies to the rite for the ancestors (*pitrya*). Because of the mention of the "divine" [nature], there is no study of the Vedas (*chando'nadhyayana*) for one invited for the sake of the ancestors. Due to the context and because of the indicative mark of his remaining in that state, the mention of the Vedas (*chandograhaṇa*) is intended for the Brahmins as well. Furthermore, this is a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*) applicable equally to the giver. For the ancestors attend upon those twice-born who have been invited; becoming like the wind, they follow them and likewise wait upon them as they sit. (3.189)
This verse is intended as praise for not transgressing [the invitation]:

"An excellent twice-born man who, having been duly invited to a rite for the gods (havya) or the ancestors (kavya), should somehow transgress [that duty], becomes a sinner and goes to the state of a pig. (3.190)

If one who has been invited with the promise, "I shall eat," does not eat, that is a transgression of this rule. But he who, having been invited to a *śrāddha*, dallies with a low-caste woman (*vṛṣalī*), incurs whatever evil deed the giver may have committed. (3.191)

By the word *vṛṣalī*, it is the Brāhmaṇī woman herself who is censured. Since she, being lustful (*vṛṣasyantī*), causes her husband to deviate from his celibacy (*brahmacarya*), that censure is appropriate for the violation of the vow, even though the fault belongs to both; for all such matters are governed by the principle of wealth. Furthermore, this fault of transgressing the rule applies to one who has not eaten; as for one who has already eaten, the author will state later: "The eater of a Śrāddha [who approaches] the bed of a *vṛṣalī*... (MDh 3.250).
"The ancestors, the ancient deities, are free from anger, devoted to purity, always practicing celibacy, having laid down their weapons, and are highly blessed. (3.192)
This verse is for the purpose of introduction: "Since the origin of all these [castes] has been explained in its entirety, learn now those rules by which they are to be served. (3.193)
The sons of all those sages— Marīci and the others, who were the offspring of Manu Hairaṇyagarbha— are recorded as the groups of Pitṛs.
The sons of Virāṭ, known as the Somasads, are remembered as the ancestors of the Sādhyas;
the Agniṣvāttas, renowned throughout the world, are the ancestors of the gods, being the offspring of Marīci.
The Barhiṣads, born of Atri, are remembered as the progenitors of the Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Uragas, Rākṣasas, Suparṇas, and Kinnaras. (3.196)
[147] Among the Brahmins they are named Somapas; among the Kṣatriyas, Havirbhujs; among the Vaiśyas, Ājyapas; and among the Śūdras, Sukālins. 3.197.
By this, they are called the "fathers" (pitṛs) of these [beings], such as the Brāhmaṇas and others. The Somapas are known as the sons of Kavi; the Haviṣmants are the Aṅgirasas;
the Ājyapas are the sons of Pulastya; and the Sukālins are the sons of Vasiṣṭha. (3.198)

One should designate as belonging to the Brahmins alone those who are consumed by fire and those not consumed by fire, those who sit upon the sacrificial grass for the *kavya* offerings, those who have departed, the *agniṣvātta*s, and the *saumya*s. (3.199)
These principal groups of ancestors that have been proclaimed— of them too, it should be understood here that their sons and grandsons are infinite.
From the sages the ancestors were born; from the ancestors, the gods and dānavas;
and from the gods, the entire world—both moving and stationary—in due succession. (3.201)

The eight verses concerning the origin of the ancestors (*pitṛs*) attain the status of praise (*stuti*) by virtue of the context; they are to be interpreted in a manner consistent with logical reasoning. Furthermore, because there is a mention of those not [ordinarily] entitled [to such rites], such as the Daityas and others, it is understood that even the *Somapās* and the rest are included under the term "Brahmins" and so forth, and thus this is a mere explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). Moreover, since ancestors of these very names are recited in the Vedas, they are celebrated here by various names. And yet, these are not [newly] born ancestors, because their status, place of origin, and eternity are established. Rather, for the sake of accomplishing ritual acts, they are eternally established as the means (*sādhana*); how then could this account of their "origin" not be for the purpose of praise? It is stated for the sake of inciting one toward the injunction (*vidhi-prarocanā*). How so? First of all, the ancestors of the gods and others themselves are to be honored with the *śrāddha* rite; how much more so, then, those of human beings? Therefore, for the purpose of honoring them, an injunction regarding the qualities of the ritual act is now being stated.
Even water, when given with faith using silver vessels or those adorned with silver, conduces to inexhaustible results. (3.202)

As for the rule regarding silver [plates], it applies to those who possess silver; or rather, for one desiring inexhaustible [results], there should be silver ones. Furthermore, in this way, the silver plates would result in being merely occasional (*naimittika*). And this is not desired, because the word "inexhaustible" is intended as a praise (*saṃstuti*). Others, however, by the logic of the "stick and cake" (*daṇḍāpūpikā*), read "golden" as well, [claiming] "those yield greater fruit. That is incorrect. Since the principle (*nyāya*) is fixed, there would be a fault elsewhere; therefore, the interpretation exactly as heard in the text is superior. The other, however, is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*).
For the twice-born, the rite for the ancestors (pitṛkārya) is superior to the rite for the gods (daivakārya);
for the rite for the gods is traditionally held to be the preliminary nourishment for the rite for the ancestors. (3.203)
Since this is so,
therefore one should first employ destiny as their protector.
For the Rākṣasas plunder a Śrāddha that is devoid of protection.

Having designated one's chosen deity, the rite for the gods should be performed first; or, without distinction, it may be for all the deities, provided that it serves as a protection for the ancestral rite. This being the case: "One should perform that [rite] beginning and ending with the gods; it should not begin and end with the ancestors.
For one who performs it beginning and ending with the ancestors, he quickly perishes along with his lineage. (3.205)

This is for the purpose of praising the injunction, "One should first employ the divine [rite]" (MDh 3.204), and because all other [details] in the *śrāddha* may be out of order; therefore, for the sake of establishing the proper sequence, [the text says] immediately after this:
"One should carefully prepare a pure and secluded place, and smear it with cow dung; one should also ensure that it slopes toward the south. (MDh 3.206)
For this reason,
the ancestors are always satisfied by what is offered in open spaces, on clean riverbanks, and indeed in secluded places. (3.207)

Even on seats that have been smeared with cow dung— or which are pure by their very nature— and which have been prepared separately, each provided with sacrificial grass (barhis) and water for sipping, he should cause those twice-born men to sit down properly. (3.208)
Having thus seated them all upon blameless seats,
one should honor them with fragrant perfumes and garlands, beginning with the gods.
Having brought water for them, as well as sesame seeds together with strainers, the Brāhmaṇa, being authorized by the Brāhmaṇas, should always perform the rite in the fire. (3.210)
Having first performed the satiation of Agni, Soma,
and Yama, he should afterwards satisfy the ancestors with the offering of oblations according to the prescribed rule.
In the absence of fire, however, one should place the offering directly into the hand of a Brahmin;
for that twice-born man is said by the Brahmins who perceive the sacred mantras to be the very fire itself. (3.212)
The ancients speak of these best of the twice-born as gods who are free from anger, full of serene faith, and intent upon nourishing the world at the ancestral rite (śrāddha). [3.213]

Therefore, these [ancestors], being free from anger, are to be served; for they are well-pleased. Having performed the circumambulation around the fire in the counter-clockwise direction (apasavya), he should pour water upon the ground with his left hand. 3.214.
Having formed three balls from the remnants of that sacrificial food, he, being composed, should offer them facing south according to the very same rite prescribed for water libations. (3.215)

Having offered those rice-balls (piṇḍas) there according to the rule with self-restraint, he should wipe that hand on those Darbha grasses for the sake of the "partakers of the smearings" (lepabhāginaḥ). 3.216.
And two [generations] are partakers of the lepa (the food smeared on the hand). Others, however, say there are three.

Having sipped water, having turned away from the water, and having slowly restrained the breaths three times, one who knows the mantras should pay homage to the six seasons and to the ancestors. (3.217)

With the mantra, “Homage to you, O fathers,” he should slowly pour out the remainder of the water near the *piṇḍas*. Then, with a concentrated mind, he should smell those *piṇḍas* in the order they were offered. (3.218)
Having taken small portions from each of the food balls in succession, he should first cause those very Brahmins who are seated to eat according to the rule. (3.219)

The fourteen verses have not been commented upon because their meaning is clear. Here, the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*—which is a Vedic rite—is included for the purpose of establishing the procedure for the *śrāddha* ceremony; even for one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* takes place at the *āvasathya* fire. Thus says the author of the Sūtras: "They say the same even for one who has maintained the sacred fires. However, while the father is still living, one should perform the offering for those who precede him.

Even though there is an injunction for giving without distinction, by virtue of the established usage (*liṅga*), when the father is living, the sacrifice is for the deceased; after the father’s death, the offering (*nirvāpa*) is properly directed toward three ancestors. For in this way, the higher world for the obligatory rite (*nitya-karma*) will be secured. Furthermore, the commonality of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) extends up to the seventh generation, and thus it will be purposeful. For instance, the rule regarding impurity alone would have its proper application even if one were to say, "the fourth cake does not go [to the ancestors]. Indeed, there is no offering of a cake for a fourth ancestor after the father; as it will be stated: "Water should be offered for three, and the cake proceeds for three" (MDh 9.186). And so says another scripture: "If father and son both possess the sacred fires (*sāgni*), the son indeed gives to those same ancestors to whom the father gives."
Or else, like a Brahmin disputant, he may resort to that ancestral rite as his own father. || 3.220 ||

And one should offer [the offerings] beyond [the father] to only two ancestors. Thus Jātūkarṇi says: "One does not offer to one who is living, according to the Śruti"; and: "The fourth rice-ball does not go [to him]. This being so, since the satisfaction of the ancestors is the goal to be accomplished, who would perform it while the father is alive? For he [the father] himself must be directly propitiated. Another view is that for one whose father is living, the ritual action ends with the *homa* (oblation), or the commencement of the rite is suspended. As it is said: "But he whose father has passed away, yet whose grandfather is still living..."
Having proclaimed his father's name, he should proclaim his great-grandfather.

In this context, the prohibition of mentioning the name of the grandfather (*pitāmaha*) is for the purpose of ceasing the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*). This is because the entitlement to perform ancestral rites, such as the worship of the *pitaras*, belongs to the deceased; as the scripture states, "one offers [the oblation] to the *pretas*. Therefore, one whose father is living should offer [the rice-balls] to the two deceased ancestors alone. An offering is not appropriate for one who is living. Nor should it be given to a fourth person beyond them, according to the statement: "The rice-ball does not go to a fourth. Therefore, it should be given to only two. And thus, even one whose father is currently living should give to only two, since the reason is the same. Why? We have already explained that "the rice-ball does not go to a fourth," and because of the capacity of the rice-ball to provide benefit, the giving should be understood as being directed toward only three. As it has been said: "The rice-ball proceeds to three" (MDh 9.186).
"Or the grandfather may eat that śrāddha," so Manu has declared;
this is the same as the latter half of the preceding verse.
"Or, being duly permitted, he may perform it himself at will. (3.222)

By whom was he authorized? By the grandfather (*pitāmaha*), because he is the subject under discussion. If one were to perform what has been stated by himself [the father], what would be appropriate? How could there be a reliance on the intention [of the grandfather] from the left side (*vāmapakṣa*)? Because all three are entitled [to the rite], and because those who have entered the state of the deceased (*pretabhāva*) are worthy of worship. A direct worship (*pratyakṣārcana*) in the form of a *śrāddha* is inappropriate [for the living]. Or rather, the grandfather might be [the recipient]; for since a living person is not to be worshipped, just as there is no entitlement for the three due to the restriction [of the rule], so too there is no entitlement for one whose grandfather is living through the offering of a *śrāddha*. It has been stated that [the rite] ends with the oblation (*homānta*). By this, one whose great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*) is living is also to be understood as explained, because the case is the same. As for the ending in *-kāra*, it is because of its similarity [to the other cases].
Having placed the *tilodaka* together with the *pavitra* into their hands, he should offer them the first portion of that *piṇḍa*, saying, "May there be *svadhā* for them. (3.223)
Having himself taken up the increased portion of food with both hands, he should place it slowly near the Brahmins while meditating upon the ancestors. (3.224)
When food that has been set aside from both hands is brought forward, the evil-minded Asuras suddenly snatch it away. (3.225)
Being self-restrained and composed, he himself should first set out the various qualities of food—soups, vegetables, and so forth—as well as milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey. (3.226)
Various kinds of food and edibles, roots and fruits, as well as heart-pleasing meats and fragrant drinks. (3.227)
Having brought these together in equal portions, he should serve them slowly and with great composure,
remaining pure and making known all their qualities.
One should never shed tears, nor become angry, nor speak untruth;
one should not touch food with the foot, nor should one shake it. (3.229)
Anger sends the hungry ghosts (preta) to the abyss; falsehood, one's enemies;
the touch of one's feet, the rākṣasa demons; and the shaking [of the body], evildoers. (3.230)
Whatever may please the learned Brahmins, that he should give without avarice; and he should engage in discourses on the Vedas, for this is what is desired by the ancestors. (3.231)

During the rite for the ancestors, one should indeed cause [the guests] to hear the private recitation of the Veda, as well as the treatises on Dharma, the narratives, the Itihāsas, the Purāṇas, and the Khilas. (3.232)
Being satisfied himself, he should gladden the Brahmins and feed them gradually;
he should repeatedly encourage them with food and praise for their virtues. (3.233)
One should diligently feed even a daughter’s son who is observing a vow at a śrāddha ceremony;
one should provide a kutapa blanket as a seat and scatter sesame seeds upon the ground.

The injunction regarding effort (*yatnavacana*) applies specifically to the father’s side because of the context, even though the daughter’s son (*dauhitra*) is engaged in a vow (*vratastha*). Thus, the mention of one “engaged in a vow” is indeed a restriction (*niyama*) by means of the three verses (*tṛca*), intended for the purpose of praising the daughter’s son, as in the passage beginning with “In the rite for the gods, like one under a vow” (MDh 2.189). Since that is so, there is no fault; we shall state the resolution for the verse “But he who might eat for the sake of the monthly [shraddha]” (MDh 11.158) in that very place. Furthermore, because the daughter’s son is not explicitly mentioned [in the primary list], his superiority is stated in comparison to the secondary (*ānukalpika*) maternal grandfathers and others. And as for the *kutapa* [time]: its prescription is made in connection with the daughter’s son; or rather, since the section on the offering of seats is unlimited, and because the *kutapa* is taught here together with the secondary daughter’s son, this [time] belongs to the secondary maternal grandfather. Why, then, is it thus? Because—
Three things are purifying at a Śrāddha: a daughter’s son, a blanket made of goat’s hair, and sesame seeds;
and three things they praise in this regard: purity, freedom from anger, and lack of haste. (3.235)
The praise of purity and the other virtues is for the purpose of enjoining them. Others, however, say: "Truth, freedom from anger, and lack of haste.
All the food should be very hot, and they should eat while remaining silent. And the twice-born should not speak of the qualities of the sacrificial offering when questioned by the giver. (3.236)
Also by way of illustration: this verse has the purpose of prescribing a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*). He states the reason:

"As long as there is heat in the food, as long as they eat with speech restrained, for so long do the ancestors eat—provided that the qualities of the sacrificial offering have not been mentioned. (3.237)
The praise of the *ūṣman* and other [sounds] serves the purpose of an injunction:
"Whatever one eats with the head wrapped, whatever one eats facing south, and whatever one eats while wearing shoes—that indeed the *rakṣas* consume. (3.238)

However, this prohibition applies to those who have arrived at a *śrāddha* where food has not been prepared; for it will be stated later: "Whether animate or inanimate" (MDh 4.117). Regarding the word "eats" (*bhuṅkte*), it indicates a connection with the hand of the recipient, because of the scriptural statement: "For the twice-born is traditionally said to have his hand as his mouth" (MDh 4.117). Furthermore, the acquisition of the object [of eating] occurs even in the act of feeding. This prohibition of the object, as applicable in certain cases, is intended as a praise for the rule governing the qualified person. And in every kind of *śrāddha*: "The Caṇḍāla, the boar, the cock, and likewise the dog..."
Neither a menstruating woman nor a eunuch should look at twice-born men while they are eating. (3.239)
Therefore, one should give [the food] after examining sites such as the banks of water or sandy shores; there is a prohibition against those who have arrived at unexamined places. For:
"In the case of an oblation, a gift, or a meal—whether in a rite for the gods or for the ancestors—whatever is looked upon by these [unworthy persons] becomes ineffective. (3.240)
These rules also apply to rites for the gods and the ancestors by virtue of the scriptural injunctions; however, he states this specifically:
"A pig defiles by its smell, a cock by the wind of its wings, a dog by the casting of its glance, and one born of a low caste by touch. (3.241)

[153] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lamp. Thus should you remember it. This is what the Blessed One said. With their minds uplifted, the monks rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One. 153. The Lamp Sūtra. Chapter 120. [End of Volume 2]. Chapter 121. The Discourse on the Great Nirvana. Part 1. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: “Bhikṣus, there are four kinds of persons in the world. What are the four? They are: the person who is like an autumn cloud, the person who is like a water bubble, the person who is like a mountain torrent, and the person who is like a fruit on a tree. What is the person who is like an autumn cloud? It refers to a person who, having committed evil deeds, does not see their own faults; they do not repent, do not confess, and do not abandon them. Because of these unwholesome roots, they fall into the three evil realms and suffer immeasurable pain. This is called the person who is like an autumn cloud. What is the person who is like a water bubble? It refers to a person who, having committed evil deeds, sees their own faults and repents; they confess and abandon them. Because of these wholesome roots, they do not fall into the three evil realms but are born among gods and humans, experiencing immeasurable joy. This is called the person who is like a water bubble. What is the person who is like a mountain torrent? It refers to a person who, having committed evil deeds, sees their own faults and repents; they confess and abandon them. Because of these wholesome roots, they do not fall into the three evil realms but are born among gods and humans, experiencing immeasurable joy. However, because they do not cultivate the path, they eventually fall back into the three evil realms. This is called the person who is like a mountain torrent. What is the person who is like a fruit on a tree? It refers to a person who, having committed evil deeds, sees their own faults and repents; they confess and abandon them. Because of these wholesome roots, they do not fall into the three evil realms but are born among gods and humans, experiencing immeasurable joy. Furthermore, they cultivate the path and attain parinirvāṇa in this very life. This is called the person who is like a fruit on a tree. At that time, the bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha: “World-Honored One, as for the person who is like an autumn cloud, the person who is like a water bubble, and the person who is like a mountain torrent—these three types of persons, having committed evil deeds, see their own faults and repent; they confess and abandon them. Because of these wholesome roots, they do not fall into the three evil realms but are born among gods and humans, experiencing immeasurable joy. However, because they do not cultivate the path, they eventually fall back into the three evil realms. World-Honored One, how can we distinguish these three types of persons? The Buddha told Kāśyapa: “If a person, having committed evil deeds, sees their own faults and repents; they confess and abandon them. Because of these wholesome roots, they do not fall into the three evil realms but are born among gods and humans, experiencing immeasurable joy. Furthermore, they cultivate the path and attain parinirvāṇa in this very life. This is called the person who is like a fruit on a tree. Why is this? Because they have severed the five lower fetters and attained the fruit of Arhatship. Therefore, they do not return to this world but attain parinirvāṇa in this very life. This is called the person who is like a fruit on a tree. At that time, the bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha: “World-Honored One, as for the person who is like an autumn cloud, the person who is like a water bubble, and the person who is like a mountain torrent—these three types of persons, having committed evil deeds, see their own faults and repent; they confess and abandon them. Because of these wholesome roots, they do not fall into the three evil realms but are born among gods and humans, experiencing immeasurable joy. However, because they do not cultivate the path, they eventually fall back into the three evil realms. World-Honored One, how can we distinguish these three types of persons? The Buddha told Kāśyapa: “If a person, having committed evil deeds, sees their own faults and repents; they confess and abandon them. Because of these wholesome roots, they do not fall into the three evil realms but are born among gods and humans, experiencing immeasurable joy. Furthermore, they cultivate the path and attain parinirvāṇa in this very life. This is called the person who is like a fruit on a tree. Why is this? Because they have severed the five lower fetters and attained the fruit of Arhatship. Therefore, they do not return to this world but attain parinirvāṇa in this very life. This is called the person who is like a fruit on a tree. At that time, the bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha: “World-Honored One, as for the person who is like an autumn cloud, the person who is like a water bubble, and the person who is like a mountain torrent—these three types of persons, having committed evil deeds, see their own faults and repent; they confess and abandon them. Because of these wholesome roots, they do not fall into the three evil realms but are born among gods and humans, experiencing immeasurable joy. However, because they do not cultivate the path, they eventually fall back into the three evil realms. World-Honored One, how can we distinguish these three types of persons? The Buddha told Kāśyapa: “If a person, having committed evil deeds, sees their own faults and repents; they confess and abandon them. Because of these wholesome roots, they do not fall into the three evil realms but are born among gods and humans, experiencing immeasurable joy. Furthermore, they cultivate the path and attain parinirvāṇa in this very life. This is called the person who is like a fruit on a tree. Why is this? Because they have severed the five lower fetters and attained the fruit of Arhatship. Therefore, they do not return to this world but attain parinirvāṇa in this very life. This is called the person who is like a fruit on a tree. At that time, the bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha: “World-Honored One, as for the person who is like an autumn cloud, the person who is like a water bubble, and the person who is like a mountain torrent—these three types of persons, having committed evil deeds, see their own faults and repent; they confess and abandon them. Because of these wholesome roots, they do not fall into the three evil realms but are born among gods and humans, experiencing immeasurable joy. However, because they do not cultivate the path, they eventually fall back into the three evil realms. World-Honored One, how can we distinguish these three types of persons? The Buddha told Kāśyapa: “If a person, having committed evil deeds, sees their own faults and repents; they confess and abandon them. Because of these wholesome roots, they do not fall into the three evil realms but are born among gods and humans, experiencing immeasurable joy. Furthermore, they cultivate the path and attain parinirvāṇa in this very life. This is called the person who is like a fruit on a tree. Why is this? Because they have severed the five lower fetters and attained the fruit of Arhatship. Therefore, they do not return to this world but attain parinirvāṇa in this very life. This is called the person who is like a fruit on a tree. Because of these wholesome roots, they do not fall into the three evil realms but are born among gods and humans, experiencing immeasurable joy.
