Because of these wholesome roots, they do not fall into the three evil realms but are born among gods and humans, experiencing immeasurable joy. Furthermore, they cultivate the path and attain parinirvāṇa in this very life. This is called the person who is

All these [verses] are explanatory statements (*arthavāda*) for the injunction "one should not look at them" (3.239). All these [beings] are impure; even by looking at them, they cause defilement. Therefore, one should not look at them, nor should they be in close proximity when the gaze falls upon the *śrāddha*. Some say that the "one born of a lower caste" (*avaravarṇaja*) refers to the *caṇḍāla*. That is incorrect, because his creation is already prohibited by the general rule itself. Therefore, the Śūdra born of a lower caste should be understood as one who causes defilement through touch during the *śrāddhas* of the twice-born, but not in his own *śrāddha*, since he is authorized therein. And among men, the one born of a lower caste intended here is specifically the *caṇḍāla*, as in the prohibition of looking: "The *caṇḍāla* and the boar... (MDh 3.239). Consequently, the phrase "born of a lower caste" in this context regarding touch is a prohibition of touch. Since touching a *caṇḍāla* is not otherwise established [as permitted], there is well-being for the Śūdra [in his own rites].
Whether he be lame or one-eyed, or even a servant of the donor, or one with deficient or redundant limbs—one should remove him from there as well. (3.242)
Those who are lame and so forth should be understood as Śūdras, by virtue of the context of the commencement of the treatise; they include both those who are servants and those who are not.
Even if he has been permitted by the Brāhmaṇas, he should, according to his ability, honor a Brāhmaṇa or even a mendicant who has approached for the sake of food. (3.243)

Having gathered food of all kinds for those invited, and having sprinkled it with water, he should scatter it on the ground in front of those who have finished eating, after they have given their permission; for this is appropriate because it was prescribed for that purpose. (3.244)

The food-remnants and that which is scattered upon the *darbha* grass shall be the share of those women of noble family who have died while performing their duties or have abandoned their lives. (3.245)
They declare that the food remaining on the ground after the meal belongs as its share to the group of slaves who are upright and free from deceit during the ancestral rite.

These three verses have a straightforward meaning: "And he who scatters [the food] upon *darbha* grasses," and so forth. It is understood that the garment should not be given on anything other than *darbha* grass, nor on the ground; for otherwise, the mention of *darbha* would be purposeless. Thus far regarding the rites for those with ancestors (*sapitṛ*). This is another point:
"For a twice-born man who has passed away, until the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is performed, one should feed him at the *śrāddha* in this very manner and offer a single *piṇḍa*. (3.247)

The sapindas should perform the *navaśrāddha* together; they should offer a single *piṇḍa*. Thus, the *śrāddha* rite would belong to one person alone, and this performance without the *sapinda* ritual occurs after one year. One should offer a *piṇḍa* to a single individual and use the singular form for the end of the mantra because of its underlying reason (*hetutvāt*). That singularity is well-known from other scriptures; therefore, one should not act otherwise. On the ground, one should offer only a single *piṇḍa*; however, when there is a merging of the *piṇḍas* based on the wording of the mantra, "O fathers, come hither to us," then—
But once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed for him according to the Dharma, the sons must perform the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa-nirvapaṇa*) by means of this very same procedure. (3.248)
By the very same rule [already] stated, his sons should give [the inheritance] to their mothers after that.
He who, having eaten at a *śrāddha*, gives the leavings to a *vṛṣala*, that fool goes headlong to the Kālasūtra hell. (3.249)
This is a specific prohibition:
"If one who has been invited to a *śrāddha* approaches the bed of a *vṛṣalī* on that day, his ancestors shall lie for that month in her excrement. (3.250)
The purpose of censuring transgression is for the sake of praising non-transgression. And the term *vṛṣalī* has already been explained.
Having asked, "Was it well-eaten? he should then cause those who are satiated to sip water; and once they have sipped water, he should dismiss them with the words, "Be happy on all sides. (3.251)
Immediately after that, the Brahmins should say to him, "Svadhāstu.
For the utterance of "svadhā" is the supreme benediction in all rites for the ancestors.
Then, once they have finished eating, he should present the remains of the food; as those twice-born ones may direct, so he should act, having been authorized by them. (3.253)

These five verses have a straightforward meaning: "At a rite for the ancestors, one should say 'It is well-savored' (svadita); at rites for cattle, 'it is well-cooked' (suśṛta); at a rite for prosperity, 'it is excellent' (saṃpanna); and at a rite for the gods, 'it is pleasing' (rucita). (3.254)

It is stated as a rule that at the time of eating, one should honor [the ancestors] with these words; or rather, permission for the meal is granted by means of these words. And this being the case, the recitation beginning with "May it be savory" (svadatām) and so forth is to be understood.

The afternoon, as well as *darbha* grass, the preparation of the site, sesame seeds, abundance, refinement, and eminent twice-born men—these are the perfections in rites for the ancestors (*śrāddha*). (3.255)

The afternoon and other times are mentioned again for the purpose of praise, or alternatively, to indicate that they may be used optionally. Darbha grass, the purifier, the forenoon, and all kinds of sacrificial food (haviṣya), as well as whatever purifier was previously mentioned—these should be understood as the perfections of the oblation. (3.256)

[155] Only the finest *darbha* grass and so forth should be employed for the perfection of the ritual in rites dedicated to the gods (*daiva*). From the word "perfection" (*sampat*), an option is inferred:
"The foods of sages, milk, soma, meat, and that which is unseasoned."
And food that is naturally free from pungent substances and salt is called *havis*.
Having stated "these are the sacrificial foods," he indicates what those sacrificial foods are: milk; the mention of milk is intended to include all its derivatives.
Having dismissed those Brahmins, being self-controlled, silent, and pure, and looking toward the southern direction, he should request these boons from the ancestors: (3.258)
"May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give. (3.259)

Having thus performed the offering of the funeral cakes, he should immediately thereafter cause a cow, a Brahmin, a goat, or the sacred fires to consume them, or else cast them into the water. (3.260)

Thus, immediately after requesting the choice of a bridegroom for his daughter, the sacrificer, having performed the offering of the *piṇḍas*, should cause those experts in the *pitṛyajña* to eat cows and other such items for the sake of the progeny honored by the ancestors. However, some say that this is the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the scattered *vikira-piṇḍas*; that is incorrect. For in that case, the prior offering of the *piṇḍas* would be contradicted; furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the middle *piṇḍa* taught in the subsequent verse, since that [middle *piṇḍa*] would be absent. But in the case of the *piṇḍas* of the *pitṛyajña*, all of this is possible without contradiction.
Some perform the offering of the funeral cakes even beforehand;
however, one should do so after the Śrāddha meal.
They cause birds to devour these [cakes], or they cast them into fire or water. (3.261)

The verses have a straightforward meaning. However, one should not give [the middle pinda] to everyone starting from the children; rather: "A devoted wife, the lawful partner, intent on the worship of the ancestors—she who desires a son should properly eat that middle pinda. (3.262)
He shall obtain a long-lived son, endowed with fame and wisdom, wealthy, possessed of progeny, righteous, and likewise virtuous. (3.263)
This verse concerns the consumption of the middle portion of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*):
Having washed his hands and sipped water, he should set aside a portion for his kinsmen (*jñāti*).
Having given that honored portion to his kinsmen, he should also honor his relatives (*bāndhava*). (3.264)
Having sprinkled water around the *śrāddha* feast, this rule is declared: food should be given to kinsmen and others, and that remnant should remain until the Brahmins have been dismissed;
thereafter, one should perform the domestic offering (*gṛhabali*)—thus the law is established. (3.265)
I shall explain in its entirety that oblation which, when offered to the ancestors according to the prescribed rule, conduces both to long duration and to infinity. (3.266)
This verse is for the purpose of introduction:
"By the offering of sesame, rice, barley, beans, water, roots, or fruits according to the prescribed rule, the ancestors of men are satisfied for a month. (3.267)
Whatever is not prohibited is initially understood to be permitted by the fact of its being mentioned as a source of knowledge.
"By the flesh of the fish, however, for two months; by the flesh of the deer, for three months; by that of the goat, for four; and by that of the bird, for five. (3.268)
For six months with the meat of a goat, and indeed for seven with that of a spotted deer; for eight months with the meat of an antelope, and for nine with that of a Ruru deer. (3.269)
They are satisfied for ten months by the meat of boars and buffaloes;
however, by the meat of hares and tortoises, they are satisfied for exactly eleven months.
For one year, however, with cow’s milk or milk-rice (pāyasa),
or with the meat of a vārdhrīṇasa, the satisfaction lasts for twelve years.
Black potherb, the great conch, the rhinoceros-horn iron,
honey, and the grains of sages— in every respect, these lead to infinity.
Whatever one might offer mixed with honey on the thirteenth lunar day,
that too shall indeed be inexhaustible during the rainy season under the asterism of Maghā.
"May he be born in our family who would give us milk-rice with honey and clarified butter on the thirteenth lunar day, during the shadow of an elephant cast toward the east."

"Two months [with fish]"—starting from this point, these seven verses are intended as specific praises for the sake of particular results, because the satisfaction of the ancestors is not directly perceived in the same way as the satisfaction of the guests; thus, they are merely for the purpose of praise. However, in the ritual manual (*kalpa*), they are appropriate. For by the statement, "What [meat] one should use month after month," the giving to the ancestors is enjoined here without distinction. Nor can any reason be stated here for why one should not offer [fish] for two months when the meat of goats and other animals is available, since it is enjoined for every month. Furthermore, these cannot logically be construed as praises for the *śrāddha* rite because they would contradict the revealed scripture (*śruti*), whether due to the capacity of the injunction or because even those who are already satisfied [by other means] could be made capable of further satisfaction. If it were so, there would be a redundancy of words, and since many brothers might be satiated by a single offering, there would be no further activity on the part of the others. Moreover, the enjoyment of the ancestors is distinguished by the enjoyment of the deities. How so? Just as there is a statement of satisfaction for those who understand the deities to be the recipients (*sampradāna*), so too should it be understood for the ancestors.
Whatever one gives according to the rule, correctly and endowed with faith, that becomes infinite and inexhaustible for the ancestors in the next world. (3.275)

This effort is for the purpose of establishing faith (*śraddhā*). This being so, the lack of contradiction with previous scriptures—due to the respectful statement "whatever he gives"—should be understood through the power of this instruction, as its intent is the praise of the *śrāddha*.
"Excepting the fourteenth day, the lunar days from the tenth onwards in the dark fortnight are recommended for the *śrāddha*, whereas other days are not so. (3.276)
Regarding that capacity, the sacrificer’s undertaking of specific gifts on the tenth day and so forth—relative to the preceding lunar day—is for the sake of a particular increase in merit.
And just as the latter fortnight is distinguished from the former fortnight, so too is the afternoon distinguished from the forenoon for the śrāddha rite. (MDh 3.278)

Because of this statement, the attainment of the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) applies to the *śrāddha*. Now, one might object that this is an unestablished example: since it is said, "Just as the latter fortnight is superior to the former fortnight" (MDh 3.278), referring to the dark fortnight being better than the bright fortnight, this [rule] does not establish the [forenoon] for this [rite], because its instruction occurs in proximity to the dark fortnight, and thus the bright fortnight is not established by this. If this is so, then in this restatement of a traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) that is not found in the original text (*agrantha*), this serves as an illustrative example. Alternatively, the establishment of both [the time and the fortnight] is understood from this very [text] through its inherent force (*sāmarthya*). Furthermore, in the work of Gautama, this traditional teaching should be seen as including the original text itself, such as "or in the presence of ten Brahmins," and so forth. This [present rule] will be dependent upon that.
Performing [the rites] on odd lunar days and under odd constellations, one attains all desires;
but by honoring the ancestors on even days, one obtains abundant progeny. (3.277)

They say that on the even lunar days (*yuk*) beginning from the tenth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇadaśamī*), and under the even asterisms (*nakṣatra*), one obtains offspring by performing worship; this is the intended meaning. This is a rite for specific desires (*kāmya*). Alternatively, because these two serve as a praise, their commencement is for the sake of a particular prosperity (*abhyudaya*). However, some derive from this *śrāddha* the instruction regarding the even and uneven days starting from the dark fortnight, as well as the even and uneven asterisms and days, treating them as optional (*kāmya*). That is incorrect, because the context is governed by the phrase "on the tenth day and so forth. Thus, this has not been observed as a direct result. Now, the subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the *śrāddha* is being stated. [158]
Just as one position is superior to the opposing position, so the afternoon is superior to the forenoon for the ancestral rite (śrāddha). || 3.278 ||
Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder, with the rites performed correctly from left to right, unwearied,
and holding *darbha* grass in his hand, he should perform the ancestral rite according to the rules until its conclusion.
This verse is intended to prescribe the qualities that are auxiliary to the *śrāddha* rite:
"One should not perform a *śrāddha* at night, for it is declared to belong to the *rākṣasas*; nor during either of the two twilights, nor when the sun has only recently risen. (3.280)

Since nights and other such times are prohibited as being unsuitable for the constituent parts of a *śrāddha*, it is understood that the *śrāddha* rite may be performed even at times other than the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*). Otherwise, the commencement of this rule would result in being purposeless. This being the case, the *śrāddha* is appropriately joined with the morning (*pūrvāhṇa*) for the sake of its attainment. As it has been said: "In the same way, for the *śrāddha*, the afternoon is preferred over the morning" (MDh 3.278). Therefore, this would apply to the option of performing a *śrāddha* with prepared food (*kṛtānna*). According to this procedure, one should perform it here constantly three times a year.
During the winter, summer, and rainy seasons, he should perform the five great sacrifices daily.
He will state immediately thereafter that this definition applies to one who has not maintained the sacred fires:
"The oblation pertaining to the sacrifice for the ancestors is not prescribed to be performed in a common fire;
nor is there a *śrāddha* without the *darśa* [new-moon sacrifice] for a twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires. (3.282)

Since the oblation pertaining to the ancestral sacrifice (*paitṛyajñika*) is not prescribed for the common fire, therefore the monthly ancestral rite (*māsānumāsika*) does not necessarily take place for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*). Furthermore, since the *śrāddha* is prescribed for one who has not maintained the sacred fires as being inseparable from the new-moon day (*darśa*), therefore the threefold annual rule also applies to one who has maintained the sacred fires. What then? Because it is a constituent part of that [ancestral sacrifice], the monthly rite necessarily takes place for him as well. "Whatever fruit the best of the twice-born obtains by satisfying the ancestors with water after bathing, by that alone he attains the entire fruit of the performance of the ancestral sacrifice" (3.283).

By this very libation of water, performed constantly day after day, the *śrāddha* rite becomes accomplished; how much more so, then, for a period of three years? Alternatively, this should be understood as being intended primarily to praise the specific *śrāddha*.
"They call the Vasus the fathers, the Rudras the grandfathers, and likewise the Ādityas the great-grandfathers—this is the ancient Vedic revelation. (3.284)

[159] Since the Vasus and others are remembered as the Pitṛs and others, therefore, for the sake of the obligatory rite (*nitya*), the *śrāddha* must be offered without disregarding the Pitṛs and others. One should not live as one who hates the Pitṛs; for it is remembered that "these are indeed gods bearing the names of Pitṛs. Alternatively, for those whose Pitṛs and others are unknown, the ancestral rites (*pitrya*) such as the offering of water and so forth should be performed by those reciting the names of the Vasus and others. "One should always be an eater of *vighasa*, or always an eater of *amṛta*."
Vighasa, however, is the remnant of what has been eaten; likewise, the remnant of a sacrifice is called amṛta.
This [verse] is intended as a praise for the performance of the duties prescribed [for each], not for the purpose of an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*).
"All this rule concerning the five sacrifices has been declared to you;
now hear this rule regarding the livelihoods of the foremost among the twice-born. (3.286)

This is the conclusion. This verse serves as an introductory summary: because of the thorough enumeration of the modes of conduct beginning with *ṛta*, the term "foremost of the twice-born" refers specifically to the Brāhmaṇa.
Thus ends the third chapter in the Commentary on the Code of Manu, composed by the teacher Gururānartīya, who has attained union (*sāyujya*) with the venerable Smṛti.
Śrī Śrī Om. (This was written in the Nandināgarī script.)

The Fourth Chapter of the Commentary on the Laws of Manu: Having adopted the position that the stages of life (*āśrama*) are to be practiced cumulatively, [the author] speaks as follows regarding how the lifespan of a person belonging to those stages should be divided into four parts.
Having lived the first quarter of his life with his teacher, the twice-born man,
having taken a wife, shall dwell in his house during the second quarter of his life.

Since the period of student life (*brahmacarya*) has already been prescribed, the statement "the fourth part of his life" is a reference to what has been mentioned for the purpose of introducing what follows. By this, the second stage [of life] is explained. By the phrase "the twice-born man shall live in the house," the performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) and other rites ordained in the third chapter is enjoined. Furthermore, that performance of rites requires wealth as its means; therefore, this treatise on the rules for livelihood (*arthavṛtti*) is now set forth. [One should live] without harming living beings, or else with minimal harm.
Adopting that mode of life, a Brahmin should live during times when he is not in distress. (4.2)

From the statement, "The *brāhmaṇa* is said to be one who is friendly" (MDh 11.35), even the permission for slight injury is improper; because by this capacity, such injury is intended for the purpose of restraint, and indeed [it applies] to violence. This being so, one should first proceed toward all beings without causing them harm in all the modes of livelihood (*vṛtti*) that will be described hereafter, since this rule applies to all purposes. An example of this is "obtaining without asking"; in its absence, it should be understood that in all modes of livelihood, this applies through obtaining without asking, provided there is only a slight offense. And thus, there is the attainment of [support] from wife and children, and the preservation of dharma. Conversely, however, there would be no transgression if it were not in times of distress (*anāpad*); this qualification is for the sake of defining the scope within this section on livelihoods, and it applies even while one is living in this manner.
For the sake of accomplishing the mere necessities of life, one should accumulate wealth through one's own irreproachable occupations, without causing distress to the body. (4.3)

One should accumulate wealth only to the extent necessary for the maintenance of the body without causing distress; no restrictive rule beyond this is prescribed. Furthermore, the accumulation of wealth must be limited to that which is prescribed by the scriptures for the sake of maintaining one's livelihood—namely, as much as is required for the performance of obligatory duties (*nityakarman*) and for the support of one’s wife and children. It should not exceed that amount. By what means? By one’s own irreproachable occupations; that is to say, by those occupations that are in accordance with the scriptures. For it is said:
"One should live by the *ṛta* and the *amṛta*, or by the *mṛta* and the *pramṛta*."
Nor, by any means, should one live the life of a dog, even if it were through truth or falsehood. [4.4]

He explains by himself, in two verses, that one does not engage in falsehood and the like except in times of distress. "Truth" (ṛta) should be known as gleaning ears of grain; "immortality" (amṛta) is what is obtained unasked;
"death" (mṛta) is alms obtained by begging; and agriculture is traditionally remembered as "repeated death" (pramṛta). (4.5)
Trade consists of both truth and falsehood, and one may indeed live by it; service is explained as the "dog's livelihood," therefore one should avoid it. (4.6)

The term *uñchaśila* is a *dvandva* compound treated as a singular, referring to two distinct objects. Words such as *amṛta* and others must be explained by some common characteristic in relation to meanings such as what is obtained without being asked for (*ayācita-lābha*). Because of the mention of receiving what is requested, the acts of officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) and teaching (*adhyāpana*), which accompany it, are also included here. Thus, the author will say later: "But the fourth [mode] lives by the *brahmasattra*. The statement, "Service (*sevā*) is explained as the dog's livelihood (*śvavṛtti*)," should be understood from the context as referring specifically to the Brāhmaṇa. For it has been stated: "Let the rule for the livelihoods of the foremost of the twice-born be heard" (MDh 3.286). Since this does not concern the other castes, Gautama says: "And all [castes] should serve each other in ascending order" (GDh 10.65). Furthermore, this prohibition of service for the Brāhmaṇa is intended with reference to normal circumstances (*prakṛti*); thus the context states "in times of non-distress" (*anāpadi*). And these modes of livelihood (*vṛtti*) are to be applied according to the requirements of performing the duties prescribed by the treatises on conduct.
He may possess grain sufficient for a granary, or enough for a single jar;
he may have enough for three days, or he may not even provide for tomorrow. || 4.7 ||

By means of these modes of livelihood (*vṛtti*), this alternative regarding accumulation (*saṃcaya*) is taught. For a householder possessed of knowledge and dispassion (*jñāna-vairāgya*), with respect to his state of having accomplished his purpose (*kṛtārthatva*), the mention of the granary (*kusūla*) and so forth is intended as an illustration of the limit of accumulation, not as a restrictive rule (*niyama*) for the locus of accumulation. However, the term *tryahaikika* is explained here: that which occurs in this world is *aihika*; what is that? It is the activity of livelihood under discussion. He who possesses three days' worth of *aihika* provisions is a *tryahaikika* householder. But one who does not provide for the morrow (*aśvastanika*) is to be understood as a *saṃprakṣālaka*. Others, however, read the half-verse of the cited *śloka* thus: "Or indeed a *tryahaikika*, or even an *aśvastanika*. For them, there is a contradiction with the subsequent verse. Because in this reading some read "five" and not "four," [as the author] will say: "And of these four... (MDh 4.8), where [the word] *mātrā* is used for the sake of establishing the sense. Now, has this not already been stated, since the objection raised at the outset is the very solution? Namely, that this alternative regarding accumulation is taught with respect to the householder’s state of having accomplished his purpose through knowledge and dispassion. Or rather, the lack of accumulation was mentioned with reference to his prior condition; likewise, the mention of "subsistence" (*yātrā*) follows. In that context, by the mention of "subsistence," the lunar day (*tithi*) is well known. But here, it is prescribed with respect to one of good deeds who has completed his duties; or else, it is for the purpose of an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). He speaks again, citing what is stated in the *Śruti*: [The verse: "One should subsist on three days' provisions, or indeed on what is sufficient for the morrow; or he may be one who gathers only what is needed for the day, or one who lives by gleaning ears of grain. [Commentary: Regarding this, the following is said: "He should always subsist on three days' provisions; or he may be one who provides for the morrow; or he may be one who gathers only what is needed for the day; or he may be one who lives by gleaning ears of grain. Among these, the one who subsists on three days' provisions is a *tryahaikika*. The one who provides for the morrow is an *aśvastanika*. The one who gathers only what is needed for the day is a *saṃprakṣālaka*. The one who lives by gleaning ears of grain is a *uñchavṛtti*. Among these, each later one is superior to the preceding one. And among these four, the one who lives by gleaning ears of grain is the most excellent. This is the settled rule. Alternatively, another interpretation is given: "He should always subsist on three days' provisions" refers to the *tryahaikika*. "Or he may be one who provides for the morrow" refers to the *aśvastanika*. "Or he may be one who gathers only what is needed for the day" refers to the *saṃprakṣālaka*. "Or he may be one who lives by gleaning ears of grain" refers to the *uñchavṛtti*. Among these, each later one is superior to the preceding one. And among these four, the one who lives by gleaning ears of grain is the most excellent. This is the settled rule. Among these four types of twice-born householders,
each subsequent one should be known as superior to the preceding in terms of dharma, and as the greatest conqueror of the worlds.

This is a praise of the contraction of one's livelihood in view of the abundance of knowledge, dispassion, and discernment. And this being so, some person, in view of the greater accumulation of ritual limbs whose purposes remain unfulfilled, becomes a performer of six duties; another proceeds with three of these;
one with two; while the fourth lives by the "sacrifice of Brahman" (brahmasattra). (4.9)

First, based on the context of the section concerning livelihoods (*vṛtti*), there is the inclusion of the six occupations beginning with officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*). Regarding those who say that the three occupations—officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts—are for times of distress (*āpad*), while the other three are not, and that these [three] are the livelihoods of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas: their view contradicts the intended meaning because of the specific mention of "teaching" (*adhyāpana*) here; furthermore, since accepting gifts from the virtuous and the wicked are treated as one, their position is subsequently untenable. As for those who, by means of the word *ṛta* (law/right), do not go so far as to propose such a construction, even for them these five [occupations] exist; and if agriculture and cattle-rearing are included along with usury, they become seven. Since this is stated to be the sixth among the occupations: "The two occupations of *śila* and *uñcha* are those which the father begs for"—thus, agriculture and trade are likewise [counted], making six occupations, because these are the subject under discussion. Alternatively, because it is explicitly mentioned, *śila-uñcha* is spoken of as one due to the proximity of the sense; thus, begging and receiving gifts are one because the cause (*nimitta*) is the same. However, officiating at sacrifices and teaching are two distinct items, as they are established by the force of the examples regarding receiving gifts, and by the association with those authorized by the sense. Thus, agriculture and trade are indeed two. Therefore, according to this construction, there are six occupations; or rather, by the application of the aforementioned logic, because *śila-uñcha* are one, and because officiating at sacrifices, teaching, receiving gifts, agriculture, and trade are five, there are six occupations; or else, by reversing the unity of the twice-born (*dvija*) in the case of *śila-uñcha* and receiving gifts, this state of having six occupations is to be expressed. There is another explanation: officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts are three; and agriculture, trade, and usury are three—thus, in this way, there are six occupations. And so Gautama says, even when not in distress: "Agriculture and trade, provided they are not done by oneself, and usury" (GDh 10.5–6). "Another proceeds by three"—the well-known three are officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts, which are to be mentioned later; they are understood here through association with the *brahmasattra*. And thus, "Receiving gifts is the lowest" (MDh 10.109); since receiving gifts is not explicitly enjoined [as a primary duty], "one [occupation] by two"—officiating at sacrifices and teaching are taken. The fourth, however, is teaching, as indicated by the phrase "he lives by the *brahmasattra*" (MDh 4.9), because the *brahmasattra* is teaching, and because that [phrase] serves as a praise. Furthermore, the superiority of these occupations over others is established by scripture and logic. "But cessation [from worldly activity] yields great fruit" (MDh 5.56)—this refers to self-restraint. This is because we see that the livelihoods of a Brāhmaṇa, such as *śila*, *uñcha*, and begging, involve restriction. This entire expansion of livelihoods, such as agriculture and trade, pertains specifically to the Brāhmaṇa in times of non-distress; it should be understood as being performed by oneself due to the context. And having done so, it was said: "Let the rule for the livelihoods of the foremost of the twice-born be heard" (MDh 3.286).
Subsisting by means of gleaning ears of corn and picking up single grains, and being devoted to the Agnihotra,
he should always perform only the Iṣṭi sacrifices prescribed for the new moon, the full moon, and the solstices.

Alternatively, having accomplished his purpose and being free from passion, he should abandon all improper modes of conduct and subsist solely by means of *śila* and *uñcha*. Maintaining himself in whatever way possible, he should remain devoted exclusively to the *agnihotra*, and he should perform the *iṣṭis*, but not those performed for specific desires (*kāmyāḥ*). What then? Those pertaining to the *parvan* and the solstices (*ayanāntīyāḥ*). A *parvan* and an *ayana* are "the *parvāyanas*"; the end of these two is "the *parvāyaṇānta*. That which occurs therein is "pertaining to the *parvāyaṇānta*" (*pārvāyaṇāntīyāḥ*), namely the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the *nava-yajña*, and the *āgrayaṇa*. This being the case, in this state there is a prohibition of all optional rites (*kāmya*), not merely of the *iṣṭis*. And such being the case, this [is the rule].
One should never follow the ways of the world for the sake of a livelihood; rather, one should live by the pure, straightforward, and honest life of a Brahmin. 4.11

"Worldly conduct" (*lokavṛtta*) refers to winning over people with verses through various stories, jests, and the like. One should never practice that for the sake of a livelihood, nor even out of compassion for the benefit of others. How then? "Straightforward" (*ajihmā*), meaning not crooked; "not deceitful" (*aśaṭhā*), meaning not dishonest through some pretext; "faithful" (*śraddadhāna*), and likewise "pure" (*śuddhā*) by abandoning all ulterior motives (*upadhā*). Alternatively, "straightforward" is an explanation of its meaning, while "not deceitful" itself constitutes the purity. One should live this "Brahmin livelihood" (*brāhmaṇajīvikā*). By the word "livelihood" (*jīvikā*), a mode of life for the purpose of subsistence is meant, because the context concerns qualities. This being so, "not deceitful" and "pure" are qualifiers of that [livelihood]. All these should be understood as its specific attributes. Now, the cause for this excellence of livelihood and for abiding in dispassion (*vairāgya*) is stated.
Relying upon supreme contentment, one who seeks happiness should become self-restrained;
for happiness has its root in contentment, while the opposite is the root of suffering. (4.12)

One who desires unsurpassed invisible happiness and one who desires visible happiness through tranquility should be thus self-restrained, as we have stated. For it is observed in this world that "happiness has contentment as its root, while the opposite is the root of suffering. And since the invisible can be inferred from the visible, one should not, for the sake of happiness, fall into the error of accepting gifts from the unworthy when they are available from the worthy, provided there is no excess. Therefore: "But a twice-born *snātaka*, living by any one of these modes of livelihood, should observe these vows which lead to heaven, long life, and fame. (4.13)

This verse is intended to provide a summary and introduction to the preceding section. Regarding this, some do not accept the combination of livelihoods (*vṛtti-samuccaya*) on the grounds of the expression "by any one [of these]. That is incorrect, because the combination is heard directly here in such passages as, "One among these shall perform six duties" (MDh 4.9). Therefore, this is merely a restatement of what was already said: that one may live in the world by any one of these aforementioned livelihoods, whether collectively or individually, according to the instruction. Others, however, read "anyarayā" (?), which is also incorrect; for since there are many livelihoods, this would be appropriate only in comparison to those who have no means or very few means. Furthermore, because these two [terms] qualify all the specific livelihoods, your explanation of them as qualifiers and your teaching of multiple livelihoods are not directly heard by you [in the text], such as "one among these shall perform six duties," and so forth. This [verse] is begun as a way of augmenting the praise of the injunction, "He should observe these vows."
[164] One should always perform, without laziness, one's own duty as proclaimed in the Vedas;
for by performing that according to one's ability, one attains the supreme goal. 4.14.

This is a restatement of the *agnihotra* and other rites prescribed in the Veda; this example is for the purpose of an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). For just as the *agnihotra* and so forth, which are declared in the Veda, [are accomplished] only through the performance of extremely difficult means, so too is the observance of the vows (*vrata*) to be described hereafter—such is the praise. And thus it has been said: "These lead to heaven" (MDh 4.13). Alternatively, because of the possibility of perception, this observance of vows is indeed declared in the Veda, just like worldly practice. Even in the case where the Smṛti is lost, although the Smṛti originates from Vedic indications (*liṅga*), one may resort to the position of inference (*anumāna*) and state that its purpose is praise, as before. Even in the position of independence, the authority of the Smṛti as an indication of the Veda has been previously stated. That this is its praise is either an unapplied comparison. How so? It is "as if declared in the Veda," though it is not actually declared in the Veda. What, then, is that? This observance of vows to be described is one's own duty (*svakarma*). Whose? Of the *snātaka*, known as a duty of man. Because of this, he should perform this constantly, unwearied. As for its fruit-rule: "For by performing this according to his ability, he attains the supreme goal. Since this is so, therefore these are called "these [vows]."
One should not pursue wealth through attachment to objects,
nor for the sake of Dharma, through cold and the like, nor by means of contradictory actions.
Neither toward objects being conceptualized, nor even in times of distress, does it [arise] from this or that. (4.15)

[The phrase] "by officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy of sacrificing" and so forth continues [to apply]. The phrase "even for the sake of dharma" also applies here. One should not accept what is unfit, even for one's own sake, nor when unasked, even if the donors are humble; nor even in times of distress—provided there is no intention to abandon the duties concerning one's sons, wife, or the sacred tradition—accepting from just anyone. Thus, this acceptance of what is unfit should not be done impulsively; rather, it is an absolute prohibition. For he will state later regarding such a situation:
"One should not indulge out of desire in any of the objects of the senses."

The objection is not raised only with regard to the objects of the tongue and the genitals; rather, it applies to others as well, such as cold and so forth, which are the objects of the ear and other senses. Therefore, the word "all" is used.
And one should restrain these excessive attachments by means of the mind. (4.16)

One should turn away even from those acts not prohibited, such as approaching one's own wife and the like, by means of the ultimate discernment (*paramārtha-prasaṃkhyāna*). Thus, this is called the instruction in the inner science (*adhyātmavidyā-anuśāsana*) regarding the "not so" (*neti*). Why is this so? It is stated here: "In this way, with effort. How indeed should he be thus? He should abandon all objects that are obstacles to his sacred study (*svādhyāya*), namely those known as attachments to sense-objects; and in whatever manner possible, remaining satisfied with mere sustenance, he should be devoted to sacred study, so that—
But teaching him accordingly—this indeed is his fulfillment of duty. 4.17

This is the state of constant private recitation (*svādhyāya*). And so says the Brāhmaṇa: "Whichever sacrifice he studies, by that very sacrifice his sacrifice becomes performed. One should conduct oneself here in accordance with the age, the occupation, the purpose, the learning, and the lineage [of others], adopting a conformity in dress, speech, and intellect. (4.18)

For those [women] whose conduct consists of service, dressing [the hair], verbal jesting, playful conversation, and devotion to virtue, wealth, and pleasure—these modes of dress, speech, and intellect, provided they do not conflict with established custom, should be practiced in accordance with the well-known worldly conventions suited to their age and other personal qualities; this is the rule being stated. Furthermore, according to the scripture, this entire scope of worldly practice is the subject matter of the verse, and having carefully examined it, it should be applied in every respect as appropriate.
These things quickly increase the intellect and are auspicious and beneficial.
He should constantly study the treatises and the Vedic scriptures. || 4.19 ||

The term *śāstrāṇi* (treatises) refers to the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*). These are those that do not contradict the Vedic scriptures, and the treatises on logic (*nyāya*) are subordinate to them. The *nigamas*, however, are well-known as works intended to teach the meanings and synonyms of words whose significance is not yet understood. Alternatively, they are called *nigamas* because by means of them the meaning of the Veda is determined (*nigamyate*); thus, the *śāstras* are their auxiliaries, and it is not that the treatises on logic and so forth are excluded from being considered supplementary to the Veda. For, "In whatever measure a person masters a treatise, to that same extent he understands it, and his understanding becomes clear. (4.20)

"These [sciences] quickly increase the intellect and are auspicious and beneficial" (MDh 4.19)—this is another praise for the acquisition of the scriptures, following the commendatory passage (*arthavāda*) of the preceding verse, and serves as a supplement to the injunction stated in the previous verse: "One should constantly study the scriptures" (MDh 4.19).

"One should never neglect the sacrifice to the sages (*ṛṣiyajña*), the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*), the sacrifice to the spirits (*bhūtayajña*), the sacrifice to men (*nṛyajña*), and the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*), according to one's ability. (MDh 4.21)

Some maintain that the commencement of these great sacrifices, such as the Vaiśvadeva and others, is for the purpose of their regular practice. However, whether that is correct or incorrect must be investigated. We, for our part, say this: the repetition of these is for the purpose of prescribing the remaining rites, or for the purpose of praise; we shall demonstrate this accordingly.
"Regarding these great sacrifices, some people who are learned in the scriptures of sacrifice, being free from worldly desire, constantly offer them into the senses alone. (4.22)

[166] Those who are learned in the scriptures concerning every kind of sacrifice, being ineligible for them, do not perform them; instead, throughout their entire lives, they constantly offer these great sacrifices into the fires of the senses. Furthermore, what is that? It is the firm conviction of faith in the afterlife, or rather, through intense absorption, this elaboration consisting of oblations becomes his mode of life in place of ordinary conduct. Some indeed offer speech into breath, and breath into speech, at all times.
Perceiving the inexhaustible accomplishment of sacrifice in speech and breath. || 4.23 ||

The function of the breath (*prāṇa*) and the organ of speech (*vāk*) occurs through mutual opposition; this is characterized by its purpose. He demonstrates this: when speech is active in activities such as recitation, the utility of the breath is observed therein, because it is subordinate and not an offering (*ahuti*). Furthermore, an offering—which involves the destruction of the self and entry into the fire—is not observed here. Therefore, this is spoken of as a figurative function (*guṇavṛtti*): "Some offer the breath into speech. By way of contrast, it should be said: "And always [offer] speech into the breath. Regarding the reason for this, he says: "Those who perceive [the offering] in speech and in the breath. Through this meditative practice (*upāsanā*) prescribed by the scripture, the functions of the sacrifice become inexhaustible, because the scripture is beyond doubt and because this instruction is intended as praise for the rule of meditation. This is an illustration of the injunction found in the preceding verse, "They offer [the senses] into the fires of the senses" (MDh 4.22); this should be understood as applying to both sides regarding the functions of all the senses and the breath. Thus, the *Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa* states: "As long as a person does not speak, so long is he unable to breathe; at that time, he offers the breath into speech. As long as a person breathes, so long is he unable to speak; at that time, he offers speech into the breath. These two he offers perpetually, whether waking or sleeping, into the infinite and the immortal. Now, other offerings are finite and merely result in ritual action (*karman*). In this very way, the wise of old did not perform the Agnihotra sacrifice. This is based on the Śruti. How indeed are these [functions] eternal? Thinking that those who are not qualified for these rituals worship in another manner and thus have no ruin, this is simply a praise of their performance. The rule for their meditation concerns persons qualified for the *vyāna*. And this interpretation of the Smṛti’s meaning is appropriate, since even in the Śruti it is said: [...text missing... By knowledge alone, other Brahmins—
meaning those who are not entitled [to ritual action] compared to those who are entitled—
perform sacrifice through that [knowledge], by means of those sacrifices.
Regarding those [vows] which we shall discuss in the immediately following verse— meaning throughout one's entire life— he states the reason for this:
"Seeing this ritual action to have its root in knowledge, in what manner..."
With the eye of wisdom. || 4.24 ||

[167] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, do you think that the Tathāgata thought: ‘By means of this dharma have I fully awakened to supreme perfect enlightenment’? Subhūti replied: “No indeed, Blessed One; certainly not, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, do you think that there is any dharma whatsoever by which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to supreme perfect enlightenment? Subhūti replied: “No indeed, Blessed One; certainly not, Blessed One. There is no dharma whatsoever by which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to supreme perfect enlightenment. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, do you think that the Tathāgata perceives the dharma of the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, as being something other than the dharma of the Tathāgatas? Subhūti replied: “No indeed, Blessed One; certainly not, Blessed One. The dharma of the Tathāgatas is not perceived as being other than the dharma of the Tathāgatas. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because of this very reason that the Tathāgata is called ‘Tathāgata. For what reason? Subhūti, the dharma of the Tathāgatas is neither real nor unreal. Therefore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata is called ‘Tathāgata. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, do you think that the Tathāgata perceives the dharma of the Tathāgatas as being something other than the dharma of the Tathāgatas? Subhūti replied: “No indeed, Blessed One; certainly not, Blessed One. The dharma of the Tathāgatas is not perceived as being other than the dharma of the Tathāgatas. One should always perform the Agnihotra sacrifice at the beginning and end of day and night;
likewise, one should perform the Darśa sacrifice at the end of a fortnight and month, and the Paurṇamāsa sacrifice as well.

At the end of the grain harvest, a twice-born man should perform the sacrifice of new grain; likewise, at the end of each season, he should perform the seasonal sacrifices; at the end of the sun's course, he should offer an animal sacrifice; and at the end of the year, he should perform the Soma sacrifices.

In the Agnihotra, the word *yajña* is recited by means of the word *juhoti*. However, in the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices, although the word *yajati* is heard [in the texts], it is to be understood through the authority of the scripture (*śāstra*). How so? In the passage "the twice-born [should worship] with *adhvaras*," this word *adhvara* is to be understood as referring to the Soma-sacrifices and the Cāturmāsya rites. This being the case, even one who is not entitled [to perform these sacrifices] fulfills them here through the aforementioned mental impression (*vāsanā*) in that very manner; likewise, he may fulfill the Great Sacrifices (*mahāyajñas*) as well. Thus, for the sake of praise, this instruction regarding one who is not entitled [to the ritual acts] is given to produce conviction. Having thus established the consistency with the logic of the scriptures, two further verses are stated by way of illustration to support the subject at hand, in connection with the *iṣṭi* and animal sacrifices.

A twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires, desiring to live a long life, should not eat new grain or meat without having first performed the sacrifice of the new harvest or an animal sacrifice. (4.27)
For his fires, greedy for new grain and meat, if not honored with an offering of sacrificial animals, desire to consume his very life-breaths. (4.28)

It has been stated that this too must be accomplished by him through non-attachment (*anaupāsana*) alone; thus, this [verse] is intended either as praise or as an instruction. Others, however, explain the meaning of the verses beginning with "And he should offer the *agnihotra*" (MDh 4.25), saying: since the obligatory nature (*nityatva*) of the *agnihotra* and other rites is directly established in the Śruti, their obligatoriness is here declared in these four verses along with the eating of human food. But whether that is logical or illogical must be investigated. This [section] is commenced because, in the context of the Great Sacrifices (*mahāyajña*), there remains something yet to be said regarding the sacrifice to men (*nṛyajña*).

For when the word *pāṣaṇḍa* is understood to have a derogatory sense—as in other instances such as "the people of the heretics (*pāṣaṇḍa*) are not dear"—then words such as *vikarmastha* (one who stands in improper action) and others, being its synonyms, serve to express an excess of censure, just as in common worldly usage. And since they serve a purpose within the Veda, both of these follow the logic of non-redundant distinctness in the construction of a restatement (*anuvāda*). As for the previous position regarding the maxim of the "cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), it should be understood as intended to show respect for the prohibition. However, when this word *pāṣaṇḍin* is a synonym for *liṅgin* (one who bears sectarian marks), then because it has both meanings, it is appropriate as a qualifier [of the former]. One should not honor with even mere speech those who stand in improper action, who are heretics (*pāṣaṇḍins*), or who bear sectarian marks (*liṅgins*). And in this very explanation, the subsequent elaboration on those "standing in action" (*karmastha*) should be understood, as before, as intended to show respect for the prohibition; or else, it is an elaboration on the cause of their standing in improper action. How so? Like those who observe the "vow of the cat" (*baiḍālavratika*), who are like cats in bearing marks (*liṅgin*) while using secret deception through the guise of the stages of life (*āśrama*) for the sake of deceiving others. Even though those who hear this—such as the followers of the Āgamas and the Lokāyatas—are intent on that purpose, the subsequent elaboration should be understood as intended to describe the distinction among the causes, such as those of "crow-like conduct" (*bakavṛtti*) who make a broken sound (*bhannabhannkāra*) in a single way. And the purpose of that is the deliberate avoidance of those distinguished by their standing in improper action. Furthermore, if these were not *aśrotriyas* (unlearned in the Vedas), then a prohibition of what was not applicable to them would be illogical; for since hospitality is applicable to them by virtue of being *śrotriyas*, the commencement of a prohibition against this specific act is appropriate. Is this an absolute prohibition of giving to them? No; for if an absolute prohibition were stated, it would contradict the statement [elsewhere] that one should not speak to those who are powerless. We shall demonstrate this later. A prohibition of what is under discussion is appropriate. And what is under discussion here is the arrival of guests in the evening, as some [have argued] based on the previous verse: "A guest should stay in the house according to one's ability, even if unhonored. Therefore, the giving in the morning is established. If that is so, then since there is no prohibition of them [elsewhere], why is this specifically commenced as an effort to apply it everywhere? The *veda* itself is *vidyā*; thus, *vedavidyā*. *Vedavidyā* and the *vratas* together constitute *vedavidyāvratāni*. One who has bathed (*snāta*) by means of these is a *vedavidyāvratasnāta*; by this term, all three types of *snātakas* are included. In that context, the expression "one who is learned in the Veda" (*śrotriya*) becomes meaningful only with reference to the *vrata-snātaka*, because one who has completed the *vedavidyā* and then bathes is so designated. This [expression] is stated even regarding the other two categories, as indicated by the mention of "those who have bathed after [studying] the *vedavidyā* and the *vratas*. It is true that being learned in the Veda (*śrotriyatva*) is already established; however, that statement is made again for the sake of excellence (*atiśaya*). Just as when it is said, "Let a maiden be given to a handsome man," it is understood to mean "to one who is more handsome," since there is no giving of a maiden to one who is not handsome at all—even so here, although being learned in the Veda is already established by the preceding [rule], the word *śrotriya* must be stated again for the purpose of signifying knowledge of the Veda along with its auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga-veda-vijñāna*). This being the case, it should be understood that for them, the giving of food during the day—other than in the case of *havya* (offerings to gods) and *kavya* (offerings to ancestors)—is not prohibited. Furthermore, the repeated instruction regarding the giving of food to a learned guest (*śrotriya-atithi*), even though it was already enjoined by the general permission to feed those associated with heretical sects (*pāṣaṇḍin*), is appropriate. Therefore, it is known from the instruction to give food even to those such as the fallen (*patita*) that there is indeed the giving of food to them, provided it is during the day and other than in the case of *havya* and *kavya*. And this [rule] would be contradicted if it were an absolute prohibition, because here it is the heretics (*pāṣaṇḍin*) who are under discussion as those from whom one does not cook. Furthermore, the mention of "beings" (*bhūta*) is a sign of respect; by that it is understood that this injunction regarding the giving of gifts, *havya*, and *kavya* applies to others than those who have completed their Vedic studies and vows (*vedavidyāvratasnātaka*). Otherwise, it would follow that it is equivalent to not undertaking the rite at all, since the giving of food to them has already been mentioned. Moreover, in the phrase "and sharing with beings," another kind of gift to divine beings (*divyadāna*) is understood apart from the giving of food. Otherwise, it would again follow that it is equivalent to not undertaking the rite, because that [giving of food] would already be established by the preceding rule.

A Snātaka who is suffering from hunger may seek wealth from a king, or from a patron for whom he performs sacrifices, or from a pupil; it is the established rule that he must not do so from anyone else. 4.33.

Because of the prohibition, "Not from one not born of the Kṣatriya caste" (MDh 4.84), he will state later that the acceptance [of gifts] is from a Kṣatriya king. The phrase "failing in this way" (*saṃsīdan*)—based on this indicative mark—is said to refer to the context of duties in times of distress (*āpaddharma*). Furthermore, after stating "from a Kṣatriya" and so forth for all stages of life (*āśrama*), the acceptance of such gifts is included among the duties in distress; or else, this is a prohibition similar to the prohibition regarding those who have been initiated (*dīkṣita*). And the mention of him "failing, desiring food, twice-born" is for the purpose of prescribing what follows, within the duties in distress. Because they provide assistance, there is no prohibition regarding the patron (*yājya*) or the pupil (*antevāsin*). And because of this effort [to clarify], when the position is that the gift is valid, this is the primary rule: "One should not accept from a king" (MDh 4.84). However, for the Brāhmaṇa and the Vaiśya, there is a prohibition regarding the acceptance of gifts from a king when the gift is invalid. Likewise, based on the indicative mark, "He who accepts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures" (MDh 4.87), this exception applies only to those two [castes]. Regarding the meaning of this verse, the venerable teacher Viṣṇusvāmin says thus. But I say: by the statement "one should seek wealth from a king," this acceptance is declared to be from a Kṣatriya king who acts according to the scriptures. What then is the reason here, since he will state right here in the section on the duties of the *snātaka* a prohibition of acceptance from a non-Kṣatriya king, saying, "One should not accept from a king not born of the Kṣatriya caste" (MDh 4.84), and "He who accepts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures" (MDh 4.87)? Since by this [verse] there is a prohibition of acceptance even from one who is a Kṣatriya but acts contrary to the scriptures, it is understood that this is not a case of accepting an invalid gift. It is as the teacher says: because there is another scriptural injunction for accepting from a Kṣatriya king, and because this is stated for the *snātaka*, it does not fall under the category of duties in distress. [Objection: Then how is it said, "The *snātaka* failing through hunger"? [Response: It is not proper to understand from this an acceptance of an invalid king's gift. Why? Because of the context and because it is an injunction of attainment, it was stated [earlier] as being final. This much, however, can be understood from this: when acceptance from other praiseworthy twice-born castes is available, one should not take from a king—even if he is righteous—because the acceptance of a righteous king is weightier than the acceptance of other twice-born castes. Or, because of the great comparison, even if the king's system is virtuous like the food of one who has been initiated, the acceptance of a righteous king should be understood as slightly weightier due to the stated reasons; or rather, this is not an invalid acceptance, but a re-authorization (*pratiprasava*) of that prohibited invalid acceptance, because it is taught in the context of duties in distress. For he will say: "A Brāhmaṇa oppressed for his livelihood may accept from anyone" (MDh 10.102); "By those failing, desiring base metals... (MDh 10.1113), and so forth. A re-authorization is appropriate to avoid a contradiction; for otherwise, there would be redundancy between the duties of the *snātaka* and the duties in distress. Likewise, there would be an obstruction to the performance of vows if it were restricted to the patrons and pupils mentioned in the section on the *snātaka*. The phrase "one should seek wealth from a king" continues [to apply] to acceptance, because these two—officiating at sacrifices and teaching—are causes for obtaining that designation [of "king"]. This being so, since there is an instruction of an option together with the patron and the pupil, and since they are equally virtuous, this is not understood as an invalid acceptance. Nor is an option between equals logical, nor an option between existence and non-existence. And because he says, "But not from another. "Stability" (*sthiti*) means from those twice-born castes who are not praiseworthy. "One should desire wealth"—this connects with something else; or else, by the word "failing" (*saṃsīdan*), the attachment to the system of Dharma is expressed. It is not the failure of the self and so forth, according to the Vedic text and the stated capacity. And likewise, he will state the duty in distress for one oppressed for his livelihood.
"One who is emaciated by lack of livelihood and suffering should practice this Dharma;

a Brāhmaṇa who has fallen into misfortune may accept gifts from anyone"—thus [it is stated] in such passages as Manu Smṛti 10.101–02. And it is indeed appropriate to interpret it in this way. For the performance of Dharma is not appropriate for one who accepts gifts from an unworthy person, as there are prohibitions against it later, such as in Manu Smṛti 12.42: "those who acquire wealth from a Śūdra," and so forth. However, the maintenance of oneself and one's family is stated by the force of the text itself, for there is no overstepping of the authority of the scriptural injunction. Having understood it thus, this becomes logically consistent.
A learned Snātaka should never suffer from hunger if he is capable [of providing for himself], nor should he wear worn-out or dirty clothes if he possesses the means. 4.34.

[171] By this [verse], the emaciation of the self and others due to hunger is prohibited, but not by the preceding one; for he will later describe the rules for times of distress (*āpaddharma*) for a *snātaka* who has fallen into such a state.
With his hair, nails, and beard clipped, self-controlled, wearing white garments, and pure—
He should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Veda and to what is beneficial for the self. 4.35.

By grooming the nails, beard, and so forth, and by bathing for purification, one should not wear the beard and such parts for no reason, because they are impure; or rather, this is an instruction regarding the specific marks [of a student]. Likewise, he states another set of marks for the *snātaka*:
"He should carry a bamboo staff and a water-pot with water;
a sacred thread, a [portion of the] Veda, and two auspicious golden earrings. (4.36)

Regarding the rule "one should carry a bamboo staff," the carrying of that object is enjoined in connection with a specific class [of persons]. As for the phrase "and a water-pot with its lid," someone here asks: Is its carrying for a transcendental purpose (*adṛṣṭa*) alone, like an earring, or for a visible purpose such as purification, like the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*)? To this he replies: Because the sentence would otherwise be redundant, the sacred thread—due to the rules governing the religious student (*brahmacārin*)—is an auxiliary to the act of touching [the water], not the water-pot, which is done without such a reason. What then? From the very rules for the religious student, one should understand that there is a restriction regarding the means for achieving purification, self-dharma, and refinement. Otherwise, it would result in an illogical equality of the water-pot’s acquisition with the girdle and other items whose acquisition is governed by scriptural injunctions; for the acquisition of the water-pot is not characterized by such scriptural authority. Thus it has been said:

"Having placed the girdle, the skin, the staff, the sacrificial thread, and the water-pot into the water when they are destroyed, he should take others with the appropriate mantras. (MDh 2.64) Now, even for the mere wearing [of these items], it is inferred by this treatise that they serve an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭaprayojana*), just like the girdle and the rest. What fault would there be in this? Here, however, the repetition would result in being purposeless. The reason is that some of the duties of the student (*brahmacārin*) have already been recited further on by means of the rule of *anuvṛtti* (extended application). For it has been said:

A twice-born man who has undergone the initiation ceremony (upanayana) should, until his formal return home (samāvartana), maintain the sacred fire, gather fuel, practice begging for alms, sleep on the ground, and perform what is beneficial for his teacher. (MDh 2.108)

And so another Smṛti says: "And this is not inconsistent with those who follow the subsequent [stages of life]" (GDh 3.10). Now, since this practice of carrying a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) is for the sake of purification, its purpose would appear to be purely transcendental (*adṛṣṭa*); thus, it might seem unworthy of being taught. However, its transcendental purpose may be established through an indirect process, just as the act of ritual rinsing (*upasparśana*) serves such a purpose here. Likewise, the rule regarding the time of day and so forth is intended to exclude other common vessels for holding water; it does not apply to anything uncommon, as is the case in both worldly practice and the scriptures. Thus Gautama says: "Having placed the water nearby" (GDh 2.41). Nor is another vessel for water worthy of being taught by implication, since at the time of eating, the student has no other [vessel] than the water-pot. And thus, by the same logic applied to the carrying of the water-pot, it applies to the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and the mendicant (*bhikṣu*) belonging to the various stages of life (*āśrama*). Furthermore, when there is a specific Smṛti text, it is appropriate that even for these [ascetics], the water-pot serves as the means for self-purification through proximity during acts of cleansing. And so another Smṛti says:
One should carry a water-pot even in all circumstances, despite impurity;
however, a wise man should not despise it, nor should he suspect it, nor defile it.
Just as one with hair is considered pure through contact with Soma,
so too the water-pot is eternally pure through contact with water.
Brahmins are pure in every respect, and their water-pot is likewise pure;
"the Brahmins" [are mentioned] first—this is the settled rule of dharma.

And Vyāsa, in the *Dānadharma*, has uttered praise for that gift: "One obtains a sixth part of the merit from bathing; there is no doubt in this matter. Furthermore, dharma is of three kinds: that which is revealed in the Vedas (*śrauta*), that which is recorded in the Smṛtis (*smārta*), and that which is practiced by the learned (*śiṣṭācarita*). Since this very [practice] is authoritative because it is practiced by the learned, so too says another Smṛti: [Note: Here, a portion of the text appears to have been lost, as no verse is cited.]

The conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) is authoritative when it is not contradicted by the scriptures (*śāstra*). And this [practice] is not contradicted by scripture. This being the case, since the conduct of the learned is authoritative, the wearing of that [sacred thread] is indeed appropriate for the sake of a visible purpose; furthermore, its purpose as a refinement of the self (*ātmasaṃskāra*) follows from the rules for religious students (*brahmacārin*), just like the sacrificial cord (*yajñopavīta*). Its efficacy (*sāmarthya*) should likewise be explained in many ways here, provided there is no contradiction with scripture or logic. [Regarding the term] *veda*, it refers to a bundle of *darbha* grass; [as for the statement] "he sweeps the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) with the *veda*," the reading here seems quite corrupted. However, if one were to take it as referring to the entire collection of Mantras and Brāhmaṇas, there would be the fault of redundancy, as it has already been mentioned. As for the phrase "two beautiful golden earrings," their beauty is not to be understood in terms of shape, but rather in terms of color (*varṇa*). Thus, their beauty is to be known through their hue.
One should never look at the sun when it is rising, nor when it is setting;
not when it is eclipsed, nor when reflected in water, nor when it has reached the middle of the sky.
One should not step over a calf’s tethering rope, nor run while it is raining;
nor should one look at one's own reflection in water—this is the rule. (4.38)
One should circumambulate clockwise clay, a cow, a deity, a Brahmin, clarified butter, honey, a crossroads, and a well-known tree. (4.39)

Neither in the scriptures nor in the world, even if under the influence of a deity, should he approach a woman when she is menstruating, even if he is intoxicated; likewise, he should not sleep with her on the same bed. 4.40.
For a twice-born man who approaches a woman covered in menstrual flow, his progeny, vital energy, fame, sight, and lifespan are diminished. (4.41)
As he avoided her who was overwhelmed by the menstrual flow, his wisdom, splendor, fame, vision, and lifespan increased. (4.42)
In both cases, due to the inherent nature of the statement, there is a praise of avoidance:
"One should not eat together with one's wife, nor should one look at her while she is eating, sneezing, yawning, or sitting at her ease. (4.43)

Regarding the statement, "The mouth of women is always pure" (MDh 5.130), even though this remains as a general permission, it is understood through this prohibition to apply specifically to the context of sexual intercourse (*rati*). For in the act of sexual pleasure, one eats together with the wife. Otherwise, since the prohibition against eating the leavings of women and Śūdras would already establish the prohibition against eating with one's wife, this further prohibition would be redundant. Nor does this permit eating with women who are not wives, nor does it permit the consumption of a wife’s leavings outside the context of eating. This being the case, by logic, traditional law (*smṛti*), and custom, my wisdom perishes when I have eaten during the three periods of the day. And therefore:
A twice-born man who desires splendor should not look at a woman applying collyrium to her own eyes, nor one who is anointed with oil, nor one who is uncovered, nor one who is urinating. (4.44)
One should not eat food while wearing only a single garment, nor should one perform a bath naked.
One should not void urine on a path, nor on ashes, nor in a cow-pen. (4.45)
Neither on ploughed ground, nor in water, nor on a sacrificial altar, nor on a mountain; neither in a ruined temple nor ever upon an anthill. (4.46)
Neither in pits inhabited by living beings, nor while walking, nor while standing;
neither having reached a riverbank, nor on the summit of a mountain. (4.47)
While looking at the wind, fire, a Brahmin, the sun, water, or likewise cows, one should never discharge feces or urine. (4.48)
One should pass by [the village] after covering oneself with wood, clods of earth, leaves, grass, or the like;
restraining one's speech, being pure, with limbs wrapped and the head covered. (4.49)
One should void urine and excrement facing north during the day;
at night, one should face south; and likewise during the two twilights, one should face south as one does by day.
In shade or in darkness, by night or by day, a twice-born man may perform [the purification] facing whichever direction he finds comfortable, as well as when there is danger to his life. (4.51)
The wisdom of one who urinates facing fire, the sun, the moon, water, a twice-born man, a cow, or the wind perishes. (4.52)
One should not blow on a fire with one's mouth, nor look at a naked woman;
one should not throw impure things into the fire, nor warm one's feet over it. 4.53.
One should not place it underneath anything, nor should one step over it; one should not treat it with one's feet, nor should one cause any injury to living beings. 4.54.
One should not eat at the time of twilight, nor should one travel, nor should one lie down;
nor indeed should one scratch the ground, nor should one remove one's own garland. (4.55)
One should not discharge urine, feces, or saliva into water; nor anything else smeared with impurities, nor blood, nor poisons. (4.56)
One should not sleep alone in an empty house, nor should one wake a superior person from sleep.
One should not converse with a woman in her courses, nor should one go to a sacrifice uninvited. (4.57)
[This verse is the scope of the reading of the *Manusmṛti* as explained by Bhāruci.
One may go at will to pay homage or to desire to see a sacrificial rite;
one who seeks wealth may wander from family to family during the menstrual period, but not without a specific purpose.
In the fire-sanctuary, in a cow-pen, in the presence of Brāhmaṇas,
during Vedic study, and while eating, one should keep the right arm uncovered.
One should not stop a cow suckling her calf, nor should one tell anyone [of it];
having seen a rainbow in the sky, a wise man should not point it out to anyone. 4.59
One should not dwell in a village that is unrighteous, nor likewise in one where diseases abound;
one should not enter a forest alone, nor should one dwell for long on a mountain.
One should not dwell in a kingdom ruled by a Śūdra, nor in one filled with unrighteous people; nor in one overrun by heretics, nor in one infested by men of the lowest castes. (4.61)
One should not eat food from which the oil has been extracted, nor should one practice overeating;
one should not eat too early, nor too late in the evening, nor having already eaten in the morning, should one eat again in the evening. (4.62)

One should not engage in useless exertion, nor drink water from the hollow of one's joined palms; one should not eat food while holding it on one's lap, nor should one ever be a seeker of idle curiosity. 4.63.
One should not dance, nor sing, nor play musical instruments; one should not clap hands, nor make harsh sounds, nor utter cries out of passion. 4.64
One should never wash one's feet in a vessel made of bell-metal;
nor should one eat from a broken dish, nor from one that is defiled by its nature.
One should not wear sandals, a garment, clarified butter, nor anything else—neither the sacred thread, ornaments, a garland, nor even a water-pot—[if they have been used by another]. (4.66)

One should not travel with many horses that are ill-trained, nor with those afflicted by hunger or disease, nor with those whose eyes or hooves are injured, nor with those whose tails have been docked. (4.67)
He should always travel with horses that are well-trained, swift, endowed with auspicious marks, and perfected in color and form, without lashing them excessively with a goad.
One should avoid the morning sun, the smoke from a corpse, and likewise a broken seat.
One should not clip one's nails or hair, nor should one tear at the nails with the teeth. (4.69)
One should not crush a lump of clay, nor should one tear grass with one's fingernails.
One should not perform an action that is fruitless, nor one that results in unhappiness in the future. (4.70)
The man who crushes clods of earth, cuts grass, or bites his nails goes quickly to destruction, as does one who practices alchemy or is impure. (4.71)
One should not engage in contentious debate, nor should one wear garlands on the outside;
riding on the backs of cows and all such things are indeed censured. 4.72
One should not enter an enclosed village or house by a way other than the gate;
and at night, one should avoid the roots of trees from afar. (4.73)
One should never play with dice, nor should one carry one's own sandals oneself;
one should not eat while reclining on a bed, nor with food held in the hand, nor while seated on a seat.
And one should not eat anything mixed with sesame from sunrise until sunset;
nor should one sleep here naked, nor ever remain in a state of impurity from food.
One should eat with wet feet, but never go to bed with wet feet;
indeed, by eating with wet feet, one shall attain a long life.
One should never attempt to see that which is beyond the range of sight; one should not look at feces or urine, nor should one cross a river by means of one's arms. 4.77
One who desires to live a long life should not step upon hair, nor ashes, bones, or potsherds; nor cotton seeds, nor chaff. (4.78)
One should not dwell with those who have fallen from their caste, nor with Caṇḍālas, nor with Pulkasas;
nor with fools, nor with the arrogant, nor with outcasts, nor with those who live on the outskirts of society. [4.79]

The verses concerning the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) for the *snātaka* have not been explained here because of their straightforwardness. He shall not give counsel to a Śūdra, nor his leavings, nor food offered as a sacrificial oblation (*havis*).
He shall not instruct him in the Dharma, nor prescribe a vow (*vrata*) for him. (4.80)

"One should not give instruction to a Śūdra. This means that one should not provide instruction for the sake of livelihood to a Śūdra who has not engaged in *dharma* and is unwilling to receive it. Someone says: "But if he asks, one should explain it, just like the instruction on penance (*prāyaścitta*). That is incorrect, because it is not established by other scriptures. For it is said: "One should not speak to anyone unless asked" (MDh 3.110). What, then, is the meaning of this? By the word "instruction," giving for the sake of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*) is prohibited in every way. But worldly matters such as making mats and the like are not prohibited, due to the force of the prohibition against instruction in *dharma*. "Not the leavings" (*nocchiṣṭam*). "Eaten" (*bhuktam*) refers to what remains after eating, situated in the vessel used for eating; this is what is prohibited. Some say it refers to food while one is still eating. That is incorrect, because this is permitted. For it will be said later: "Food that is leavings should be given" (MDh 10.125). Thus, this would contradict the present rule. Let these two Smṛti rules—one prohibiting and one permitting—not be mutually contradictory; therefore, this is the meaning. Or perhaps: the rule permitting leavings refers to food remaining from cooking intended for guests and others, and thus there is no contradiction. That is also incorrect, because this meaning is established elsewhere by such passages as "The Vaiśya and the Śūdra also attain [the right to study]" (MDh 3.112). Consequently, the contradiction remains in that state.
