Furthermore, if this were stated merely to explain the meaning of the Smṛti, there would be an option regarding the restriction: "For Śūdras who live according to the law, shaving should be performed monthly" (MDh 5.140), and "and eating the leavings of the twice-born" (MDh 5.140)—this will be stated later. Therefore, one of these two must have a specific purpose, and now another indication follows. For it is stated in the section on *Śrāddha*: "The dried-up remnant of the food of one who is not crooked and not deceitful, belonging to the class of servants—that shall be declared as the share for the father" (MDh 3.248). And among all the *dharma*s of the Smṛtis, Śūdras and others are not excluded when the leavings of a Brāhmaṇa are permitted; it cannot be denied without a valid authority. Likewise, Gautama says: "Eating leavings and subsistence through a craft" (GDh 10.59–60). Moreover, the specific prohibition: "He who, having eaten at a *Śrāddha*, gives the leavings to a *Vṛṣala* (Śūdra)" (MDh 3.249) shows that the giving of leavings is possible outside of the *Śrāddha*. Otherwise, since the general prohibition "not leavings" (MDh 2.56) would already suffice, this specific prohibition would be meaningless; therefore, this is stated as a permissive statement. Now, if you think that this prohibition of the *Śrāddha* context is for the sake of a permanent rule, and thus the prohibition "not leavings" permits occasional giving elsewhere than at a *Śrāddha*, so that both prohibitions are established—this is incorrect, because it contradicts the logic of the scriptures. If that were not the case, this would be consistent; but even if it were permitted, it is called non-permanent. Even the remainder of the sacrificial oblation (*haviḥśeṣa*) is given to a Śūdra, for that is not given apart from the *Śrāddha* leavings. This contradicts established practice. Therefore, this is the meaning of the aforementioned Smṛti. Others, however, believe that the entire sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and so forth, once offered to the deities, is prohibited as "leavings. That is incorrect, because this meaning is not well-known either by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) or by etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the word "leavings" (*ucchiṣṭa*). This word-meaning is not established in common usage or in the scriptures. Nor is it possible to derive it through the meanings of the root and suffix like the word "cooking" (*pāka*). There is no context or anything else to determine the word-meaning. Nor is it stated as a permission based on the connection with that established meaning. By the subsequent phrase "not the sacrificial oblation" (*na haviṣkṛtam*), the aforementioned meaning is not achieved. How could the sacrificial oblation be requested? From where would there be the acquisition of the remainder of the oblation? Therefore, this is nothing. What is its meaning? We say: the meaning is "not leavings. Not all leavings are prohibited by this in a general sense. What then? What remains is the remainder of what was offered, the leavings of a Brāhmaṇa; that should not be given to a Śūdra by a *Snātaka*. How is this known? By the power of inference through elimination (*pariśeṣa*). If there were a general prohibition of all leavings, the Smṛti rules permitting them at a *Śrāddha* would be sublated, and they are not to be sublated by the aforementioned logic. Furthermore, there might be another meaning for the word "leavings" involving women and the like, whereas here the general giving of leavings is what remains; therefore, this refers to the remainder of the sacrificial cake and so forth belonging to a Brāhmaṇa. Practice among the learned is exactly like this, and there is no contradiction with other Smṛtis; the capacity [of the text] is thus justified. Now, as for the counter-argument: since this is the scriptural meaning, and furthermore: "As long as he is not born by means of the Veda, he is equal to a Śūdra" (MDh 2.172), it is not given even to uninitiated twice-born men because of their similarity to Śūdras. Therefore, this is the meaning. By the proximity of the word "sacrificial oblation" (*haviṣkṛtam*), this meaning is understood even more clearly. We shall demonstrate the capacity of this very word in its explanation later. It may be argued: "In that case, there is a redundancy with the subsequent word 'not leavings' (*nocchiṣṭam*). But it is not redundant because of the word "sacrificial oblation. Why? Because it is a different word, and because the scripture is intent on instruction regarding things mixed with the remainder of the oblation, the listener proceeds according to the instruction. Therefore, the prohibition of what is mixed with the remainder of the oblation does not allow us to understand a prohibition of those leavings. Thus, what is not prohibited by the phrase "not the sacrificial oblation" is properly prohibited by the other word "not leavings. In this way, this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the general Smṛti rule. How? The Smṛti "Leavings of
For he who explains his doctrine and he who instructs him in the vow—both go together with that very person into the darkness called "the unrestrained. (4.81)

[180] If, by this reasoning, the instruction of Dharma were permitted for a Śūdra when they are situated together at one time, then this exception would not be appropriate: "He goes with that very darkness called unrestrained. This statement of censure is appropriate because it contradicts the qualification [of the rule]. Therefore, otherwise, the instruction of Dharma according to the qualification is for the purpose of praising the instructor.
One should not scratch one's own head with both hands joined together.
One who is impure from eating should not touch this [the water-pot], nor should one bathe without it. 4.82.

Because the instruction concerns [the hand] when it is joined together, there is no prohibition against [scratching] when the two hands are not joined. Because scratching is prohibited, other actions such as touching and so forth are not prohibited. Because the term "self" (*ātman*) is used, there is no prohibition against another person scratching with both hands even when they are joined together. And because the term "head" is used, there is no prohibition against scratching other parts of the body. Even with both hands joined together, one should not touch oneself; this applies whether the hands are joined or unjoined when one is impure (*ucchiṣṭa*). Furthermore, one should not bathe without that [water], except for obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, but not for a purpose based on visible utility (*dṛṣṭārtha*), and by implication [this applies] here as well. In all cases, this distinction between what is more serious (*guru*) and what is lighter (*laghu*) must be demonstrated.
One should avoid seizing others by the hair and striking them on the head;
moreover, having bathed one's head, one should not touch any part of the body with oil. (4.83)
One should not accept gifts from a king who is not born of the Kṣatriya caste, nor from those who possess slaughterhouses, oil-presses, or taverns, nor from those who live by prostitution. (4.84)

There is a prohibition against accepting gifts from a king who is not a Kṣatriya, or from a Śūdra, except in times of distress. Since the term *rājanya* refers specifically to a Kṣatriya who is the offspring of a king, the phrase *tatprasūtiḥ* means one born of that lineage—that very caste. *Arājanyaprasūtiḥ* thus means one not born of a Rājanya lineage; the meaning is "from a Śūdra who is not born of a Rājanya lineage. This is stated by virtue of his lack of capacity for the administration of a kingdom. Thus, this constitutes a prohibition of what was otherwise permitted by the scriptural injunction, "One should seek wealth from a king" (MDh 4.33). Furthermore, by implication, the acceptance of gifts from butchers and others is also prohibited.
A cart is equal to ten slaughterhouses; a banner is equal to ten carts;
a brothel is equal to ten banners; and a king is equal to ten brothels. (4.85)
A king is considered equal to a butcher who maintains ten thousand slaughterhouses; therefore, accepting gifts from him is a terrible thing. (4.86)

This censure of accepting gifts from a king who is not a Kṣatriya is intended to bring about desistance from such practice. The phrase "equal to ten slaughter-houses" serves to establish their mutual purity [in comparison]. Therefore, it should be understood with effort that this is for the purpose of censuring the king; or, even on this alternative view, the mention of "slaughter-houses" establishes the censurability of those [other sins] as well, through a tenfold progressive increase. This being so:
"He who accepts gifts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures, goes in succession to these twenty-one hells. (4.87)
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, Raurava,
the hell Kālasūtra, and likewise Mahānaraka.
Saṃjīvana, Mahāvīci, Tapana, Saṃpratāpana,
Saṃhāta, Kākola, Kuddāla, and Pūtimṛttika.
The Iron Spike, the Residue, the Path, the Śālmalī River,
the Forest of Sword-leaves, and likewise the Iron Barbs.
Having understood this, learned Brahmins who discourse on Brahman and who desire the highest good after death do not accept gifts from a king. 4.91

The prohibition against accepting gifts from a non-Kṣatriya king when there is no distress should be understood from the context. By stating the prohibition of acceptance for a specific reason, [the author] shows that he permits acceptance even from a Śūdra who does not act contrary to the scriptures; likewise, there is a prohibition of acceptance from a Kṣatriya who acts contrary to the scriptures, because the underlying reason is the same. This being the case, when a legal dispute arises concerning dharma, the subordinate status [of the king] should be understood.
One should wake during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and reflect upon dharma and artha, as well as the physical hardships rooted therein and the true meaning of the Vedas. (4.92)

The *brāhma-muhūrta*—the final watch of the night—is well known in the *Yoga-śāstra* and other treatises. Having awakened at that time, one should reflect upon Dharma and Artha by way of their practice, their relationship as goal and means, and their mutual non-contradiction; likewise, one should reflect upon the afflictions (*kleśa*), the performance of Dharma which is rooted in those [afflictions], and the true meaning of the Vedas along with its six auxiliary limbs (*ṣaḍ-aṅga*). What is the injunction here? What is the counter-injunction (*pratiprasava*) regarding the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*)? For what purpose? What is the restatement (*anuvāda*)? This knowledge of ritual action (*karma-vidyā*) is indeed a supplement to ritual action in the *Upaniṣads*; this [knowledge of Brahman], however, is not a supplement to ritual action, but is independent and connected to its own fruit. This [knowledge] is combined with that [ritual action]; this is optionally substituted for that; this is the qualification for this [ritual action]; and through ritual action, there is neither this nor that fruit—namely, worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). Furthermore, the deity who is a limb of ritual action is of such a nature, whereas for one who performs only ritual action, the worlds are perishable; but for one who effects the combination of worldly knowledge [with ritual action], there is the state of Brahman (*brahmatva*). One should reflect on such categories of meaning. At that time, one’s intellect is serene, unassailed by delusion and the like. Thus...
Having risen and performed his necessary duties, having purified himself and composed his mind,
he should stand for a long time reciting prayers during the morning twilight, and likewise at its proper time during the evening twilight.
[182] His praise:
By virtue of performing the long twilight devotions (*dīrghasaṃdhyā*), the sages attained a long life.
Wisdom, glory, fame, and indeed the splendor of sacred knowledge.

This statement is repeated for the sake of prescribing a long duration [for study], due to the fear that it might obstruct the time for the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) of one who maintains the *agnihotra* fire; furthermore, there is another time for twilight worship even for the religious student (*brahmacārin*). And that [other time] is "until the stars appear" (?). Moreover, in the case of the school that maintains the *agnihotra* offering after sunrise, there is no such obstruction of the twilight worship by the time of the *agnihotra*. Having performed the commencement of study (*upākaraṇa*) according to rule on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada, a Brahmin, being disciplined, should study the Vedas (*chandas*) for one month and four and a half months. (4.95)

This rule regarding the ritual implements is appropriate; because of the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa," it indicates the exclusion of the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya by implication, and this should be understood to apply to both cases regarding the "four and a half" months. This is an option based on specific conditions: for the Adhvaryus, the commencement of study (*upākarma*) takes place on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, while for the Chandogas, it is on the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada.

"A twice-born man should perform the external suspension (*utsarjana*) of the Vedas under the asterism Puṣya, or when the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha has arrived, during the forenoon. (4.96)
The verse is intended to explain the procedure for the ritual abandonment (utsarga).

Having thus performed the abandonment of the Vedic meters outside [the village] in accordance with the scriptures, he should cease [recitation] for a night with its two flanking days—that is, for one full day and night. (4.97)

In both cases, it is said that [the study lasts for] a pakṣāpakṣiṇī (a day and night) and an ahorātra (a full day and night). From this point forward, however, one who is self-restrained should recite the Vedas during the bright fortnights,
and all the Vedāṅgas during the dark fortnights.

This distinction [between mantra and brāhmaṇa] applies after the general rule [of the Veda's division], because there is no separate mention of the brāhmaṇa; thus, the mention of *chandas* (Vedic texts) may include the brāhmaṇa as well, since even in those three verses [of the preceding context], the mantras and brāhmaṇas are already divided by their inherent nature. In some parts of the Veda, one should not recite it indistinctly, nor in the presence of Śūdras. Nor, having finished his Vedic study at the end of the night while still fatigued, should he go back to sleep. (4.99)

Because of the prohibition [against reciting] in the presence of a *vṛṣala* mentioned later on, the reading here as "in the presence of women" (*strījana-saṃnidhau*) is appropriate. Alternatively, by the etymological derivation of *vṛṣala*, it refers to one who is unrighteous (*adhārmika*) there, not a *vṛṣala* by birth; therefore, this very reading is superior. A twice-born man, being disciplined, should always recite the Veda composed in meters according to the prescribed rule, and likewise that which is composed in the *brahma*-meter, except in times of distress. (4.100)

[183] A verse for the purpose of summary: One who studies these [texts] should always avoid them when they are not fit for recitation— namely, those composed in the *brahma*, *brāhmaṇa*, and *chandaḥ* meters, and the mantras following the *gāyatrī* meter, in both cases, whether in the *brāhmaṇa* or in the *chandas*.
And while teaching his disciples according to the prescribed rule, || 4.101 ||

The inclusion of the word "constant" (*nitya*) is for the sake of emphasis, so that the avoidance of study on forbidden days (*anadhyāya*) may be carried out with great effort. Alternatively, the inclusion of "constant" is intended to indicate that the section concerning forbidden days applies not only to the seasonal course of study (*vāriṣika-adhyayana*) but to other forms as well; thus it is said in that very context: "When the wind is audible to the ear at night, and when there is a cloud of dust by day—these two are declared by those who know the rules of study to be times of non-study during the rainy season. (4.102)

By this [rule], those occasions for which there is no study during the rainy season are explained; Manu has declared that when lightning, thunder, and rain occur together, or when there is a falling of great meteors, one must abstain from study for the remainder of the day. (4.103)

Not at all times; [except] during a thunderbolt strike. One should know that when these have arisen while the fires have been kindled, then one should know it to be a time unfit for study, as well as when there is the appearance of clouds out of season. (4.104)

But they know these [clouds] as *dādan*. When one sees them at the time of twilight (*saṃdhyākāla*), then there is no study (*anadhyāya*). Because of the context, this [period of non-study] lasts until the same time the next day; otherwise, it would be purposeless. This non-study is understood to apply to the rainy season (*varṣā*). Regarding those [clouds] such as *vidyut* and so on, it has been stated that during the rainy season and at twilight, the non-study lasts until the same time the next day. Therefore, if it were prescribed again at twilight, it would be redundant; thus, the lack of authority [to study] during the rains ceases. It is said that in these cases, the authority for the "until-the-same-time" period continues. Alternatively, since the term "not in the dry season" (*anṛtau*) is indeed present here, we shall take it to serve both purposes; and that being so, the particle *ca* serves as a further alternative. Some say it means "and when there is no appearance of the dry season. We, however, consider it to be a supplement to the preceding verse, intended as a restrictive specification of the desired time for the restatement (*anuvāda*).

In the event of a thunderclap, an earthquake, or an eclipse of the heavenly bodies, one should know these to be occasions for the suspension of study until the same time the following day, even during the proper season. 4.105.

Since portents such as thunderclaps are generally seen during the rainy season, the phrase "even in the [proper] season" is stated; by the word "even," it is implied that they also apply outside the season. But when the fires have been kindled, at the sound of lightning and thunder, there shall be no study for as long as the light lasts; the remainder of the night is like the day. (4.106)

There is, however, another interpretation: one should offer oblations when the fires have been kindled; furthermore, even if either of the two signs—lightning or thunder—is encountered, there shall be a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) as long as the light remains. This means "during the day" alone. As for the remainder of the three mentioned in the context—lightning, thunder, and rain—the rule here in this verse is that when lightning and thunder occur, there is a suspension of study during the day even if rain has not yet fallen; or else, if the "remainder" is still visible, there is a suspension at night as well. Alternatively, because the "remainder" of the evening twilight follows the morning twilight, the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*) applies to the lightning and thunder as well. By taking it thus, even the "remainder" of those two, being grasped, causes a suspension of study at night, just as lightning and thunder occurring during the morning twilight cause a suspension during the day. And this alternative sequence of rules should be understood as not applicable to the entire section on study. We shall demonstrate the indicators of these alternatives in each verse right here.
For those who desire proficiency in dharma, there shall be a perpetual suspension of study in villages and cities, as well as everywhere in the presence of a foul odor. (4.107)
There is no study when a corpse is inside a village, nor in the presence of a *vṛṣala*, nor while there is weeping, nor in a great gathering of people. (4.108)
While in water, at midnight, when voiding excrement or urine, or while impure from eating at a *śrāddha* feast, one should not entertain [such thoughts] even in the mind. (4.109)

[This applies] even for those who are not Śūdras. [The editor notes here that there appears to be a gap in the manuscript. Furthermore, the term *vṛṣala* was explained previously. One who has discharged urine or excrement in water, or at midnight, being impure from having eaten a *śrāddha*, should not even mentally contemplate the Veda. This statement of emphasis is intended to preclude any doubt; it does not, however, permit mental recitation during other occasions of suspended study (*anadhyāya*).

"Having accepted an invitation to an *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, a learned twice-born man shall recite the Veda for three days. He shall likewise do so during the period of impurity following the death of a king, and during an eclipse of Rāhu. (4.110)

In the *ekoddiṣṭa* and *navaśrāddha* rites, where there is a single [deceased] and a modification (*ūha*) of the mantras, the learned one, having accepted the mantra, omits the word "api" (even). However, some say: "Not for three days; rather, as long as the oil and the smearings of the *ekoddiṣṭa* remain on the body of a learned Brahmin, so long should he not recite the Veda. (4.111)

There shall be a three-day suspension of study for an *anuddiṣṭa* (a funeral rite not specifically designated), or until the oily residue has been absorbed. One should not study while lying down, nor with feet raised on a seat, nor having crossed one's legs;
nor after eating meat, nor after food that makes a hissing sound when eaten. (4.112)

The taking of meat is for the purpose of those who lack faith. Because of the statement regarding the suspension of Vedic study (*anadhyāya*) due to eating food from one in a state of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), there is no suspension of study when eating food that is otherwise unfit to be eaten.
"In mist and at the sound of an arrow, during both twilights, on the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the lunar fortnight, and on the full moon and *aṣṭakā* days. (4.113)

*Bāṇa* means a lute (*vīṇā*), because we see its usage in the expression “he stretches (or plays) the *bāṇa*” (*bāṇaṃ vitanvati*), and because in other treatises it is mentioned alongside other stringed instruments; thus, *bāṇa* refers to a lute. The mention of *bāṇa* here is intended as an illustration for all types of musical instruments (*ātodya*), based on the rule regarding the sounds of the *bherī*, *mṛdaṅga*, *gartta*, and *ārtta* drums. This inclusion of the *tṛcāṣṭaka* is not for its own sake, but for the purpose of including the eighth and ninth days, due to its association with the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) and other such occasions. This being the case, the rule that “on the *aṣṭakā* and other such days there is a fast for a day and night” becomes meaningful. As it is said: “The new moon destroys the teacher; the fourteenth day destroys the pupil.”
Therefore, one should avoid those [days], including the Brahmāṣṭaka and the full moon days. || 4.114 ||

From this specific statement, it is understood that there is no recitation for one who has not studied on the fourteenth day and other such occasions. Likewise, Śaṅkha and Likhita state that there is constant non-recitation on the festival days (*parvan*):
"In the case of a dust storm, when the quarters of the sky are aflame, when a jackal howls, and likewise when dogs, donkeys, or camels cry out, a twice-born man should not recite in a row. (4.115)

One should not study at the edge of a cremation ground, at the edge of a village, or likewise in a cow-pen; nor after wearing a garment used for sexual intercourse, nor after accepting a gift related to a funeral rite (śrāddha). 4.116.

Whether it be animate or inanimate, whatever may be offered at a śrāddha ceremony, upon touching even that there shall be no study; for the twice-born is traditionally said to have his hand as his mouth.
When a village is plundered by thieves, during a panic caused by fire,
and in the case of all extraordinary portents, one should know that there is a suspension of study for the duration of the day.

Marvelous portents occurring in the heavens, the atmosphere, and on earth are to be understood from the *Atharvaveda*, and some of these have been taught by the authors of the Sūtras in the *Yajurveda*.
Regarding the suspension of Vedic study, it is traditionally prescribed that a three-night interruption occurs at the commencement (*upākarma*) and the conclusion (*utsarga*) [of the term];
however, a one-day and one-night interruption is prescribed during the *Aṣṭakā* festivals and on the nights marking the end of the seasons. (4.119)

There are four *aṣṭakā* festivals, according to the statement, "The winter season consists of four *aṣṭakās*. Others say that the term refers to the eighth day (*aṣṭaka*) itself. Furthermore, there is a suspension of study on the final nights of the seasons. One should not study while mounted on a horse, nor on a tree, nor on an elephant; nor in a boat, nor on a donkey, nor on a camel; nor while standing on barren ground, nor while traveling in a vehicle. (4.120)
By the instruction regarding vehicles such as horses, it is implied by the force of the context that other vehicles, such as carts and the like, are also taught.

[186] Not during a dispute, nor in a quarrel, nor in an army, nor in battle; not immediately after eating, nor when food is undigested, nor while traveling with a companion, nor when one has consumed sour food. (4.121)

There is no study when disputes or quarrels have occurred within oneself; nor should one study while in an army, even if not in uniform or unobserved, nor likewise during a battle (*saṅgara*). What, then, is the distinction between these two? An army is one where fighting has not yet commenced; a battle is one where fighting has already commenced. These two terms are to be explained according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*). And having taken leave of a guest, or when the wind blows violently, or when blood flows from the body, or when it is wounded by a weapon—4.122.
One should never recite the Ṛgveda or Yajurveda while the sound of the Sāmaveda is being heard;
likewise, after reaching the end of the Veda, or having studied the Āraṇyaka, one should not recite them.

A learned man, even if he does not intend to avoid a day unfit for study (*anadhyāya*), should certainly not [neglect] such rules as "he should always avoid... (MDh 4.127). Even one who has studied the *Āraṇyaka* alone, though he has not yet begun the formal study of the Veda, states here a certain apparent reason, which is actually an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*):
"The Ṛgveda has the gods as its deity; the Yajurveda belongs to humans;
the Sāmaveda is remembered as belonging to the ancestors; therefore, its sound is impure. (4.124)

This is stated by someone on the basis of a certain similarity with the *arthavādas*: "There is a conflict between those of equal strength; therefore, in this case, the *smṛti* is sublated by the *śruti*, because the *śruti* is stronger. And this being so—having understood this, the wise, having daily practiced the essence of the three Vedas (*trayīniṣkarṣa*) in sequence first, afterwards study the Veda itself. (4.125)

Having thus understood this very nature consisting of the ancestors, humans, and the self (*ātman*), one should first practice the study of the Veda three times daily in sequence—consisting of the *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *sāvitrī*, which is the essence of the three Vedas—and thereafter study whichever Veda one chooses. Since the cause of doubt regarding knowledge is [the lack of such study], for one who is being initiated, this [study] is ordained as possessing these qualities for the sake of conquering the three worlds of Brahmā, consisting of gods, ancestors, and humans; by the mere act of such study, it becomes endowed with these virtues. [The phrase] "another [is] the attainment of disciples" [is explained as follows]: although this matter ought to have been stated in the section concerning the teacher (*ācārya-prakaraṇa*), it is mentioned here because the prohibition of the former [teacher's duties] is intended to be supported by this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
If any of these—cattle, frogs, cats, horses, snakes, or mongooses—should pass between [the teacher and student], one should know that there is a suspension of study for a day and a night. (4.126)

And some, based on the word "paśu" (animals), maintain that there are seven domestic animals as qualifiers: the cow, sheep, goat, horse, mule, donkey, and human; and seven wild animals, such as the *uṣṭra* (camel) and others. [187] [This verse is found only in the reading of the *Manusmṛti* as explained by Bhāruci.]

Others, however, maintain that in the case of the animal sacrifice itself—such as in the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal"—just as a goat is understood from the general injunction and its specific application through the mantra-text "Recite the invitatory verse for Pāyus," so too here, a goat must be established by some inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*). But the former view, which concerns the meaning of the non-specific injunction, is seen to be superior here, not the other, because there is no observation of such inherent capacity [for a specific animal]. However, this is now stated for the purpose of defining all possible types of non-study days (*anadhyāya*):
"One should always diligently avoid only two non-study days."
A twice-born man [should avoid] an impure place for Vedic study and his own impurity. (4.127)

Because of the inclusion of the word *nitya* ("constant"), it is understood that here the rule regarding all [days] of non-study (*anadhyāya*) is optional. For if there were a specific purpose [for restriction], the inclusion of the word *nitya* for the sake of emphasis would not be appropriate. What then? It is for the sake of making the days of non-study constant; thus, as it has been stated in various places, there are signs of their non-constancy. Furthermore, this [rule] should be seen as an option for students regarding the days of non-study with respect to the fulfillment of their duty; the rule for Vedic study is not based on one's own desire, but rather by the force of the instruction of the Smṛti. And from the Śruti: "Indeed, of that other Brahma-sacrifice, there are two [factors]: [one] by which the self is impure, and [the other] by which the place [is impure]. If this Smṛti statement regarding the days of non-study is assumed to concern the Brahma-sacrifice, then the non-censurability of the days of non-study is to be understood through the aforementioned signs alone. This [statement] beginning with "One should always avoid these two" is not [intended] because of its connection to general custom; rather, having concluded that section on the days of non-study, this very instruction is stated again.
On the new moon day, the eighth, the full moon, and the fourteenth, a twice-born *snātaka* should always remain celibate, even during the fertile period. (4.128)

However, because there would otherwise be a lapse of the proper time, the reading "on the festival days (*parvasu*)" is joined for the purpose of exclusion. This reading is also supported by the text: "A twice-born man who has taken the bath [of initiation] [should approach her] during the season (*ṛtau*). And so it has been said: "He may approach her except on the festival days" (MDh 3.45). For this reason, the alternative reading "not during the season (*anṛtau*)" is set aside, as it is redundant, meaningless, or synonymous, since it is not the word of a seer (*ārṣa*).
One should not perform a ritual bath after eating, nor when ill, nor at midnight, nor constantly with one's clothes on, nor in an unknown body of water. (4.129)

This rule applies to one who has bathed for the sake of an unseen spiritual purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). As for bathing for the sake of purification (*śaucārtha*), because it is occasional (*naimittika*) and because such occasions are restricted to specific times, there is a prohibition against it at all other times. The mention of the "sick person" is not intended to exempt them from penance (*prāyaścitta*); for otherwise, in the absence of a specific statement regarding the sick, they would incur a transgression of the rule. Since the penance is established, it is not a great matter. Thus, even though staying overnight is occasional, the Smṛti prohibits it as a constant practice for the *snātaka*, seeing that he must always remain clothed (*bahuvāsāḥ*). [188]

One should not intentionally step upon the shadow of deities, of one's teacher, of a king, of a *snātaka*, of an *ācārya*, nor of a brown-colored person or one who has been consecrated for a sacrifice. (4.130)

Because the deities are formless (*amūrta*), for the sake of their manifestation, the learned ones worship them as having a firm physical form through this very vision; thus it is said that "Babhru worships. Even though this is the designation of Soma when it has become a constituent part of the ritual (*karmāṅga*), the word *babhru* is not heard there either. Alternatively, a tawny cow (*kapilā gauḥ*) is denoted by the word *babhru*, according to the Vedic text: "She [the cow] saw Babhru with her eyes as marks. Others say that the meaning of the word *babhru* refers to a religious student (*brahmacārin*), because his hair is tawny (*kapila-śiroruha*) and because of his desire. This statement is understood by implication to be for the purpose of removing the need for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in the case of unintentional [offense].
At midday and at midnight, after eating a śrāddha meal containing meat, and during both twilights, one should not frequent a crossroads. (4.131)
One should not intentionally step upon fragrant unguents used for rubbing the body, water used for ritual bathing, feces, urine, blood, phlegm, spittle, or vomit. (4.132)
One should not serve an enemy, nor the companion of an enemy, nor an unrighteous person, nor a thief, nor the wife of another. (4.133)
Indeed, nothing in this world is seen to be so detrimental to longevity as a man's pursuit of another's wife in this world. (4.134)
The meaning of these verses is clear. "Out of desire" has already been explained.
One who wishes to prosper should never, under any circumstances, despise a Kṣatriya, a serpent, or a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas, even if they are weak. (4.135)

The inclusion of the examples of the *kṣatriya* and the snake is for the purpose of illustrating the [wrath] of a virtuous Brahmin who has been slighted. For these three, when insulted, can utterly consume a man;
this is said in reference to their connection with both seen and unseen [consequences].
Therefore, a wise person should never despise these three things. 4.136

Others also say: since the purpose of all three [classes] is invisible (*adṛṣṭārtha*), this prohibition is understood to apply even to those Kṣatriyas and Sarpas who, though established by their capacity, are not very learned (*abahuśruta*). Because of the subsequent prohibition against those with deficient limbs and so forth—which functions like the "stick-and-cake" logic (*daṇḍāpūpikayā*)—the non-inclusion of Kṣatriyas and others is established. However, because they are superior, this specific prohibition is either for the sake of a specific penance (*prāyaścitta*) or is a prohibition specifically regarding Kṣatriyas and others:
"One should not despise oneself on account of former failures."
Seeking prosperity until death, one should not consider this [prosperity] difficult to attain. 4.137 ||

"One must not despise oneself"—this is a restrictive rule (niyama) whose purpose is transcendental (adṛṣṭārtha). For through self-contempt, one might at some point engage even in improper acts such as consuming poison.
"One should speak the truth; one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak an unpleasant truth, nor should one speak a pleasant falsehood—this is the eternal dharma. (4.138)

In this regard, it has been stated that one should speak the truth. Now, for the sake of specifying its particular application, it is enjoined that one should speak what is true by way of stating another related matter: "one should speak what is pleasant. This specific rule is now being explained: one should not speak an unpleasant truth. For example: "O Brāhmaṇa, your daughter is pregnant. First of all, this is an exception to the general injunction to speak the truth; now, speaking what is unpleasant is being set aside. Furthermore, one should not speak a pleasant falsehood. For example, when a daughter has been born, saying: "O Brāhmaṇa, a son has been born to you. In such a case, since a truthful course is possible, one should resort to ignorance [of the facts]. However, a falsehood may be told to avoid causing pain to others. Here, the word "para" (other) implies that out of compassion, one should resort to untruth for the purpose of preventing the arising of suffering in another. This should be understood to apply to all unpleasant matters, such as the death of a relative and so forth. But in the case of testimony in a legal proceeding, where the pain of one party might be paramount, there must necessarily be a favor toward both sides. In that situation, it is proper and even possible to say that untruth should not be spoken because of the fault attached to speaking it; thus, this truthfulness regarding pleasant matters is defined by the discernment of the specific context. It is not [defined] by the [prohibitions against] falsehood and so forth, which apply to truth itself.
One should say "auspicious, auspicious," or simply say "auspicious";
one should not engage in domestic enmity or dispute with anyone. (4.139)

The expression "inauspicious" (*abhadra*) is used as "auspicious" (*bhadra*) for the sake of emphasis. Thus says Gautama: "They call inauspicious 'auspicious'" (GDh 9.20). This being the case, there is no restriction on the word here; if the word *bhadra* were repeated a second time, that repetition would be for the purpose of restricting the term, just as the particle *eva* is used. Or rather, in the phrase "he should say only 'bhadra'," this very word is thus restricted.
[He should not go] too early, nor too late, nor at midday when [the sun] has reached its zenith.
He should not travel with an unknown person, nor alone, nor with *vṛṣalas*. (4.140)
One should not despise those who have missing limbs, those with extra limbs, those lacking in learning, those advanced in age, those deficient in beauty or wealth, or those of low birth. (4.141)
A Brahmin who is impure from eating should not touch with his hand a cow, a Brahmin, or fire;
nor, while remaining in good health, should he look at the hosts of celestial luminaries in the sky while he is himself impure.
Having touched these while being impure, one should always touch the vital breaths with water, as well as all the limbs and the navel with the palm of the hand. [4.143]

Having seen these lights, one who is impure should perform this very rite; for since both [the sight and the impurity] are prohibited, the penance for the transgression is equal, by virtue of the capacity of the injunction.
One who is not ill should not touch his own orifices without a specific cause, and he should avoid all the hair of his private parts. (4.144)
This verse is explained by its own words:
"He should be endowed with auspicious conduct, self-restrained, and have his senses conquered;
he should mutter prayers and offer oblations into the fire daily, without weariness. (4.145)

That which is performed during the sight of bad dreams and the like is for the purpose of averting harm; that is *maṅgala*. Alternatively, let it be pleasing for the sake of prosperity (*abhyudaya*) while being performed. The touching of the head and other parts of the body—whether not performed or performed—is a transgression (*pratyavāya*). Just so is the practice of *maṅgala*, such as truthful speech and the like. If [the rule] regarding the practice of *maṅgala* has already been stated, then its repetition here is for the purpose of an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). If, however, it is appropriate [to state it here], then its statement is indeed appropriate for the purpose of an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*). And thus he will say later. Alternatively, this is said with reference to the householder’s position where there is an absence of a ritual seat (*sādana*); it is a praise of this [practice], meaning that it is to be accomplished by the self alone as the means, independent of others, and performed in due order.
For those who are devoted to auspicious conduct, who are constant and self-controlled,
and who recite prayers and offer oblations, no downfall is found.
This is stated in order to demonstrate that conduct is paramount for him:
"He should constantly recite the Veda at the proper times without sloth; for they declare that to be his supreme duty (*dharma*), while any other is called a secondary duty (*upadharma*). (4.147)
The censure of improper conduct is intended for the purpose of praising the study of the Vedas:
"By the constant study of the Vedas, by purity, by austerity alone, and by non-injury toward living beings, one remembers one's former birth" (4.148).
Remembering his former birth, the twice-born practices the Veda;
and through the constant practice of the Veda, he enjoys infinite happiness. (4.149)
The repetition regarding the study of the Vedas is for the purpose of praise.
He should constantly perform the Sāvitra and the propitiatory oblations (śānti-homa) on the Parvan days;
and he should always worship the ancestors on the Aṣṭakā days and the Anvaṣṭakā days. (4.150)

[191] Because of the statement, "The *sāvitra* and the *śānti-homa*s," the oblation should be performed with clarified butter (*ājya*), rather than with any other primary substance used as a means for the oblation.
One should perform urination at a distance from one's dwelling, washing the feet at a distance, and likewise the disposal of food remnants and waste at a distance. (4.151)
The meaning of this verse is well known:
"One should perform the act of friendliness, grooming, bathing, cleaning the teeth, applying collyrium, and the worship of the deities during the forenoon alone. (4.152)
The commencement of this treatise is for the purpose of establishing a restrictive rule:
"On the sacred festival days (parvan), one should visit deities, righteous and most excellent twice-born men, the sovereign for the sake of protection, and likewise one's teachers. (4.153)
He should salute his elders and offer them his own seat;
he should attend upon them with palms joined in reverence and follow behind them as they depart. (4.154)
The good conduct is restated for the sake of what follows:
"One should, unwearied, practice that good conduct which is the root of dharma—the dharma proclaimed by the Śruti and Smṛti, and established in one's own duties. (4.155)
The accomplishment of all this results from conduct.
For through conduct one obtains long life; through conduct, desired offspring;
through conduct, inexhaustible wealth; and conduct destroys inauspicious marks. (4.156)
For a man of evil conduct is indeed censured in the world;
he is a partaker of suffering, and moreover, he is diseased and short-lived. (4.157)
Even if he is devoid of all auspicious marks, the man who possesses good conduct, is full of faith, and is free from malice, lives for a hundred years. (4.158)

The four verses intended to praise the performance of proper conduct (*ācāra*) are to be understood as being applicable in both ways due to the inherent nature of the statements. In the first chapter, the praise of conduct was stated for the purpose of praising the treatise (*śāstra*), beginning with the words, "Conduct is the highest dharma" (MDh 1.108). Here, however, in this section on the injunctions regarding conduct, the praise should be understood as pertaining to its own specific context.
One should carefully avoid whatever action is dependent upon others.
With the intention, "Who has accomplished what was to be done? Who specifically will sacrifice or serve? one should engage in receiving gifts and other such acts;
for whatever is under one's own control, that one should cultivate with effort. (4.159)
This is also observed in the world:
"Everything dependent on another is suffering; everything dependent on oneself is happiness.
One should know this, in brief, to be the definition of happiness and suffering. (4.160)

The restraint of the senses (*indriyasaṃyama*)—consisting of the taking of wealth through gifts and other means for the sake of enjoying one's own objects in this very world, and bringing the self under control by being devoted to contentment—is described here as a further mode of sense-restraint; though already mentioned, it is restated again in these two verses. Regarding the performance of the prescribed conduct, even though there is a great variety of such conduct:
Whatever action, while performing it, brings satisfaction to his inner self, that he should perform with effort, but he should avoid the opposite. (4.161)

This specific enjoined action, when performed with a mind that is contrary [to its requirements], leads to no transgression; this is for the purpose of praising the purity of intention regarding that subject.
"One should not harm the teacher, the expounder, the father, or likewise the mother, nor Brāhmaṇas, cows, or any ascetics. (4.162)

Indeed, violence toward those who do no harm is not permitted in any circumstance. For one should not injure even teachers and others, even though they may be harmful; and what is called "violence" (*hiṃsā*) regarding teachers and others refers to acting in opposition to them, not their killing. Thus it has been said: "And likewise one who opposes the teacher" (MDh 3.153). This is the meaning [of the prohibition] which serves as a restriction against what would otherwise be applicable. And so it is stated in the *Mahābhārata*: Arjuna struck Yudhiṣṭhira only by acting in opposition to him. [Furthermore: Atheism, reviling the Vedas, and disparaging the deities...
One should avoid hatred, arrogance, pride, anger, and hypocrisy. || 4.163 ||

That [is said] for the purpose of demonstrating a specific kind of aversion, and for the purpose of avoiding [such acts] even toward teachers and others. "One should not raise a staff against another, nor, when angry, should one strike him down; except in the case of a son or a pupil, one may strike those two for the sake of discipline. (4.164)
A twice-born man who merely threatens a Brahmin with the intent to kill him revolves in the Tāmisra hell for a hundred years. (4.165)
Having intentionally struck [a being] even with a blade of grass out of agitation, one shall be born for twenty-one lifetimes in the wombs of the wicked. [4.166]
By causing blood to flow from the body of a Brahmin who is not fighting, a man, through his lack of wisdom, incurs very great suffering after death. (4.167)
For as many particles of dust as the blood gathers from the surface of the earth, for that many years shall the shedder of blood be devoured by others in the next world. (4.168)
"By others" means by those such as tigers and so forth.
Therefore, a twice-born man should never even threaten Brahmins;
he should not strike them even with a blade of grass, nor should he cause blood to flow from their body. (4.169)

And this should be understood from the illustration of the Brāhmaṇa for the purpose of avoiding injury to all living beings; likewise, he will later prescribe penance [for such acts]. Furthermore, royal punishment applies not only to the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, but to the injury of any living being whatsoever. However, the mention of the Brāhmaṇa is intended to indicate the gravity of the transgression. And so it is observed in the world:
"A man who is unrighteous, whose wealth comes from falsehood, and who always delights in violence—such a person does not prosper in happiness in this world" (4.170).
And this being so—
though one may be sinking, by means of the dharma existing in the form of a formal arrangement known as "self-constriction"—
One should direct the mind toward unrighteousness, in the form of violating the established order of the treatises. For what reason?
Because one quickly perceives the reversal of the fortunes of those who are unrighteous and sinful. (4.171)
If this is seen [in the world], it is not seen [directly] through scripture. What is the reason?

Because—“Unrighteousness practiced in the world does not bear fruit immediately, like a cow. [The word] “cow” refers to the earth, as it possesses horns. For the sake of establishing the subject at hand, examples should be stated by means of both similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
But when a task is undertaken slowly and turns back, it cuts away the very roots of the doer, depending as it does on factors such as place, time, and cause. (4.172)
[194] The cutting of the root is the praise of its virtues, for the purpose of excellence. It leads the doer to the state of no further rebirth. And this being so:
"If not in oneself, nor in one's sons; if not in one's sons, then in one's grandsons."
But an unrighteous act that has been committed never becomes fruitless for the doer. (4.173)

In this case, because a result is observed, one must not understand that undesirable karma is fruitless. What then? It ripens gradually through the enjoyment of desired fruits by sons and grandsons; thus, undesirable karma [is exhausted]. Furthermore, this is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) intended to deter people from improper actions by showing the connection of sons and others with undesirable results, for otherwise there would be the fallacy of "acquisition of what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*), the fault of "loss of what was done" (*vipraṇāśa*), and contradiction with the scriptures. Thus, one should not act here by disregarding the scripture and thereby violating its established order; for while the primary factor is that which is inherent in the self—namely, the violation of the scriptural order—it cannot effect the increase of the face [of the agent] through that [external result]. Moreover, the word *tāvat* (so much/for so long) is to be explained as being accompanied by a nod of the head due to the requirement of syntactic expectancy.
Someone prospers through unrighteousness; then he sees auspicious things, because his own conduct is not contrary to reality due to the inherent nature of things. Then he conquers his rivals.
One attains the second human goal—the cessation of misfortune through prosperity—by perceiving its true nature through direct perception. This occurs at the time of death;
however, it perishes along with its very root. (4.174)

The authority of the scripture is established by its being the standard for the determination of dharma and adharma; and thus says the worldly proverb: "Inference is to be drawn from the science of Ayurveda and from common worldly experience. Furthermore, the destruction of the root was explained in the preceding verse.

One should always exert oneself toward truth, dharma, noble conduct, and purity; and one should instruct disciples in accordance with dharma, employing speech, arms, and the belly [as appropriate]. (4.175)

This is a restatement for the purpose of providing an offering for all the duties of a *snātaka*. Since it was stated in the verse taught at MDh 2.224—"But the three-fold aim [of life] is established"—in reference to that, this is now said: "One should abandon wealth and pleasure if they are devoid of righteousness (*dharma*); and one should also abandon righteousness if its future result is unhappiness or if it is censured by the world. (MDh 4.176) In the passage, "Even if he is suffering through righteousness, he should not turn his mind toward unrighteousness" (MDh 4.171), that which was taught in the verse—"The three-fold aim is established"—is what is being considered here. Therefore, this is stated with reference to that.

Wealth and pleasure should be such that they are connected with righteousness (*dharma*). Therefore, even when one possesses the duty of embracing the three aims of life (*trivarga*), one should avoid that which results in unhappiness; for that which results in unhappiness is not desired by one who is incapable, since wealth is required for that which is suitable for the self. Just as in matters of visible purpose, so too in matters of invisible purpose, because of the scriptural injunction regarding the protection of the self, a practice contrary to worldly consensus (*lokasaṅkruṣṭa*) is performed as a sacrifice for the sake of appearing similar to that [righteousness]. Or rather, all this is already established; however, the matter of what is contrary to worldly consensus is taken up again. If that [act] were superior—such as the slaughter of a cow, or the sale of *soma* by one obstructing the constituent parts of a sacrifice—it is prohibited, as in the case of the student (*brahmacārin*), the unchaste woman, or the reviler. Because of the force of the injunction, or because of the prohibition against speaking of it as "white" (*śukla*), it should not be performed. Others, however, cite adultery as an example, or the destruction of living beings despite speaking the truth, because of the instruction on penance (*prāyaścitta*) such as "with oblations dedicated to the deity Speech" (MDh 8.105), and so forth. This being the case:
One should not be fickle with hands or feet, nor fickle with the eyes, nor crooked; one should likewise not be fickle with speech, nor have a mind intent on deeds that harm others. (4.177)
This verse has been explained by its very recitation. Now, another cause for the practice of the True Dharma is being stated:
"One should travel by that path of the virtuous which one's fathers have traveled, and by which one's grandfathers have traveled; traveling by that path, one does not come to ruin. (4.178)

Regarding the phrase "the path of the virtuous" (*satāṃ mārgam*), the term "virtuous" (*santaḥ*) refers—based on its indicative mark—to those who know the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and the Śāstras, namely one's father and grandfather; one should follow the sacrificial practice performed by them. How so? Even if one is personally incapable of discernment for the sake of entering upon one’s own duty (*svadharma*), nevertheless, considering that it was practiced by them, one enters upon it out of devotion to them. Others say that this is stated as a cause for entering upon the true dharma through another means: being instructed by prior usage even without direct instruction.
[This is taught] by the officiating priests, the family priest, the teacher, the maternal uncle, guests, and those who provide shelter.
By children, the elderly, the sick, physicians, kinsmen, relatives, and friends. || 4.179 ||
One should not engage in dispute with one's mother or father, sisters, brother, son, wife, daughter, or the group of servants. (4.180)
By abandoning disputes with these, one is liberated from the sins of serpents;
and having conquered them, the householder conquers all these worlds. (4.181)

For this reason, it is said: "The teacher is the lord in the world of Brahmā; the father is the master in the world of Prajāpati; the guest is the lord in the world of Indra; and the officiating priests are the lords of the world of the gods. (4.182)

Sisters-in-law belong to the world of the Apsarases; kinsmen belong to the world of the Viśvedevas; maternal relatives belong to the world of the waters; and one's mother and maternal uncle belong to the world of the earth. (4.183)
The young, the old, the emaciated, and the sick should be known as lords of space (ākāśa).
An elder brother is equal to a father; a wife and a son are one's own body. (4.184)
One's own shadow is one's own slave-folk, and a daughter is the ultimate object of pity; therefore, when reviled by these, one should always endure it without feverish distress. (4.185)
The mention of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others in these seven verses is intended merely to indicate their connection [to the topic].
Even one who is capable of receiving gifts should avoid attachment to them;
for by the act of receiving gifts, his spiritual luster (*brahmatejas*) is quickly extinguished. (4.186)

Although this was already stated in the verse, “For the sake of accomplishing mere subsistence” (MDh 4.3), it is stated again here. I shall speak specifically for the purpose of prohibiting particular [forms of] action for one who has completed his duties. And since [the rule] is thus established, [this section] is intended to describe specific types of acceptance—either for the sake of a particular excellence in prosperity resulting from the restraint of livelihood regarding the acceptance of gifts, or for the sake of what follows. Accordingly, he shows:
“Without knowing the righteous rule for the acceptance of things, a wise man should not accept a gift, even if he is perishing from hunger. (MDh 4.187)

The lawful rule is that wealth is for the purpose of sacrifice. Having understood this—that the deity of the substance is [stated] thus, beginning with "a horse to Varuṇa, a cow to Rudra"—the deities of substances are mentioned in another scripture. Whether ending with acceptance (*pratigraha*) or being common, or even if destroyed; this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), "even perishing from hunger," is for the purpose of praising the rule of acceptance. And thus, even when one is perishing from hunger, what is taken—even if unintentionally—is not for the sake of sin. This also follows from the word [of the text]. Now, he shows the substance to be accepted.
But the ignorant man who accepts gold, land, a horse, a cow, food, clothing, sesame seeds, or clarified butter is reduced to ashes like wood. (4.188)

Or rather, this refers to the specific substances. This injunction is for the purpose of illustrating those substances, because their mention is intended as a general praise of the rule concerning the acceptance of gifts that has been under discussion. Thus, the mention of gold and the other items is intended to be significant; this is stated for the sake of respect, in order to prohibit the acceptance of specific things:
"Gold [bestows] long life, food, land, a cow, and offspring;
a horse [bestows] sight, a garment [bestows] skin, ghee [bestows] luster, and sesame seeds [bestow] progeny. (4.189)
Since this is so:
"But that twice-born man who is devoid of austerity, who does not study, and who delights in accepting gifts, sinks along with him in the water like one using a stone as a raft. (4.190)

This being the case, it should be understood from the instruction here that austerity is accompanied by knowledge (*vijñāna*). And the acquisition of Vedic study (*adhyayana*) is according to the previous rule, by virtue of the context of knowledge. This is to be understood either for its own sake, for the sake of austerity, or as a qualification of austerity. He now concludes the subject at hand:
"Therefore, an ignorant man should fear [accepting] from whatever source; for an ignorant man sinks even through a very small gift, like a cow in the mud. (4.191)

It is not only [the case] that one who has not studied [the Veda] is forbidden from accepting gifts such as horses and the like; by stating "nor even one who is unlearned," he prohibits even that person from accepting gifts of a teacher's property, provided he has studied the Veda and is learned and ascetic—even when he possesses knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas. "A knower of Dharma should not give even water to a twice-born man who acts like a cat, nor to a sinful man who acts like a heron, nor to one who does not know the Veda. (4.192)

"One should not honor with even a mere word those Brahmins who follow the 'cat-vow' (baiḍālavratika)" (MDh 4.30). Although this is already established [by other rules], it is stated again; we shall explain the purpose for which it is so stated. In the phrase "not even water," the word "even" (*api*) indicates that water is intended for all purposes, as has been stated in the verse: "Grass, ground, and water... (MDh 3.101). Thus, by prohibiting the gift of water—which is otherwise well-known to be for all purposes—he prohibits the gift of other substances as well. By the force of the aforementioned reasoning, he will later state regarding those following the cat-vow, the heron-vow, and the Kaulas: "...not one who is ignorant of the Veda. By this, he refers to one who has not mastered the meaning of the Veda. This is distinct from the case where giving is prescribed to a *śrotriya* (Vedic scholar) even if he is ignorant [of the meaning], or to one who has studied the Veda according to the scriptures but has not heard the meaning of the scriptures. Equating these two is improper, as it contradicts both scripture and logic. Since that [equivalence] is unheeded and lacks logical force, the meaning must be understood exactly as stated. Furthermore, "one who knows Dharma" here refers to one who knows the prohibitive scriptures, not anyone else. This explanatory passage (arthavāda) regarding the prohibition is intended to effect desistance through the expression of aversion.
For wealth, even if acquired according to the law, when given to these three types of persons, leads to misfortune for both the giver and the recipient in the next world. (4.193)

He does not merely produce those [gains] from censurable persons according to the law; rather, he renders them [unlawful] by performing another prohibited act. Thus, because of the mention of wealth, there is no prohibition here of what was previously permitted for those such as the *baiḍālavratika* (those with the conduct of a cat) and the *udvratika* (those who have transgressed their vows). This is also the logic of specific prohibitions mentioned in the verse concerning heretics (*pāṣaṇḍin*). Otherwise, if there were a total prohibition here, it would contradict the logic stated previously. Alternatively, since there is an option between what is prescribed and what is prohibited, this shows that there is no restriction regarding the aforementioned food, unlike the case of a guest. But another says: It was stated there that one should not give to the *baiḍālavratika* and others, whereas here the undertaking is intended to show that one should not accept gifts from the *baiḍālavratika* and others. Since that rule has already been stated, its meaning is restated here. Furthermore, in the explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) regarding the seeking [of wealth], the state of being a hidden sinner is difficult to discern; therefore, with the intention of defining its characteristics, this is stated again. What was expressed in the previous verse—"wealth acquired even by lawful means"—is that when given to these [persons], it does not lead to prosperity but results in misfortune; this is the perceived purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) in analyzing its nature.
Just as one who attempts to cross water with a boat made of stone sinks, so too do the ignorant donor and recipient sink to the bottom. 4.194

What is the meaning of the simile here? Just as a boat sinks by its own nature because it is unable to support what is mounted upon it, so too he who receives what is given to him according to the rule, yet bends down and sinks, being incapable of supporting the giver—because this state is now difficult to discern due to the fault of being concealed, this definition is undertaken for the sake of distinguishing and avoiding it:
"One who displays the banner of righteousness, always greedy, deceitful, and a deceiver of the world;
such a person should be known as one who follows the 'cat-vow' (baiḍālavratika), who is violent and a subverter of all. (4.195)

Or rather, he is called such by someone because of his connection with that [hypocritical] action and those qualities, due to some similarity in behavior, for the purpose of censure. Others, however, recite the second verse for that very purpose in this region:
"He whose banner of dharma is always raised high like the banner of Indra, yet whose sins are concealed—that is the vow known as 'the cat-vow' (baiḍāla)."

That is incorrect, because the meaning has already been stated by the preceding verse; there is no further purpose for this verse on that same subject. Nor is it heard even in the traditional recension: "The twice-born who looks downward, who is cruel, intent solely on achieving his own ends, deceitful, falsely humble, and a practitioner of the crane's vow. (4.196)

This [verse] is for the purpose of censuring false Brahmins; although some of what is here may be a repetition of what was stated in the preceding verse, it should nevertheless be understood that such repetition is not intended [as a fault]. For, in this case, nothing is either enjoined or prohibited by it. Thus it is said: “Those Brahmins who follow the vow of the heron (baka-vratinaḥ) and those who bear the marks of a cat (mārjāra-liṅginaḥ), they fall into the Andhatāmisra hell because of that sinful deed. (4.197)
Because it has the result of deceiving others, this [false claim] is likewise a downfall; therefore, any other action involving hypocrisy is also censured for the purpose of avoidance:
"Having committed a sin, one should not perform a vow under the pretext of dharma;
by concealing the sin with a vow, one practices deception upon women and Śūdras. (4.198)
For such Brahmins as these are censured both in this world and after death by those who discourse on the Veda; and whatever vow is practiced through hypocrisy goes to the Rākṣasas. (4.199)
Therefore, one should not perform penance under the pretext of practicing dharma; this is another instance equal to that.
He who, though not a bearer of the marks, lives off the livelihood of those who bear the marks, takes upon himself the sin of those bearers of marks and is born in the womb of an animal. (4.200)

This [verse] is exactly like that, and should therefore be explained in the same manner; here, one must imagine a contradiction in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding the absence of prohibition and so forth. Because of their association, bathing was mentioned for these two previously in the verse: "Combing the hair, bathing, [and wearing fragrant substances] belong to Mitra" (MDh 4.152). Since that was intended as a rule regarding the means [of purification], it is now commenced [again]. One should never bathe in reservoirs belonging to others. For by bathing there, one becomes tainted by a portion of the evil deeds of the maker of the reservoir. (4.201)

A *nipāna* is a watering place such as a lotus pond (*puṣkariṇī*) or the like, so called because people drink there (*nipīyate*). One should never bathe in one belonging to another; "never" (*kadācana*) means at no time whatsoever. Even for a visible purpose, such as for one's own purification, if one has been touched by a *caṇḍāla* or similar person, one should not bathe there for the sake of that [external] purification, much less for the sake of *dharma*. A *snātaka* who does not bathe here is not tainted by even a fraction (*aṃśa*) of the fault of its maker. Regarding this, some maintain that the word "fraction" (*aṃśa*) denotes a fourth part, because a third is heard later on. That is incorrect, because this is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). This being the case, the status of being a fourth part is not intended here. However, a transgression is understood for one who acts in violation of the scripture. He states an illustration in this regard:
For he who makes use of another's vehicles, beds, seats, wells, gardens, or houses without they being given to him, indeed commits the third [offense]. (4.202)

For just as one who uses vehicles, beds, seats, and so forth—things prepared for his own enjoyment but not given to him—commits a fault against another, so too [is it with water] because of the statement that "the drinking-troughs belonging to others are not to be used without permission. Regarding drinking-troughs intended for the benefit of all, he at one time permits bathing; and even in the case of those not so intended, if they have been permitted, it is likewise [allowed]. Furthermore, just as in the case of [public] squares (*śūrya*) and so on, even when not explicitly relinquished, such usage is indeed considered permissible simply by the force of the word "other" (*para*). In this way, the gifts of lotus-ponds (*puṣkariṇī-dāna*), which are well-known everywhere in the world, become logically consistent. This being the meaning of the Smṛti, otherwise these would lack the characteristics of a scriptural injunction (*śāstra-lakṣaṇa*), and that is not desired. Therefore, the meaning of the Smṛti is exactly as stated. Now, however, another means for bathing is mentioned for the purpose of further qualifying that [topic].
One should always perform one's ritual bathing in rivers, in natural pools dug by the gods, in large tanks, in lakes, and also in pits and springs. (4.203)

In this context, if rivers are of both kinds, then this very word here is appropriate to be studied as having three genders because it serves as a qualifier for them; and in other cases, it is understood by implication. Let its gender be unexpressed (*aśruta*). It is not so; therefore, because it qualifies things such as *taṭāka* (ponds), it should be studied with that same gender. (The combined intention of these two sentences is unclear. Furthermore, ponds and the like are indeed well-known to be of both kinds, and the word "constant" (*nitya*) is fixed for the purpose of qualifying the ritual bath for merit (*dharmasnāna*). However, regarding the occasional (*naimittika*) and the visible-purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) baths, such a restriction is not understood. Alternatively, the mention of "constant" should be understood as being for the sake of emphasis: one must first strive to rely upon the primary rule for the ritual bath for merit. First, with a mind free from worldly attachment, one should bathe in rivers and the like; even today, the ritual bath for merit may take place in reservoirs that are either abandoned or authorized. But for the other two—the occasional and the visible-purpose—there is no restriction on the choice of location. Moreover, the absolute prohibition of all three types of baths in reservoirs belonging to others is understood from the force of the commencement of the preceding verse. And this detailed exposition of the meaning of the three verses is understood through the power of the treatise, not by mere assertion. How so? Because of the statement regarding bathing in rivers and the like. Since there is a prohibition against reservoirs belonging to others, it is understood from the subsequent prohibition that, by the logic of the restriction of the three baths, bathing is permitted in abandoned reservoirs. Otherwise, the preceding illustrative verse would have been unnecessary. This has also been stated: it is repeated in every verse and again at the end of the section to clarify its meaning, lest there be confusion. The restraints and observances (*yama-niyama*) of the *snātaka* have been stated. Now they are described in order to demonstrate their relative weight and lightness.
A wise person should constantly practice the *yamas* and not always the *niyamas*; for one who fails to perform the *yamas*, even if they worship only the *niyamas*, they fall. (4.204)

In this context, the *yamas* consist of abstentions such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and so forth; the *niyamas*, however, consist of observances such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and so forth. Thus, when there is a violation of the *yamas*—such as the killing of a Brahmin—the person is no longer qualified for ritual acts, whether Vedic (*śrauta*) or traditional (*smārta*), due to that lapse in the *niyamas*. To this effect, Gautama says: "Falling [from caste] is the loss of eligibility for the duties of the twice-born" (GDh 21.4). And so, because the *yamas* are more powerful, this is stated: one should constantly practice the *yamas* for the sake of respect toward their performance, whereas one may neglect the *niyamas* due to their relative lightness; thus, the performance of the *niyamas* is indeed non-obligatory. Therefore, the wise person does not [regard] the *niyamas* as obligatory. However, this is not a rejection of the performance of the *niyamas*; rather, the scripture is non-optional due to the force of the instruction regarding both. Accordingly, the tradition of the learned (*śiṣṭas*) records: "One who possesses the *niyamas* but is unattached to the *yamas* does not perish, even if he is indolent in the observance of the *yamas*. Having thus reflected upon both *yamas* and *niyamas*, one should fix the intellect upon the path where the *yamas* predominate—even for those for whom *yama* and *niyama* are merely technical designations.
Non-violence, truthful speech, celibacy, freedom from guile,
and non-stealing— these five are both the restraints (yamas) and the observances (vratas).
Absence of anger, service to the teacher, purity, moderation in food,
and vigilance— these are the five observances (niyamas) and the minor vows (upavratas).

Having stated that this same principle (*nyāya*) is to be understood for them as well [and not another], and since the performance of the observances prescribed for those who have completed their studies is rooted in purity of food, this section concerning the purity of food for the *snātaka* is now commenced: "A Brāhmaṇa should never eat at a sacrifice performed by one who is not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*), nor at one performed by a priest who officiates for an entire village (*grāmayājika*), nor at one offered by a woman or a eunuch. (4.205)

When a sacrifice has been commenced by one who is *aśrotriya*—that is, one who has not studied the Veda—from what is this known? From the force of the context (*sāmarthya*). Since the mere possibility of study would otherwise be assumed, this prohibition is stated. "A Brāhmaṇa should never eat" applies here, whether at an *abhyudaya-śrāddha* or in the case of one who performs sacrifices for a village (*grāmayājaka*) or for many (*bahuyājaka*), because the capacity for commencement is established even for such an *aśrotriya*. The term "by a woman" (*striyā*) refers to both a wife and a maiden. For whom is the offering (*homa*) prescribed? It is said to be for certain individuals, because of the statement "the woman's evening [offering]" (*strīsāyam*). In the *pākayajñas* of the *Chandogas*, since that [offering] is prohibited, this is stated for the purpose of forbidding it. Regarding "an offering made by a woman," where sacrifices are performed primarily by a woman, this mention of a "woman" refers specifically to the case of a substitute (*pratinidhi*) for the sacrificer, because she lacks the status of an *aśrotriya*. Alternatively, once the prohibition of a woman is already established, her specific mention is for the sake of providing an illustrative example (*arthavāda*). By this, the mention of a eunuch (*klība*) is explained; the eunuch is prohibited because he lacks the status of an *aśrotriya*. Furthermore, the inclusion of the terms "lacking Vedic study" (*aśrotriyatva*) and so forth should be understood as intended to demonstrate general conduct; this is the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*).
This is unseemly for the virtuous, wherein these men offer oblations;
this is contrary to the will of the gods, therefore one should avoid it. (4.206)

The food of these [people] is unseemly and unworthy of praise. In what manner? According to the opinion of the virtuous and the refined (*śiṣṭa*). For it is in this regard that they offer the oblation (*havir juhvati*); those who act as village-priests are excluded from the mantra-recitation during that sacrifice. Here, for those who recite [the mantra] in an improper way, it is loathsome and indecorous (*aślīla*). And so it is said: "Indecorousness is harsh speech; this is contrary to the refined, opposed to them, and unrefined"—this is the meaning. Of whom? Of the gods. This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) concerning the preceding [rule]. Indeed, because of the introduction of the sentence and the context of its result, [the text] shows that it is indeed a matter of dharma in the section concerning forbidden food. That [forbidden nature] is fourfold: produced by possession (*parigraha*), inherent nature (*svabhāva*), association (*saṃsarga*), and time (*kāla*).
One should never eat the food of those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted; nor that which is infested with hair or insects, nor that which has been intentionally touched by the foot. (4.207)

The intended meaning is to be understood from the phrase "of those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted," or as far as "intoxicated" and so forth. Furthermore, the mention of "hair" here is for the purpose of illustrating body hair, nails, garlands, and the like. The mention of "insects," however, should be understood as including small creatures similar to them by common usage. And the term "intentionally" (*kāmataḥ*) is a qualifier for "touched by the foot," intended to permit eating when it is done unintentionally. "Food looked upon by a killer of an embryo, touched even by a woman in her courses, pecked at by a bird, and likewise touched by a dog [is unfit]. (4.208)

The mention of the "slayer of a Brahmin" (*brahmaghna*) is intended to indicate those who are equal to him; furthermore, since looking at such a person is forbidden, it is established by implication that touching them is even more defiling. The mention of the *udakyā* (a woman in her courses) includes all those who are perpetually impure, such as women recently delivered, because of the prohibition against contact with a menstruating woman, which implies a prohibition against looking at her as well. The mention of "falling birds" (*patatri*) should be understood from the context as referring to unclean birds such as crows and the like.
And food smelled by a cow, and especially food [announced] by public proclamation (*ghuṣṭānna*).
The food of a group and the food of a courtesan are both despised by the wise. (4.209)
And by one who is learned and knows the connection with the causes of defilement, or by another who is well-known [for his expertise].
[One should not eat the food] of a thief, a singer, a carpenter, a usurer, an initiated person, a miser, one who is bound, or one who wears fetters. (4.210)
[202] A thief is one who steals property other than gold. Those who commit mortal sins (pātakin) will be described later in the section on the assembly (pariṣad). A usurer is one bound in shackles.
[Of one accused, of a eunuch, of an unchaste woman, and of a hypocrite...]
[One should avoid] sour gruel, food that has stood overnight, and the leavings of a Śūdra. || 4.211 ||

A *puṃścalī* is an unchaste woman, not a slave; for a slave is separately prohibited by the rule, "and the food of a courtesan" (MDh 4.209).
