The mention of *śukta* (fermented) and *paryuṣita* (stale) food here again is either for the purpose of prescribing an expiation or for the sake of a specific qualification. Even though these two are already included in the section on forbidden foods, "the food left over after being eaten by a Śūdra" (*śūdrocchiṣṭa*) refers specifically to that which has been cooked as a remnant of what was consumed by a Śūdra. Others read: "and likewise the leavings of one who is not a Guru. The food of a physician, a hunter, a cruel person, and one who eats leavings;
the food of an *ugra*, the food of a woman who has recently given birth, and that from which water has been sipped but not the ritual rinsing (*anirdaśa*): (MDh 4.212)

The prohibition of physicians is connected to the rules on livelihood (*ājīva*). Regarding hunting, because it is mentioned separately later on for the king, it refers here to one who is cruel by nature, meaning like a *śūdra* who eats leavings. By the force of the scriptures, the king is called *ugra*; this is indicated by the mark [in the text]: "An *ugra*, a Madhyama-śarī, or... Furthermore, he will state: "He takes away the splendor of the king" (MDh 4.218), which is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). It is not possible to designate the king in this context, as he is distinct from those [others] and not [included] in that group. We shall speak of him simply as a "servant" (*bhṛtya*), as it is said: "In every city, he should thus carry out the consideration of all affairs" (MDh 7.121). Among the duties of kings, some call the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) an *ugra*; that is incorrect, because of the statement "of one who is consecrated" (*dīkṣita*). Food during impurity (*sūtaka*) refers to the food of parents; or it refers to the period of the fortnight. Or it is a prohibition against a woman eating her own wealth when she has given birth after her husband's death. "Paryācāntam" means occupied with sipping water (*ācamana*). "Anirdiṣṭam" refers to the milk of cows and other such animals.

Meat that has not been honored, meat obtained for no purpose, the food of a woman who has no hero (husband), the food of an enemy, the food of a city, the food of one who has fallen, and food upon which someone has sneezed—[these one should avoid]. 4.213.

Even food fit for the consumption of the learned, if not honored—that is, if it is not offered with due respect by the giver to those such as guests who are worthy of honor—is unfit to be eaten. Likewise, meat that is "vain" (*vṛthāmāṃsa*)—meaning meat consumed merely for one's own pleasure or for gratification—and that which is not honored even when intended for guests and the like, is forbidden. This is because this rule is taught in proximity to the prohibition against eating what is not honored by its preparer. As will be shown later in the verse: "Vain is *kṛsara* and *saṃyāva*" (MDh 5.7), the prohibition of vain meat is established by the term "unconsecrated meat" (*anupākṛtamāṃsa*); thus, its non-redundancy with regard to the later statement, "One may eat consecrated meat" (MDh 5.27), is proven. "A woman without a brother, without a son, or without a husband" refers to a widow. "The city" (*nagarī*) is as will be described. "A royal servant": for he will say, "In every city, one [should appoint a magistrate]," etc. (MDh 7.121). The rest is straightforward.
[203] The food of a slanderer and a liar, of one who sells the results of sacrifices, the food of an actor and a tailor, and likewise the food of an ungrateful person; 4.214.

Regarding the actor (*śailūṣa*), the *Bhārata* states that he is so called because of his performance of useless [roles]: "Like an actor, O King. This being the case, even Brāhmaṇas and others who perform such actions are likewise designated by that term on account of their qualities. Others, however, declare that an actor is one whose wife is a commodity for sale; as well as a blacksmith, a Niṣāda, a stage-manager, a goldsmith, a bamboo-worker, and a seller of weapons. (4.214)

All these—being performers of those respective acts—are thus prohibited by their specific designations, such as "Brāhmaṇas" and so forth, because of the force of the prohibition against those who have already entered upon such occupations. In the previous case, even one who was merely colored on the stage was referred to by that term [actor] because he performed the work of a *śauṇḍika* (liquor-seller). Here, however, even a man who performs the work of entering the stage is censured, as is the weaver (*yāyaka*). A dancer (*nartaka*) was mentioned previously; here, however, the dancer and others are included. [The verse continues:
"Of those who keep dogs, of liquor-sellers, and of the washerman of clothes; of the cruel dyer, and of him in whose house a paramour resides. (4.216)
This verse has already been explained:
"Those who tolerate a paramour, those who are entirely dominated by women, food from a deceased person within ten days of death, and that which is simply unpalatable. (4.217)

And those who tolerate a paramour—this is the distinction between him and the actor (*śailūṣa*). For the former sends away his wife out of greed for profit; the latter, however, will be described [later] as "an actor is called a *naṭa*. And in this alternative view, there is no fault of tautology.
The food of a king takes away one's splendor (*tejas*); the food of a Śūdra, one's Vedic luster (*brahmavarcasa*);
the food of a goldsmith, one's longevity; and the food of a leather-cutter, one's fame. (4.218)
The food of artisans destroys one's progeny, and that of a washerman destroys one's strength; the food of a guild and the food of a courtesan cut one off from the higher worlds. (4.219)
The food of a physician is pus; the food of an unchaste woman is semen;
the food of a usurer is excrement; and the food of a seller of weapons is filth. (4.220)
But those others who have been described in succession as persons whose food should not be eaten—the wise declare that their food consists of skin, bone, and hair. (4.221)

From the transgression of dharma, one becomes a beast; this statement regarding various fruits is for the purpose of desisting from such acts, as in the passage: "The food of a king takes away one's luster," and so forth. How indeed could it be that "one should not practice what is censured"? For even among those whose food is otherwise fit to be eaten, they are declared unfit to be eaten on these grounds; and likewise, while these causes—the sale of sacrifices and the like—are not inherently prohibited, their performance is declared improper through this censure. Now, one might object: since the sale of dharma is impossible, this transgression has been mentioned. Whether there actually be a sale of dharma or not, the meaning of the scripture is simply that because such a transgression is impossible—given that dharma is formless—it must never be performed under any circumstances. Furthermore, the general reference made in this section is to be explained according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (where the specific is included within the general).

Having unintentionally eaten the food of any one of these, one should fast for three days; this is the meaning of "kṣapaṇa. Kṣapaṇa means non-eating, because of the statement, "having eaten the food of any one of these. Although this instruction is stated with reference to those who have accepted [the food] or those who have not, nevertheless, it should be understood that it includes those who are impure due to contact and so forth, since this is intended as an illustration. This is known from the force of the instruction given in a single section and because these are designated as being distinct from that.
Having eaten intentionally, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance.
The *kṛcchra* penance performed is not the *prājāpatya*. To this effect, we shall cite from the Gautama-smṛti alone: "And [the consumption of] semen, feces, and urine... (4.222).

In this context, that [penance] is connected with drinking unintentionally (*amatipāna*), because of its proximity to the drinking intentionally (*matipāna*) and by virtue of the authority of another Smṛti. For Gautama, having stated: "For drinking *surā* unintentionally, one should consume milk, clarified butter, water, or air, heated daily, for one *sakṛcchra*; thereafter, his purification (*saṃskāra*) [is performed]" (GDh 23.2), says this: "And in the case of consuming urine, feces, a corpse, or semen, this same *taptakṛcchra* is the purification. Since this is the meaning of the scripture, Manu also will say: "Having drunk *vāruṇī* through ignorance, one becomes pure only through purification" (MDh 11.147). Because it is accompanied by the *taptakṛcchra*, it must be made explicit in this way by the authority of another Smṛti, and not according to the literal reading. Although this penance is taught here outside of its specific context in both these scriptures, it should be understood as being for the sake of an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) and not for its own sake as a primary injunction. Now, this is commenced for the purpose of providing a counter-exception regarding the eating of food for a virtuous *śūdra* householder, since there is a general prohibition against *śūdras*.
A learned twice-born man who does not perform śrāddha rites should not eat the cooked food of a Śūdra;
he may, however, take raw grain from him for a single night in case of distress.

The mention of *śrāddha* here is understood by implication to indicate all the duties of a Śūdra, such as truthful speech and so forth, which apply everywhere. For one who has not abandoned other [prescribed] duties, a Śūdra does not venture to perform a *śrāddha* or provide food for a single meal; therefore, this mention of *śrāddha* should be understood as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for a "good" (*sat*) Śūdra. From such a person—one who is not a "bad" (*asat*) Śūdra—one should receive only traditional knowledge (*āgama*), and not cooked food, nor even for a single night. Furthermore, regarding one who exists outside the [social] fold (*bāhyavṛtti*), there is no examination of strength and weakness; thus, he says the following for the purpose of praising faith (*śraddhā*).
[205] O gods, having deliberated upon both the miserly Vedic scholar and the liberal usurer, you have ordained that their food is equal. 4.224.
Prajāpati said to them: "Do not do this; make the unequal equal.
That which is purified by faith belongs to the generous man; that which is devoid of faith is destroyed. (4.225)

Since both [the eating of food from a non-Śrotriya and from one who has not performed the *avakīrṇin* penance] are prohibited, and since the former is for the purpose of praising faith (*śraddhā*), there is no counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) regarding the generosity [of the donor]. If, however, it were on account of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), that would apply only to that specific case; therefore, based on the explanatory passages, there is no counter-exception. And because food devoid of faith is impure even for a *śrotriya*, therefore:

"Let him always perform sacrifices and works of public utility with effort, provided they are done with faith; for when performed with faith and with well-acquired wealth, those two become inexhaustible. (4.226)

Since this is so, therefore one should constantly practice the duty of giving— both that pertaining to sacrifices and that pertaining to works— with a completely satisfied disposition, whenever a worthy recipient is found, according to one's ability. (4.227)
One should always give a gift for the sake of prosperity with faith; this may be for the purpose of initiating an undertaking or for the purpose of a funeral rite (*śrāddha*).
Whatever little may be given when asked, one should do so without malice;
for such a worthy recipient (*pātra*) will arise who delivers one from everything. (4.228)

When asked, one should give even a small amount without regard for the worthiness of the recipient; for there will arise a worthy recipient—this is indicated by the scriptural mark that giving even to an unworthy person exists. Now, [the author] shows the nature of the substance to be given along with the means, together with an explanatory passage (arthavāda): "The giver of water attains satisfaction; the giver of food, inexhaustible happiness;
the giver of sesame seeds, desired offspring; the giver of a lamp, supreme vision. (4.229)
The giver of land obtains land; the giver of gold, long life; the giver of a large house, excellent dwellings; and the giver of beauty, supreme beauty. (4.230)
The giver of lodging attains the same world as the Moon; the giver of horses, the same world as the Aśvins;
the giver of a bull, abundant prosperity; and the giver of a cow, the realm of the Sun.

The giver of vehicles and beds obtains a wife; the giver of fearlessness obtains sovereignty; the giver of grain obtains eternal happiness; and the giver of the Veda attains equality with Brahmā. [206] 4.232
Of all gifts whatsoever—water, food, cattle, land, clothing, sesame seeds, gold, and clarified butter—the gift of the Veda is preeminent. (4.233)

These five verses are all *arthavādas* concerning the results [of giving]. Alternatively, they are instructions regarding the results; however, since heaven (*svarga*) is to be inferred and because this contradicts the treatises on logic (*nyāyaśāstra*), it should be understood that their purpose is not perceived (i.e., they are not directly perceptible). Furthermore, water and the other items are intended to demonstrate the modes of faith and the honoring with which all things to be given should be donated. Thus, by stating these, those not mentioned are not excluded. And so it is said:
"With whatever disposition one bestows whatever gift, one receives that very thing, honored by that same disposition. (4.234)

Indeed, this is also seen in the section on the praise of faith (*śraddhā-stuti-prakaraṇa*): "One should constantly practice the duty of giving (*dāna-dharma*), both that pertaining to the *iṣṭi* sacrifices and that pertaining to the *pūrta* works, with a state of complete satisfaction" (MDh 4.227). This is formulated for the purpose of praising this [state]—which is the effect of faith, whether it be called *prabhāva-prasāda* or *śrāddha*. Having performed that [act], at the time of giving, the state of mind described by the words "with whatever state of being" and so forth is a clarity of mind (*citta-prasāda*) preceded by faith for the sake of honoring the recipient; it is not faith itself, nor is there an absence of honoring the recipient. Because this [clarity of mind] is inferior, middling, or superior, this praise is made in connection with its corresponding results. Others, however, reconcile this with the connection to *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. This being the case, it is stated that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the instrument, while the action is primary and external things like substances are secondary. And such being the case, the meaning of the sentence is: "The mind should be given with supreme faith."
He who accepts what has been honored and he who gives what has been honored—both of them go to heaven; but in the opposite case, they go to hell. (4.235)

It is appropriate that heaven awaits one who accepts what has been honored [with due respect], because of the statement: "Of his six duties, three are his means of livelihood" (MDh 10.76), which shows that acceptance has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*). And thus, the passage "But hell in the opposite case" is not meant for anyone else; this is an *arthavāda* intended to praise giving with honor. How indeed could such a thing be said—namely, that this gift given with honor, accepted merely through the grace of faith, is so distinguished that one can say, "Heaven belongs even to the acceptor of what is honored, how much more so to the giver"—if it were intended to prohibit such taking? It is possible to understand it thus: "But hell in the opposite case" refers to when acceptance is performed at the request of a recipient who is indifferent to his own interest, solely for the sake of favoring the giver. This ascetic, however, having obtained a specific recipient for this [gift] other than one eating at a *śrāddha*, it is thus appropriate, like Agastya and others, because no other motive for the acceptance is perceived. Alternatively, this is a statement of praise referring to the duty of restraint (*niyamadharma*) resulting from a particularly distinguished acceptance; and by the context, it indicates that another thing is also to be prohibited, in connection with the prohibition of praising gifts.
One should not take pride in one's asceticism, nor should one speak untruth after performing a sacrifice;
even when distressed, one should not revile Brahmins, nor should one boast after giving a gift. (4.236)

The phrase "having sacrificed with the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices, one does not speak falsely" is stated again for the sake of a specific qualification; thus, it should be understood that this establishes a distinct expiation (*prāyaścitta*). There is no established expiation for the omission of the *snātaka* vows. Regarding the transgression of this [present rule], there is a deprecatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*): "Sacrifice perishes through falsehood; austerity perishes through pride; longevity through reviling Brahmins; and a gift through boasting. (4.237)

Since this is so, one should not practice what has been forbidden. Furthermore, from the section concerning the praise of giving and so forth, it follows that a *snātaka*, out of devotion and faith, should daily give even a very small amount of whatever he possesses to those who ask—gradually accumulating merit like termites building an anthill—without causing distress to anyone, for the sake of having companions in the next world. (4.238)
The reason for this is stated here as a formal argument:
"For neither father nor mother stands there in the next world to provide assistance;
neither son, nor wife, nor kinsman remains—only Dharma alone abides. (4.239)
Therefore, with that in view, one should certainly not accumulate wealth. What then? One should indeed give away whatever little one has every day, gradually. For it is said:
"Having cast off the dead body upon the earth like a piece of wood or a clod of earth..."
Relatives depart with averted faces; only Dharma follows him.
Therefore, one should always gradually accumulate Dharma for the sake of a companion;
for with Dharma as a companion, one crosses over the darkness that is difficult to traverse. 4.241
And because of this: "Therefore, it is not for the sake of one's mother and others—beings are born alone, and alone they die;
alone one experiences the fruit of good deeds, and alone one undergoes the result of evil deeds. (4.242)
Therefore, one should not set aside wealth for the sake of one's mother and others, since they will be without assistance in the next world.
[Here the text repeats verses 240 and 241] And because:
The radiant one, whose body is ethereal, swiftly leads that man who is devoted to dharma and whose sins have been destroyed by austerity to the other world.

What is that? It is *dharma*. And for this reason—since it is said that one should gradually accumulate *dharma* by giving to those who ask, even making that [virtue] a companion in all calamities—it is now stated, for the purpose of specifying a particular relationship with *dharma*, while remaining on this very point:
One desiring to lead one's family to excellence should always form connections with the most excellent; one should abandon the base and avoid those who are base. (4.244)

It is not only with distinguished recipients that a *snātaka* should seek connection; rather, all forms of relationship—matrimonial and otherwise—are to be sought by all of these [classes], because they are the cause of excellence. This applies without distinction to those mentioned here, and it should be understood that for a person of a single caste (*ekajātīya*), this refers to the highest goal achieved through the perfection of qualities such as noble lineage (*abhijana*) and so forth. In the absence of such [superior qualities], however, one may associate even with equals, but never with inferiors, even in times of distress. Thus, the following statement of praise is appropriate: "One should approach the most excellent and indeed the excellent, and avoid the inferior."
A Brāhmaṇa attains excellence, but through transgression, he falls to the state of a Śūdra. (4.245)

And thus, by relying on such association— a twice-born man who acts with firm resolve, who is gentle and self-controlled, who does not dwell with those of cruel conduct, and who is non-violent— shall conquer heaven through self-restraint and charity. (4.246)
It is stated that for a *snātaka*, through association and practice, there arises firmness of character and a connection with distinguished results. And so Vyāsa says:
"Whatever one habitually pursues by deed, mind, or speech—that very thing carries him away; therefore, one should perform what is auspicious."

Alternatively, the reading "diṣṭakārī" is explained as one whose nature is to perform what is prescribed. Now, since all forms of association with the virtuous have been taught, the acceptance of gifts from the wicked is not permitted except in times of distress; this is the beginning of the discussion regarding who might be such a person.
[209] Wood, roots, fruits, food, and whatever is offered to one;
One may accept honey from anyone, as well as the gift of safety.

The acceptance of gifts from those who do not honor [the recipient] and who are Śūdras is prohibited for one who does not live by such means; however, for those very same persons, fuel, water, and so forth are permitted even outside of times of distress (*anāpadi*). By the force of the instruction regarding the section on non-distress, it follows by implication that one should accept these after having requested them—specifically fuel and water—due to the restriction concerning prepared food (*kṛtānna*) and that which is "held out" (*abhyudyata*). Otherwise, the term *abhyudita* (or *abhyudyata*), being connected with food, would be unnecessary because it would serve no purpose. Furthermore, by the rule of the "staff and water-jar" (*daṇḍopānahikā*), the non-rejection of fuel, water, and so forth when they arrive unasked is established, since the acquisition of what is obtained without asking possesses a lighter force. Alternatively, this word *abhyudyata* may be merely an adjective qualifying all things, including fuel, water, and so forth. Consequently, this acquisition without asking applies to all types of objects, not to food alone. Thus Gautama, having stated that accepting gifts from the twice-born is commendable, says: "Fuel, water, and so forth, which cannot be refused, may be accepted from everyone" (GDh 17.2–3). This is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) to the present rule.
Prajāpati considered that alms brought forward and offered spontaneously, even by one who has performed evil deeds, are to be accepted. 4.248.

And this [alms] has been brought—that is, it has been carried to that place where the recipient is present and where it is intended to be given as a gift. Or, "brought and offered" (*āhṛtābhyuditā*) means that living beings such as cows have been brought, or that highly valuable non-living things such as gold have been offered. Furthermore, one should know that for a person with a body, this alms—previously unasked for—may be accepted by oneself, by one commissioned by him, or by another through some sign of knowledge. Prajāpati considered this very specific kind of alms. The mention of Prajāpati is for the purpose of praising the gain obtained without being asked. "Even from one of evil deeds" refers to one who is outside the caste system (*varṇāpaśada*). How much more so, then, from those of the twice-born or even from Śūdras? Here, *api* (even) expresses possibility rather than conjunction, because such people do not exist [in the context of being sources of blame]. This praise of obtaining what is unasked—which might otherwise be suspected of being unacceptable like wood—is intended to encourage [the practice]. One should understand this point through the praise: since the gain obtained without asking is faultless, or at least involves little fault, praise does not proceed from anything else. Regarding the purpose for oneself, what is unasked is not necessarily to be accepted; however, when it serves a purpose for a teacher or others, its acceptance will be restricted. For this reason, he speaks of its rejection: [The verse continues: "One should not reject it, thinking, 'This is an evil deed,' nor, 'He is a man of evil deeds. Even from a low-caste person, one should accept it, provided it is not impure. One should not reject it on the grounds that "this is an evil deed," nor that "he is a man of evil deeds. Even from a person of low caste, one should accept it, provided it is not impure. If it is impure, it must be rejected. But if it is pure, it should be accepted even from a low-caste person. The ancestors do not eat for fifteen years, nor does the fire carry his oblations, for him who treats her with contempt. (4.249)

In this case as well, it is not logical that there should be a censure of non-acceptance without cause; therefore, a rule of non-acceptance for him is understood. And the rule mentioned here concerns the acceptance of what is unasked for the sake of one's teacher, dependents, guests, and the gods, because such use serves a great purpose, whereas for one who lacks the means [to provide], otherwise, by not accepting it, his *dharma* would lead to the sin of failing to support them. This being so, this statement censuring the acceptance of wealth for its own sake becomes meaningful, and self-restraint is heard of here. When it is said "this [is] therein," this refers to the Self which is elevated above the enjoyment of nearby material objects. Therefore, the meaning exactly as stated is appropriate. And since this is so, therefore—
One should not refuse a bed, a house, kusha grass, perfumes, water, flowers, jewels, curd, parched grain, fish, milk, meat, or even vegetables. (4.250)

Because of the mention of water (*udaka*), this is simply a collective inclusion of all substances; it is not a different category. Otherwise, the repeated mention of water—already listed in the verse concerning firewood and water (*edhodaka*)—within the context of beds and other items would be redundant. Thus, Gautama lists firewood, water, and so forth together with beds and other items in a single sūtra: "Firewood, water, fodder, roots, fruits," and so on (GDh 17.3). Furthermore, by the mention of milk (*payas*), clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and the like are excluded. By the mention of parched grain (*dhānā*), other prepared foods (*kṛtānna*) are excluded. However, fish and meat are mentioned separately because they have different sources: meat from fowlers and the like, and fish from fishermen. Alternatively, just as in the case of the word *śloka*, in common usage one might ask, "Is this meat (*māṃsa*) or fish (*matsya*)?"—thus the separate mention of fish is made, much like the expression "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvarda*). But here, the author speaks by resorting to a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Indeed, there is acceptance (*pratigraha*) of both categories—firewood, water, etc., and beds, etc.—provided there is a need for them. Therefore, this non-exclusion of beds and other items refers specifically to acceptance when they are unasked for; the term "exclusion" (*praṇoda*) does not imply that their acceptance is forbidden by rule. If it were so, one would incur sin by not accepting them; and since this [acceptance] serves a visible purpose, its permissibility or impermissibility must be deliberated upon. Since this is the case, therefore—
Desiring to support his teachers and dependents, and wishing to honor the deities and guests, he may accept gifts from all sources, but he himself must not be satisfied by them alone. (4.251)

The "elders" are the father and others; the "dependents" are the wife, children, and so forth. Desiring to uplift them when they are stuck in the mire of hunger, and wishing to honor the deities, he should accept [gifts] from them. However, because the deities lack the capacity for hunger and because the word *atra* (here) is used [to exclude them], this term does not apply to them. Just as there is no such thing as "provisioning" (*saṃbharaṇa*) for the elders in the same way as for the teacher, the same should be said regarding guests. For it has been stated: "He may accept from all quarters for the sake of honoring them, even from low-caste twice-born men and Śūdras. But this does not refer to those prescribed in the rules for times of distress (*āpadkalpa*), nor to those who are utterly unworthy, because of the difference in context and because this [acceptance] is for the purpose of supporting the elders and others. Furthermore, for one who is emaciated by lack of livelihood, the instruction on the rules for times of distress is given: "One who is emaciated by lack of livelihood and suffering should practice this dharma" (MDh 10.101). The purpose of accepting gifts for the sake of the elders and others is through the livelihood of clothing and food for one emaciated by lack of means. As for the statement, "But he should not satisfy himself with that," its explanation has already been provided.
But when the teachers have passed away, or when living at home without them, seeking his own livelihood, he should always accept [gifts] from a virtuous person. (4.252)

[211] And from this it is understood that this acceptance during times of distress for the purpose of honoring one's teacher and others is not [permitted] even from those who are absolutely unworthy. It has been stated that a Śūdra’s food is unfit to be eaten because of his occupation, but not that of another; as in the verse: "One should not eat the cooked food of a Śūdra" (MDh 4.223). Furthermore, the fitness of the food of others to be eaten is intended, since the following is commenced for the purpose of establishing what was previously unestablished: "A ploughman, a family friend, a cowherd, a slave, and a barber..."
These are the Śūdras whose food may be eaten, as well as those who offer themselves [to the Brāhmaṇa]. (4.253)

The half-share is the one who takes a portion. Who is he? The *pāraśava*; he is one whose food may be eaten by those of that lineage who are *snātakas*. Others, however, say he is one who acts in concert with others in activities such as agriculture; he is a family friend whose connection has continued through his father and grandfather. Cowherds, slaves, and barbers are indeed one's own people. As for gardeners (*śāka*), even if they are not entitled to invitations to ancestral rites (*aśrāddhin*), Śūdras are ones whose food may be eaten, because they offer themselves [to their masters]. He shows that others besides these also demonstrate this offering of oneself: "Whatever his nature may be, and whatever he intends to do..."
And just as one should serve him, so should one offer oneself. || 4.254 ||

In whatever manner his character may be—whether by means of new occupations and the like—and whatever he intends to do for himself, whether for the purpose of protection or for some visible or invisible goal, or with the desire to please a Brāhmaṇa, he should serve him according to the relative importance of both [the master’s and his own interests] through crafts, agriculture, trade, and so forth; but not as a slave, because that would entail the faults already mentioned. For it is said: "The cowherd, the slave, and the barber... (MDh 4.253). Likewise, having restrained himself, he should report everything truthfully and not otherwise:
"He who represents himself to virtuous men as one thing when he is another... (MDh 4.256).
He is the greatest evildoer in the world, a thief who steals his own self. || 4.255 ||
This is an explanatory statement (arthavāda). For it is said:
"All objects of speech are fixed; they have their root in speech and have issued forth from speech.
That man who steals that speech is a thief of everything. (4.256)

The organ of speech has been mentioned. The word *artha* (object/meaning) refers to speech. By virtue of its quality (*guṇataḥ*), all objects denoted by it are dependent upon that speech, because words—the means of perceiving those objects—have their root in speech; they do not become perceived otherwise. And since the practical engagement with objects proceeds through the perception of those [words], they are said to have "issued forth from speech. For this reason, it is said by way of its quality to be like the rain and the harvest. This being the case, when it says, "But he who would steal that speech," a person is called a thief of everything because he speaks untruth for the purpose of concealing his own self. This is a declamatory statement (*arthavāda*) intended to censure such untruth regarding speech, for the sake of preventing falsehood in the disclosure of one's self. And thus, the passage beginning with "Of whatever sort his self may be" (MDh 4.254) is established. Furthermore, this which is stated for the Shudra to disclose his self should be understood as applying to the student (*brahmacārin*) and others as well, due to the commonality of the task. Thus, the householder is properly instructed.

Having discharged his debts to the great seers, the ancestors, and the gods according to the prescribed rule, and having entrusted everything to his son, he should live adopting an attitude of neutrality. [4.257]

Having attained freedom from debt toward the sages and others through Vedic study, and having discharged his obligations toward the ancestors through the performance of ancestral rites and sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, that householder—having completed what was to be done and possessing matured wisdom—should spend a portion of his second life in the village itself, maintaining neutrality for a time while occupied with duties pertaining to his sons. This should be understood as applying to the view that does not advocate the combination [of all stages], and not to the other two views. And thus, having reached the highest stage of division, he should always reflect alone in solitude upon what is beneficial for himself.
Reflecting alone and constantly, one attains the supreme good. (4.258)

In that case, the performance of the rules taught by the Brāhmaṇa is the means for attaining the highest good; regarding this, he says: "This eternal mode of life for the Brāhmaṇa householder has been declared, as well as the ritual of the Snātaka vows, which is supreme for purifying the inner being. (4.259)

And because of the mention of the "Brahmin," the duties of the *snātaka*—like those of his mode of conduct (*vṛtti*)—should belong specifically to him alone, and not so for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya. By this very mode of conduct, one who knows the Vedic scriptures, living constantly free from impurity, is glorified in the world of Brahmā. (4.260)

By this conduct, the Brahmin undertakes the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) taught in the section on the *snātaka*. By the mention of one who "knows the Veda and the scriptures," both knowledge and action are intended. And this implies the following meaning: these two—knowledge and action—alone are capable of accomplishing the goal. This is a statement of praise for the performance of the *snātaka* duties, meaning that if the duties of the *snātaka* are connected with these [qualities], they are effective, and not otherwise; or rather, it means that the realization of the Supreme Self does not depend [exclusively] upon those duties. How so? Because even without ritual actions, the knowledge of the Supreme Self, when accompanied by the duties of a *snātaka*, is capable of leading to the attainment of Brahman, as such is heard in the scriptures. Thus, even in this way, these [duties] have the nature of being for the purpose of praise.
Thus ends the fourth chapter.
The fifth chapter is the commentary on the Institutes of Manu.

Having heard these duties of the *snātaka* as they have been declared, the sages spoke thus to the high-souled Bhṛgu, who was born from fire: 5.1. Having heard these duties of the *snātaka* as they have been declared, the sages spoke thus to the high-souled Bhṛgu, who was born from fire.

In the first chapter, Bhṛgu was declared to be descended from Manu, as in [Manu Smṛti] 1.34: "I, desiring to create offspring... In this verse, however, he is called "born of fire" (*analaprabhava*). Here is the resolution: because he dispels the darkness of ignorance by illuminating the true nature of all dharmas, he is metaphorically described as being born of fire. Alternatively, due to his abundance of the quality of *sattva*, or according to the perspective of the Purāṇas regarding the cause and effect of that [birth], it is heard that Bhṛgu’s descent from fire occurred at the sacrifice of Varuṇa. Now, he demonstrates what was stated previously—that the great sages possess knowledge—by saying:
O Lord, how does death prevail over those brahmins who, as previously described, perform their own duty and are learned in the Vedas and the scriptures? (5.2)

The word *katham* is used here in the sense of censure: "How can there be death [for them]? This is because their conduct is such that it has been stated here: "For through right conduct one obtains long life," and so forth. But how is it that those who know the Vedas and the Śāstras are not subject to old age and death, since he speaks thus? It is said in reply: no, because this contradicts what is perceived and because it would contradict the Śāstra by teaching the performance of rituals for them. What then? Death at an improper time—known as *akālamṛtyu*—is improper even before the lifespan ordained by the Vedas and Śāstras has expired. Likewise, the statement "there are one hundred and one deaths" is a mark (*liṅga*) from the Atharvaveda concerning untimely deaths. And thus, how could death prevail over one whose full lifespan has been reached? In this way, [death prevails] when the collection of causes for [the end of] life is present.
That righteous-souled Bhṛgu, the son of Manu, said to those great seers:
"Listen, by what fault Death seeks to slay the Brahmins. (5.3)
Considering their reply to deserve respectful instruction, he addressed those sages directly and spoke these words of solemn promise with great reverence:
"Through the lack of study of the Vedas, through the abandonment of right conduct, through laziness, and through the defects of food, Death seeks to slay the Brahmins. (5.4)

The question—"Thus, for those Brahmins who perform their own duty (*svadharma*) as previously described" (MDh 5.2)—is followed by the reply beginning with "by not neglecting the Vedas," and so forth. However, that reply is not logically consistent, because the question specifically asked about those "performing their own duty. This is the resolution: the matters previously mentioned, such as the study of the Vedas and so on, do not constitute *svadharma* exclusively. What then? This is another aspect of that duty, known as the avoidance of its faults, which will be explained hereafter. This dialogue consisting of questions and answers is intended primarily to instruct on the gravity of that matter. And having established this, there is a separate treatment of this [topic], because even for consuming garlic and other forbidden substances—which are more serious than the previously mentioned substances like clarified butter—one hears of specific expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) merely from the hearing [of the rule].
Having intentionally eaten mushrooms, a boar, garlic, a village cock,
onion, or leek, a twice-born man shall fall [from his caste].

"Having unknowingly eaten these six, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra or the Yati-Cāndrāyaṇa; regarding the remaining [forbidden foods], one should fast for a day. (MDh 5.19–20). This being the case, just as the non-study of the Vedas, the abandonment of proper conduct, and laziness are causes of death even for one who has reached a full lifespan, so too is this specific fault [of eating garlic and the like]. Furthermore, the demonstration of the gravity of garlic and other such items should be understood as intended to inspire respect for their avoidance. Now, this defect of food is being discussed.
Garlic, leeks, onions, and mushrooms, as well as anything originating from impure substances, are not to be eaten by the twice-born. (5.5)

"Mushrooms and *katyuḍuka* (? are not to be eaten by the twice-born (*dvijāti*). The mention of "twice-born" is for the purpose of excluding the *śūdra*. And it was stated that the conclusion of this very section will be made in this very manner. Regarding the phrase "the edible and non-edible for the twice-born without exception," the mention of "Brāhmaṇa" occurs in the context of the previous prohibition on food, as taught in the fourth chapter:

"A Brāhmaṇa should never eat at a sacrifice offered by one who is not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*), nor at one offered by a village-priest (*grāmayājī*); likewise, he should not eat at a sacrifice offered by a woman or a eunuch. (MDh 4.205)

Because of the statement, "of those whose livelihood is the foremost of the twice-born" (MDh 3.286), this pertains specifically to Brāhmaṇas. In the preceding section on food that should not be eaten, it was specifically for Brāhmaṇas; however, here, because of the statement "of the twice-born," it pertains to all three castes. Thus, a distinction between the two sections is appropriate. And [he should avoid] beans and other such things produced from impure substances.
He should carefully avoid red exudations from trees, as well as those produced by felling them, and *selu*, cow's milk during the first few days after calving (*pīyūṣa*). (5.6)

[The term] *selu* refers to red resinous exudations from trees such as the *sallakī*, and also non-red ones produced by felling [trees] such as the *kapittha*. It is understood to refer to the cream (*pīyūṣa*) of boiled milk because of its association with that term. Furthermore, he will state that cow's cream is the milk of a cow within ten days [of calving]. This present undertaking is for the purpose of prohibiting the cream even of a cow whose ten days have passed. If, by some chance, this [cream] occurs for anyone—even for one whose ten days have passed—the prohibition therein is to be understood. Others, however, say that *selu* is the *śleṣmāntaka* tree.
In vain are *kṛsara*, *saṃyāva*, milk-rice, and cakes; likewise, meat that has not been consecrated, food intended for the gods, and sacrificial oblations. (5.7)

That which is prepared for one's own sake, such as *kṛsarā* and the like, without dedicating it to the gods and other [deities], is in vain. And because of established usage (*samācāra*), the mention of *kṛsarā* and so forth is intended to illustrate *modaka* and similar items; furthermore, since all food intended for the gods and others is unfit to be eaten, this serves to specify the particular expiation (*prāyaścitta*) required for such a sin. That *kṛsarā* and the rest are taught here is understood from the force of the context. Now, one might object: "Unconsecrated meat (*anupākṛtamāṃsa*) should be understood as meat that has not been offered, just like *kṛsarā* and the like. Thus, because of their similarity, its inclusion here together with *kṛsarā* and the others is appropriate. If that is so, then since the word "in vain" (*vṛthā*) is already the governing term, the word "unconsecrated" (*anupākṛta*) need not be mentioned here as a qualifier of meat; rather, its mention in this metrical work is appropriate only for the purpose of completing the verse. This being the case, the consumption of unconsecrated beef is not what is being addressed by this [rule]. In this way, the redundancy with what will be said later—"One may eat meat that has been consecrated" (MDh 5.27)—is avoided. But surely there is no duplication, since "meat in vain" (*vṛthāmāṃsa*) was already mentioned in the section on forbidden foods in the fourth chapter? It is replied: it was stated that in that instance the teaching was directed at the eater due to the force of the context, not at the preparer. Therefore, for this reason, its double teaching is established. The "foods of the gods" (*devānnāni*) are those dedicated [to them]. Others, however, say: that which is prepared with faith, even if it is naturally substantial like a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), is unfit to be eaten. For he will state later that the remainder of the oblation (*haviḥśeṣa*), even if stale, is fit to be consumed provided it is properly enclosed. Therefore, the oblations (*havīṃṣi*) are taken outside by the vigilant deities; or rather, this prohibition applies to things that have been set aside for the status of an oblation (*haviṣṭva*).

The milk of a cow within ten days of calving, that of a camel, that of one-hoofed animals, that of a sheep, the milk of a *saṃdhinī* cow, and the milk of a cow whose calf has been taken away—[these are forbidden]. (5.8)

The perpetual prohibition of speaking the single word "camel" (*uṣṭra*), as well as [the milk] of sheep and ewes, should be understood from other Smṛti texts on penance and from established custom. Regarding *saṃdhinī* milk: that cow which was not milked in the evening but is milked in the morning is called *saṃdhinī*. A pregnant cow is also *saṃdhinī*. For those who recite *saṃdhinī* milk because of its connection with pregnancy, an intensification of the fault is intended. This reading applies even to one whose calf has been taken away (*vivatsā*)—meaning one deprived of her calf—or one whose calf is dead (*mṛtavatsā*). Because of the mention of the "cow," there is no prohibition regarding the goat or the buffalo.
And among all wild animals, with the exception of the buffalo, as well as the milk of females and all fermented acids, these indeed must be avoided. (5.9)

[Editor's Note: In the first half of this verse, regarding the reading "mahiṣam" (the male buffalo) in the phrase "sarveṣāṃ mṛgāṇāṃ mahiṣam," a variant reading "mahiṣīm" (the female buffalo) has been extracted as an alternative interpretation.]

Even though the masculine gender is indicated [in the compound], in the prohibition against drinking the milk of the *mṛga* and *mahiṣa*, their reference to females must be understood from the context. Alternatively, the mention of the [masculine] kinship term implies that gender and number are not intended to be significant (*avivakṣā*). Furthermore, in this alternative reading—“and of all wild female deer except for the *mahiṣī*”—there is no room for such an objection. In the rule “the milk of females is also to be avoided,” the word *eva* (also) indicates that this prohibition is universal. The phrase “even in cases of ignorance, etc. serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to the statement “all fermented acids” (*sarva-śuktāni*).
Curd is fit for consumption among sour substances, as is everything produced from curd,
and those [liquors] which are distilled from pure flowers, roots, and fruits.

[216] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Great Exposition. Thus should you remember it. This is what the Blessed One said. With their minds uplifted, the monks rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One. 216. The Discourse on the Great Exposition is concluded. 217. The Discourse on the Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “It would be good, Bhante, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dharma in brief, so that, having heard the Dharma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Ānanda, whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past have been Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, all those Blessed Ones taught the Dharma to their disciples in brief thus: ‘All phenomena are impermanent; all phenomena are suffering; all phenomena are non-self. Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will be Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, all those Blessed Ones will teach the Dharma to their disciples in brief thus: ‘All phenomena are impermanent; all phenomena are suffering; all phenomena are non-self. Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the present are Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, all those Blessed Ones teach the Dharma to their disciples in brief thus: ‘All phenomena are impermanent; all phenomena are suffering; all phenomena are non-self. Now, Ānanda, when you have heard this teaching in brief, what practice do you intend to undertake? “Bhante, when I have heard this teaching in brief from the Blessed One, I intend to undertake the practice of mindfulness of the body. “Good, good, Ānanda! It is well that you, having heard this teaching in brief from me, intend to undertake the practice of mindfulness of the body. For, Ānanda, when mindfulness of the body is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness; when the four foundations of mindfulness are developed and cultivated, they fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment; when the seven factors of enlightenment are developed and cultivated, they fulfill true knowledge and liberation. And how, Ānanda, is mindfulness of the body developed and cultivated so that it fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him, ever mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out. Breathing in long, he knows: ‘I breathe in long’; or breathing out long, he knows: ‘I breathe out long. Breathing in short, he knows: ‘I breathe in short’; or breathing out short, he knows: ‘I breathe out short. He trains thus: ‘Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe out. He trains thus: ‘Tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe out. Just as a skilled turner or his apprentice, when making a long turn, knows: ‘I make a long turn,’ or when making a short turn, knows: ‘I make a short turn’—so too, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, when breathing in long, knows: ‘I breathe in long’... he trains thus: ‘Tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe out. This, Ānanda, is called the development of mindfulness of breathing in brief. Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu contemplates the body in the body internally, contemplates the body in the body externally, contemplates the body in the body both internally and externally. He contemplates the nature of arising in the body, he contemplates the nature of passing away in the body, he contemplates the nature of arising and passing away in the body. Or else, mindfulness that ‘there is a body’ is simply established in him to the extent necessary for bare knowledge and mindfulness. And he abides independent, not clinging to anything in the world. This, Ānanda, is called the development of mindfulness of the body in detail. Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu reviews this very body, however it is placed, however disposed, as consisting of elements: ‘In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element. Just as a skilled butcher or his apprentice, having killed a cow, would sit at a crossroads with the carcass divided into portions, so too, Ānanda, a bhikkhu reviews this very body... as consisting of elements. This, ĵĀnanda, is called the development of mindfulness of the body in detail. Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu reviews this very body, upwards from the soles of the feet, downwards from the hair of the head, enclosed in skin, as full of many kinds of impurities: ‘In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin; flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys; heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs; bowels, entrails, gorge, dung; bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat; tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil-of-the-joints, urine. Just as if there were a bag with an opening at both ends full of various kinds of grain, such as hill rice, red rice, beans, peas, millet, and white rice, and a man with good eyesight, having opened it, were to review it: ‘This is hill rice, this is red rice, these are beans, these are peas, this is millet, this is white rice’—so too, Ānanda, a bhikkhu reviews this very body... as full of many kinds of impurities. This, Ānanda, is called the development of mindfulness of the body in detail. Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu reviews this very body, however it is placed, however disposed, as being composed of the elements, by way of its open and closed apertures: ‘In this body there are openings of the eyes, ears, nostrils, mouth, and below the navel the opening for excrement and urine. Just as if there were a tree trunk, hollow and empty, with openings at top and bottom, and a man with good eyesight, looking in, were to review it: ‘This tree trunk is hollow and empty, with openings at top and bottom’—so too, Ānanda, a bhikkhu reviews this very body... as composed of the elements, by way of its open and closed apertures. This, Ānanda, is called the development of mindfulness of the body in detail. Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu reviews this very body, however it is placed, however disposed, as being subject to impermanence, as being subject to suffering, as being subject to change. Just as if there were a bowl of water left in the heat in the sun, with bubbles and froth rising to the surface, so too, Ānanda, a bhikkhu reviews this very body... as subject to impermanence, as subject to suffering, as subject to change. This, Ānanda, is called the development of mindfulness of the body in detail. Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu reviews this very body, however it is placed, however disposed, as being subject to death. Just as if a bhikkhu were to see a corpse thrown aside in a charnel ground—one day dead, two days dead, three days dead—swollen, discolored, and festering, he compares this very body with it: ‘This body, too, is of the same nature, it will be like that, it is not exempt from that fate. This, Ānanda, is called the development of mindfulness of the body in detail. Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu reviews this very body, however it is placed, however disposed, as being subject to disintegration, as being subject to dispersion. Just as if a bhikkhu were to see a corpse thrown aside in a charnel ground, bleached to the color of a shell, reduced to a pile of bones, or reduced to a scattered collection of bones, he compares this very body with it: ‘This body, too, is of the same nature, it will be like that, it is not exempt from that fate. This, Ānanda, is called the development of mindfulness of the body in detail. Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu reviews this very body, however it is placed, however disposed, as being devoid of self, as being soulless. Just as if a bhikkhu were to see a corpse thrown aside in a charnel ground, a skeleton with flesh and blood, held together by sinews, or a fleshless skeleton smeared with blood, held together by sinews, or a skeleton without flesh and blood, held

In this context, although there is a prohibition against *śukta* (fermented liquids), it specifically prohibits *śukta* made from flour. Regarding the phrase "with auspicious flowers, roots, and fruits," because there is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) for items of that same category, those flowers, roots, and fruits which are naturally sour (*śukta*) by their very nature are not prohibited. Furthermore, since bathing and other rites are generally performed with flowers and fruits, the mention of "flowers and so forth" should be understood as referring to those; it is not a prohibition of sugarcane juice, molasses, and the like. This being the case, one must interpret the meaning of the *Smṛti* in a way that does not contradict established custom. Moreover, since auspicious substances are permitted, the prohibition applies to non-auspicious substances such as *śīdhu* (a type of spirituous liquor) and similar drinks.
One should avoid all carnivorous birds, as well as those dwelling in villages, single-hoofed animals that are not specifically permitted, and the ṭiṭṭibha bird. (5.11)

The term *kravyāda* refers specifically to meat-eaters; thus, there is no prohibition against others such as peacocks and the like, who eat both [meat and non-meat]. Similarly, regarding village-dwellers, although they are not meat-eaters, the *pārāvata* (dove) and others are mentioned, while in another scripture (*śāstrāntara*), only the single-hoofed animals (*ekaśapha*) are prohibited. Furthermore, horses and the like are specifically pointed out. If it is argued that since the eating of single-hoofed animals is established by the *Ādhvaryava-śruti*—which states, "One should quickly sacrifice a mare," and "One desiring offspring should eat the flesh of a large donkey"—this present text need not be commenced, we say no. Because one might otherwise proceed to eat them based on that [other] observation, this prohibition is necessary. Just as in the case of the Vedic injunction, "Those which have membranes [are to be eaten]," even though the *ṭiṭṭibha* bird is pure and edible, one should avoid it.
The kalaviṅka, the plava, the haṃsa, the cakrāhva, the domestic cock, the sārasa, the rajjudāla, the dātyūha, the parrot, and the maina. 5.12

The *kalaviṅka* is said to be the village sparrow (*grāmacaṭaka*) in the treatises on towns. When there is a prohibition against those that dwell exclusively in villages, the *kalaviṅka*—which dwells in both—is also prohibited; for they become forest-dwellers during the rainy season. The prohibition regarding the village cock is for the purpose of permitting the wild variety. Even though the dwelling of these two is distinct, they are nevertheless confused because they belong to the same species. If it is argued that in the list of edible birds the letter *e* is used [to denote them], then even for peacocks (*mayūra*) and others, the vowel *ā* changes in different regions and so forth. Therefore, since this species dwells in both places, it is logical to treat it exactly like the *kalaviṅka*. As for the *rajjudāla*, whether it is *rajjudāla* or *arañjudāla*, it is a bird and should be identified from the fowlers, as it is listed among them. Others, however, identify the *rajjudāla* as the *śleṣmātaka* tree. Their inclusion among animals and the application of the same penance for cutting it as for bone-bearing creatures is incorrect, especially since it is taught in the middle [of the list]. Moreover, it has been stated that the term *śleṣmātaka* is used with the word *selu* in the passage, "the *selu*, cow's milk, and fresh butter" (MDh 5.6), showing its usage in other regions. The rest is well known.
Pecking birds, web-footed birds, the koyaṣṭi, claw-scratching birds, those that dive for fish, meat from a slaughterhouse, and dried meat; 5.13.

Those which eat by pecking are *pratuda*s. Although the prohibition of the *plava*, *bhāsa*, and *cakrapāda* is established by the inclusion of the term "web-footed" (*jālapāda*), that term is included for the sake of establishing a permanent rule. Thus, it is inferred that there is an option regarding the prohibition of web-footed *pratuda*s. The *koyaṣṭi* is to be identified from those who deal in vegetables. A *viṣkira* is so called because it eats by scattering food with its claws; however, chickens and the like are not *viṣkira*s. Consequently, since village chickens are prohibited, wild ones are permitted. How then are peacocks, quails, and so forth eaten? According to the opinion of Āpastamba, "the chicken is not among the *viṣkira*s. Thus, peacocks and the like are permitted, while there is no prohibition against the wild chicken. When two rules of equal force conflict, an option must be resorted to. Even dried meat from a slaughterhouse is among the foods to be eaten.
The crane, the heron, the raven, the wagtail, those that eat fish, village pigs, and all kinds of fish; 5.14.

Since the prohibition of the *bakā*, *balākā*, *kākolā*, and fish-eaters is already established, the specific mention of "fish" (*matsya*) implies that for those other than these, the prohibition is optional. Fish-eaters include even non-birds; by the mention of "fish-eaters," those such as the *menakādatta* (or *maukalyādayaḥ*) are to be understood as unfit for consumption, because the word "fish-eater" (*matsyāda*) is based on the act [of eating]. The *kākola* is the hawk (*śyena*), as established in other regions. This is stated thus regarding those living near the ocean. Furthermore, from the prohibition of the village-pig (*viḍvarāha*), the permission for wild ones is inferred. And the prohibition of village-born birds and so forth, mentioned previously in the context, should be understood as referring to specific types of birds. In this way, the mention of the village-pig here becomes meaningful. The statement "and all kinds of fish" is a general rule (*utsarga*) concerning fish in common, serving as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended to express the condemnation of fish.
He who eats the flesh of another is said to be an eater of that very being;
a fish-eater is an eater of all kinds of flesh; therefore, one should avoid fish. (5.15)

"Just as [the eating of] man-eaters, snake-eaters, and cats [is forbidden], so it is here. Now, by recourse to specific sub-species of those [animals], the consumption of meat that was previously prohibited is being re-permitted: "The *pāṭhīna* and *rohit* fish are to be eaten when employed in offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*); likewise, the *rājīva*, the *siṃhatuṇḍa*, and all *saśalka* fish [may be eaten]. (5.16)

By this [verse], the *pāṭhīna* and *rohit* fish are permitted for offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*). This is understood from the use of the word "and" (*ca*), which serves the purpose of conjunction, implying that they must be eaten as a mandatory rule (*niyogataḥ*). However, because of the statement "but those with scales may be eaten in all cases," and because of the specific mention of the *rohit*, it is inferred that the eating of scaled fish is permitted optionally (*vikalpena*), even in the absence of a mandatory injunction.
One should not eat animals or birds that wander alone, nor those that are unknown;
likewise, one should avoid all five-toed animals, even if they have been designated among those fit for consumption. (5.17)

Serpents and the like move alone; deer and birds are likewise unknown to those of their own species. Therefore, even among those animals not prohibited as food by the learned or others who frequent their habitats, they are "as if pointed out" (*samuddiṣṭāḥ*)—meaning they are recognized by the signs of having been eaten and thus remain objects of doubt. Likewise, regarding five-toed animals (*pañcanakha*), he says this for the purpose of providing a counter-exception to the prohibition on eating them: "The porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, the tortoise, and the hare. [218]
Among five-toed animals, they say that those with a single row of teeth, excluding the camel, are edible.

Regarding cows, sheep, goats, and deer, he will state the rule by means of two scriptural passages. Although this is not the primary context, this expiation is now stated for the purpose of excluding those [animals] that are currently well-known as forbidden—namely, cows, sheep, goats, and deer. As the Arthavāda says:

[Here the Editor inserts: "Of the cow, the sheep, and the goat" is understood as the meaning of *go'vyajasya*. In the usage of this compound word, Bhāruci generally employs the singular; however, in his commentary on the twenty-seventh verse, the use of the plural is also observed. As for whether the use of the singular is to be justified by considering it a collective dvandva compound, those who know the faults [of such interpretations] are the authority.
The mushroom, the village-pig, garlic, and the village-cock.
Having intentionally eaten onions or leeks, a twice-born man shall fall [from his caste].
Having unintentionally eaten these six, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance or the Yati-Cāndrāyaṇa; for the remaining [forbidden foods], one should fast for a day.

Intentional consumption [of forbidden food] is a sin equal to the drinking of liquor; because it shares this commonality, [the author] will declare its atonement later: "Eating forbidden food and so forth—these six are equal to the drinking of liquor" (MDh 11.57). Now, regarding a Brāhmaṇa who eats the food of a Śūdra and whose fault of contact was unknown, [the author] says this for the sake of purification:

"A twice-born man of the highest rank shall perform even a single Kṛcchra penance during a year for the sake of purifying himself from eating what was consumed unknowingly; but for that which was known, the penance is specifically greater. (5.21)

The nature, contact, time, and transformation of all that is unfit to be consumed depend upon the ownership [of the thing]. Therefore, one who desires his own welfare should diligently avoid foods, drinks, and edibles that are not to be eaten. In the scripture, violence is defined by its characteristics; for this reason, he says:

"Excellent wild animals and birds are to be killed by Brahmins for the sake of sacrifice, and likewise for the sake of maintaining their dependents; for Agastya acted in this manner in the past. (5.22)

It is enjoined by the Śruti that wild animals and birds are to be killed in sacrifice. Although this is established by the Śruti, the following is stated in order to demonstrate the similarity between [the killing for] taking them away and [the killing for] supporting dependents (*bhṛtya*). Thus, this example shows that just as these may be killed for the sake of sacrifice, so too may they be killed for the sake of supporting dependents. Regarding this, Agastya provides an illustration of the underlying reason: Agastya prepared them without the ritual sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), and since there was no other divine [purpose] for his dependents, there was no fault for one who follows such a practice. Furthermore, the mention of the *brāhmaṇa* here is for the sake of illustration; likewise, Yudhiṣṭhira and others accepted wealth for the purpose of honoring guests and the like. This being the case, when citing the example of Yudhiṣṭhira and others, the statement—"wild animals and birds are praised when killed by Brāhmaṇas for the sake of sacrifice"—is intended solely as an illustration for the support of dependents. And so says the Brāhmaṇa: "In the same way, when a king has arrived for a man, they slaughter for him a bull, a rhinoceros, or a pregnant cow; even so, they slaughter for him this [fire], for fire is the animal of the gods among those produced by friction. This Brāhmaṇa passage from the Ṛgveda regarding the slaughter of wild animals and birds in the thirty-six-year [Sattra] sacrifice should be understood here. And because there is no sacrifice to a deity in that month, as seen in the Śruti, he says this: [The text continues: "Just as when a king has come to a man, they slaughter for him a bull, a rhinoceros, or a pregnant cow, even so they slaughter for him this [fire], for fire is the animal of the gods among those produced by friction. This Brāhmaṇa passage from the Ṛgveda regarding the slaughter of wild animals and birds in the thirty-six-year [Sattra] sacrifice should be understood here. And because there is no sacrifice to a deity in that month, as seen in the Śruti, he says this: [End of excerpt].
For in ancient times, during the sacrifices of the ṛṣis and the rites of the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, the sacrificial cakes were made from the flesh of wild animals and birds. (5.23)

In the thirty-sixth year, the killing of wild animals and birds is permitted by this Smṛti; therein, for some, hunting is allowed when life is at stake and for the sake of maintaining dependents, as there is no contradiction with the Smṛti. Whatever food, whether solid or soft, is mixed with oil and is not censured, that may be eaten even if it has stood overnight, as may what remains from a sacrificial oblation (haviḥ-śeṣa). (5.24)

Since food that has been kept overnight is generally prohibited, this exception is made for it when it is mixed with oily substances such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Furthermore, that which is not censured—even if it has come into contact with something else—is understood to include the remnants of sacrificial oblations (*haviḥśeṣa*), even if they are not mixed with oil, by virtue of the context of the passage.

"However, all food produced from barley and wheat, as well as preparations of milk, may be eaten by the twice-born even if they have stood for a long time, provided they are not smeared with oil. (5.25)

This is a specific permission for the consumption of preparations made from barley and wheat that have stood for a long time, provided they are not mixed with oil or fat; it is undertaken because such food was not permitted by the preceding rule.
Thus has been declared in its entirety what may and may not be eaten by the twice-born.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the rules regarding the eating and the avoidance of meat. (5.26)
This verse serves as a summary and presentation of the two preceding sections:
"One may eat meat that has been consecrated with sprinkling, or at the desire of Brāhmaṇas, or when enjoined according to the rule, or when there is a danger to one's life. (5.27)

In this context, that which is called *prokṣita* (consecrated by sprinkling) refers to the meat of cows, sheep, and goats—which, as parts of the Vedic ritual (*śrutikarma*), have undergone the consecration of sprinkling—and which remains after the portions have been offered in the sacrifice (*avadāna-homa*). This applies also to the *puroḍāśa* cake, which originates from the animal; the word *prokṣita* is used here figuratively (*guṇavṛttyā*) to refer to these. One should eat that. Now, this is not an injunction (*vidhi*) regarding eating, because eating is already established by the nature of the situation. Nor is any sin (*pratyavāya*) heard of in the scriptures for eating such meat. However, as will be explained later, there is a fault in transgressing what is not prescribed. Therefore, this is not accepted as having the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyamārthatva*). Rather, as will be shown later by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), this is an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) intended to prohibit other means of obtaining meat. How so? Just as the eating of the meat of cows and other animals is not prohibited and is thus obtained by implication, so too the eating of the meat of cows, sheep, and goats—though already established—is here prohibited. Furthermore, one should not eat the meat of cows and others after it has been taken by some means such as purchase and consumed by guests and so forth. But how is it that the word *prokṣita* specifically includes only cows, sheep, and goats, when the sacrificial scriptures teach that only these are worthy of sprinkling? It is because of their excellence (*atiśaya*). How then [is this justified]? Passages such as "by goat-meat for six months" (MDh 3.269) must be understood with reference to *prokṣita* meat; they are merely statements (*vacana*) and not part of the Veda itself. There is no *madhuparka* (honey-mixture) involved here. Rather, in the case of occasional cow-slaughter, the eating of its meat would not be permitted because it is not *prokṣita*. But it is indeed permitted, since this is the authoritative source (*pramāṇa*) for that time. If this were not the case, eating that meat would be improper. Alternatively, in the view of general permission (*utsarga-pakṣa*), the cow is the subject here. Or, as stated regarding the meat of rams and goats at a *śrāddha*, there would be no fault due to the scriptural statement concerning those of a different caste (*vijātīya*). Some, however, conceive of this as a restrictive rule for eating meat, as will be explained later. Whether that is logical or not must be deliberated upon, because an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) for a restrictive rule of eating is impossible, as already stated. Nor is an injunction against eating meat appropriate here. As for those who say that although the eating of meat as a part of the ritual is enjoined based on the authority of the Vedic scriptures, this is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the sake of praising the subsequent injunction—for them, let the eating of goat-meat and the like remain permissible even in the absence of this restrictive scripture; what is the harm? But surely this will be stated later: "A Brahmin should never eat animals not consecrated with mantras" (MDh 5.36). If that is so, then the prohibition of eating the meat of cows, sheep, and goats is established from this very scripture. This need not be said, as it would result in redundancy (*paunaruktya*) through mere naming. To this it is replied: An explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is rightly stated either to praise the remainder of an injunction or prohibition, or to express aversion, as in the verse beginning "But one who is appointed according to rule" (MDh 5.35). For this reason, even a single instructional sentence is capable of both types of action—engagement or withdrawal—due to its inherent nature. Otherwise, all explanatory passages would be useless, leading to their total non-existence. And it is observed that a meaning is postulated which generates an inclination toward the performance of the enjoined act. Nevertheless, one should not eat that meat, because the author says: [The text continues with the verse: "One should not eat the meat of an animal not consecrated with mantras. (MDh 5.36) Thus ends the section.
A Brahmin should never eat animals that have not been consecrated with mantras;
however, abiding by the eternal rule, he may eat those consecrated with mantras. [MDh 5.36]

And regarding the phrase "and at the *madhuparka*" (MDh 5.41), this should be understood as an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) intended for glorification, which serves to specify the enjoined matter. This being the case, whether the term *vṛthāmāṃsa* (meat not prepared for a sacred purpose) has the same meaning [as the meat mentioned in the injunction] or a different meaning, the specific understanding of its sense cannot be obtained except through the scriptural rules concerning consecrated (*prokṣita*) meat that is to be eaten; and there is no scripture [other than this] by which these two scriptural passages could be considered fit to be mere descriptive supplements (*śeṣa*). Otherwise, they would be non-existent. Since there is an absence of a restrictive rule regarding the meat of cows, goats, sheep, and so forth—which are not prohibited—there would necessarily follow the eating of their meat; nor can it be maintained that this is a supplementary statement (*śeṣapratipādana*). The phrase "and at the desire of Brāhmaṇas" (brāhmaṇānāṃ ca kāmyayā) connects with "he may eat. Who, then, is this? It refers to the guest at the *madhuparka*, the *arghya*, and the cow or animal—at the time of the slaughter or the release [of the animal]. According to the principle that "the cow should never be the *arghya*," one should eat the meat of the cow or animal as a rule, even if it is normally forbidden, when there is the desire of Brāhmaṇas as the cause—that is, by the request of the giver—for the sake of favoring the purpose of the gift characterized by the scriptures. One should eat according to this *Gṛhya-smṛti* or the *Manu-śāstra-smṛti*. How so? Because for one who has not been prohibited from eating meat that is obtained by the nature of things and is [normally] released, there is an eligibility here [for this rule] based on the scripture: "But abstention yields great fruit" (MDh 5.56). Alternatively, for one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), who is prohibited from eating the meat of animals not intended for sacrifice, and who by implication eats meat that is neither released nor prohibited, this mandatory scriptural rule (*niyoga-śāstra*) becomes meaningful for him, as he is one who eats meat that is not released and is not prohibited. Thus, this [rule] becomes purposeful, and it is appropriate to construe it in such a way. And thus it is purposeful, as we have stated. This is not an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) as in the previous case; rather, it is a restriction (*niyama*). Consequently, since eating is enjoined as necessary, there is sin (*pratyavāya*) in avoiding it, just like the transgression of a ritual injunction. And so he will say: "At the *madhuparka* and at a sacrifice... (MDh 5.41), etc., referring to the specific explanatory praise and the general rule: "But one who is appointed, according to the rule" (MDh 5.35). This being the case, it has been said that this is not an injunction of another means for one who is already eating, due to the force of the instruction. Nor does sin arise for one who eats meat at the desire of Brāhmaṇas when he has already desisted from eating prohibited meat, because the eating is for the sake of another. Here, for one whose self is restrained by the aforementioned scripture, it is for the sake of favoring the giver; therefore, there is no transgression of Dharma, just as in the case of eating meat [under certain conditions], or like the student (*brahmacārin*) eating food from a single source. Just as for a student, when there is a prohibition against eating food from a single person, the text says: "If requested, he may eat at will; his vow is not violated" (MDh 2.189)—due to the force of this scriptural instruction, eating food from a single person or eating meat when requested does not constitute a violation of the vow—so it is here as well. [Objection: The comparison is unequal. For in the case of the student, it is proper that he should enter [the meal] because of the instruction, and thus his eating is not opposed to his vow, provided he avoids meat. But here, for one who has desisted from eating prohibited meat, if he eats meat at the desire of Brāhmaṇas despite the collection of scriptural prohibitions, there is the fault of transgressing the rule of desistance. [Response: To this it is said: Meat-eating should not be cited as the example. Rather, it is the eating of food from a single person and the monthly eating that should be considered. Having done so, just as there is no contradiction in the scripture permitting eating in a specific context at the request of a Brāhmaṇa-giver, so it is here. Therefore, it is logical that for those two who eat in this manner, there is no fault of transgressing the scriptural rule on meat.
