Others, however, explain: Just as there is a rule that the guest should eat at the desire of the Brāhmaṇa-giver, so too this instruction regarding eating as a rule is for the guest at the desire of the Brāhmaṇa-giver. Others say it refers to sacrifices, weddings, and so forth; others to a friendly meeting; others to a dining party. Some say all these are synonyms for a restrictive rule (*niyama*). These various explanations of the word "at the desire of Brāhmaṇas" (*brāhmaṇakāmyayā*) must be deliberated upon as to which form is most appropriate. It has been stated that when one is properly engaged in a rite for the gods or ancestors, or at a *śrāddha*, the Brāhmaṇa should eat according to the rule and the capacity of the situation. This is reasonable. Even in the event of the loss of life, in distress, or due to disease—even without the two previously mentioned causes—this would be the same state; and in such a condition, one who eats meat is authorized by this scripture. For one who lives, there is a requirement for the avoidance of sin. And thus the effort to preserve human life is taught in the scripture: "Performing actions here, one should desire to live a hundred years" (ĪśU 2). This being so, in this state, one who eats meat becomes a destroyer of the self (*ātmahā*), and the destruction of the self is contrary to the scripture. As the scripture says: "This, indeed, is not remembered again for the sake of life; for that becomes worldless" (ŚB). And thus, this is better.
"Sunless indeed are those worlds, shrouded in blind darkness;
to them go after death those people who are slayers of the Self. [Īśopaniṣad 3]

Gautama and all other authors of *Dharmaśāstras* have stated: “One should protect oneself from everything that destroys the self” (GDh 9.34). Therefore, it is established that meat must necessarily be eaten when invited by a Brahmin and in similar circumstances. If this is so, then even for a religious student (*brahmacārin*), eating meat would result from such causes as being invited by a Brahmin, since the reason is the same as in the cases of eating meat that has been offered or is otherwise prohibited. This is not correct, because of the prohibition [of meat] in the rule of counter-exception (*pratiprasava*). For even regarding the monthly meal, it is said: “He may eat at his pleasure when requested; his vow is not thereby violated” (MDh 2.189). By this scripture, food is prescribed for one observing a vow as being free from honey and meat. Furthermore, there is an expiation for him if he eats meat while observing a vow: “But he who, while observing a vow, should somehow eat honey or meat” (MDh 12.159), and so forth, in the case of being invited by a Brahmin. [Objection: Then how is it in the case of officiating at a sacrifice (*ārtvijya*) or when life is in danger? [Response: It is said: Because the cause is the same, eating meat by him is likewise improper in those two other circumstances. Thus, when the eating of animals, birds, cows, and so forth—which are not prohibited—would otherwise be obtained through the rules, and when the scripture prescribing restrictions prohibits other means of eating, this scripture of counter-exception is commenced to regulate the eating of meat again within the scope of that prohibition, once the eating that was naturally obtained has been negated by the two aforementioned types of prohibitory scriptures. And thus, there is prosperity (*abhyudaya*) through the eating permitted by these three scriptures. What then? There is merely the avoidance of sin (*pratyavāya*). Indeed, there is sin in not eating, due to the force of the commencement of the scripture. And thus he will say: “But when appointed, according to the rule” (MDh 5.35). Others, however, say: Just as there is sin for one who does not eat, so there must be prosperity for one who eats. But its status as being like the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) is to be reconsidered, because that rule is subject to deliberation, whereas the twilight worship is a natural requirement and lacks the nature of a restrictive rule (*niyama*). The phrase “only in the event of the loss of life” is a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*).
Prajāpati fashioned all this as food for the vital breath (prāṇa): everything that moves and everything that is stationary is the sustenance of the vital breath. 5.28.

In this context, the name *prāṇa* belongs to the fivefold wind (*pañcavṛtti-vāyu*) which is the cause of the stability of the body and the senses. Others, however, describe *prāṇa* as a collection of specific functions of the senses located in the heart. Some logicians (*tārkika*), moreover, do not accept that. As for its being the cause of stability, because it is conditioned by the presence of that [wind], food is what sustains the bodily state and so forth. It is not merely a modification of rice and other grains; rather, everything—beasts, wood, grass, leaves, and so on—is designated as food for the bodily *prāṇa* in some way, because it is the cause of its stability. Thus, by that very means, it is swallowed by it. Since the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) exists as the enjoyer, this is called its "food," by which the *kṣetrajña*'s entitlement to experience (*bhoga*) is established. This being the case, the genitive case is not used here with reference to the relationship between the enjoyed and the enjoyer; rather, it should be understood through the force of the context and the aforementioned meaning for the sake of emphasizing the weight of the subject matter. Now he shows its cause: "Thus Prajāpati fashioned [it]," as previously stated. Its cause is not inherent. And this conceptualization of the meaning is attributed to Prajāpati in the *Prāṇasaṃvāda-upaniṣad*: "Whatever exists here, starting from insects and moths—that is your food. Because of this statement, he now explains "everything": that which moves, following after living beings, and that which is stationary, the opposite of that—all that is the food of *prāṇa*. Thus, it is not merely a matter of worldly convention. This is said to be the commentary (*bhāṣya*) upon this aphorism (*sūtra*).
The immobile are the food of the mobile; those without fangs are the food of those with fangs; the handless are the food of those with hands; and the timid are the food of the brave. (5.29)

This is indeed relative, and it is observed thus in the world: among moving creatures, those with little speed, such as pigeons and the like, are called slow compared to those possessing greater velocity, such as hawks; and among fanged creatures, such as tigers and the like, animals without fangs, such as jackals and the like, are so designated. In the same way, handless creatures such as snakes are the food of those with hands—namely, mongooses and others—who possess hands and feet and are capable of the actions of approaching and retreating. This is for the purpose of providing an illustration. Likewise, among the brave, the timid are always the food of those who possess the specific activity of constant connection with power. Other cases of the opposite nature should also be understood in this manner. And such being the established order of Prajāpati:
The eater does not incur sin by eating the creatures that are fit to be eaten, even day after day; for both the eaters and those fit to be eaten were created by the Creator himself. (5.30)

This explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is intended for the purpose of praising the rule regarding the eating of the flesh of animals that have reached the end of their life-span; it should be understood as being for the sake of encouraging its performance. Furthermore, what is the reason for this being merely an explanatory statement exactly as it was heard? Because of the efficacy of the instruction prohibiting the injury of all living beings, and because of the instruction regarding its transgression, there is no option (*vikalpa*). If this were the actual cause for it, it would not be an explanatory passage; consequently, the established order of the scripture (*śāstra-vyavasthā*) would be undermined, since the underlying reason would be the same [in both cases]. But such is not observed. For me, however, its meaning lies precisely in its being stated as it is.
"The eating of meat for the sake of sacrifice—this is remembered as the divine ordinance."

This is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) for that [rule]. This *smṛti* is intended to encourage the observance of the rule regarding the consumption of meat during the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), the hospitality rite (*atithya*), and the ancestral offering (*śrāddha*). Alternatively, this is an illustrative explanatory passage. How so? Just as in the ritual procedure of a sacrifice, the consumption of meat—which is an auxiliary part of it—is necessarily performed by the officiating priests at the desire of the Brahmins, so too in the *śrāddha*, the consumption of meat must necessarily be performed in order to avoid transgression. And thus he will say: "But one who is appointed [to the task] should act according to the rule" (MDh 5.35). Furthermore, for those for whom even the consumption of consecrated meat (*prokṣita*) is mandatory, this [passage] is a qualification; it is an explanatory passage applicable to all three cases.
But conduct contrary to this is called the demonic way. || 5.31 ||

This [verse] is indeed a *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) for the purpose of praising the eating of consecrated meat and thereby excluding the eating of unconsecrated meat; for it serves as the introduction to the meaning of the subsequent verse. This being so, what other Smṛti rule exists for the prohibition of eating unconsecrated meat? And another [rule], intended for the eating of meat under specific restrictions, is stated thirdly for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa’s desire, at a Śrāddha, or in cases of life-threatening danger, in order to exclude other means:
"Having purchased it, or produced it himself, or even obtained it from another, one does not incur sin by eating meat after having worshipped the gods and the ancestors. (5.32)

And thus, by means of such methods as ritual action (*kriyā*) and so forth, one should indeed consume what remains after the offering, as well as other meats of the cow, sheep, goat, and deer. Here, because the self-production of meat is mentioned without being emphasized, there is no permission [for it]; for this reason, no restrictive rules regarding the production of meat are taught here, since these [rules] are defined by their purpose (*artha*). Furthermore, there is a statement made without the intention to prescribe, even though the root [of the verb] implies that meaning. For example, [the rule] "having died, one should perform this *jartva* [rite]"—if the purpose is not in contradiction with the context, then it will mean "one should produce it oneself for the sake of sacrifice. And in this way, non-contradiction is maintained according to possibility, relying on the *avatka* (?). This reference to the production of meat—"to the gods and ancestors, preceded by the *arghya* offering"—is a restatement of the duties of a householder (*gṛhastha-dharma*). Thus, this does not differ from the duties of a householder; for every cooking of a householder is of such a nature. And this purpose of restating the duties of a householder is stated so that there may be a specific mental disposition (*citta-viśeṣa*) regarding the specific expiation for the omission of the *snātaka-vrata* of the teacher’s feet. Otherwise, for one who consumes that [meat], it would be like *kṛsara* (rice and peas) and so forth, as was said previously. And this being the case—
A twice-born man who knows the law should not eat meat contrary to the rule when there is no distress;
for by eating meat contrary to the rule, he becomes a ghost and is helplessly devoured by those very creatures. (5.33)
This other verse of qualification, which serves as a general supplement to the preceding statement, has been [inserted by someone]:
"The sin of a hunter seeking wealth is not so great as that which befalls one who eats meat in vain after death. (5.34)

These two verses are intended as a censure of eating meat for which one has paid; they do not constitute a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*). What then? The previous injunction—that eating only after consecration (*prokṣita*) and so forth—is the primary rule; thus, this [present passage] is either a praise of that prior scriptural teaching, or, because of its immediate proximity, it is intended solely as a praise of the injunction regarding the *krīta* (bought) meat and the others. Therefore, meat must not be eaten otherwise than in this manner; this is said for the purpose of praising the eating [of meat] when one is so enjoined. Now it is stated: "But that twice-born man who, being duly appointed, does not eat meat according to the rule..."
Having passed away, he goes to the state of a beast for twenty-one successive births.

Thus, this [passage] is first an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) for the Vaiśeṣika practice of eating meat when commissioned; however, by means of ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), it is made into an entire injunction by the scripture: "But one who is commissioned should [eat] according to the rule" (5.27). "A Brahmin shall never eat animals that have not been consecrated with mantras;
but established in the eternal Dharma, he may give [meat] that has been consecrated with mantras. (5.36)

By the rule, "And [the meat of] animals with two rows of teeth" (MDh 5.18), since cows, sheep, and goats possess two rows of teeth, they would prima facie be considered edible; however, this verse is intended to prohibit that by means of other scriptural injunctions regarding purchased meat and so forth. As for what was stated, "One may eat consecrated meat" (MDh 5.27), this present meaning should be understood as a restrictive exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) supplementary to that, on account of its inherent capacity. Thus it has been said: its repetition is for the sake of an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), whereas its instruction serves the purpose of an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*). Furthermore, the context is explained either in this way or by positing a different subject matter. Its repetition was mentioned previously: it is for the purpose of prohibiting the unavoidable slaughter of goats and other animals in rites such as the *sītā-yajña* when accompanied by mantras. If, however, one were to harbor the false notion that grain and other necessities cannot be obtained without the slaughter of animals, then—out of such desire—[the prohibition applies].
In times of distress, one may perform a sacrifice with clarified butter as the victim, or likewise with a victim made of flour;
but one should never, under any circumstances, desire to kill an animal in vain.

In the *Saṅga*, at the place where the sacrificial animal (*paśu*) is normally located, one should offer clarified butter (*ghṛta*) in place of the animal, because the animal is not to be slaughtered there; for the Śruti declares, "Clarified butter is indeed brilliance" (*tejo vai ghṛtam*). One should thus make an offering of clarified butter in the place of the primary animal, or perhaps of substances in the form of fat. By means of that, one should make an animal out of flour using ground flour—not by a method contrary to the scriptures? For it has been said regarding the slaughter of animals in vain: "As many hairs as there are on the body of an animal, so many times does the slayer of an animal in vain undergo death after death in birth after birth. (5.38)

But this fault does not apply to the slaughter of goats and other animals for sacrifice, because: "Animals were created by the Self-Existent One himself for the sake of sacrifice; and sacrifice is for the prosperity of all. Therefore, killing in sacrifice is no killing. (5.39)
It is not merely because of the absence of the harmful effects of violence that this is said; rather, it is also because [the victims] perform an act of favor toward him. And so he shows:
"Herbs, animals, trees, beasts, and likewise birds, having met their death for the sake of sacrifice, attain higher states once again. (5.40)

Furthermore, based on the characteristic qualification of being human, one should understand from the authority of the scripture that [the birth] occurs in a different continent or region. Thus, this is the meaning of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the desire of the Brāhmaṇas:

"In the honey-mixture offering (*madhuparka*), in a sacrifice, and in rites for the ancestors or deities—it is only here that animals may be killed, and nowhere else; so Manu has declared" (MDh 5.41).

This being the case, the killing of the animal does not merely result in the absence of sin; rather, by way of its very nature as a subordinate element (*bhṛtya*) of the primary ritual action, it serves both the sacrificer and the animals—just as it does in a sacrifice, so too in the *madhuparka* offering. This should be understood through the force of the context as being intended for the praise of the consumption of the meat of the sacrificial animal worthy of honor (*arghya*). And just as that [killing] is a benefactor in sacrifices and other rites, there is this further scriptural authority: "A twice-born man who knows the true meaning of the Veda, while killing animals for these purposes, [incurs no fault]."
It leads both oneself and the sacrificial animal to the highest state. || 5.42 ||

It is logical that animals are elevated when they exist as means for accomplishing the act of favoring gods, ancestors, and humans; for they are the very instruments of the ripening (*vipāka*) that establishes the attainment and avoidance of merit and demerit, being established by the authority of the scriptures (*śāstra-pramāṇa*), and there is no contradiction whatsoever with the Vedas or the *Smṛti* texts. This is just as in the case of the status of a *Śūdra* and so forth, whereby we do not fail to understand this point. For example, elsewhere it is said: "Everything is the property of the Brāhmaṇa" (MDh 1.100), and so on. And as for one who might think that the elevation of animals and other materials used as means for the sacrifice—performed for the sake of the sacrificer—does not apply to them as it does to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), that view must be refuted. Just as animals and others attain the status of being auxiliary members (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice through their own destruction, the priests do not; therefore, they should be elevated from the ritual in the same way, and not otherwise. Furthermore, if even from a fruitless ritual an incidental (*ānuṣaṅgika*) worldly result is seen for the priests in the form of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), then from that same ritual, even though the animals and others are not for that purpose, there would be an invisible incidental result. If it is argued that because they are authorized (*adhikṛta*), they have a claim to that result, we reply: their authorization would arise from the scriptural injunction itself, provided they have an intention toward the incidental result, just as in the case of the priests; and this is indeed observed. Even in the case of work performed for another’s sake, such as carrying a load, the laborers who are the means of accomplishing it receive an incidental benefit attached to the primary result. If it were thus here as well, then— [The text continues: ...in this being the case—
Whether living at home, with his teacher, or in the forest, a self-possessed twice-born man should never practice violence not ordained by the Veda, even in times of distress. (5.43)
And here he states the reason:
"One should know that very violence which is ordained by the Vedas and restricted to this world of moving and non-moving beings as being indeed non-violence."
For indeed, because it is free from the effects of the fault of violence, Dharma shone forth from the Veda, which is honored by the world.

Not from another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, since the Veda, Smṛti, and Āgama are authoritative here through a distinction of scope regarding the performance of violence and its prohibition, one should respond as follows: "Violence is not merely the production of suffering in another, nor is there a lack of concern for it merely in the production of suffering in another; for deviation is observed in both cases. Even that which is beneficial to others, though followed by further suffering, is absolutely true and non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) itself. Otherwise, the scriptures would be rendered ineffective across all philosophical systems (*dṛṣṭi*), and this is not desired. Therefore, it is logical that "Dharma indeed shone forth from the Veda. This is another verse for the purpose of prohibiting violence; by the force of the context, it is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) for the prohibition of eating meat not prescribed by rule.
He who harms harmless beings out of a desire for his own pleasure finds no happiness anywhere, whether he is alive or even dead. (5.45)

Thus, it is shown that the killing of tigers, robbers, and the like involves no small transgression; for they are [regarded as] harmful, and there is the instruction regarding those who are non-harmful. And so it is said:
"He who desires to bring about the suffering of binding and killing for living beings, yet seeks the happiness of all—such a person enjoys ultimate happiness. (5.46)
[227] This is as before. But the meaning of "pride" (*māna*) is as follows: that which one meditates upon, that which one performs, and wherein one fixes one's delight.
He who harms nothing whatsoever attains that without effort. || 5.47 ||

All these verses, beginning with "From tigers and so forth," although intended for the purpose of abstaining from violence, should be understood—by virtue of the context—to have the purpose of prohibiting the eating of meat that is not prescribed by rule. For he who eats meat without following the prescribed rule has effectively committed the slaughter of an animal himself; since the animal is killed solely for the sake of his meat, this censure of eating meat without rule results in the praise of eating meat according to the rule. Therefore: "Meat is never produced without having first committed violence against living beings."

Therefore, by this [reasoning], even though there are various contexts regarding the relationship between a cause and its effect, the presentation of the prohibition of violence should be understood as having this purpose:
that the killing of living beings is not [permissible] because it constitutes violence.
Since [meat] leads to heaven [only when obtained] according to the rule,
one should therefore avoid meat. 5.48.

Now, this enumeration—which takes the form of an explanatory praise (arthavāda)—is stated for the purpose of avoiding the consumption of meat by one who eats it contrary to the rule, as well as other types of prescribed consumption:
"Having fully considered the origin of meat, as well as the slaughter and imprisonment of embodied beings, one should desist from the eating of all meat. (5.49)

Having understood that the origin of meat is from the semen and blood of the mother and father—both utterly impure—and having realized that even for embodied beings, slaughter and bondage in an impure place within the womb are cruel means for the production of meat, one should desist from eating all meat; this is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise), not a [logical] reason (*hetu*). Otherwise, even the eating of meat permitted by other rules would be contradicted, since this reason would apply equally to it. Thus, the inclusion of the term "all" (*sarva*) is supported here. And this being so:
He who does not eat meat, even while disregarding the [prescribed] rule like a flesh-eating demon (piśāca), becomes beloved in the world and is not afflicted by diseases. (5.50)

Through the connection with this perceived purpose, this is a censure of the eating of meat not prescribed by rule, as well as a praise of its avoidance; and this arises from the eating of meat intended for others:
[228] "The one who consents, the one who dissects, the killer, the buyer, and the seller..."
The preparer, the server, and the eater are all killers. (5.51)

[Editor’s Note: Regarding the fourth quarter of this verse, the reading “ścāṣṭa” was indicated in the commentary as an alternative to “śceti,” and a lack of approval for that reading was demonstrated; furthermore, the identity of the buyer and the seller was presented as the reason for this.]

How so? Just as for the killer and the consenter, this [text] is established by another scripture; this is merely an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) intended to disparage the consumption [of meat] by one who violates this injunction. This being the case, even though the eating of forbidden meat is prohibited, the expiation for the slaughter of a living being does not apply to the killer. Furthermore, there is another form of disparagement: if even those who perform the ritual slaughter of a flour-elephant (*piṣṭapaśu*)—namely, the butcher, the buyer, the seller, the preparer, and the thief—are considered killers in the absence of any other prohibitory scripture, how much more so the eater, for whose sake the animal is slaughtered? Thus, since these [roles] would lack utility if even one of them were missing, this injunction is for the sake of the eater; it must be explained in two ways as an *arthavāda* disparaging the consumption of meat. Like the previous [case], this too must be explained. And because the buyer and seller are a single unit, the reading "eight" (*aṣṭa*) does not apply here. Therefore, one should adopt this alternative reading: "The eaters and the killers are [the same]. Nor is there any contradiction with the scripture in this reading, nor is there any special favor in the reading "eight," because this is an *arthavāda*. Since this is so, therefore—
There is no doer of unmeritorious deeds greater than he who, without having honored the ancestors and the gods, desires to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another. 5.52
This is another praise of the subject at hand, a praise for abstaining from meat that is not otherwise forbidden:
"He who might perform the horse-sacrifice every year for a hundred years, and he who does not eat meat—the merit and fruit of these two are equal. (5.53)
One does not obtain that fruit by eating pure fruits and roots or by consuming the food of sages, which one obtains from the total avoidance of meat. (5.54)

These two verses are for the purpose of abstaining from meat. Regarding which meat? They prohibit [it]. From the context, it is understood that what is prohibited is meant. For it is known from the statements, "The fruit of merit for those two is equal," and "One does not obtain that fruit which comes from the total avoidance of meat. Therefore, this is a statement of praise regarding the renunciation of what remains after guests and others have eaten—[that is], meat that is not prohibited. Since, in this case, the avoidance of what is prohibited has as its fruit merely the non-occurrence of transgression, and while the visible [fruit] is seen, the invisible [fruit] may likewise be inferred to be of such a nature, and since safety can somehow be conceived even from that, this is thus appropriate; now, by means of an etymological explanation (*nirvacana*), he again renders it an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) for the sake of avoiding what is prohibited: ... [text continues] ... Thus, having explained the meaning of the name, he concludes with a eulogy for the purpose of avoiding what is forbidden. *Note: The provided source text contains several archaic or corrupted variants (e.g., *svati*, *vijñayate*). The translation above attempts to convey the logical structure and intent of the argument as found in the original.*
"He shall eat me in the next world, whose flesh I eat here"—the wise declare this to be the true nature of "flesh" (māṃsa). (5.55)
[229] Now, it must be stated regarding the dharma of abstaining from meat; therefore, this is spoken in connection with that:
"There is no fault in eating meat, nor in intoxication, nor in sexual intercourse."
This is the way of beings; however, renunciation yields great fruit.

First, regarding the subject of prohibition, this statement—"there is no fault in eating meat"—is meaningless, because we observe that prohibitions are directed toward those for whom an act is already considered faulty. Furthermore, even if one were to argue that the prohibitory scripture would otherwise be rendered purposeless, what relevance would that have here, since there is no suspicion of fault in an area not subject to a formal injunction? This being the case, this statement—"there is no fault in eating meat"—must be understood as referring to what remains after [the meal] of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), by virtue of its contextual force; and furthermore, that which remains after guests and others have eaten, or the residue of consecrated meat (*prokṣita*), is to be known as "not prohibited by the learned. As for that which must necessarily be eaten at *śrāddha* ceremonies and the like, there is a scriptural hearing of fault in its rejection, as it has been said: "But one who is appointed [to eat], according to the rule" (YDh 5.35). The explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating "this is the way of beings" is intended to praise abstention. And this being so, the abstention from what is either not practiced by the learned or is prohibited, when performed by one's own will, yields great fruit; it does not depend on a prohibitory scripture. Thus, the performance of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) repeatedly is equal to [eating] roots and fruits; this is not a praise of the excellence of the meal resulting from non-abstention, but rather an illustration for the sake of all such abstentions. Likewise, the conduct of the learned in abandoning the anus and salt serves as a perfect example of this. The abstention from liquor and sexual intercourse, which concerns what is not practiced by the learned and is not prohibited, should be understood as explained according to one's specific qualification. Now—
I shall now declare the purification of the deceased as well as the purification of objects, for all four castes, duly and in their proper order. (5.57)

"Thus has been stated in its entirety what is edible and what is inedible for the twice-born" (MDh 5.26). From this conclusion of the section on forbidden foods mentioned above, although all social classes (*varṇas*) have authority regarding the section on meat, this repeated statement—"for all four classes"—is for the sake of emphasis. And he will demonstrate that emphasis later. Now, we shall explain the purification according to the specific rules: "When one has teethed, when one has been born [to a younger sibling], when the tonsure ceremony has been performed, and upon death—likewise in the case of birth—all relatives are impure. (5.58)

Regarding the terms *dantajāta* (one whose teeth have appeared) and *anujāta* (one born after): the meaning of *anujāta* is one younger than the one whose teeth have appeared. Regarding *kṛtacaule* (one for whom the tonsure has been performed), by the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that this also applies to those for whom the initiation (*upanayana*) and other rites have been performed. When such a person has died, the term "non-worldly relatives" (*alaukikā bandhavaḥ*)—as distinguished from those characterized by the rules of impurity in the scriptures—refers specifically to the *sapiṇḍas*. This is because the author will specify this in the following verse: "And the same is said regarding birth-impurity (*sūtaka*). Since this is a common rule, it is introduced here even though it was not the immediate subject. Now, he demonstrates the nature of that impurity: "Impurity (*āśauca*) due to death (*śāva*) is ordained for ten days among the *sapiṇḍas*."
Until the collection of the bones has taken place, [the impurity lasts] for three days or indeed for one day alone. (5.59)

[230] Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”—“Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? The form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. These, bhikkhus, are the five aggregates subject to clinging. Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir; it is marvelous, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘Bhikkhus, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging. Yet, venerable sir, when I consider the five aggregates subject to clinging, I do not see any other dhamma that is so utterly hollow, so utterly empty, so utterly vain, so utterly insubstantial as the five aggregates subject to clinging. “It is so, Ānanda, it is so! When you consider, Ānanda, the five aggregates subject to clinging, you do not see any other dhamma that is so utterly hollow, so utterly empty, so utterly vain, so utterly insubstantial as the five aggregates subject to clinging. For what reason? Because, Ānanda, whatever is felt, therein is craving; wherever there is craving, therein is delight; wherever there is delight, therein is attachment; wherever there is attachment, therein is bondage; and wherever there is bondage, therein is the five aggregates subject to clinging. Therefore, Ānanda, it is because of this that when you consider the five aggregates subject to clinging, you do not see any other dhamma that is so utterly hollow, so utterly empty, so utterly vain, so utterly insubstantial as the five aggregates subject to clinging. Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how should one know, how should one see, for the mind to be liberated from the five aggregates subject to clinging? “Ānanda, one should know form as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is form, this is the arising of form, this is the cessation of form. One should know feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is consciousness, this is the arising of consciousness, this is the cessation of consciousness. It is when one knows and sees thus, Ānanda, that the mind is liberated from the five aggregates subject to clinging. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘One should know form as it really is with correct wisdom... Now, venerable sir, I understand the five aggregates subject to clinging, and I also understand the origin of the five aggregates subject to clinging, and I also understand the cessation of the five aggregates subject to clinging, and I also understand the way leading to the cessation of the five aggregates subject to clinging. “It is so, Ānanda, it is so! You have understood the five aggregates subject to clinging, Ānanda, and you have understood their origin, their cessation, and the way leading to their cessation. Therefore, Ānanda, you should dwell contemplating impermanence in the five aggregates subject to clinging, contemplating suffering in what is impermanent, contemplating non-self in what is suffering, contemplating disenchantment in what is non-self, contemplating dispassion in what is disenchanting, and contemplating cessation in what is dispassionate. It is by doing so, Ānanda, that you will soon attain the deliverance of mind that is taintless through exhaustion. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, the Venerable Ānanda rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words. [230] Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Therefore, Ānanda, you should dwell contemplating impermanence in the five aggregates subject to clinging, contemplating suffering in what is impermanent, contemplating non-self in what is suffering, contemplating disenchantment in what is non-self, contemplating dispassion in what is disenchanting, and contemplating cessation in what is dispassionate.
