When the *sapiṇḍas* have passed away, this fourfold rule applies; for those who are *samānodakas*, he will state a different rule. This is an option determined by circumstances. It depends on one's study of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*). And so he will say: "One should not prolong the impurities" (MDh 5.84), and so forth. Gautama also says: "Immediate purity," "and for kings, for the sake of not interrupting their duties," and "for a Brāhmaṇa, for the sake of not interrupting his Vedic study" (GDh 14.44–46). Just as in the case of childhood, this specific determination depends on [the state of] Vedic study; it does not apply only to non-Brāhmaṇas, because of the subsequent instruction regarding Kṣatriyas and others. Furthermore, the phrase "until the collection of the bones" (*saṃcayanād asthnām*) is an indicator for the bones themselves, since of that statement it must be understood that it refers specifically to those who maintain the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), based on the scriptural injunction: "Until the collection of the bones. Now he demonstrates the nature of *sapiṇḍatā*:
The sapinda relationship ceases with the seventh person; however, the state of being a samānodaka (distant kinsman) persists as long as the birth and the name are not forgotten. 5.60.

Sapiṇḍatā ceases upon passing beyond six generations when the seventh is reached; for it is by this [status] that, while the three ancestors beginning with the father are living, the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) is prescribed for the three descendants. This being so, "sapiṇḍatā extends to six generations," whereas *samānodakatā* (the status of having common water) exists as long as there is no forgetting of birth or name. When, however, the name of an earlier ancestor is known—such as "we belong to the lineage of so-and-so"—and his birth is known—"this person is born into our family"—then water must be offered to him who is deceased; this shall be explained as the impurity (*āśauca*) of the *samānodakas*, both on account of death (*śāva*) and birth (*sūtaka*).
For those who desire purity with precision, even in the case of birth, it should be exactly thus:
for all [relatives], there is impurity due to death (śāva), but for the mother and father alone, there is impurity due to birth (sūtaka). (5.61)

By virtue of the context, the ten-day period for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is prescribed specifically for the *sapiṇḍas*. This is stated as such because it would otherwise contradict established custom (*ācāra*) and because it is interrupted by the procedure for the collection of bones (*saṃcayana*). For one who acts according to the primary rule (*prakṛti*), the period is indeed ten days and no other. This is the primary rule regarding birth, whereby there would be impurity due to birth (*sūtaka-aśauca*) for all *sapiṇḍas*. And this is the secondary alternative (*vikalpa*): "or that of the mother and father. If it were the case that this same [impurity] would apply to birth as well, then the alternatives should be understood as optional. Furthermore, if the mother's *sūtaka* were to follow the alternatives of one day and so forth, it would contradict established custom; nor is this desired. Therefore, only the single alternative of ten days and so forth is extended [to the case of birth]. Thus says the *Gṛhyaśāstra*: "On the ninth day, having raised [the child] and fed the Brahmins, the father performs the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*)."
The birth-impurity shall belong to the mother alone; having performed the ritual sipping of water, the father becomes pure.
But having emitted semen, a man becomes pure simply by touching water;
however, due to the connection arising from seminal emission, he should observe impurity for three days.

This is stated for the sake of providing an alternative for the father: where [the text] teaches a specific bath by the mere rejection of semen, which is superior to the obligatory [bath], one might ask: why, in that case, would there not be a three-day period of *sūtaka* (birth-impurity) following the birth of offspring, according to the scriptural rule, "The bath for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse is prescribed" (MDh 5.144)? Furthermore, the mention of the father’s three-day period is intended to demonstrate all possible alternatives; for the sake of establishing these alternatives, the word "father" is used, though many various readings (*pāṭhavikalpa*) regarding this matter have not been stated here for fear of making the book too voluminous.
Those who touch a corpse are purified in this way by one night and day, or indeed by three nights; those who offer water [for the deceased] are purified after three days. (5.64)

The *śavaspṛśaḥ* (those who touch a corpse) are the *pretahāra*s (bearers of the deceased), not those merely touched by them; for the author will prescribe a bath with one's clothes on (*sacelasnāna*) for them. In the verse concerning the *divākīrti* (MDh 5.85), this period of ten nights is taught for those who touch a corpse, following the constraints of the metrical composition of the verse. Likewise, he will state in the subsequent verse: "In that case, one becomes pure after ten nights along with the bearers of the deceased" (MDh 5.65). Regarding the rule "after three days for those who offer water," when there are those who offer water during the rainy season, only those who offer water alone—along with their *samānodaka* (sapindas)—are included here, and no others, due to the force of the context.
But a disciple performing the funeral rites for his deceased guru becomes pure after ten nights, together with those who carry away the corpse. (5.65)
[Note: This verse is cited as the commentary on verse 11.197; therein, for the reading "samācaran," the reading "samācaret" is adopted.

And this is understood through the force of the term *asapiṇḍa*. For instance, regarding one who touches a corpse, as stated in the previous verse, the author will later say concerning a student who performs the *apitṛmedha* rite: "They declare that the impurity lasts for three nights when the teacher has passed away" (MDh 5.80).
In the case of a miscarriage, one is purified by nights equal in number to the months [of gestation].
When her menstrual flow has ceased, a virtuous woman who was menstruating becomes pure through bathing.
This verse has been explained by its very recitation:
"For men whose tonsure ceremony (*caula*) has not been performed, purification is declared to take one night;
but for those who have undergone the tonsure ceremony, purification is held to occur after three nights. (5.67)

This should be understood as a specific rule for him: it is for one day alone, not for three days. In the absence of rain, for those whose *caula* ceremony has been completed, the rule of three days applies exclusively, and not the other periods such as ten days and so forth. Those who have completed their *caula* are understood here as being even prior to their initiation (*upanyana*). And for those who undergo another sacramental rite characterized by initiation, a different designation arises, namely, "the initiated. [232] Relatives should place a deceased child less than two years old outside the village.
Having adorned [the body], they should place it on pure ground, except for the collection of the bones.

The tonsure ceremony (*caulakaraṇa*) for one whose year has been completed may take place in the third year. This being the case, it should be understood that, following this rule in the third year, this [text] refers to the reception [of the deceased] for one whose tonsure has not yet been performed, based on another Smṛti:
"Neither the fire-consecration nor the water-rite should be performed for him;
having abandoned him in the forest like a piece of wood, one should observe impurity for only three days. (5.69)

And in this verse, the rule for those three days is prescribed for those who have not yet had the tonsure ceremony (*caula*). This being so, prior to the tonsure, there is one day or three days; but after the tonsure, it is exactly three days.

"The water-rite (*udakakriyā*) should not be performed by relatives for one under three years of age; however, they may perform it for one whose teeth have appeared, or even when the naming ceremony has been completed. (5.70)

Since the permission for water [libations] was granted for those who have teethed and for those for whom a name has been made, the performance of the fire-rite (*agnisaṃskāra*) is also thereby prohibited along with them, by implication, in the preceding verse. Here, however, the eligibility [for the rites] is permitted: "When a fellow student has died, a one-day fast is prescribed;
but upon the birth [of such a child], purification for those entitled to offer water (*ekodaka*) is held to occur after three nights. (5.71)

A "fellow religious student" (*sabrahmacārī*) is understood here as one who is closely related through having the same preceptor (*ekopādhyāya*). Others, however, maintain that it refers to any fellow religious student whatsoever. A "moment" (*kṣaṇa*)—in this context, a period of impurity (*āśauca*) during which study is suspended—is what is intended. For every *śrotriya*, a three-night period will be prescribed; therefore, this present rule is commenced for the sake of those who are not *śrotriyas*, with regard to their proximity. Regarding birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), purification for those who share the same water-libation (*ekodaka*) but are not *sapiṇḍas* occurs after three nights. For *sapiṇḍas*, however, it is according to the rule already stated. And this impurity due to birth for those who are not *sapiṇḍas* should be understood to apply to the case where all *sapiṇḍas* are subject to birth-impurity, and not otherwise.
But for the kinsmen of women who have not undergone the sacraments, purification occurs after three days;
however, those of the same lineage (sanābhayaḥ) are purified according to the rule already stated.

For those who have not undergone the *saṃskāras*, who have not had their tonsure (*cūḍā*), or who have not yet taken vows, the relatives and kinsmen become pure three days after the performance of the *cūḍā* ceremony; this is understood by implication to apply to those who are not *nābhi*-related (i.e., non-blood relations). However, those who are *nābhi*-related (blood relations) are purified only according to what has been previously stated; that is, uterine siblings are purified in ten nights. Furthermore, regarding those who have already been married and are experiencing the status of being wives, the aforementioned rule is to be understood as applicable. Thus says the *Gṛhyaśāstra*: "Others [the blood relations] should perform the water-libation for them, and they [the married women] for those [the blood relations]. Gautama also says: "The offering of water is performed by the *sapiṇḍas* for one whose hair-tuft has been formed; so too for women. Some say this applies to those who have been given away in marriage. (GDh 14.34–36).
[233] They should eat food that is neither pungent nor salty, and they should not bathe for three days; they should abstain from eating meat and sleep separately on the ground. (5.73)
The meaning is: "for as long as the impurity due to death lasts.
This rule for impurity caused by death has been proclaimed for when one is present;
this procedure is to be known by relatives and kinsmen for when one is absent. (5.74)

"Relatives" (*saṃbandhin*) are those connected by birth, such as one's wife; or alternatively, "relatives" (*saṃbandhin*) are the *sapiṇḍas*, and "kinsmen" (*bāndhava*) are the *sodakas*. For the word "kinsman" (*bāndhava*) is seen used elsewhere as well, for example: "and the kinsmen who are the mother’s relatives" (MDh 5.102). "But he who hears that [a relative] has died while residing in a foreign land, provided it is before the tenth day, shall remain impure only for whatever portion of the ten nights remains. (5.75)
This rule regarding those residing abroad is stated according to the ten-day alternative; the same applies elsewhere as well.
However, when the ten days have elapsed, one shall remain impure for three nights. This [ten-day] alternative applies likewise in other cases, as far as possible.
But when a year has passed, one becomes pure even by merely touching [the corpse].

If ten days have elapsed, purification lasts three nights until the end of one year; but after a year, it is immediate purity. Having heard of the death of a relative whose ten-day period has passed, or the birth of a son, one becomes pure immediately by plunging into water with one's clothes on. (5.77)
If the ten-day period has expired, immediate purification is prescribed; or else, the previously mentioned three-night period applies.
When a child, one residing in a foreign land, or a sapinda relative has died, one becomes pure immediately after immersing oneself in water along with one's clothes. (5.78)

Non-existence (*abhāva*) is perceived as being located in another place. Regarding that [non-existence], a one-night purification (*aikarātrikī śuddhi*) was previously stated: "For men whose tonsure ceremony (*caula*) has not been performed, impurity is declared to last for one night" (MDh 5.67). But here, immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is prescribed for it. This [rule] regarding the child is optional (*vaikalpika*). Thus it has been said: "Whether the teeth have emerged or not yet emerged" (MDh 5.58). And regarding "being in another place": even for one who is not a child, there is immediate purification. Due to the difference in time—prior to a year—here, even when less than ten days have passed, immediate purification is prescribed for one situated in another place. As for the phrase "by those who do not perform the three-day [rite] or give [the offerings]," this other rule of immediate purification is handed down specifically for the death of those for whom a three-day period was previously mentioned in the case of the simultaneous death of separate *piṇḍas*. It is an optional alternative depending on the specific Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) required.
If death or birth should occur again within ten days, the Brahmin shall remain impure for as long as that period has not yet reached its tenth day. (5.79)

This too is improper and must be explained according to another Smṛti: "Impurity due to birth (*sūtaka*) does not apply when [another] impurity of the same or a different kind falls within the ten-day period, nor does [impurity due to] death fall within the ten-day period. What then? It is specifically this [impurity due to birth] of the same kind that is being indicated. And so Gautama says: "If that [period of impurity] should recur within [the first], they shall be purified by the remainder" (GDh 14.6). In this context, the mention of "that" (*tat*) must be explained with reference to the subject under discussion. Others, however, interpret both [types of impurity] as applying to both [situations], based on the statement of Śaṅkha: "Now, if [another birth or death] should occur in the interval, or if one should die."
When a teacher has passed away, they say that impurity lasts for three nights;
likewise for his son and his wives, it lasts for a day and a night—this is the settled rule. (5.80)
This verse has been explained by its literal recitation:

"But upon the death of a learned Śrotriya who is well-qualified, one shall remain impure for three nights; in the case of a maternal uncle, a pupil, an officiating priest, or a kinsman, one shall remain impure for a night with its two wings (a pakṣiṇī rātriḥ). (5.81)

One who has received initiation (upasaṃpanna) is dependent [on others]. For some reason, he might have to stay overnight with his maternal uncle; this "overnight period" (*pakṣiṇī rātri*)—so called because it encompasses two days—is metaphorical. A student [is impure] through both the text and its meaning; likewise, officiating priests through their connection to the ritual acts of recollection; and relatives such as the *abhyādayaḥ* (?). When a king dies, one who resides within his realm remains impure for as long as the light lasts. But when a non-Vedic person dies, the impurity lasts for a full day; the same applies when a teacher who has mastered the Vedas (*anūcāna*) passes away. (5.82)

If one resides or stays within the territory of a king, the impurity lasts for as long as that light [i.e., the reign] endures; however, at night, it should not be observed. But if the king is not a *śrotriya* (one learned in the Vedas), the impurity lasts for the whole day; if he is a *śrotriya*, it is said to last for three nights. Some, however, interpret this as a qualification of the king himself; that, moreover, remains to be considered. Regarding the teacher and the venerable person, there is this other rule concerning those who are not *sapinda* relatives:
"A Brahmin is purified in ten days, a Kshatriya in twelve days, a Vaishya in fifteen days, and a Shudra is purified in a month" (5.83).

The Brahmin’s ten-day period is stated again with the intent of prescribing an alternative. Regarding its meaning, some say: “This is optional, whereby the previous rule applies only to the four [castes]. And so he will state: “Those who desire merit and know the Dharma... (MDh 10.127), and so forth. Others, however, on account of the proximity [of the texts], construe this [as applying to all]. Gautama, however, does not accept this; and that must be demonstrated:
“One should not prolong the days of impurity, nor should one interrupt the rites performed in the sacred fires.
Nor does one who performs those rites become impure, even if he is a kinsman. (5.84)

This prohibition is for the purpose of abandoning the aforementioned days. For someone, there might be an obstacle to Vedic study (*adhyayana-vighāta*) or other such impediments. Accordingly, other Smṛti texts should be cited as examples. This being the case, the person under obligation—driven by laziness with the thought, "I shall remain inactive and live happily"—should generally not let the days joined with sin increase; nor should he cause them to be interrupted, meaning he should not fail to perform the Vaiśvadeva and other rites. Alternatively, the sense may be that he should dissolve [the interruption]. However, because they are obligatory, he must certainly perform those rites even when they have been excessively delayed. Both of these positions are supported by the Gṛhya-smṛtis. For it is said therein: "Because they are obligatory, the days should not be omitted, except in cases where one follows the teachings of the Vaikhānasa school. And: "One who performs that rite does not become impure, even if he is a relative. The phrase "connection with men" is intended as a praise of the performance. Thus it is stated in the Gṛhya-sūtra: "These [rites] should be performed on the same day."
Having touched a divākīrti, a menstruating woman, an outcaste, a woman who has recently given birth, a corpse, or one who has touched a corpse, one becomes pure by bathing. 5.85.

The *divākīrtya* is a *caṇḍāla*. Thus says Gautama: "A fallen man, a *caṇḍāla*, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman," and so forth (GDh 14.30). Others say: "This bath is required for touching a *divākīrtya* during the act of shaving, but not for touching him on other parts of the body. However, that is an incorrect interpretation, as it contradicts the force of other *smṛti* texts; moreover, in the dialogue between the cat and the mouse, Vedavyāsa explicitly states that the *divākīrtya* is a *caṇḍāla*, whereby the meaning remains exactly as stated previously.

Having sipped water and being purified, one should always recite, upon seeing something impure, solar mantras according to one's enthusiasm and the *pāvamānī* verses according to one's ability. (5.86)
If one should see impure objects that are not among those [specifically] mentioned in the *divākīrtya* [list], [the rule for] touching has already been stated:
"Having touched a human bone that is still moist with fat, a Brahmin becomes pure by bathing;
but if it is dry of fat, he is purified simply by sipping water and then either touching a cow or looking at the sun. (5.87)
This verse is already explained by its literal recitation (*nigadavyākhyāta*).
One who has been initiated (*ādiṣṭī*) shall not perform the water-libation (*udaka*) until the completion of his vow.
Upon completion, he shall perform the water-libation; he becomes pure after three nights alone. (5.88)

One should not offer water to a relative who departs while observing a vow until the completion of that vow; there is also a prohibition regarding ancestors. As it has been stated: "Having bathed daily, being pure, one should perform the libations for the gods, the seers, and the ancestors" (MDh 8.176). Upon completion [of the vow], having performed the water-libation, one becomes purified from all deceased persons after three nights alone. Regarding this, [the following is said]: "The rite of water-libation shall cease for those born of illicit unions, for those who persist in heretical mendicancy, and for those who have committed suicide. (5.89)

He who is born in vain is he who does not honor the gods, the ancestors, or men. Sons and others who have been appointed [to such duties] are excluded due to prohibitions in the scriptures. Renunciation (*pravrajyā*) is permitted for those born of mixed castes (*saṃkara*), and that is characterized by the scriptures. Because it occurs in association with transgressions, the offering of water (*udaka-dāna*) should be withheld from those who commit suicide by means of poison and other such methods; this is a prohibition regarding what is otherwise established by scripture. Impurity (*āśauca*) should likewise be understood to be exactly like the water-offering, by virtue of its logical consistency. And [the same applies] to those who have resorted to heretical sects (*pāṣaṇḍa*) and to women who live according to their own lust.
And also for women who harm the fetus or their husband, and for those who drink liquor. || 5.90 ||

And here, because of its association with transgression (*vyatikrama*), the prohibition regarding the offering of water applies; therefore, this [prohibition] should be understood as applying to twice-born women according to the specific prohibitions. Thus, the transgression of drinking *surā* should be recognized as a mark of their fallen status (*patitatva*) due to their being *udakyās*. [The same applies to] killing a Brahmin and stealing gold. Regarding this, another says: even though there is no distinction in the meaning of the caste term, the prohibition against drinking *surā* is understood to apply specifically to the male Brāhmaṇa by rule, based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the verse, "Eating the sacrificial oblation of the gods" (MDh 11.95). However, for women, there is no such prohibition as there is for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas; with this intention, some read the word "Brāhmaṇa" [in the general sense]. Thus, under the view that it is a restrictive rule (*niyamapakṣa*), this censure of its transgression is to be understood in every respect, but not as a state of being fallen (*patitatva*). And so says another Smṛti: "Having purchased *surā* through deception, one should make Brāhmaṇīs endowed with noble lineage, character, and conduct drink it along with those who have performed a hundred *Caṇḍī* rites, for the sake of their mothers. This is also an exhaustive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*). In the Gautama Dharma Sūtra: "In the case of killing an embryo or serving a man of lower caste, a woman falls" (GDh 21.9); regarding this point of disagreement, the venerable gods of the earth (*bhūmidevas*) are the authority for the final decision.
Having carried out the funeral rites for one's own teacher, sub-teacher, father, mother, or guru, the one observing a vow is not deprived of his vow by that act. (5.91)

"But having turned away from another, one is separated [from the impurity]"—this statement regarding the prohibition against carrying out a deceased person other than one's own preceptor (*vratin*) is to be understood by implication. Furthermore, because of the mention of "one's own," that which might otherwise apply when the preceptor’s own preceptor is present—namely, the rule "one should behave toward the preceptor’s preceptor as toward the preceptor himself" (MDh 2.205)—is hereby prohibited. One should carry out a dead Śūdra through the southern gate of the city;
but for the twice-born, through the western, northern, or eastern gates, as appropriate. (5.92)

This undertaking is for the purpose of defining the directions. Furthermore, because the removal of a corpse is inauspicious, it should be understood that the instruction here is given by reversing the usual order of the social classes (*varṇa*).
There is no fault of sin for kings, nor for those observing vows or performing sacrificial sessions (*sattra*); for they always abide in the station of Indra, being one with Brahman. (5.93)

For the sake of establishing the discipline of all the world, he bestows sovereignty upon the station of Indra; because of his connection to the qualities of kings through the means [of his office], there is immediate purification for him. This is a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*) intended to praise the fact that he is presided over by the gods and not otherwise, and it serves as an injunction regarding immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*). [237] In this way, it should be explained as before, on account of the fact that those engaged in ritual procedures (*prakriyā*) and those performing sacrificial sessions (*sattrin*) have become one with Brahman. Since this is so, therefore: "Immediate purification is ordained for a king in his high-souled station;
and the reason for this is his seat [of authority] for the sake of protecting his subjects. (5.94)

That place where the Great Self resides, or that which belongs to Him—this is the "majestic" (māhātmyaka) [status]. For the king who dwells therein, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*), because he exists for the sake of protecting the subjects in that very place. And thus it shows this: "And here, the seat is the cause. Therefore, this refers to a king by virtue of his office alone; by the word "king," one who possesses qualities such as consecration and who protects living beings is meant. Furthermore: "And for those killed in a riot or in battle, by lightning, or by the sovereign;
for the sake of cows and Brahmins, and for whomever the lord of the earth desires [to be purified immediately]. (5.95)
[Editor's note: In the commentary on the fourth quarter, regarding the phrase "cecchati bhūmipaḥ," there is an alternative reading: "vecchati pārthivaḥ."]

*Ḍimba* refers to a great crowd, a tumultuous mass of people mixed with those who have fallen, or a conflict without weapons; whereas *āhava* is a conflict involving weapons. *Vidyut* is lightning; *pārthiva* is a king. And [this applies] both by means of him and in a situation where there is no battle. Thus Gautama says: "In the case of death due to the king's anger in battle," he declares immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*). There is also immediate purification for the sake of cows and for the sake of Brahmins, even if it is not in battle. Regarding the phrase "whomsoever the king desires," this refers to a minister or similar official for the purpose of ensuring his own business is not obstructed, or another person because, since he is like a deity to him, there is the scriptural injunction for the immolation of an animal. And thus he shows: "Whom many sacrifices know as the sacrificial fire. And because—
The king assumes the form of the eight guardians of the world: Soma, Agni, Arka, Anila, Indra, Citrāpatī (Varuṇa), and Yama. (5.96)
And this being so:
"A king is empowered by the Lord of the World; no impurity is prescribed for him.
For the purity and impurity of mortals originate from and dissolve back into the Lord of the World. (5.97)
But this is not because gods lack the qualification [for sacrifice]. Therefore, this is understood as an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) for those who have been slain in battle at that time:
"For one slain according to the duty of a Kṣatriya by weapons raised in battle, the sacrifice is immediately completed; no impurity is prescribed for him" (5.98).
"In connection with that [sacrifice], for one who remains at the sacrifice, there is impurity just like that of the sacrificer.
"A Brahmin becomes pure by touching water; a Kṣatriya, his mount and weapon;
a Vaiśya, his goad or staff; and a Śūdra who has performed the required rites, his staff. (5.99)
At the end of the ten-day period and others, this purification consisting of ritual bathing with water and so forth should be performed as the preferable method.
O best of the twice-born, this purification regarding sapinda relatives has been declared to you; now learn the rules for the purification after death regarding all non-sapinda relatives. (5.100)
This verse serves the purpose of introducing the concluding summary:
"Having carried out a deceased twice-born man who is not a sapinda, a Brahmin becomes pure after three nights, as if for a kinsman; likewise for the maternal relatives on his mother's side. (5.101)
The meaning of this verse is straightforward:
"If he eats their food, however, he is purified in ten days; if he does not eat their food, he is purified in a single day, provided he does not dwell in that house. (5.102)

For one who does not eat and does not stay there, purification occurs immediately; for one who stays there but does not eat, it is as stated in the immediately preceding verse—three days. But for one who eats his food, it is ten days.
"If one follows a deceased person out of desire, whether he be a relative or a stranger, he becomes pure by bathing with his clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter. (5.103)
Bathing and the consumption of ghee should be performed in all such cases.
One should not have a deceased Brahmin carried by a Śūdra while his own kinsmen are present;
for that [funeral] would be defiled by contact with a Śūdra, resulting in the loss of heaven and the failure of the sacrifice. (5.104)

This instruction regarding that which is seen therein is for the purpose of establishing a rule. Now, for the sake of providing an illustration, the Veda composed by [the sages] themselves (svārṣa) is being stated here concerning the corpse (śava). In the section on purification:
"Knowledge, austerity, fire, food, earth, mind, water, acquisition, wind, action, the sun, and time—these are the agents of purification for embodied beings. (5.105)

He will state the purification of the intellect (*buddhi*) by means of knowledge (*jñāna*): "The intellect is purified by knowledge" (MDh 5.109). Or [it refers to] that of the person (*puruṣa*): "By austerity, those most learned in the Vedas... (MDh 5.107). That [is purified] "by re-firing, as is an earthen vessel" (MDh 5.122)—that is, by fire. By food, meaning by eating sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) and the like. By clay, in the case of something smeared with impure matter (*amedhya*). Because of the statement, "The mind is purified by truth" (MDh 5.109), here too one should reverse the order and say, "One should speak speech purified by the mind" (MDh 6.46?). Water is well known for the purpose of purification. And [purification occurs] not by acquisition or smearing in the case of the mind; for there is the statement, "A house [is purified] by sweeping and whitewashing" (MDh 5.122). Wind is [purified] by its natural attachment (? for the sake of purification. Precisely because of this effort, in accordance with the conduct of the cultured (*śiṣṭa*), it should be understood as a means of purification in certain cases, such as when grass or wood has been touched by a *caṇḍāla* or similar outcaste. By this, the sun and time are also explained. Regarding the phrase "those who have committed sin," this purification is stated—as before—because of the context of rites such as the *agniṣṭoma*.
Of all forms of purity, purity in wealth is declared to be the highest;
for he who is pure in wealth is truly pure, not he who is purified by earth and water. (5.106)

For those who act with disinterestedness toward wealth and conduct themselves with purity in worldly affairs, this statement—made with regard to the perceived purity that arises in social dealings—is also consistent as being intended as an illustration:
"The wise are purified by patience; those who have committed forbidden acts are purified by charity;
those whose sins are concealed are purified by silent recitation; and those most learned in the Vedas are purified by austerity. (5.107)
This will be demonstrated in the section on penance (*prāyaścitta*). Others, however, read: "The wise are purified by forbearance.
"What is to be cleansed is purified by earth and water; a river is purified by its current;
a woman defiled in mind is purified by her menses; and the best of the twice-born are purified by renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). (5.108)

The mention of "water" is for the sake of illustration. Since [the text] states that the flow of a river and other such causes of purification are [effective] when there is water—otherwise [it would follow that land] is even purer than a stationary object—it is by this means that the purification of riverbanks, which abound in impurities, is declared. Likewise, "a woman is defiled by her menses" refers to one whose mind is corrupted; however, the author will later prescribe an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for one who is defiled by action. Furthermore, regarding the best of the twice-born (*dvijottama*) who, by renouncing prohibited acts, does not perform what ought not to be done, his purification is established; the specific mention of the "best of the twice-born" is not for the sake of mere illustration. Alternatively, this should be understood as referring to the well-known state of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) by virtue of the authority of the scripture itself. And this is taught for the purpose of defining the scope of the aforementioned means of purification, such as knowledge and the rest.
The limbs are purified by water; the mind is purified by truth;
the inner self (bhūtātman) is purified by knowledge and austerity; and the intellect is purified by wisdom. 5.109.

And this detailed exposition on the purification of knowledge and so forth is supported by way of an explanatory praise (arthavāda) in connection with the previously mentioned ritual purity (*śauca*). Just as these [purifications of] knowledge and so forth are themselves the agents of purification, so too should this impurity caused by death (*śāvāśauca*) be understood; for their purification occurs through their own inherent capacity, according to the context, the connection, and the specific application of the rules.
This determination regarding the purification of the body has been declared to you.
Now hear the determination regarding the purification of various kinds of substances. (5.110)
The meaning of this verse is well known:
"For luminous gems, for all things made of stone, and for [objects made of] earth, purification has been declared by the wise to be by means of ashes, water, and clay. (5.111)
In this case, there is a combination with water of the two alternatives, earth and ashes.
A golden vessel that is free from stains becomes pure by being washed; likewise, a vessel made of lotus-material, stone, or silver, provided it is not ornamented. (5.112)

In this manner, for metallic objects that have a coating, one should use the previously mentioned method; for those without a coating—namely iron, gold, and silver—one should use water alone. Since the conch was not under discussion in the previous verse, its inclusion here [as an example] refers back to that previous rule. Regarding the gem and the lotus: since the previous verse dealt with both the lotus and the non-lotus gem, this is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) concerning them.
Furthermore, through the union of fire and water, gold and silver came into being.
Therefore, for those two, purification by means of their own origin is more excellent. || 5.113 ||

For it is stated in the Śruti: "Agni indeed desired Varuṇānī. And here, the rule for Agni is heard to be gold, while for Varuṇānī it is silver. This being so, the cleansing of those two—gold and silver—with the ashes produced by this [fire] and with water is more effective. Because this is an explanatory passage (arthavāda), this same rule should be understood to apply to iron and other metals as well:
"For copper, iron, bell-metal, silver, tin, and lead, purification should be performed as appropriate with alkaline substances, acids, and water. (5.114)

The protective measures for copper and other metals are now stated. Ashes, which are the means for purification, are denoted by the word *kṣāra* (alkali), and nothing else, because this is well-known among the Bāhlīkas. Regarding *amlodaka* (sour water): although not explicitly mentioned in every case, it applies to any sour substance or sour gruel (*kāñcika*). Since *amlodaka* is intended specifically for copper, it may also apply to silver and so forth; if copper is beneficial [for a particular metal], then it should be employed there as well. The mention of *kṣāra* is repeated here with the intention of prescribing *amlodaka*. The mention of silver is for the purpose of establishing the use of *amlodaka* [in its case]. For in the case of silver and gold, only pure water or ashes are used. Therefore, this repetition is for the sake of using ashes and water for silver. Furthermore, this purification is prescribed as being practical. Accordingly, in another Smṛti, specific purifications are stated according to the specific nature of the defilement, such as Bodhāyana’s rule: "For metallic objects defiled by impure substances, purification consists of heating them in fire until they glow red."
The purification of all liquids is by means of straining; that of solid objects is by sprinkling, and that of wooden items is by planing. || 5.115 ||

The injunction regarding *utpavana* (purification by sprinkling) is declared in the Veda. For all substances, such as water and the like, the practical purification (*prāyogika*) must be performed using two blades of *kuśa* grass. For the learned do not desire purification through *utpavana* even when the defilement by ants and similar creatures is slight. Likewise, for solid objects such as seats and beds, sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is the practical purification. However, for those that are extremely defiled, scraping and washing are required. Regarding the cleansing of sacrificial vessels with the hand during a sacrificial rite:
the purification of the *camasa* cups and the *graha* ladles is indeed by means of washing. (5.116)

The cleansing of sacrificial vessels by wiping them with the hand or with the limbs of the Veda is understood to be a constituent part of the sacrificial rite; therefore, they must be taken for the sake of the *camasa* cups. This shall be the rule for the practical purification of the *camasa* cups and similar items. For the *prāśitra-haraṇa* spoons, which have not been specifically mentioned, this same rule applies. For those that are damaged, the rule of local custom shall be either to plane them down or to discard them.

The purification of the *caru* pots, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, as well as the wooden sword (*sphya*), the winnowing basket, the cart, the pestle, and the mortar, is performed with hot water. (5.117)
This verse has been explained by its very recitation. However, for large quantities of grain and clothing, purification is performed by sprinkling them with water;
but for small quantities, purification by washing with water is prescribed. (5.118)

The mention of "small" is for the sake of restatement; smallness and greatness are relative and should be understood in terms of place and time. This rule also applies primarily to articles used for practical purposes.
"The purification of skins is like that of clothes, and the same applies to woven baskets;
the purification of vegetables, roots, and fruits is held to be like that of grain. (5.119)

That which is prescribed for clothes would also apply to items made of palm leaves and the like, on account of their common nature as "things to be used" (*kārya*); furthermore, since the term "grain" (*dhānya*) is mentioned [in the rule], it follows that even vegetables and such are considered "clothes" (*cela*) by virtue of the word's application. Thus, it is established that the purity of vegetables and the like is determined by one's own satisfaction (*ātmanas tuṣṭi*). This [rule] also pertains strictly to practical usage (*prāyogika*) based on established custom (*samācāra*). However, in the event of defilement (*upaghāta*), another *smṛti* text or customary practice must be sought. [Silk and wool are purified] with alkaline salts (*ūṣa*); blankets (*kutapa*) with *ariṣṭaka* fruits; fine cotton cloths (*aṃśupaṭṭa*) with *bilva* fruits; and linen (*kṣauma*) with white mustard seeds (*gaurasarṣapa*). (5.120)
The meaning of this verse is straightforward:
"For conch shells and horn, as well as for objects made of bone or ivory, purification should be performed by one who knows the law with cow's urine and water, just as in the case of linen. (5.121)

Even though the conch shell possesses the specific quality of being born from a different species (*vijāti*), this very same rule would apply; it is not the case that the previous one does not apply anywhere.
[142] Grass, wood, and straw are purified by sprinkling;
a house by sweeping and smearing with cow-dung; and earthenware by re-firing. (5.122)

The re-initiation of the discussion regarding grass and other materials that have been gathered together is for the purpose of stating what follows, namely, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) which has already been established. Through sweeping (*mārjana*) and smearing (*upāñjana*), purification occurs; however, in cases of defilement upon the first entry [into a house], there may also be re-cooking (*punar-pāka*), depending on the degree of the defilement. For those items that are excessively defiled and cannot be saved, they must be discarded; for those not so defiled, sprinkling is prescribed. [Earthenware touched by intoxicating liquors, urine, excrement, spittle, pus, or blood is never purified by re-cooking. (5.123)
The ground is purified by these five means: by sweeping, by smearing with cow dung, by sprinkling water, by scraping, and by the dwelling of cows. (5.124)
Purification is achieved through many methods—whether combined or individual—as appropriate, according to established practice.
That which has been pecked by birds, smelled by a cow, blown upon, sneezed at, or defiled by hair or insects, is purified by the scattering of earth. (5.125)

The specific types of birds and insects should be understood from other Smṛti texts. Regarding which substances require earth and which require the application of earth: "In all purifications of objects, as long as the odor and the stain caused by the impure substance do not depart from that which has been smeared by it, so long should earth and water be applied. (5.126)

This is stated for the purpose of indicating that all substances may be purified by speech, or else it should be understood as referring specifically to Śūdras, being intended as a teaching on general purification. This should be known as a slight reduction from the prescribed rules of purification. Now, this [next verse] is commenced for the purpose of prohibiting the sin associated with contact for one who takes an object whose purity or contamination is unknown:
"The Vedas ordained three purifiers for Brāhmaṇas:
that which is unseen, that which is cleansed with water, and that which is commended by speech. (MDh 5.127)

The mention of the *veda* here should be understood as being for the sake of showing respect. Since the mention of the *brāhmaṇa* is primary, the vow (*vrata*) is not required elsewhere; for no contradiction is seen through perception, inference, or scripture. That which has a connection with a cause of invisible harm (*adṛṣṭopaghāta*)—this refers to that which is connected to an invisible cause of injury—the gods, even though it was thus injured, ordained it to be pure through non-contact (*asaṃsarga*). Therefore, from the authority of the scriptures, one should understand that there is an absence of transgression (*pratyavāya*) at the beginning of its connection with that invisible [cause]. Or, when there is doubt regarding what is injured, it is purified by water; and when there is doubt regarding the purity of the cleansing performed, it is praised by speech, or rather, such praise by speech is prescribed for the learned (*śiṣṭa*). Water, however, is taken as an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), because its status as a means of praise for other things has already been stated. This being so, just as that which is purified by water is pure, so too is that substance which is praised by speech regarding the invisible and which serves as a means for the act of eating without forgetfulness. But how is this [to be reconciled] with the rule: "O best of the twice-born, one should perform even a single *kṛcchra* penance for the purification of what has been eaten unknowingly, but especially for what is known" (MDh 5.21)? This should be understood as follows: the application of this penance pertains to the use of a substance that is impure by its own nature (*guṇasvabhāva-aśuci*) but whose impurity was unknown, whereas the present case concerns that which is impure due to contact (*saṃsarga-aśuci*), such as food pecked at by birds and the like. Therefore, both of these rules should be understood as authoritative according to their respective domains. Alternatively, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between what is prescribed and what is prohibited, for the state of the two subjects of Dharma remains established as in the original rule. Or else, this is a general rule while the specific exception (*apavāda*) is the statement "the gods have three purifiers" and "one should perform even a single [penance] for a year," and so forth.
Water on the ground is pure if it can quench the thirst of a cow, provided it has not been contaminated by impurities and possesses its natural fragrance, color, and taste. (5.128)

Water is indeed pure by its very nature. It is not like earth, which is [impure] in both ways. Thus, regarding those waters that have fallen upon the ground or been touched by it, when there is a suspicion of impurity, [the text] shows their purity to the extent that they would satisfy the thirst of a cow—provided that, even if there were only a small amount, the cows' thirst would be quenched; for the phrase "having bathed, he places the cow's [water]" implies that the water reaches up to the knee or the thigh. And thus, this indicates a large quantity of them. The exception to this is: "if they are not pervaded by impurity. This means that even if they are abundant, if they are pervaded by impurity, they become unclean. How, then, is the contact with impurity to be understood? Those [particles] which possess the smell, color, and taste of the impure substance [are affected]; in the absence of these, they are unpervaded and remain pure. And this being so, this is not a qualification of the water itself, but rather of the impure substance.
The hand of an artisan is always pure, as is merchandise spread out for sale;
almsfood received by a student of sacred knowledge is always pure—this is the settled rule. 5.129

The hand of an artisan is pure for the purpose of work, but it is not pure when there is defilement; its purification is prescribed [only] upon contact with the impurity of death and the like—this is the meaning of the term "taking hold" (*grahaṇa*) as used here. Even in the case of one who sells barley-meal, rice, and so forth, there is no fault from the touch of his hand. Almsfood received by a religious student (*brahmacārin*) is to be known as pure even if it has been defiled by being brought out from a place impure due to urine or feces. "The mouth is always pure; a bird is pure in causing fruit to fall;
a calf is pure while suckling; and a dog is pure in seizing game. (5.130)

Because eating together with one's wife is prohibited, and because another Smṛti states, "and women, in the context of sexual union," it is understood that this [prohibition] pertains to the subject of sexual enjoyment and not otherwise. However, some believe that because of the inclusion of the word "always" (nitya), eating together is permitted; that is incorrect, because eating together with a woman is forbidden and because a penance is prescribed for eating her leavings. Furthermore, this instruction concerns women of all castes. Since the prohibition of leavings is identical in the rule "eating the leavings of a woman or a Śūdra," the mention of the Śūdra there includes the Śūdra woman as well. The use of the term "woman" (strī) in the sense of a generic class designation should be understood as including an Ārya woman. This being so, there is no specific contradiction regarding an Ārya woman; therefore, since the prohibition applies to all, it is logical that the permission should also apply to all. And since this is the case, therefore...
Manu has declared that the flesh of an animal killed by dogs is pure, as is the flesh of one killed by other carnivorous beasts or by outcasts, bandits, and the like. (5.131)

Regarding raw meat, the leavings of dogs and other such animals, and the statement that these are pure, the same rule applies to the discarding of other types of leavings; by this, one should understand that food touched by *caṇḍālas* and others is also treated in the same way.
"The apertures above the navel are all pure, while those below are impure, as are any places from which filth has fallen" (5.132).

Because the orifices below the navel are impure, one should avoid contact with them; likewise, the excretions that fall from the body are impure. It should be understood that phlegm and other secretions are also considered unholy even when they remain on the body.
One should declare flies, droplets of water, shade, a cow, a horse, the rays of the sun, dust, earth, wind, and fire to be pure to the touch. (5.133)

But it is not the case that for flies and the like, which do not leave a smear, purity exists merely through contact. As for droplets, however, even though there is no specific statement [to the contrary], according to established practice, one should apply earth and water as appropriate during the effort to purify oneself after the voiding of urine and the like;
this applies to all twelve types of bodily impurities and their purifications. (5.134)

"Having purpose" means neither too little nor too much, but rather that amount by which the removal of bodily impurities may occur; this undertaking is for the sake of a restrictive rule (niyama) so that there may be just enough earth and water for the purpose of removing physical filth. And considering these to be "bodily impurities," this is commenced:
Fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, earwax, nasal mucus, phlegm, tears, rheum of the eyes, and sweat—these twelve are the impurities of men. (5.135)
The mention of "man" is for the purpose of indicating others who possess similar wealth.
One application of earth should be made to the penis, three to the anus, ten to one hand, and seven to both hands by one desiring purification. (5.136)
This is the rule of purification for householders; it is twofold for students, threefold for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics. (5.137)

Even when the stains and odors have been removed from an impure substance, the required number [of washings] must still be completed; and once that number is reached, the removal of the stains and odors must indeed be performed thereafter, according to the statement: "As long as the impurity does not depart from that which was smeared with it" (MDh 5.126). In this way, the status of both injunctions as explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) is not contradicted. "Having voided urine or feces, one who has sipped water (*ācānta*) should touch the cavities of the body; likewise when about to study the Veda, and always when eating food. (5.138)
Seeking bodily purity, one should first sip water three times and then wipe the mouth twice; however, a woman or a Śūdra should do so once each. (5.139)

In the section concerning the religious student (*brahmacārin*), it was stated [in MDh 2.62], “A Brahmin is purified by [water] reaching the heart,” and so forth; this present commencement is for the sake of women and Śūdras. Thus, a settled option regarding the two subsequent ritual rinsings (*upasparśana*) should be understood as pertaining to virtuous and non-virtuous Śūdras respectively. In connection with this very topic of virtuous Śūdras, this other [rule] is enjoined for them: “Śūdras who live according to the law must have their heads shaved every month; their rules of purification are like those of Vaiśyas, and they may eat the remnants of food left by the twice-born. (5.140)

For *śūdras* who are true [to their caste] and perform rites such as the *pākayajña*, because they depend upon Brāhmaṇas, shaving (*vapana*) must be performed monthly, just like the twice-born; and regarding internal purity, the rule "like a Vaiśya, [they should observe] purification of the body" is understood to apply to them. Furthermore, purification from the impurity of death (*śāva-śuddhi*) lasts for half a month. However, for the other [type of *śūdra*], bathing (*upasparśana*) is prescribed after a full month. This has been explained in detail in the context of eating the remnants of food from the twice-born, according to the verse: "But a woman and a *śūdra* [should rinse] once, once" (MDh 5.139). This was also stated in that same verse under the rule: "One should not give advice to a *śūdra*, nor [give him] the remnants of food" (MDh 4.80). Thus it is said in the section concerning *śūdras* dependent on Brāhmaṇas:
"For in whatever measure one who is free from malice abides in virtuous conduct,
in that same measure he, being beyond reproach, attains both this world and the next" (MDh 10.128).
The principal [limbs] do not become impure by drops that fall upon them;
nor are the beard hairs considered part of the mouth, nor what remains stuck between the teeth. (5.141)

This is a prohibition for one who has attained [the state of] being learned in the scriptures. And this is a counter-exception to the prohibition: "The drops that fall from the mouth [into the limbs] as one swallows the last [mouthful]... Furthermore, according to another Smṛti, the authoritative rule is that there is no fault in touching with the tongue what remains between the teeth, nor in those [drops] accompanied by falling or scattering. "Those drops which touch the feet of one who is giving water for sipping to others are to be known as equal to those on the ground; one does not become impure because of them. (5.142)
[246] This must be refuted by oneself on the basis of the opponent's own statement:
"But if one who has something in hand is somehow touched by what is left over from a meal..."
Without even setting that object down, one who has sipped water (ācānta) shall attain purity. || 5.143 ||

Gautama, however, maintains the position that one must set the object down; for he reads an additional statement to the effect of setting it down in the sūtra: "One who has something in hand and is impure shall set it down and perform *ācamana*," interpreting the phrase "one who has something in hand" as referring to the purpose of setting it down. Because of this addition of words, even though the two views are otherwise equal, Gautama’s position is understood to be that of setting it down. Thus, because they possess equal force, there is an option (*vikalpa*) in case of conflict. "One who has vomited or purged, having bathed, should consume clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
One who has eaten food should simply perform *ācamana*; bathing is prescribed for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse. (5.144)

"One should sip water after eating food. Just as there is purification through sipping water (*ācamana*) at the conclusion of a meal, so too for one who has vomited or purged, there is purification by consuming clarified butter (*ghṛta*) after bathing; if that is the case, then [the rule regarding] sipping water applies as well. Because this is stated as an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭāntavāda*), it is employed for the sake of another [rule], not for its own sake, since that [purification] has already been stated. Furthermore, this illustration is to be understood by implication as being for the purpose of illustrating all occasions for sipping water. And for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse, bathing is the proper course; or, avoiding the forbidden lunar days (*parvan*), he may approach his wife and bathe. This is taught as a distinguished rule due to its superior merit, being an addition to the obligatory [daily] rite. Others, however, maintain that it refers to a single act [of intercourse] only.
Having slept, having sneezed, having eaten, having spat, having spoken untruths, having drunk water, and when about to recite the Veda—even if already pure—one should sip water. 5.145.

There are other reasons for sipping water (*ācamana*). Here, the repetition of "Vedic study" (*svādhyāya*) is for the purpose of showing that sipping is an auxiliary part of Vedic study; whereas previously, it was stated to be for the purpose of purification. This being the case, there are these two rules: "The pure, having sipped water and being composed, should study. By this [repetition], however, sipping is prescribed for the times of eating when one is alone. For a religious student (*brahmacārin*), the time for consuming alms-food is mentioned here twice. And in this context, for the religious student, that [sipping] is an auxiliary part of the meal, whereas in the passage "having again performed [the sipping] after voiding urine or feces," it is for the sake of ritual purity (*prayatna*); here, however, it is for the sake of intending to perform other [acts].
This entire rule for purification, as well as the purification of liquids, has been declared to you for all social classes; now learn the duties of women. (5.146)
Whether she be a child, a young woman, or even an old woman, a female should not perform any action independently, even within her own home. (5.147)

This is an instruction regarding her lack of independence: because she purifies herself through dharma even before [marriage], and because both [parents] would otherwise perish, a woman should remain under the control of her father in childhood, under that of her husband while in youth, and when her husband has died, under that of her sons; a woman must never enjoy independence. (5.148)
"Even at any time" means excessively. And this being so:
one would not desire separation from oneself even from one's father, husband, or sons.
For by illicit intercourse with these, a woman would bring reproach upon both families. (5.149)
And this is another duty of hers: she should always be cheerful, skillful in household affairs, keep the utensils well-maintained, and be not wasteful in expenditure. (5.150)
Furthermore:
To whomsoever her father or her brother—by the father’s consent—may give her, she should serve him while he lives, and once he has passed away, she must not transgress against him. (5.151)

He shows that in the absence of the father, the brothers and others shall inherit [the property]. By the phrase "and she must not transgress [her duty] once he has passed away," he declares her non-deviation from her husband after his death. Her dependence on the husband begins from the time of betrothal, not from the marriage ceremony itself. For the sake of auspiciousness, the *svastyayana* rite and sacrifice to Prajāpati are performed at marriages; however, the formal giving away (*pradāna*) is the cause of [the husband's] ownership. (5.152)

The *svastyayana* rite performed at a wedding consists of the application of mantras for the sake of auspiciousness; it is not the cause of [the husband’s] ownership. For if [ownership] already existed, this auspicious application through the verbal betrothal (*vāgdāna*) would be appropriate—just as in the case of a woman accepted in marriage through the mantras and oblations of Prajāpati, such as “Place ten sons in her, and make the husband the eleventh” (RV 10.85.45), and so forth—it is joined with the verbal betrothal. Furthermore, from the injunctions, “She should serve him while he lives, and she must not transgress him when he has passed away” (MDh 5.151)—by which [it is understood that] the husband is one who has performed the sacramental consecration (*mantrasaṃskāra*) both out of season and during the fertile period (*ṛtukāla*).
A wife is the constant giver of happiness both in this world and in the next. || 5.153 ||
Whether he be lacking in virtue, given over to lust, or devoid of good qualities, a husband must always be served by a virtuous wife like a god. (5.154)
For women there is no separate sacrifice, nor a vow, nor even a fast; by that which consists in serving her husband, she is exalted in heaven. 5.155
This is an explanatory praise (arthavāda) for the purpose of commending the preceding rule. And so it is said:
"A virtuous wife, desiring the world of her husband, should do nothing unpleasant to her husband, whether he be living or dead. (5.156)
[248] She may indeed emaciate her body with pure flowers, roots, and fruits;
but she must not even mention the name of another man once her husband has died. 5.157.
And even if a livelihood is impossible, she should remain until death— patient, self-restrained, and chaste— desiring that supreme dharma which belongs to women devoted to a single husband. (5.158)

He would not even act for the sake of a son, because his husband had passed away; for many thousands of brahmin youths have gone to heaven while remaining celibate from their youth, without having established a lineage for their family. (5.159)
When her husband has died, a virtuous woman who remains steadfast in celibacy goes to heaven even if she is childless, just like those who are lifelong celibates. (5.160)
In the very same way, even though she knows this prohibition:
"But that woman who, out of greed for offspring, transgresses against her husband, incurs reproach in this world and is excluded from the next. (5.161)
And because:
"There is no offspring born of another, nor is there possession by another; and for virtuous women, a second husband is nowhere prescribed. (5.162)
And because— she who, having abandoned her own inferior husband, serves (or attends upon) a superior one—
even while serving a superior, she—
She becomes censurable in the world and is called "one who has had a previous husband. || 5.163 ||
Not only is this a fault, but there is also this other [fault] that is even more extreme:
because of infidelity toward her husband, a woman is not only...
In this world, he incurs censure;
after death, he enters the womb of a jackal and is tormented by sinful diseases. (5.164)
Therefore, one should not transgress against one's husband out of greed for visible rewards; and so it is shown:
"She who does not transgress against her husband, being restrained in mind, speech, and body..."
She attains the worlds of her husband and is called "virtuous" by the righteous. (5.165)
By this conduct, a woman who has restrained her mind, speech, and body attains supreme fame in this world and the world of her husband in the hereafter. (5.166)

This verse is intended as a summary of the duties of women. Regarding the statement that "the duties of women are straightforward," no detailed exposition has been provided here. However, this much is taught for the sake of instruction: just as a man may engage again in ritual acts with another woman, so too [a woman] "must not transgress what is established" (MDh 5.151), whereby she has no further engagement with anyone else; and just as by the rule "she goes to heaven even if childless" (MDh 5.160), procreation is prohibited except in times of distress. Yet, that procreation will be permitted again by the Smṛti on *niyoga*. Thus, the production of offspring is subject to option because it is both enjoined and prohibited. It is impossible to determine which of these two Smṛtis is superior, since one prescribes offspring while the other prescribes self-restraint. We understand that both are intended as praise.

A twice-born man who knows the law should cause his wife of equal caste, who has conducted herself in this manner and dies before him, to be cremated with the sacred fires and the sacrificial implements. (5.167)

This verse is a restatement of what is established by logic. Thus, because she possesses ownership over it, her consecration by means of the *agnihotra* is indeed appropriate; this is cited again for the sake of emphasis:
"Having given the fires to his wife who has died before him at her funeral rites, he may again perform the act of taking a wife and likewise the re-establishment of the sacred fires. (5.168)

This is stated as a separate entitlement (*adhikāra*) together with another [text], and not as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) that is supplementary to the section on dependence (*adhīnatva*). However, when one is incapable of procreation or the performance of ritual acts, then, due to the absence of assistance, there would be an entitlement to the stage of forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) or wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*), which would constitute a contradiction [with the previous rule]. Thus says the Śruti: "Indeed, by old age he is released from this," which implies the cessation of the purpose [of procreation]. Others, however, say: the word "when" (*yadā*) will be supplied here; by this, the lack of contradiction with the scriptural injunction for lifelong oblations (*yāvajjīvahoma*) will become clear.
Following this rule, a Brāhmaṇa living in his home during the second stage of life should never neglect the five great sacrifices. (5.169)

This concluding verse is for the purpose of summarizing the five sacrifices and for the successful accomplishment of all ritual acts. Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Commentary on the Code of Manu composed by Bhāruci.

The Sixth Chapter: Having thus remained in the householder stage of life according to the rules, the twice-born who has completed his Vedic studies shall dwell in the forest, self-restrained, duly controlling his senses.
This verse is for the purpose of introduction:
"But when a householder sees wrinkles and gray hair upon himself, and indeed the offspring of his offspring, then he should take refuge in the forest. (6.2)

The mention of "wrinkles and grey hair" serves as an indicator for the third stage of life; the mention of "sons" is for the purpose of indicating their completion [of duty]. The mention of "grandsons" is because of the connection to the discharge of debts (*ṛṇa*). He must necessarily perform the completion of his sons' duties. Furthermore, since the rule of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is prescribed for this third stage, the procreation of sons is precluded. Therefore, when the third stage of life has arrived, one who has produced sons should resort to the forest, abandoning all village food and every possession.
Having entrusted his wife to his son, he should go to the forest, either alone or together with her.

This is not an optional alternative based on specific qualifications; rather, it is a fixed alternative depending on the purpose of his wife: "Taking with him the *agnihotra* fire and the household implements for the sacred fires, having departed from the village for the forest, he dwells there with his senses restrained. (6.4)

And here, the word *agnihotra* has another meaning for the purpose of praise. Thus Gautama says: “Having established the fire according to the *śrāmaṇaka* rite” (GDh 3.27); therefore, from that time forward, one should maintain that very same fire while exercising restraint over the senses. This restatement is for the sake of specification: “With various kinds of pure food fit for sages, or with vegetables, roots, and fruits, he should perform these very Great Sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) according to the prescribed rule. (6.5)
He will describe the forest-food of a sage:
"He should wear either a skin or a garment of bark; likewise, he should bathe in the evening and in the morning;
and he should always bear matted hair, as well as his beard, body hair, and nails. (6.6)
He will later state that this bathing is obligatory, though even the three daily ablutions may be performed optionally for him:
"From whatever food he may have, he should offer the bali-oblation and give alms according to his ability;
he should honor those who come to his hermitage with water, roots, fruits, and alms. (6.7)
One should be constantly devoted to self-restraint, self-controlled, friendly, and composed;
always a giver and never a taker, compassionate toward all living beings. (6.8)

The study of one's own Veda (svādhyāya) is for the purpose of grasping the unchanging [Reality]. One who is self-controlled according to his own scripture, namely that of the Vaikhānasa, has the acceptance of gifts and such things prohibited; however, the performance of the duties of his stage of life (āśrama) is required as a means for the sake of his daily obligations.
